dishes.name: Creole Hanger Steak
dishes.serviceNote: Ask temperature, best medium-rare to medium. Chili crisp brings real heat, warn spice-shy guests and offer it on the side if the kitchen agrees. Pumpkin seeds; the chili crisp may contain soy or sesame, ask. Different plate from the breakfast/lunch hanger.

kept.a: Offer the hanger to a steak lover who likes spice, or a guest who wants something bolder than a classic steak. Ask the temperature with the order. Pour the Durban at $19, served cool; for a classic steak-and-Bordeaux guest, the Moulin d'Issan at $16; without alcohol, the Personality. Say: “Our Creole Hanger Steak has our own Creole spice, Madeira-glazed broccolini, a pumpkin seed persillade and chili crisp for heat.”

The Creole Hanger Steak is a dinner entrée at $42, bold, spiced and fun.

Hanger is a butcher's favorite cut, loose-grained and very beefy, and ours is Creekstone Farms beef seasoned with our own housemade Creole spice. Broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the fortified wine, so it is a little sweet and nutty. Persillade, pair-see-YAHD, is chopped parsley and garlic, and we add pepitas, pumpkin seeds, for crunch. Chili crisp, a crunchy chili oil, brings real heat.

The guest gets sliced steak with the glossy broccolini, the green persillade and the chili crisp over it. It tastes beefy and spiced, with crunch, heat and a sweet-savory glaze.

It is the dinner hanger, spicier than the daytime one and with no egg. The Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge is the pour: ripe and generous, with soft tannins and a peppery note that love a little spice, served cool so its alcohol does not lift the heat.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: the chili crisp has real heat, so the red should be ripe and soft, served cool, and the Durban is that wine.

Answer: The chili crisp brings real heat. If you are spice-shy, I will check with the kitchen whether it can come on the side.

Asked: What is persillade?

Answer: Pair-see-YAHD: chopped parsley and garlic. Ours has pumpkin seeds for crunch.

Asked: How should I have it cooked?

Answer: Hanger is at its best medium-rare to medium, but it is your call.

Warn spice-shy guests about the chili crisp, and offer it on the side only if the kitchen agrees. Ask the temperature with the order. Do not mix it up with the daytime Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, $38, the steak and eggs with béarnaise. Serve the Durban at about 58°F, a few minutes in the ice bucket, so the alcohol does not amplify the chili. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

The Housemade Pork Sausage Patty is a breakfast and lunch side at $9, and the one breakfast meat we make ourselves.

We make our own pork sausage in house and form it into a patty, the classic Southern breakfast way. A Southern breakfast sausage is traditionally fresh pork shoulder seasoned with salt, black pepper and sage, often with red pepper and a touch of brown sugar; what goes into ours, and how much heat it carries, is a question for the kitchen.

It belongs to the breakfast Owen Brennan made the event: in a city whose restaurants served lunch and dinner, he made breakfast the reason to come, and the sides are how a guest builds that breakfast out. The Eggs Sardou and the Crab & Corn Omelette carry no meat, so the sausage is the natural add; it also sits well beside the cheddar grits, the Brabant potatoes or an egg any style.

A buttermilk biscuit is the Southern breakfast bread. The classic method is soft flour and cold butter or lard, buttermilk reacting with baking soda to lift the dough, a few folds for layers and a hot oven. The buttermilk makes it tender and gives it a gentle tang. How ours is made each morning is a question for the kitchen.

dishes.name: Cheddar Grits
dishes.serviceNote: Dairy (cheddar, likely butter). Corn is gluten-free, confirm preparation.

kept.a: Offer the grits to a first-time visitor from out of town, a guest building a lighter breakfast from sides, or anyone ordering bacon or sausage. Suggest an egg on top for $3 more. Say: “Have you tried grits? Ours are creamy, with cheddar stirred in: Southern comfort in a bowl.” For a table, a bowl to share beside the egg dishes lets everyone taste them.

The Cheddar Grits are a breakfast and lunch side at $7, the Southern breakfast staple.

Grits are coarsely ground corn, cooked slowly until creamy, the Southern answer to polenta. Ours have cheddar stirred in, so they are rich and a little sharp.

The guest gets a warm bowl of creamy, pale gold grits. They taste creamy, rich and a little sharp from the cheese, with the gentle sweetness of corn.

They are the side for a guest who has never had grits, because cheese makes them friendly, and for anyone who wants Southern comfort beside the eggs. An egg any style on top turns them into a small meal, and they sit well beside the thick-cut bacon or the housemade sausage patty.

They are not the grit cake on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits: that one is made with pimento cheese, set and fried. And they are not the rice grits under the Blackened Tofu at dinner, which are broken rice from Two Brooks Farm.

Asked: What are grits?

Answer: Coarsely ground corn, cooked slowly until creamy, like a Southern polenta. Ours have cheddar stirred in.

Asked: Are these the grits on the shrimp and grits?

Answer: No. Those are a pimento cheese grit cake, set and fried. These are creamy cheddar grits in a bowl.

Asked: Can I add an egg?

Answer: Yes, an egg any style on top is a favorite, $3 more.

Do not confuse the three grits on our menus: the creamy cheddar grits side, the fried pimento cheese grit cake on the Shrimp & Grits, and the rice grits under the dinner Blackened Tofu. How the grits are prepared, butter included, is a question for the kitchen, never a guess. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Brabant Potatoes
dishes.serviceNote: Confirm the kitchen’s finish (garlic butter, parsley) and fryer for gluten and dairy.

kept.a: Offer Brabant potatoes with any egg dish, the bacon or the sausage, and to a guest who wants something crisp and familiar beside the sauces. They are the friendliest side for a visitor: everyone loves crisp potatoes, and the name gives you a story. Say: “Can I add Brabant potatoes? They're the old New Orleans side: crisp cubes of potato, finished with garlic and parsley.” For a shared table, one bowl goes a long way.

Brabant Potatoes are a breakfast and lunch side at $7, and an old New Orleans restaurant classic.

They have been in the Picayune's Creole Cook Book since the early 1900s, and they are usually said to be named for the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands. Potatoes are cut into cubes and cooked until golden and crisp outside and fluffy inside, then traditionally finished with garlic butter and parsley; the kitchen confirms tonight's finish at lineup.

The guest gets a bowl of golden cubes, flecked with green. They taste crisp, fluffy, buttery and garlicky.

They are the side every egg dish wants, and the best partner for the housemade sausage or the thick-cut bacon. An egg any style with a bowl of Brabant potatoes makes a small breakfast of its own. They also appear on the children's breakfast menu, with the popcorn shrimp and the grilled cheese.

The name trips people up: the guide prints bra-BAHNT, and bra-BAHN and the local bruh-BANT are both heard, so learn the house's way at lineup.

Asked: What are Brabant potatoes?

Answer: An old New Orleans side: cubes of potato cooked golden and crisp outside, fluffy inside, traditionally finished with garlic butter and parsley.

Asked: Where does the name come from?

Answer: They are usually said to be named for the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands, though no one has proved it. They have been in New Orleans Creole cookbooks since the early 1900s.

Asked: How do you say it?

Answer: The guide prints bra-BAHNT; bra-BAHN and bruh-BANT are both heard here. I say it the way the house does.

Learn the house pronunciation at lineup: bra-BAHNT, bra-BAHN or bruh-BANT. How the potatoes are finished, the garlic butter and parsley, and which fryer they go through, are questions for the chef, never a guess. Fire them with the eggs so they land crisp. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Say: “Would you like creamed spinach with the steak? It's rich and silky, the classic steakhouse side.” For a table sharing sides, it pairs well with the Brabant potatoes: crisp and creamy side by side.

The Creamed Spinach is a breakfast and lunch side at $7, a New Orleans and steakhouse classic.

It is spinach cooked down in a rich cream sauce until it is silky and spoonable. The menu prints nothing more, so how the kitchen builds it, whether with Parmesan like the spinach under the Eggs Sardou and whether the sauce is thickened with flour, is confirmed at lineup.

The guest gets a warm bowl of deep green spinach in its cream. It tastes rich and silky, green and savory.

It is the natural partner for the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, where something green and creamy balances the beef and the béarnaise, and it sits comfortably beside any of the egg dishes. A guest who loves the Eggs Sardou will recognize the idea: that plate carries Parmesan creamed spinach under its eggs.

At $7 it is one of the easier sides to add, and one that turns a lighter plate into a fuller meal.

Asked: Is it the same spinach as on the Eggs Sardou?

Answer: The Sardou has Parmesan creamed spinach. Whether this side is made the same way is on the lineup list, so I will check with the kitchen.

Asked: What goes well with it?

Answer: The hanger steak above all, and any of the egg dishes.

Asked: Is it very rich?

Answer: It is rich and silky, spinach cooked down in a cream sauce, so it is lovely shared.

The menu prints only creamed spinach: whether it carries Parmesan, like the Sardou's, and whether it is thickened with flour are questions for the kitchen, so do not describe either until the chef confirms. dishes.serviceNote: Pork (bacon), not vegetarian. Seasonal; confirm tonight’s vegetables.

kept.a: Offer the succotash with the Chateaubriand or the poussin, or to a table that wants a seasonal vegetable side with a little smoke. Name the bacon: Nueske's is a story in itself. Say: “The succotash is glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon, sweet and smoky, lovely with the Chateaubriand.” For a table of two sharing the Chateaubriand, it is the vegetable to add beside the mushrooms.

The Succotash is a dinner side at $12, and a seasonal one.

Succotash is a Native American dish of corn and beans, some four hundred years old, that the South adopted; traditionally it is corn and lima beans. Ours is a mix of glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon, a Wisconsin bacon known since 1933 for its deep applewood smoke.

The guest gets a bowl of bright, glossy vegetables with pieces of smoky bacon through them. It tastes sweet and bright from the glazed vegetables, savory and smoky from the bacon.

It is a great partner for the Roasted Chateaubriand or the Poussin à la Moutarde, and a way to bring something green and seasonal to a rich dinner.

It changes with the season: the dinner menu is a late summer one, and tonight's vegetables are confirmed at lineup. It is not a meatless side, because of the bacon, so say so when a guest asks for vegetables.

Asked: What is in it tonight?

Answer: Glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon. The vegetables change with the season, and I learn tonight's at lineup.

Asked: What is Nueske's?

Answer: A Wisconsin bacon, known since 1933 for its deep applewood smoke.

Asked: Is it a traditional succotash?

Answer: Traditionally succotash is corn and lima beans, a Native American dish the South adopted. Ours is a summer vegetable version with bacon.

The succotash carries bacon: never offer it as a meatless side. It is seasonal, so confirm tonight's vegetables at lineup before you describe them. The house pronunciation of Nueske's is contested; ask the manager how the kitchen says it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Offer the cauliflower to a guest who likes bold flavors, to anyone ordering the tofu or the papillote, and to a steak table that wants a vegetable with character. Say: “The smoked cauliflower is finished with preserved lemon and harissa: smoky, bright and a little spicy.” For a table of four, it is the side that gets talked about.

The Smoked Cauliflower is a dinner side at $12, smoky, bright and gently spicy.

We smoke the cauliflower so it picks up a deep, savory flavor, then finish it with preserved lemon, lemons cured in salt, which taste intensely citrusy and a little floral, and harissa, hah-REE-sah, the North African chili paste with warm spice.

The guest gets the smoked cauliflower dressed with the harissa and the preserved lemon. It tastes smoky and savory, then bright and citrusy, with a moderate warmth from the harissa.

It is the vegetable side with the most going on, and a good partner for the Blackened Tofu or the Gulf Fish en Papillote; it also gives a steak dinner something lively and green-tasting beside the richness.

The heat is moderate, so it is worth a word to a spice-shy guest. Whether it suits a guest's diet is a kitchen question: the service note marks it as one to confirm.

Asked: What is harissa?

Answer: Hah-REE-sah: a North African chili paste with warm spice, which gives the cauliflower its color and its warmth.

Asked: Is it spicy?

Answer: Gently: the harissa gives a moderate warmth, balanced by the preserved lemon.

Asked: What is preserved lemon?

Answer: Lemons cured in salt; they taste intensely citrusy and a little floral, and they brighten the smoke. It is lovely beside the Blackened Tofu or the Gulf Fish en Papillote.

The harissa brings moderate heat: mention it to spice-shy guests. Questions about whether it suits a diet go to the kitchen, never to memory, since the service note marks it as one to confirm. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Offer the shells and cheese with the Chateaubriand or the hanger steak, and to any mac and cheese lover. The Mimolette and the Abita Amber are the story. Say: “Our Shells and Cheese is a grown-up mac and cheese: a Mimolette fondue made with Abita Amber beer, with Grana Padano.” For a couple sharing the Chateaubriand, it and the mushrooms make a full feast.

The Shells & Cheese is a dinner side at $12: our grown-up mac and cheese.

Pasta shells hold the sauce in every curve, and the sauce is a fondue of Mimolette, mee-mo-LET, a bright orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and a little sweet as it ages. It is made with Abita Amber, the Louisiana lager brewed at Abita Springs since 1986, for a malty depth, and finished with Grana Padano, the hard, nutty Italian cheese, for a salty finish.

The guest gets a bowl of shells in an orange cheese sauce. It tastes rich, nutty and malty, with a salty edge.

It is the side to put beside the Roasted Chateaubriand or the Creole Hanger Steak, and a favorite with anyone who loves mac and cheese.

The beer goes into the sauce, and cooking takes most of its alcohol but not all, so a guest avoiding alcohol should hear that it is made with beer.

Asked: What is Mimolette?

Answer: Mee-mo-LET: a bright orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and a little sweet as it ages.

Asked: Is there beer in it?

Answer: Yes, Abita Amber, a Louisiana lager, goes into the fondue. Cooking takes most of the alcohol but not all.

Asked: What goes well with it?

Answer: The Chateaubriand or the Creole Hanger Steak.

It is made with beer: tell a guest who avoids alcohol, since cooking does not take all of it. Say Mimolette as mee-mo-LET and Abita as uh-BEE-tuh. Fire it with the entrée so it lands hot beside the steak. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

TABLESIDE SAFETY: (1) Set the cart where nothing hangs overhead and away from drapes, décor and air vents; clear menus, napkins and paper from it. (2) Guests seated and back from the cart; no one leaning in; watch children, loose sleeves and long hair. (3) Measure the rum into a small vessel first, never pour from the bottle near a flame. (4) Pull the pan off the flame to add rum, then tilt the far edge toward the flame to ignite, away from you and the guests. (5) Never add alcohol to a lit pan. (6) Keep a lid or cover within reach to smother, and know where the extinguisher is. (7) Let the flame burn out before plating; turn the burner off before you leave the cart. Flambéing doesn’t remove all the alcohol, tell guests who avoid it. Dairy (butter, ice cream); ice cream likely contains egg. On the breakfast tasting it comes with Congregation Coffee & Chicory.

kept.q: Does the recipe use banana liqueur as well as rum?
kept.a: Our published recipe uses both banana liqueur and rum, in equal measure; the menu prints rum. Say rum and a splash of banana liqueur once the kitchen confirms the cart build.

Seed Bananas Foster with the entrée order, so the cart is ready: every first visit, every celebration, every guest who asks what Brennan's is famous for. Remind the table it is for two or more. With it, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle at $80 when the sommelier confirms it is still poured, or a cup of our coffee with chicory at $11. Say: “Save room for Bananas Foster: it was invented here in 1951, and we flambé it right at your table.”

World Famous Bananas Foster is the dessert Brennan's gave the world, $14 at every meal, flambéed at the table, with a minimum of two people per order.

It was invented here in 1951. Owen Brennan asked for a banana dessert, and chef Paul Blangé created it; the house's own telling credits Ella Brennan with Blangé. It is named for Owen's friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission, and New Orleans was then the main port for bananas from Central America. 2026 is its 75th year.

At the cart, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melt into a caramel; banana liqueur goes in as our published recipe has it, then the bananas to soften; then the rum is lit. As it burns, the caramel deepens. The bananas are spooned over our housemade vanilla ice cream, then the warm sauce.

It tastes warm, caramelized and boozy-sweet over cold, creamy vanilla. It closes the Traditional Breakfast with Congregation Coffee & Chicory.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Rum, butter, brown sugar and flambeed caramel sit in the caramel and nut group, whose textbook partners are oxidative fortifieds, so Banyuls Reserva would lead and the Auslese would be the bright second for contrast. The Auslese stays first in this pack because the Banyuls is a tasting pour and is not confirmed a la carte; nothing changes until that answer exists.

Asked: Was it really invented here?

Answer: Yes, in 1951, by chef Paul Blangé at Owen Brennan's request; the house's own telling credits Ella Brennan with him. It is named for Richard Foster, Owen's friend.

Asked: Does the alcohol burn off?

Answer: Not all of it. Flaming leaves much of the alcohol in the sauce, so I tell anyone avoiding alcohol.

Asked: Can I order one for myself?

Answer: It is made in one pan at the table for at least two people, so the minimum order is two. For a flambé just for you, let me ask the manager what the kitchen can do tonight.

A minimum of two per order; whether the $14 is per person or per order is a lineup question, so never quote it either way until a manager says. A new server never lights a pan before sign off: who performs the flambé, and the house procedure, are lineup questions for the manager. Pour any wine before the flambé starts, so no glass sits near the flame. Follow the tableside safety steps in the service note every time. The origin is disputed between the guide and the house page: use the house's telling once a manager confirms it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Fruit lovers and guests who find caramel too sweet lean here. Pour the Banyuls if the sommelier confirms it à la carte; otherwise our coffee with chicory at $11. Say: “If you'd like a second flambé, Cherries Jubilee is tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce, flamed at the table over vanilla ice cream.”

Cherries Jubilee is our other tableside flambé, a Brennan's signature the guide prints at $14. It is not on the current dessert menu, so confirm with a manager that it is served before offering it.

It is older than Bananas Foster: Escoffier is credited with it, for Queen Victoria's jubilee in the 1890s. Fresh, tart black cherries go into a warm Luxardo sauce. Luxardo, loo-KSAR-doh, is the Italian family house famous for maraschino cherries and the liqueur, founded in 1821 and making it at Torreglia, near Padua, since 1947.

At the table the sauce is lit, and as the flame burns the sauce deepens and the cherries soften. Then it all goes over our housemade vanilla ice cream, warm and cold together.

It tastes warm and tart-sweet, the cherries bright against the cold vanilla, fruitier and lighter than the Foster's caramel.

It is the flambé for a guest who is not in the mood for bananas, or the second flambé for a table that wants both. Banyuls, a sweet red from the south of France tasting of fig, caramel and cocoa, is the pour once the sommelier confirms it is poured à la carte.

Asked: How is it different from Bananas Foster?

Answer: Both are flambéed at the table over our vanilla ice cream. The Foster is bananas in butter, brown sugar, cinnamon and rum, rich caramel; the Jubilee is tart black cherries in Luxardo sauce, brighter and fruitier.

Answer: I will check with the kitchen before you order, and warn you if they are not.

Answer: The menu prints no minimum, unlike the Foster's two; I confirm it at lineup.

It is not on the current dessert menu: confirm with a manager before offering it. Follow the same tableside safety steps as the Bananas Foster, and pour any wine before the flame. dishes.serviceNote: Gluten, eggs, dairy, tree nuts (pecans in the pralines). Contains whiskey in the caramel.

kept.a: Offer the bread pudding to a guest who wants comfort, to anyone who has never had a New Orleans bread pudding, and to a table sharing desserts beside a flambé. Pour the Auslese half-bottle at $80 if it is confirmed at lineup, or our coffee with chicory at $11. Say: “Our bread pudding is warm, with a whiskey caramel, tangy buttermilk ice cream and pralines, the New Orleans pecan candy.”

The New Orleans Bread Pudding is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: New Orleans' comfort dessert, done our way.

Bread pudding began as an old European thrift dish for stale bread and became a New Orleans staple; the Picayune's Creole Cook Book of 1901 already prints one. It is bread soaked in a sweet custard and baked until soft inside and golden on top. The warm whiskey sauce became a New Orleans restaurant signature in the 20th century; ours goes a step further with a whiskey caramel, rich and a little boozy, buttermilk ice cream with a gentle tang, and pralines, PRAH-leens, the New Orleans candy of pecans, butter and brown sugar, for crunch.

The guest gets the warm pudding with the caramel, a scoop of ice cream and the crumbled pralines. It tastes warm, soft and custardy, sweet and tangy, warm and cold.

The Dr. Hermann Auslese, honeyed with lively acidity, is the pour; the Banyuls may lead once a manager confirms it is poured outside the tasting.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Whiskey caramel, brown sugar and pecan praline bridge to fortified wine, so the Banyuls would lead and the Auslese would be second. The Auslese stays first here until the Banyuls is confirmed a la carte.

Asked: Is there alcohol in it?

Answer: Yes: the caramel is made with whiskey.

Asked: What are pralines?

Answer: PRAH-leens, never PRAY-leens: the New Orleans candy of pecans, butter and brown sugar, crumbled on top for crunch.

Asked: Which whiskey is in the caramel?

Answer: That is on the kitchen's question list for the dessert cards, so I will check with the kitchen and tell you.

The caramel carries whiskey: say so to anyone avoiding alcohol. Say pralines as PRAH-leens. The whiskey's name is a lineup question for the chef, so do not guess one. Pour the Auslese 2 to 3 oz, as the dessert order fires. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Offer The Snickers to a chocolate lover, to a guest who wants something playful, and to anyone who smiled at the name. On the dinner tasting it arrives as the fifth course, with Banyuls. À la carte, pour the Banyuls if it is confirmed by the glass, or our coffee with chicory at $11. Say: “The Snickers is our grown-up candy bar: milk chocolate Bavarian cream, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts.”

The Snickers is our grown-up candy bar, $15 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the dessert that closes the dinner tasting.

You can guess the inspiration. Each part of the candy bar becomes its own element: a milk chocolate Bavarian, a light, set cream somewhere between a mousse and a custard; a silky caramel custard; nougat turned into ice cream; and roasted peanuts for salt and crunch.

The guest gets a plated dessert with all the flavors they know, laid out as separate pieces. It tastes creamy, chocolatey and caramel-sweet, with salty, crunchy peanut.

It is nostalgic and fun, but refined. On the dinner tasting it is poured with a 4 oz glass of Banyuls, a sweet fortified red from the south of France, whose cocoa and coffee notes are chocolate's best friend and whose sweetness keeps the chocolate from turning the wine bitter. The tasting pour is the guide's Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva, confirmed at lineup.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: chocolate makes dry wine bitter and salt makes a sweet wine sweeter; 4 oz is generous, 2 to 3 oz is the norm.

Answer: No: each part of the candy bar becomes its own plated dessert, milk chocolate Bavarian cream, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts.

Asked: What do you pour with it on the tasting?

Answer: Banyuls, a sweet fortified red from the south of France, with cocoa and coffee notes.

dishes.serviceNote: Eggs (meringue, mousse), dairy, gluten (pastry). The lightest dessert, suggest it after a rich meal.

kept.a: Offer the Lemon Tart after a rich meal, after the Hussarde or the Chateaubriand, to a guest who says they are too full for dessert, or to someone who loves citrus. Pour the Auslese half-bottle at $80 once you know it is still offered, or keep it light with the Personality at $16. Say: “If you'd like something bright after all that richness, our Lemon Tart is yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and toasted meringue.”

The Lemon Tart is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the lightest dessert on the menu.

It has everything a lemon meringue tart has, built in layers. A yuzu mousse, YOO-zoo, is the heart of it: yuzu is a fragrant Japanese citrus that tastes like lemon, lime and mandarin at once. With it come a lemon jelly, a sweet pastry crumb for crunch, and toasted meringue, soft and marshmallowy.

The guest gets the layers of pale mousse and bright jelly over the crumb, with the browned meringue on top. It tastes bright, tart and airy, with sweet crunch.

It is the dessert to suggest after a rich meal, when a guest wants something refreshing rather than heavy. Citrus desserts are hard on wine, but a sweet Mosel Riesling loves them: the Dr. Hermann Auslese has the acidity to match the lemon, which is why it is the match, as a half-bottle, and why Banyuls is not.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: only sweet plus piercing acid survives the yuzu and lemon; the Banyuls avoid line is right.

Asked: What is yuzu?

Answer: YOO-zoo: a fragrant Japanese citrus that tastes like lemon, lime and mandarin at once.

Asked: Is it a classic lemon tart?

Answer: It has all the flavors of a lemon meringue tart, built in layers: yuzu mousse, lemon jelly, a sweet pastry crumb and toasted meringue.

Asked: Which dessert is lightest?

Answer: This one: tart, airy and refreshing.

Do not pour Banyuls or another low-acid dessert wine with it: lemon makes them taste flabby, and red fruit clashes with yuzu. The Auslese comes only as the $80 half-bottle, 2 to 3 oz pours, unless a manager says it can be poured by the glass. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.serviceNote: Gluten (puff pastry), dairy, eggs (anglaise, mousse).

kept.a: Offer the tarte Tatin to a guest who loves fruit desserts, who wants something lighter than a flambé, or who knows the French classic. Pour the Auslese half-bottle at $80, whose pineapple notes mirror the tart, when it is confirmed on the list, or the Oh! What It Seemed to Be at $16, fig and cinnamon, for no alcohol. Say: “Our Pineapple Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down tart made with charred pineapple, with a condensed milk anglaise and vanilla mousse.”

The Pineapple Tarte Tatin is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: tropical, buttery and bright.

Tarte Tatin, tart tah-TAN, is the famous French upside-down tart, usually apples caramelized in butter and sugar on crisp pastry. We make it with pineapple, charred so it is caramelized with a little smoky edge, on puff pastry for flaky layers. The anglaise, a pourable vanilla custard, is made with sweetened condensed milk for a rich, caramel-milk flavor, and a whipped vanilla mousse keeps it light.

The guest gets the caramelized pineapple on its pastry, with the custard sauce and the mousse. It tastes caramelized, tangy and flaky, with creamy vanilla.

It is a French classic with a tropical twist, and a lighter alternative to the flambés. The Dr. Hermann Auslese is the pour: it carries pineapple and honey notes of its own, so the wine mirrors the tart, and it stays bright enough to cut the pastry and the custard.

Asked: What is a tarte Tatin?

Answer: Tart tah-TAN: the French upside-down caramelized tart, usually apples. Ours is charred pineapple on puff pastry.

Asked: What is the anglaise?

Answer: A pourable vanilla custard, made here with sweetened condensed milk for a caramel-milk flavor.

Asked: Is it very sweet?

Answer: It is caramelized, but the pineapple's tang and the light vanilla mousse keep it bright.

Avoid Banyuls and dry wines with it: red fruit clashes with pineapple, and dry wines taste sour against the caramel. Pour the Auslese 2 to 3 oz as the dessert fires. Say Tatin as tah-TAN. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

The Roost Burger is the one full plate on the Bubbles at Brennan's bar snack list, $17, served in the Roost Bar and the courtyard on weekday afternoons from 2 to 6.

The current menu prints the build: two beef short rib patties, bacon, cheese, pickles, onions, tomato jam and a special sauce. The guest gets a double burger. It tastes rich and beefy, salty from the bacon, sharp from the pickles and onions, with the sweetness of the tomato jam.

It is the plate for a guest who wants a proper meal at the bar rather than snacks. With it, the Moulin d'Issan, a classic Bordeaux with tannin for the beef, or the Rumors are Flying, our barrel aged Rittenhouse rye with tart cherry juice, brown sugar syrup and orange bitters.

wines.serviceNote: The Binwise list read on 3 October 2026 prints the glass at $28; the current Wines by the Glass and Birthday Bubbles pages, pasted the same day, both print $30. Confirm at lineup and quote the list in hand.

kept.a: Show the label and say the name as it reads: Brennan's Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in a tulip or white-wine glass, from an ice bucket half ice and half water. Offer the house Champagne at the greeting, to anyone celebrating, and with the turtle soup, the oysters and the Hussarde. It is the easiest first glass at either meal. kept.a: Our house Champagne is a Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut bottled under the Brennan's name, a very dry style; a blend of all three Champagne grapes from the Piper-Heidsieck house. Piper-Heidsieck spells its own cuvee Essentiel. Say 'labeled for us', not 'made for us', until a bottle is checked, and do not quote a dosage or a lees age until the sommelier confirms which cuvee is in the bottle. The Binwise list of 3 October prices the bottle at $140; the current Bubbles at Brennan's page lists no bottle of it.

Brennan's Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut is our house Champagne, poured by the glass at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: $28 a glass on the Binwise list and $30 on the current menu, so the price is confirmed at lineup.

It is a Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut labeled for us, a blend of all three Champagne grapes, Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay, made by the traditional method. Extra Brut means 0 to 6 grams of sugar per liter in the finished Champagne. It overlaps Brut; the label alone cannot rank two bottles by dryness. Piper-Heidsieck spells its own cuvée Essentiel; the dosage and lees age wait on the sommelier confirming which cuvée is in the bottle.

In the glass it is pale and lively, with fine bubbles. It tastes very dry and crisp: citrus, orchard fruit and a little brioche, with a firm, chalky finish.

That dryness and those fine bubbles cut through rich, salty food, which is why it is the first pick with the turtle soup, the Grand Isle Jewel oysters and the Eggs Hussarde, and the second choice with the Louisiana Oysters, the Creole Caesar and the omelette. It is the house bubbles, morning and night.

Asked: What does Extra Brut mean?

Answer: It means 0 to 6 grams of sugar per liter in the finished Champagne, a very dry style. It does not state the amount of sugar added at dosage.

Asked: Is it made for Brennan's?

Answer: It is a Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut labeled for us. I say labeled for us, not made for us, until the sommelier confirms which cuvée is in the bottle.

Asked: What does it go with?

Answer: The turtle soup, raw oysters and the Eggs Hussarde above all: its dryness and bubbles cut through rich, salty food.

wines.name: Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d’Alsace NV

kept.a: Show the label and say it as pee-AIR SHPAR. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in a flute or tulip, from an ice bucket half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease the cork out quietly. Tilt the glass and pour in two stages so the creamy mousse does not overflow, guests first and the host last. Say: “The Pierre Sparr, a sparkling rosé from Alsace: all Pinot Noir, dry and berry-bright.”

Offer the Pierre Sparr to a guest who wants something pink and festive, at brunch celebrations, and with the steak tartare cannoli, the fried hen and the Sardou or the Owen. It is the friendlier-priced bubbles beside the house Champagne. Say: “If you'd like something pink and festive, the Pierre Sparr is a sparkling rosé from Alsace, made like Champagne, dry with bright berry fruit.”

The Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d'Alsace is our sparkling rosé by the glass, $18 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Pierre Sparr, pee-AIR SHPAR, is an Alsace house. Crémant means the wine is made the same way as Champagne, with the second fermentation in the bottle, and in Alsace a rosé crémant must be all Pinot Noir.

In the glass it is pink and lively, with a creamy mousse. It tastes dry, with strawberry and red currant.

It is Champagne's method at a friendlier price, and the red fruit is what makes it useful at the table: it is the first pick with the Steak Tartare Cannoli, where red fruit suits the raw beef and the bubbles cut the fried shell and the crème fraîche. It is also the second choice with the Eggs Sardou, the Eggs Owen and the Poussin à la Moutarde, and a natural for a brunch celebration.

For a guest who wants bubbles but something pink with the Hussarde, it is all Pinot Noir and dry, with red fruit for the marchand de vin.

Asked: What is a crémant?

Answer: A sparkling wine made the same way as Champagne, with the second fermentation in the bottle, from outside Champagne. This one is from Alsace.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is a Brut: dry, with strawberry and red currant fruit.

Asked: What grape is it?

Answer: All Pinot Noir: in Alsace a rosé crémant must be.

Say Pierre Sparr as pee-AIR SHPAR. It is a sparkling rosé, not Champagne: never call it Champagne. The creamy mousse foams quickly, so pour in two stages. It is not a match for the sweet starters: the curds and the coulis make it taste tart. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: The Binwise list and the Birthday Bubbles page print Rare Brut 2012 by the glass; the current Wines by the Glass page prints a 2013 Rare Millésime at the same $75. The bottle list carries both vintages. Read the label at lineup before naming the vintage.

kept.a: Bring the bottle to the table and present the label: the guest is paying for the name. Serve it at 46 to 50°F, a touch warmer than the house bubbles so the vintage complexity shows, in a tulip or white-wine glass. Lift the Coravin Sparkling stopper, pour, and reseal it straight away. Say the vintage only once you have read it on the label. Say: “This is Rare, the prestige vintage: toasted almond and candied citrus. Happy celebration.”

Offer Rare to a table celebrating, an anniversary or a guest who loves Champagne, as the step up from the house glass with the oysters, the turtle soup or the Hussarde. Tell them it is a rare chance to taste a wine like this without buying the bottle. Say: “For a special occasion, we pour Rare by the glass: a prestige vintage Champagne with toasted almond and candied citrus.”

Rare Brut 2012 is our prestige vintage Champagne by the glass, $75 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, poured from a bottle kept fresh under a Coravin Sparkling stopper.

Rare began as Piper-Heidsieck's prestige cuvée and is now run as its own house, Rare Champagne; its first vintage was 1976, and only about a dozen vintages have ever been declared. It is Chardonnay-led, with Pinot Noir, from a single vintage and Grand Cru sites, with about ten years on its lees. Because the opened bottle sits under a Coravin Sparkling stopper, which re-pressurizes it, a single glass is possible.

In the glass it is golden, with a long, fine mousse. It tastes of white peach, candied citrus and toasted almond.

It is the celebration step up: from the house Champagne with the turtle soup, the oysters, the Hussarde and the omelette, and wonderful with crab claws or on its own. The Binwise list and the Birthday Bubbles page print 2012, and the current Wines by the Glass page a 2013 Millésime, so the open vintage is read at lineup.

Charles Lafitte Brut is the pairing Champagne on both of our tasting menus, poured as a 4 oz glass; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Charles Lafitte, sharl lah-FEET, is a house with roots to 1834, now part of the Vranken-Pommery group. This is a traditional method Brut, a blend led by Pinot Noir and Meunier with Chardonnay.

wines.serviceNote: New on the current Wines by the Glass page (3 October 2026), printed there as Argyle Vintage Brut and on the Birthday Bubbles page and the Binwise list as Argyle Brut, all 2022 at $15. Confirm at lineup that it is one bottle and that it is poured.

kept.a: Show the label and say Argyle Brut, from the Willamette Valley in Oregon. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in a flute or tulip, from an ice bucket half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease the cork out quietly. Tilt the glass and pour in two stages so the mousse does not overflow, guests first and the host last. Say: “The Argyle Brut, a dry sparkling wine from Oregon. Cheers to the 80th.”

Offer the Argyle to a guest who wants bubbles at a gentler price than the house Champagne, to a table toasting a birthday or the 80th, and with the Louisiana Oysters or the Bubbles snacks. At $15.00 it is our lowest priced sparkling glass, below the Pierre Sparr at $18. Say: “For a glass of bubbles, the Argyle Brut is a dry sparkling wine from Oregon's Willamette Valley, $15.”

Argyle Brut 2022 is the newest sparkling wine on our by-the-glass list and the friendliest priced, $15 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner. It is printed twice: on the Wines by the Glass page as Argyle Vintage Brut, and on the Birthday Bubbles page, under Champagne by the Glass, as Argyle Brut.

Argyle is the producer, in the Willamette Valley, wil-AM-it, in Oregon. So it is an American sparkling wine, not Champagne, whatever the page heading says, and we call it sparkling wine. Brut means dry, and 2022 is the vintage both lists print. It is made the Champagne way, with the second fermentation in the bottle, from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with a little Meunier in recent vintages; the sommelier confirms this bottle's blend.

The guest gets a flute of dry bubbles: shortbread and apple, citrus zest and a saline finish.

It is the glass for a guest who wants bubbles to toast the 80th without the house Champagne's price. Dry bubbles cut salt and fat, so it suits the Louisiana Oysters, and at Bubbles the popcorn shrimp and the fries with pink sauce.

Asked: Is it Champagne?

Answer: No, it is a sparkling wine from Oregon's Willamette Valley. The Birthday Bubbles page lists it under Champagne by the Glass, but only wine from Champagne in France is Champagne.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is a Brut, which means dry.

Asked: What grapes are in it?

Answer: Recent vintages are Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with a little Meunier, the Champagne grapes, made the Champagne way; I will confirm this bottle with the sommelier.

Never call it Champagne: it is an Oregon sparkling wine, even under the Birthday Bubbles page's Champagne by the Glass. The glass list prints Argyle Vintage Brut, and the Birthday Bubbles page and the Binwise list print Argyle Brut, all 2022 at $15: confirm at lineup that they are one bottle. wines.name: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022

kept.a: Show the label and say C.H. Berres as BEH-ress. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, with no decanting, and keep the bottle well chilled between pours. Pour a standard glass for the guests first and the host last. If the guest asked about sweetness, tell them what you tasted at lineup. Say: “The Berres Riesling, from old vines in the Mosel: light, racy and a touch sweet.”

Offer the Berres with anything spicy: the gumbo, the shrimp and grits, the dinner hanger or the tofu, and with the duck confit waffle. It is a $14 glass, an easy yes. Say: “With anything spicy I love the Berres Riesling from the Mosel: light, racy and a touch sweet, so it cools the heat.” For a guest who says they do not like sweet wine, explain the touch of sweetness is what tames the spice.

The C.H. Berres Old Vines Riesling 2022 is our Riesling by the glass, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and one of the two least expensive glasses on the list.

C.H. Berres, BEH-ress, is an old Mosel family estate at Ürzig in the Middle Mosel, with roots to 1510. This is Riesling from old vines on the Mosel slate, fermented to leave a touch of sweetness: about twenty grams of sugar a liter, at only 11.5% alcohol.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes light-bodied, with green apple, peach, a slaty mineral note and racy acidity under that touch of sweetness.

That little sweetness is what cools spice, and the low alcohol keeps heat from flaring, so it is the first pick with the Seafood Gumbo and the Duck Confit Waffle, where its fruit meets the maple. It loves the chili crisp on the hanger and the ’nduja on the lobster, and it is the second choice with the baked apple, the lobster, the shrimp and grits and the tofu. Six pairings hinge on how sweet the open bottle tastes, so it is tasted at lineup.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Off-dry: a touch of sweetness, about twenty grams of sugar a liter, balanced by racy acidity. We taste it at lineup, so I can tell you honestly how today's bottle reads.

Asked: Why Riesling with spicy food?

Answer: The touch of sweetness and the low alcohol, 11.5%, cool the heat rather than amplifying it.

Asked: Where is it from?

Answer: An old family estate at Ürzig in Germany's Mosel, from old vines on slate.

Taste the open bottle at lineup and record the label alcohol: six pairings hinge on whether it reads dry or off-dry, and the guide hedges on it. Keep it well chilled with spicy dishes; heat reads hotter with warm wine. Say C.H. Berres as BEH-ress. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025

kept.a: Show the label and say PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, with no decanting, and return the bottle to the ice between pours. Pour the guests first and the host last. With the Caesar, mention the smoked oyster dressing as you pour. Say: “The Albariño from Spain's Atlantic coast: lemony and fresh, with a salty edge.”

Offer the Albariño with seafood: the Caesar, the papillote, the oysters for a still wine, and fried seafood at the bar. It suits a guest who likes crisp, dry whites and does not want oak. Say: “The Albariño comes from Spain's Atlantic coast: citrusy, unoaked, with a salty edge made for seafood.”

The Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025 is our Albariño by the glass, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Pazo das Bruxas, PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas, means manor of the witches: it is the Familia Torres estate in Rías Baixas, on the Atlantic coast of Galicia in Spain. Albariño is the crisp, saline white grape of that coast, and this one is unoaked and bottled young for freshness.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes of lemon and white peach, with an almost sea-spray, saline snap, dry and fresh.

That salty freshness makes it a natural with seafood: it is the first pick with the Creole Caesar, whose dressing is made with smoked oysters, and with the Gulf Fish en Papillote, with its olives and tomato; it is the still white offered with the Grand Isle Jewel oysters. It also suits the Marcona almonds on the papillote and the popcorn shrimp at Bubbles.

Its freshness fades as it warms, so it is kept iced between pours.

Asked: What does Pazo das Bruxas mean?

Answer: Manor of the witches. It is the Familia Torres estate in Rías Baixas.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: No: unoaked and bottled young, so it is fresh, with lemon, white peach and a salty snap.

Asked: What goes with it?

Answer: Seafood: the Creole Caesar with its smoked oyster dressing, the Gulf fish en papillote, and oysters if you want a still wine.

Keep it iced between pours: its saline freshness fades as it warms. Confirm at lineup that the vintage is still the 2025, since young whites roll over. Say Pazo das Bruxas as PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Famille Durand Val de Loire Sauvignon Blanc 2024
wines.serviceNote: The current Wines by the Glass page prints Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024; the Binwise list read the same day prints Domaine Durand, Loire Valley, 2025, both at $14. Read the label at lineup before naming the producer or the vintage.

kept.a: Show the label and say the producer and vintage as the label reads, Durand as dur-AHN, and name the Loire. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, with no decanting, and keep the bottle in the ice bucket. Pour the guests first and the host last. Say: “Our Loire Sauvignon Blanc from the Durand family: crisp, herbal and bone-dry.”

Offer the Durand with the Eggs Sardou above all, and with the tomato tostada, the crab claws and anything herbal. It suits a guest who likes crisp, dry whites, and at $14 it is an easy glass. Say: “Artichokes are tricky with wine, but a Loire Sauvignon Blanc loves them: the Durand is crisp and herbal.”

The Sauvignon Blanc by the glass is our Loire white, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, one of the two least expensive glasses on the list. The current menu prints it as Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024; the Binwise list still prints Domaine Durand, 2025, so the label is read at lineup.

The Durand family, dur-AHN, makes it in France's Loire Valley from Sauvignon Blanc. Val de Loire names the region and no village, so it is called a Loire Sauvignon Blanc, never a Sancerre. The guide described the 2025 as fermented in steel with no oak; the sommelier confirms the 2024.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes bone-dry and zippy, with grapefruit, cut grass and a flinty note.

Artichokes make most wines taste oddly sweet or metallic, but this one's sharp, herbal acidity stands up to them, which is why it is the first pick with the Eggs Sardou. It also loves tomatoes and fresh herbs, so it is the second choice with the Creole Tomato Tostada and the leaner choice with the Louisiana Crab Claws.

Asked: Is it a Sancerre?

Answer: It is a Loire Sauvignon Blanc. The menu prints Val de Loire, the region, and no village, so I never call it Sancerre.

Asked: Why with artichokes?

Answer: Artichokes make most wines taste oddly sweet; a bone-dry, herbal Sauvignon Blanc survives them and joins the artichoke instead.

Asked: Which vintage is it?

Answer: The menu prints 2024 and our wine list 2025, so I read the label before I name it.

The producer and vintage are disputed: the current menu prints Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024, and Binwise Domaine Durand, Loire Valley, 2025. Read the label at lineup, and never call it Sancerre. Whether the 2024 is steel fermented with no oak is a lineup question for the sommelier. Keep it in the ice bucket so its acidity stays sharp. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say GAY-nee. Serve it at 50 to 54°F in a larger white or Chardonnay glass, with no decanting; if it is too cold, let it rest out of the ice a few minutes so the creamy texture shows. Pour the guests first and the host last. Say: “The Gainey Chardonnay from Santa Barbara County: creamy, with lemon curd and baked apple, and fresh.”

Offer the Gainey with butter sauces and cream: the BBQ oysters, the pecan fish and the poussin. It suits a guest who asks for Chardonnay or something rounder. The Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé at $40 is the step up for a Burgundy lover. Say: “For something rounder, the Gainey Chardonnay from Santa Barbara County has a creamy texture but stays fresh.”

Gainey farms in both the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills and its Chardonnays have carried either appellation; confirm the appellation on the bottle in service. The 'Santa Barbara County' phrase in the say it line is safe either way.

The Gainey Estate Vineyards Chardonnay 2023 is our California Chardonnay by the glass, $17 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Gainey, GAY-nee, is a Santa Barbara County estate that farms in both the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills, and its Chardonnays have carried either appellation, so the one on the bottle is confirmed in service. It is cool-climate Chardonnay: the ocean cools the vineyards, which keeps the acidity bright.

In the glass it is golden. It tastes of lemon curd and baked apple, with a creamy texture and bright acidity.

That pairing of creaminess and freshness makes it the first pick for butter and cream: the Louisiana Oysters in their BBQ butter sauce, the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Poussin à la Moutarde with its mustard cream. It is also worth offering with the two crab dishes, keeping the Leflaive as the step up, once the sommelier confirms it tastes fresh rather than oaky.

It is served a little warmer than the crisp whites, so the creamy texture shows.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: It is creamy, from a cool climate that keeps it fresh. Whether today's bottle reads fresh rather than oaky is something the sommelier confirms, and I will check with the sommelier if you dislike oak.

Asked: Where in California?

Answer: Santa Barbara County, where the ocean cools the vineyards; the exact appellation is on the bottle.

Asked: What goes with it?

Answer: Butter and cream: the BBQ oysters, the pecan Gulf fish and the poussin with mustard cream.

Confirm the appellation on the bottle, Sta. Rita Hills or Santa Ynez Valley; Santa Barbara County holds either way. Ask the sommelier whether it reads fresh or oaky: the answer decides whether you offer it on the crab dishes. If it comes out too cold, rest it a few minutes out of the ice. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Present the label first: the estate name matters to Burgundy lovers. Say luh-FLEV, mah-KAWN vair-ZAY. Serve it at 50 to 54°F in a white Burgundy bowl. Pour through the Coravin needle, cork left in, and return the bottle to the cooler. Guests first and the host last. Say: “Domaine Leflaive's Mâcon-Verzé, poured by Coravin: citrus, white flowers and a chalky finish.”

Offer the Leflaive to a white Burgundy lover, with the crab dishes and the redfish, and as the step up from the Gainey. At $40 a glass, name the price and the estate. Say: “If you love white Burgundy, we pour Leflaive's Mâcon by the glass, a legendary estate: rich enough for butter, fresh enough for seafood.”

The Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé 2022 is our white Burgundy by the glass, $40 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, poured by Coravin.

Domaine Leflaive, luh-FLEV, is one of Burgundy's great white-wine estates, best known for Puligny-Montrachet. This is its Chardonnay from Verzé, mah-KAWN vair-ZAY, in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy. The Coravin is a needle through the cork: the wine is poured without the cork being pulled, which is why a single glass of a wine like this is possible.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of citrus and white flowers, with a fine, chalky texture and a gentle richness.

That balance of richness and freshness is why it is the first pick with the Crab & Corn Omelette, the Louisiana Crab Claws and the Redfish Véronique in its beurre blanc, and the still white offered with the turtle soup. It is the step up from the Gainey with the oysters, the pecan fish and the poussin, and on the lobster course.

The estate's name matters to Burgundy lovers, so the label is always presented.

Asked: Who is Leflaive?

Answer: Luh-FLEV: one of Burgundy's great white-wine estates, best known for Puligny-Montrachet. This is their Mâcon-Verzé.

Asked: How do you pour it by the glass?

Answer: By Coravin: a needle through the cork, so the bottle is never opened and stays fresh.

Asked: Why with the redfish?

Answer: Beurre blanc and white Burgundy are a classic: the wine has the richness for the butter sauce and the brightness for the preserved lemon.

It is poured by Coravin, needle through the cork: never pull the cork, and return the bottle to the cooler after each pour. Which device and log procedure the bar uses is a lineup question. At $40 a glass it is the first pick with a $28 omelette, so offer the Gainey as the lower priced creamy choice once it is confirmed fresh. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Fichet ‘Château London’ Mâcon-Igé 2024

kept.a: Show the label and say fee-SHAY, mah-KAWN ee-ZHAY, once you have confirmed it is tonight's pour. Serve it at 50 to 53°F in a white-wine glass, from a bottle opened at the start of service and kept in a cooler so it does not over-chill. Pour exactly 4 oz just before the lobster lands, guests first and the host last. Say: “With the lobster, a Mâcon-Igé from Domaine Fichet: round enough for the butter, fresh against the spice.”

You sell the Fichet by selling the dinner tasting's $120 pairing; it is the white that meets the lobster. Name it as you pour, and tell the parcel story: guests enjoy that Château London has no castle. If a guest wants a glass on its own, check with the sommelier. Say: “With the lobster we pour a Mâcon from Burgundy: Chardonnay with body for the lobster and a fresh finish.”

The Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé 2024 is the dinner tasting's white, a 4 oz pour with the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Domaine Fichet, fee-SHAY, is a family estate at Igé, mah-KAWN ee-ZHAY, in the Mâconnais, farmed by the Fichet brothers; it is not the Meursault Fichet. Château London is a named vineyard parcel on old limestone, with some vines over a hundred years old: no castle, and nothing to do with England. The wine is made mostly in steel with a touch of old oak.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of apple and citrus, with a gentle roundness and a fresh finish.

That roundness gives it the body for lobster and butter, and the fresh finish lifts the palate after the spicy ’nduja, which is why the guide and the current menu both pour it on that course.

Asked: Is there a castle?

Answer: No. Château London is a named vineyard parcel at Igé, on old limestone; no castle, and nothing to do with England.

Asked: Is it from Meursault?

Answer: No, this Fichet is a family estate at Igé in the Mâconnais, not the Meursault Fichet.

Asked: Can I have a glass on its own?

Answer: It is poured on the tasting pairing and not on the glass list, so I will check with the sommelier.

The guide and the current menu both print this Fichet with the lobster; read the supplement card at lineup all the same. It is an included 4 oz pour on the pairing: never double-pour. Open it at the start of service and keep it in a cooler, not an ice bath. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Minuty ‘Prestige’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024

kept.a: Show the label and say mee-nu-TEE. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, from an ice bucket half ice and half water, with no decanting. Pour where the guest can see the pale Provence color, guests first and the host last, and return the bottle to the ice. Say: “The Minuty, a classic Provence rosé: pale, dry and refreshing.”

Offer the Minuty on a warm day, in the courtyard, with the tomato tostada, the shrimp and grits and the papillote, and to any guest who asks for rosé. Say: “The Minuty is a classic Provence rosé: pale, dry and refreshing, lovely with tomatoes and shrimp.” Pour it where the guest can see the pale color.

The Minuty Prestige Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024 is our still rosé by the glass, $17 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Minuty, mee-nu-TEE, is one of the classic names of Provence rosé. The Prestige is a Grenache-led wine, pressed pale and bottled young, so it keeps its freshness.

In the glass it is the pale color Provence is known for, and the color is part of the appeal. It tastes dry and refreshing: white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest, with a light mineral finish.

Its freshness and red fruit are made for tomatoes and shrimp, which is why it is the first pick with the Creole Tomato Tostada, whose raw tomatoes need a wine as bright as they are, and with the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, where the acidity meets the tomato-based Creole sauce and the fruit cushions the tasso. It is the second choice with the Gulf Fish en Papillote for the tomato and olive, and a natural glass in the courtyard on a warm afternoon.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is dry: white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest with a light mineral finish.

Asked: Where is it from?

Answer: Provence, in the south of France. Minuty is one of the classic names of Provence rosé.

Asked: What goes with it?

Answer: Tomatoes and shrimp above all: the Creole tomato tostada and the shrimp and grits.

Confirm at lineup that the vintage is still the 2024: young rosé rolls over. Keep it iced, half ice and half water, and pour it well chilled. Say Minuty as mee-nu-TEE. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say dah-mee-EN mar-TAN, and name the Bourgogne. Serve it at 55 to 58°F in a Burgundy bowl, with no decanting; chill the bottle briefly if the bar runs warm. Pour the guests first and the host last. Say: “Our Bourgogne Pinot Noir from Damien Martin: light and silky, with red cherry and a touch of earth.”

Offer the Damien Martin to a guest who wants red but a light one: with the tofu, the duck, the egg dishes' marchand de vin and the gumbo. It is the red for breakfast. Say: “If you'd like a red that won't overpower the plate, our Bourgogne Pinot Noir is light and silky with bright cherry fruit.”

The Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir 2023 is our light red Burgundy by the glass, $18 on the current menu at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; the Binwise list still prints $17.

It comes from a father and son family domaine, Domaine Robert et Damien Martin at Davayé in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy, founded in 1982 by Robert and run by his son Damien, dah-mee-EN mar-TAN.

In the glass it is a translucent ruby. It tastes light and silky: red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, with light tannin and fresh acidity.

A light red like this goes where a big red would bully the food. It is the first pick with the Blackened Tofu, whose earthy mushrooms it loves, and the second choice on six plates: the Rohan duck and the duck confit waffle, the steak tartare cannoli, the gumbo, the Eggs Hussarde, where it meets the red wine in the marchand de vin, and the Pecan Gulf Fish if the bordelaise is red-wine based.

It is served slightly cool, around 55 to 58°F, so it stays fresh.

Asked: Red with eggs?

Answer: A light one, yes: the marchand de vin on the Hussarde is a red wine sauce, and this Pinot Noir is light enough for the yolk.

Asked: Where is it from?

Answer: A father and son family domaine at Davayé in the Mâconnais, in southern Burgundy.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: No: light and silky, with red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, and light tannin.

The glass price is disputed: the current menu prints $18 and Binwise $17, so confirm at lineup and quote the list in hand. Serve it slightly cool, 55 to 58°F; if the back bar runs warm, give the bottle ten to fifteen minutes in the ice bucket. The producer and importer are a lineup question for the sommelier. Say Damien Martin as dah-mee-EN mar-TAN. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say loo-EE zhah-DOH, BOHN, Premier Cru, once you have confirmed it is tonight's pour. Serve it at 57 to 60°F in a Burgundy bowl, from a bottle opened 20 to 30 minutes ahead. Pour exactly 4 oz just before the redfish lands, guests first and the host last. Say: “With the redfish, a Premier Cru Beaune from Louis Jadot: light and bright, lovely with the grapes.”

You sell the Beaune by selling the dinner tasting's pairing, and by explaining it as it is poured: red with fish surprises guests, and the explanation is the pleasure. For the Chateaubriand table, offer it only if the sommelier confirms it à la carte; otherwise the Moulin d'Issan at $16. Say: “With the redfish we pour a Premier Cru Beaune, a light, bright red Burgundy that loves the pickled grapes.”

The Louis Jadot Beaune 1er Cru 2023 is the dinner tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Redfish Véronique on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Louis Jadot, loo-EE zhah-DOH, is the Burgundy house behind it, and Beaune, BOHN, is the wine capital of Burgundy. Premier Cru is Burgundy's second-highest vineyard tier, and the highest in Beaune, which has no Grand Cru. This is Pinot Noir from Premier Cru vineyards there.

In the glass it is bright ruby. It tastes of bright red fruit, with a silky texture and a savory edge.

It is a talking point for red with fish: light enough for the redfish, low in tannin, and its red fruit loves the hibiscus-pickled grapes. It is also the second choice the guide offers with the Chateaubriand, finesse over power, but only if it can be poured à la carte. It is opened 20 to 30 minutes ahead so the young wine shows its perfume.

Asked: Red wine with fish?

Answer: A light red, yes: Pinot Noir with low tannin is gentle with fish, and its red fruit loves the hibiscus-pickled grapes.

Asked: What does Premier Cru mean?

Answer: Burgundy's second-highest vineyard tier, and the highest in Beaune, which has no Grand Cru.

Asked: Can I order a glass?

wines.name: Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge 2024

kept.a: Show the label and say Domaine de Durban, BOHM duh vuh-NEEZ. Serve it at 58 to 62°F in a standard red glass, with no decanting; with spicy plates, chill it a few minutes in the ice bucket first. Pour the guests first and the host last. Say: “The Durban, a Southern Rhône red: ripe and generous, with soft tannins for the spice.”

Offer the Durban with the Eggs Owen, the dinner hanger steak and anything spicy or braised, and to a guest who wants a red that is ripe and soft rather than tannic. Say: “The Durban is a Southern Rhône red, ripe and generous with soft tannins, so it handles spice and richness beautifully.”

The Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge 2024 is our Southern Rhône red by the glass, $19 on the current menu at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; the Binwise list still prints $18.

Domaine de Durban, dur-BAHN, is famous for its sweet Muscat, but this is the estate's dry red: a Grenache and Syrah blend from the Beaumes-de-Venise cru, BOHM duh vuh-NEEZ, in the Southern Rhône.

In the glass it is deep ruby. It tastes ripe and generous: dark cherry, plum, dried herbs and pepper, with round, soft tannins.

That ripeness and pepper stand up to spice and braise. It is the first pick with the Eggs Owen, whose short rib is braised in red wine under a red wine sauce, and with the Creole Hanger Steak and its chili crisp, where soft tannins keep the heat from turning bitter. It is the second choice with the daytime Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. The sommelier may also suggest it with the duck on the dinner tasting.

Grenache is generous in alcohol, so a few minutes in the ice bucket keeps it in check with spicy plates.

Asked: Isn't Beaumes-de-Venise a sweet wine?

Answer: The village is famous for sweet Muscat, but this is Durban's dry red, Grenache with Syrah.

Asked: Will it be too strong for the spice?

Answer: Its tannins are soft and its fruit ripe, so it soothes the chili; we serve it a little cool so the alcohol does not lift the heat.

Asked: What does it taste like?

Answer: Dark cherry, plum, dried herbs and pepper, with round tannins.

The glass price is disputed: the current menu prints $19 and Binwise $18, so confirm at lineup and quote the list in hand. Serve it at 58 to 62°F, and with the chili crisp a few minutes in the ice bucket: warm Grenache makes heat burn. Say Beaumes-de-Venise as BOHM duh vuh-NEEZ, and never call it sweet. The printed 2024 blend is a lineup question for the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Domaine de Châteaumar's Cuvée Vincent Côtes du Rhône is the breakfast tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Petite Filet Mignon on the Traditional Breakfast; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Châteaumar, shah-toh-MAR, grows it as all Syrah from fifty year old vines on two parcels beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, nine kilometers from Orange, farmed organically without certification. That is unusual in the south, where Grenache usually leads.

In the glass it is deep purple-red. It tastes juicy and soft: black raspberry, black pepper and gentle tannins.

It is just right for red meat at breakfast: its soft tannins meet the lean filet gently, its pepper picks up the garlic spinach, and its freshness cleans up the crisp rösti. It is served slightly cool, 58 to 60°F, to stay fresh in the morning.

The menu prints the 2023; read the label before naming it, and remember it is the Côtes du Rhône, not the estate's Châteauneuf of the same name.

The Moulin d'Issan Bordeaux Supérieur is our Bordeaux by the glass, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner. The current menu prints the 2021 and the Binwise list the 2023, so the vintage is read at lineup.

It comes from the team behind Château d'Issan, a classic estate in Margaux, and it is named for a ruined seventeenth century windmill: moulin, moo-LAN, is French for mill. The menu heads it a Cabernet Sauvignon blend; the blend of the 2021 is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is deep ruby. It tastes of cassis, plum and cedar, medium-bodied with polished tannins.

That structure is what a steak with béarnaise wants: the tannin binds with the beef and the butter, and the acidity resets the palate. It is the first pick with the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at breakfast and lunch, and the second choice with the Petite Filet Mignon and the dinner Creole Hanger Steak. It is the classic, gentler priced alternative to a $70 glass of Rubicon with the Chateaubriand, and it suits the Roost Burger at the bar.

If a table takes a bottle, it is opened or decanted 20 to 30 minutes ahead.

La Miraja Le Masche Barbera d'Asti 2023 is the newest red on our by-the-glass list, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and our one Italian glass.

Barbera, bar-BEAR-ah, is the grape, and Asti the hill country of Piemonte in northwest Italy where it grows; La Miraja is the producer and Le Masche the name of the wine. How long it spends in barrel, and what Le Masche means, are questions for the sommelier.

In the glass it is deep ruby. Barbera is known for bright acidity and soft tannin, so it drinks juicy and medium-bodied: dark cherry and plum, fresh rather than heavy.

That acidity makes it a food red. It meets tomato, Creole sauce and cured pork, so it suits the shrimp and grits with their tasso and the Creole tomato tostada, and its soft tannin never fights a spicy plate. It is the first pick with Maggie's mushrooms, whose earthiness it lifts. On the list it sits between the light Damien Martin and the riper Durban.

kept.a: Present the label: it is a Napa icon, and the guest will want to see the 2010. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a large Bordeaux glass. kept.a: Stand the bottle upright a day ahead; pour with Coravin if the house uses it for this wine, otherwise stopper, refrigerate and sell through the same night; never decant it for more than about thirty minutes. An opened sixteen year old wine fades within about a day. Confirm the house method at lineup.

Inglenook Rubicon 2010 is our grand red by the glass, $70 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Rubicon is Inglenook's flagship, a Cabernet Sauvignon based wine from Rutherford in the Napa Valley, and our glass is the 2010, sixteen years old: a Napa legend with real age on it.

In the glass it is deep garnet. Age has softened the tannins, so it tastes powerful but silky: blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth.

That depth is made for the Roasted Chateaubriand and its sauce Foyot, whose lean tenderloin a young, firm Cabernet would dry out, and it suits both hanger steaks. It is the step up with the Petite Filet Mignon on the breakfast tasting and with the daytime hanger.

An older wine can throw sediment, so the bottle is kept upright and poured slowly, leaving the last inch behind, and the label is always presented. At $70 a glass, two glasses come close to a bottle, which is when the sommelier is the better call. How the open bottle is preserved between pours is confirmed at lineup.

Asked: Why is it $70 a glass?

Answer: It is Inglenook's flagship, and our glass is the 2010, sixteen years old: a rare chance to taste an aged Napa legend by the glass.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: Powerful, but age has made it silky: blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth.

Asked: Will it have sediment?

Answer: It can, at sixteen years; I pour slowly and leave the last inch in the bottle.

Stand the bottle upright ahead of service, pour slowly and leave the sediment behind; never decant it for more than about thirty minutes. How it is preserved between pours, and that it is still the 2010, are lineup questions. At $70, two glasses near a bottle's price: bring in the sommelier for a table drinking more. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say Paul Hobbs, KOOMZ-vil. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a Bordeaux glass, from a bottle opened or decanted 30 to 60 minutes ahead. Pour exactly 4 oz just before the duck lands, guests first and the host last. Say: “With the duck, Paul Hobbs Cabernet from Coombsville: dark fruit, cocoa and a firm, fresh structure.”

The Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 is the dinner tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Paul Hobbs is the Napa winemaker behind it, and Coombsville, KOOMZ-vil, is one of Napa's cooler corners, near the town of Napa, so its Cabernet keeps its freshness.

In the glass it is deep, dark red. It tastes of dark fruit and cocoa on a firm structure.

The guide's reasoning is that duck breast is red and fatty enough to carry Cabernet: the tannin binds with the fat and the wine tastes rounder, the dark fruit meets the glazed peaches, and the candied hazelnuts echo the cocoa. A young Napa Cabernet against cane syrup peaches is a real tension, which is why the Damien Martin Pinot Noir stands as the lighter alternative.

It is young, so it is opened or decanted 30 to 60 minutes ahead. The duck plate itself is disputed, so the garnish it meets is confirmed with the kitchen.

Asked: Cabernet with duck?

The Dr. Hermann Erdener Prälat Riesling Auslese 2014 is our sweet wine, sold as a 375 ml half-bottle at $80, at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; it is the only sweet wine sold à la carte.

Dr. Hermann, HAIR-mahn, is the Mosel estate behind it. Auslese, OWS-lay-zuh, means selected harvest, a tier above late-harvest Spätlese, and the fruit comes from the steep Erdener Prälat vineyard, one of the Mosel's famous slopes. Twelve years of age add depth.

In the glass it is golden. It tastes of apricot, honey and pineapple, with electric acidity that keeps the sweetness lively.

Because it is sweeter than our desserts, it never tastes sour beside them, so it is the first pick on seven plates: Bananas Foster, the bread pudding, the Lemon Tart, the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, and the sweet breakfast starters, the trifle, the Framboise French Toast and the baked apple. The half-bottle pours about four dessert glasses of 2 to 3 oz, so it is a wine to share and carry from a sweet starter to dessert.

Asked: Can I have just a glass?

Answer: It is sold as the $80 half-bottle, about four dessert glasses. Whether a single pour can be rung is a manager's call, so I will check before promising it.

Asked: What does Auslese mean?

Answer: OWS-lay-zuh: selected harvest, a tier above late-harvest Spätlese, so it is sweet and honeyed.

Asked: Will it be too sweet with dessert?

Answer: Its electric acidity keeps it bright, and because it is sweeter than the dessert, the dessert tastes fruitier, not sour.

kept.a: Show the label and say lah TOOR vee-AY, bahn-YOOLS. Serve it slightly cool, about 55°F, in a small dessert glass: 4 oz on the tasting, 2 to 3 oz otherwise, with no decanting. Pour it before the dessert lands, guests first and the host last. Say: “To close, Banyuls from La Tour Vieille: fig, caramel and coffee, the classic with chocolate.”

You sell the Banyuls with the dinner tasting's pairing, as the Snickers lands. À la carte, offer it with the chocolate and caramel desserts only once the sommelier confirms it is poured by the glass and at what price; otherwise our coffee with chicory. Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva is the dinner tasting's dessert wine, a 4 oz pour with The Snickers on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Banyuls, bahn-YOOLS, is a sweet fortified red, a vin doux naturel, from the schist terraces around Banyuls-sur-Mer in Roussillon, French Catalonia. It must be at least half Grenache noir, and the fermentation is stopped with neutral grape spirit so the grape's own sugar stays in the wine. La Tour Vieille, lah TOOR vee-AY, ages its Reserva the oxidative way.

In the glass it is a deep, browning red. It tastes of dried fig, walnut, caramel, coffee and orange peel.

It is the classic wine for chocolate: its sweetness keeps chocolate from turning it bitter, and its cocoa and coffee notes echo the dessert. It is the first pick with The Snickers, the Cherries Jubilee and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, and the sommelier may lead with it on Bananas Foster and the bread pudding, once a manager confirms it is poured outside the tasting.

Asked: What is Banyuls?

Answer: Bahn-YOOLS: a sweet fortified red from Roussillon, in French Catalonia, mostly Grenache. Grape spirit stops the fermentation so the wine stays sweet.

Asked: Is it like port?

Answer: It is made in a similar way, a fortified sweet red, but from Grenache in the south of France.

Asked: Can I order a glass?

Answer: It is poured on the dinner tasting; whether it is poured à la carte is a question for the sommelier, so I will check.

Whether it is poured à la carte, at breakfast or at dinner, and at what price, is a sommelier question: until it is answered, the coffee cake, the Jubilee and the Snickers are coffee only à la carte. The guide and the current menu both print this Banyuls on the tasting. Lead with fig, caramel and coffee, not fresh black cherry. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Drappier, drah-pee-YAY, is a Champagne house, and Carte d'Or, kart DOR, is its Brut: a dry, non-vintage Champagne made by the traditional method. Our wine list carries Drappier among the grande marques, and lists the same Carte d'Or in a six liter Methuselah. Cesarini Sforza Rosé Brut is the gentlest priced sparkling rosé on our bottle list, $55, filed under Selections Under $100, and a first pick for the popcorn shrimp at the Roost Bar.

Cesarini Sforza is a sparkling house in Trento, the city in the Trentino Alps of northern Italy that gives its name to the Trento DOC. Trento sparkling wine is made the way Champagne is: a still base wine is bottled with a little yeast and sugar, ferments a second time in the bottle and rests on its lees before release.

This rosé is mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir, which brings the pale pink color. In the glass it is dry and bright, with small red berries, a cool mountain acidity and a soft, easy mousse.

It is on the list for the guest who wants real bubbles at a friendly price. With the Crystal gastrique and fried shrimp, its cold fizz and red fruit cool the heat and scrub the batter.

Asked: Is this Champagne?

Answer: No, Champagne only comes from Champagne in France. This is from Trento in northern Italy, made the same way, with the second fermentation in the bottle.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is Brut, so it is dry. The berry fruit can make it seem a little softer than it is.

Asked: What grapes are in it?

Answer: Mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir for the color; the sommelier can give the exact blend.

Jansz Premier Cuvée Brut 2022 is the only Tasmanian sparkling wine on our list, $65, under International Sparkling, Australia, and a first pick for the Creole spiced nuts.

Jansz makes sparkling wine on Tasmania, the island south of mainland Australia. It is the coolest wine region in the country, and cool weather keeps the acidity high, which is what sparkling wine needs. Premier Cuvée is made by the traditional method, the Champagne method: a second fermentation in the bottle, then time on the lees before it is disgorged. The blend in this bottling is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles. It tastes crisp and clean, citrus and green apple, with a touch of brioche from the lees and a salty snap at the finish.

It is here for the guest who wants a crisp bottle of bubbles at a friendly price. Salt and Creole spice make you thirsty, and its bubbles and acidity refresh after every handful.
