Answer: It is the island south of mainland Australia, the coolest part of the country, which keeps sparkling wine crisp.

Asked: Is it made like Champagne?

Chapel Down Rosé Brut is the English sparkling rosé on our list, $75, filed under Selections Under $100, and the value bottle for the steak tartare cannoli.

Chapel Down is one of the best known sparkling wine producers in England, in the county of Kent in the southeast. Southern England is cool, with chalk soils much like those of Champagne, and the grapes keep the bright acidity sparkling wine needs. The rosé is made by the traditional method: a second fermentation in the bottle and time on the lees. The blend in this bottling is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is pale salmon pink with fine bubbles. It tastes dry and light, strawberry and red currant over a bright, almost tart acidity.

It is here for the guest who wants a pink sparkling wine that is a little unexpected. With the tartare, its red fruit sits beside the raw beef and its bubbles lift the crème fraîche and the crisp potato.

Asked: They make wine in England?

Answer: Yes, and sparkling wine above all. Kent and Sussex are cool with chalky soils, and Chapel Down is one of the best known houses.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Asked: What grapes are in it?

It is on the list for brunch: a bottle of real traditional method bubbles that leaves room in the check for a second course. Its bright acidity cuts hollandaise and soft yolk, and the toast in it suits the Canadian bacon of the Hussarde.

Suggest the Pétillant when a table orders the fried pickles and wants something more interesting than a beer, or to a guest who loves Loire whites or finds Champagne too sharp. The Huet Pétillant 2019 is a lightly sparkling Vouvray, $90, filed under Selections Under $100, and a first pick for the fried pickles.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire River near Tours, and it grows only Chenin Blanc, in three famous vineyards: Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and the Clos du Bourg. Our list carries all three as still wines. Pétillant means lightly sparkling: the wine is made by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in the bottle, but at a lower pressure than Champagne.

In the glass the bubbles are softer and creamier than Champagne’s. It tastes of quince, baked apple and honeysuckle, with the high, bright acidity Chenin keeps, and it is dry or very nearly so.

It is on the list as a sommelier’s bottle at a value price. Vinegar flattens most wines, but Chenin’s acidity stands up to the pickles, and the gentle bubbles lift the batter and the chive cream.

Asked: What does pétillant mean?

Answer: Lightly sparkling. It is made the Champagne way, but with gentler pressure, so the bubbles are soft and creamy.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: It drinks dry or very nearly so, with bright acidity. If a guest needs it bone dry, I will check the bottling with the sommelier.

Asked: Who is Huet?

Answer: One of the great Vouvray estates. We also carry three of its still Chenin Blancs.

Huet appears several times on our list: this is the sparkling one, bin 32641, 2019, $90. The still wines are Le Haut-Lieu Sec (a full bottle and a half-bottle), the Le Mont demi-sec half-bottle and the Clos du Bourg demi-sec, so check the bin. Ease the cork out gently. Its exact sweetness is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Ferrari is the best known sparkling house of Trento, in the Italian Alps, and it is no relation to the cars. It is run by the Lunelli family and makes only traditional method wines, with the second fermentation in the bottle, under the Trento DOC.

JM Sélèque Solessence is a grower Champagne, $100, listed under Grower Producers, Vallée de la Marne, and a first pick for the fried pickles.

JM Sélèque is a family grower in Pierry, on the slopes just south of Épernay: they farm their own vines and make the wine themselves. Solessence blends Chardonnay and Meunier with a little Pinot Noir from seven villages, and part of it is fermented in oak barrels. It is Extra Brut, so very little sugar is added after the second fermentation.

In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles. It tastes of white flowers, ripe citrus and almond paste, with a chalky, precise finish, very dry and very clean.

It is on the list as a door into grower Champagne at a sweet spot price. Its dryness stands up to vinegar and its freshness lifts fried batter, which turns a snack at the Roost Bar into a bottle worth remembering.

Louis Roederer is a family Champagne house in Reims, best known for Cristal, which is also on our list. Its non-vintage Brut is called Collection, and each blend carries a number. Collection 244 is built on the 2019 harvest and blended with wines from the house’s perpetual reserve, a store of older wine it tops up every year, with a small part of oak-aged reserve. In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles. It tastes fresh and precise: citrus, white peach and a light pastry note, crisp and long.

Chartogne-Taillet Rosé Brut is a grower rosé Champagne, $125, under Grower Producers, Montagne de Reims on our list, and the sweet spot bottle for the steak tartare cannoli.

Chartogne-Taillet is a family grower in Merfy, a village northwest of Reims, and the family makes the wine from its own vines. The rosé is colored by blending in a little red wine made from Pinot Noir grown in Merfy. The rest of the blend is a question for the sommelier.

Larmandier-Bernier Longitude is an all-Chardonnay grower Champagne, $135, under Grower Producers, Côtes de Blancs on our list, and the sweet spot bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

Larmandier-Bernier is a family grower in Vertus, at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs, the chalk slope where Champagne’s finest Chardonnay grows. Longitude is a Blanc de Blancs, all Chardonnay, rated Premier Cru and named for villages that lie along the same line of longitude. It is Extra Brut, with very little sugar added.

wines.serviceNote: Bin 3226 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 750 ml, $155. A famous name and a section anchor; no dish tier. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the bottle with the yellow label toward the host and say Veuve Clicquot, vuhv klee-KOH. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in a tulip or white-wine glass, from an ice bucket half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease the cork out with a quiet sigh. Host last. Say: “Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label: round and toasty. Happy celebrating.”

Offer the Veuve when a guest asks for a Champagne they know, for birthdays and anniversaries, and with brunch. Do not talk them out of a name they love. If they want something they have not tried, Billecart-Salmon Réserve or a grower such as Larmandier-Bernier is a fresh alternative. Say: “Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label, the classic: round, toasty and generous, a beautiful way to celebrate.”

Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label is the famous orange-labeled Champagne, $155 on our list among the grandes marques, and the name many guests ask for first.

Veuve Clicquot is a great house in Reims. Veuve means widow: Barbe-Nicole Clicquot took over the house after her husband died and ran it in the early nineteenth century, and she is remembered for the riddling table, the rack that gathers the yeast in the neck of the bottle so it can be removed. Yellow Label is the house Brut, Pinot Noir-led with Meunier and Chardonnay.

The label is called yellow but looks orange, and guests know it on sight. In the glass it is gold with lively bubbles. It tastes generous and toasty: ripe apple, citrus, brioche, round and dry.

It is on the list because guests ask for it by name, and a server should be able to say yes. It suits a toast, brunch, the turtle soup or the meat pies.

Asked: Why is the label yellow when it looks orange?

Answer: The house calls it Yellow Label; the color has always been that orange yellow, and guests know it on sight.

Asked: What does Veuve mean?

Answer: Widow. Barbe-Nicole Clicquot ran the house as a widow in the early nineteenth century.

Moët & Chandon Nectar Imperial Rosé is a sweet rosé Champagne, $180 on our list, and the sweet spot bottle for the Framboise French toast.

Moët & Chandon is the largest of the great Champagne houses, based in Épernay. Nectar Imperial Rosé is its demi-sec rosé: after the second fermentation it is finished with noticeably more sugar than a Brut, so it tastes gently sweet. It is Pinot Noir-led, with Meunier and Chardonnay.

In the glass it is a deep salmon pink with a creamy mousse. It tastes of ripe strawberry and raspberry with a soft, creamy sweetness, and the bubbles keep it from feeling heavy.

It is on the list for sweet plates. A sweet dish makes a dry wine taste sharp and thin, so a sweeter wine is the match. With the French toast, its berries echo the raspberry coulis and its bubbles lift the mascarpone mousse.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Yes, gently. Demi-sec means it carries more sugar than a Brut, so it suits a sweet dish.

Asked: Is this the Moët rosé from happy hour?

Answer: No. Bubbles pours the Imperial Rosé Brut, which is dry; this is the Nectar, the sweeter one.

Asked: Will it be too sweet with dessert?

Answer: Not with fruit or cream; with very sweet chocolate I would ask the sommelier for something richer.

This is the sweet one. The Bubbles list prints Moët Imperial Rosé Brut, which is dry, while Binwise lists only this Nectar Imperial Rosé Demi Sec, bin 32453, $180, so do not swap one for the other or promise a dry wine. Pour it well chilled. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: Bin 32362 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 750 ml, $210. A first pick for the Creole Spiced Nuts. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the bottle and say Charles Heidsieck Réserve, SHARL HIDE-sick. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a tulip or white-wine glass, from an ice bucket half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease the cork out with a quiet sigh. Host last. Say: “Charles Heidsieck Réserve: rich, toasty and creamy.”

Offer the Charles Heidsieck to a guest who says they like a rich or toasty Champagne, at the Roost Bar with the spiced nuts or the cheese board, or with the turtle soup. For the grandest version of that style with the nuts, Krug Grande Cuvée is the celebration bottle. Say: “Charles Heidsieck Réserve is rich and toasty, roasted nuts and brioche, and it was made for those spiced nuts.”

Charles Heidsieck Réserve Brut is one of the richest non-vintage Champagnes on our list, $210 among the grandes marques, and a first pick for the Creole spiced nuts.

Charles Heidsieck is a Champagne house in Reims, and its wines age in the chalk cellars dug beneath the city. The Réserve is known for a high share of reserve wines, older wines held back from earlier harvests, blended into the Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier of the new year, and for long aging on its lees.

In the glass it is a deeper gold than most, with fine bubbles. It tastes rich and toasty: roasted nuts, brioche and dried apricot, creamy in texture, dry, with a long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who loves a fuller Champagne. Its nutty, toasted flavors echo roasted nuts and soften Creole spice, and it is lovely with the sherry in the turtle soup.

Asked: Is this the same as Piper-Heidsieck?

Answer: No. The houses share a family history and a name, but Charles Heidsieck is a separate house and wine; Piper-Heidsieck makes our house Champagne.

Asked: Why is it so toasty?

Answer: It uses a lot of older reserve wine and ages a long time on its lees in the chalk cellars of Reims.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is Brut: dry, though rich and creamy.

Do not mix up Charles Heidsieck with Piper-Heidsieck, which makes our house Brennan’s Essential and Rare. This is bin 32362, $210. It drinks best a touch warmer than the house bubbles. The share of reserve wine in the current bottling is a question for the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Bollinger Special Cuvée is the classic full-bodied Champagne on our list, $250 the 750 ml bottle, and the sweet spot bottle for the turtle soup.

Bollinger is a family-owned Champagne house in Aÿ, a Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir. Special Cuvée is its non-vintage Brut: Pinot Noir-led with Chardonnay and a little Meunier. Part of the wine is fermented in oak barrels, and the house keeps its older reserve wines in magnums, which is unusual and adds depth.

In the glass it is a deep gold with fine, firm bubbles. It tastes rich and structured: baked apple, toasted nuts and a little spice, with a firm, dry finish.

It is on the list as the anchor of the rich style. With the turtle soup, its nutty depth echoes the aged sherry and lifts the brown butter spinach. For a party, the Birthday Bubbles list pours the same wine in magnum.

Armand de Brignac Brut Gold is the Champagne known as Ace of Spades, $325 on our list among the grandes marques. Guests ask for it by sight.

It is made by the Cattier family in Chigny-les-Roses, on the Montagne de Reims, and today it is owned in partnership by Shawn Carter, the artist known as Jay-Z, and Moët Hennessy. The Brut Gold blends Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier.

The bottle is the story: opaque, metallic gold, with a pewter ace of spades on the front. In the glass the wine is gold, with a soft, creamy mousse. It tastes ripe and generous, white peach, brioche and a touch of honey, dry but round.

It is on the list for the celebration that wants to be seen. Present it so the table can see the bottle, open it with care, and keep it iced: the metal-finished bottle takes longer to chill. It suits the oysters, the turtle soup and the BBQ lobster.

Asked: Who makes it?

Answer: The Cattier family in Chigny-les-Roses on the Montagne de Reims; it is owned in partnership by Jay-Z and Moët Hennessy.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, the Gold is Brut: dry, with ripe, round fruit.

It is bin 32573, $325, the Gold Brut only; if a guest asks for the rosé or a larger gold bottle, check with the sommelier before promising one. The opaque bottle chills slowly, so put it on ice the moment it is ordered. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Pol Roger Blanc de Blancs 2015 is a vintage, all-Chardonnay Champagne, $335 on our list, and the celebration bottle for the Poussin à la Moutarde.

Pol Roger is a family Champagne house in Épernay. Winston Churchill was its most famous admirer, and the house named its prestige cuvée Sir Winston Churchill after his death. This Blanc de Blancs is made only from Chardonnay grown in the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, and only from the 2015 harvest, so it is a vintage wine.

In the glass it is pale gold with a very fine, creamy mousse. It tastes of lemon, white flowers and chalk, with a long, precise finish and the first notes of toast that come with age.

It is on the list as a vintage Champagne for dinner, not only for a toast. With the fried Cornish hen, its chalky freshness cuts the crust and the mustard cream sauce and keeps each bite light.

Bollinger is the family house in Aÿ, a Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir. Its PN series is a Blanc de Noirs, white Champagne made only from Pinot Noir, a black grape, and each edition is led by one village. TX20 is led by Tauxières, on the southwest slopes of the Montagne de Reims, and built on the 2020 harvest, with older reserve wines making up the rest.

In the glass it is gold with fine, firm bubbles. It tastes full and powerful: red apple and white peach, a chalky tension and a long, firm finish.

It is on the list as the Champagne for big flavors. With the barbecue oysters, its weight matches the buttery, peppery sauce while its bubbles clear the fried saltine crumble.

Asked: What does PN TX20 mean?

Answer: PN is Pinot Noir; TX stands for Tauxières, the village that leads the blend; 20 is the 2020 harvest it is built on.

Asked: Can a white Champagne be all Pinot Noir?

Asked: Is it dry?

Answer: Yes, it is Brut: dry, with a firm finish.

Billecart-Salmon is a family Champagne house in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, founded in 1818, and the house that made our Brennan’s 80th Anniversary Sous Bois. The house took its name from the marriage of Nicolas François Billecart and Elisabeth Salmon, and its grandest rosé carries her name. Asked: Is a 2009 still fresh?

Asked: Is it dry?

Bollinger La Grande Année 2015 is the vintage Champagne of Bollinger, $495 on our list, and a first pick for the crawfish meat pies.

Bollinger is the family house in Aÿ, a Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir. La Grande Année means the great year: it is made only from a harvest the house judges worthy, and this bottle is all 2015. It is Pinot Noir-led with Chardonnay, and every part of it is fermented in oak barrels, which is rare for Champagne and builds depth.

In the glass it is a deep gold with fine bubbles. It tastes rich and layered, baked apple, hazelnut, honey and spice, held together by firm acidity, with a long finish.

Jacques Selosse Initial is the cult grower Champagne on our list, $560, under Grower Producers, Côtes de Blancs, and a first pick for the fried pickles.

Jacques Selosse is a grower house in Avize, a Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs. Anselme Selosse, who took over from his father, made Champagne the way a great Burgundy domaine makes white wine, fermenting and aging in oak barrels, and inspired a generation of growers. Initial is a Blanc de Blancs, all Chardonnay, blended from several harvests, and the list prints its disgorgement date, 10.16.23, the day its yeast was removed.

In the glass it is a deep gold with fine bubbles. It tastes intense and vinous: ripe citrus, hazelnut, honey and a salty, mineral grip, with vivid acidity.

It is here because collectors ask for it and it is hard to find. Its acidity and salt meet the pickles head on and turn a snack into an occasion.

Asked: Why is Selosse so famous?

Answer: Anselme Selosse made Champagne like great white Burgundy, in oak barrels from his own vines, and growers everywhere followed him.

Asked: What is the date on the label?

Answer: The disgorgement date, when the yeast was removed: our list prints 10.16.23.

Asked: Should we drink it from a flute?

Answer: A wine glass is better; it opens up like a white Burgundy.

It is bin 31713, $560, and scarce, so confirm it is in the cellar before you describe it at length. Serve it in a white-wine glass, a touch warmer than other Champagnes. The list prints the disgorgement date, 10.16.23; check that the bottle matches. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Krug is a Champagne house in Reims, founded in 1843, that makes only prestige Champagne. Grande Cuvée is blended from wines of many years and many plots, often well over a hundred wines, each first fermented in small oak casks. Louis Roederer Cristal 2015 is one of the most famous Champagnes in the world, $775 on our list, and a first pick for the popcorn shrimp.

Roederer is a family house in Reims. Cristal was first made in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II of Russia, who asked for a clear bottle, and it has come in clear glass ever since. It is the house’s prestige vintage, made only in good years from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, here the 2015 harvest. Because clear glass lets light in, each bottle travels wrapped.

In the glass it is pale gold with silky, very fine bubbles. It tastes precise and pure: citrus, white peach, chalk and a light toast, with a long finish.

It is on the list because guests ask for it by name. Its precision cuts fried batter and makes the popcorn shrimp an occasion, and it is grand with the oysters and the crab claws.

Asked: Why is the bottle clear?

Answer: It was first made in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II, who wanted to see the wine; it has stayed in clear glass ever since.

Asked: Is 2015 a good year?

Answer: It is a vintage Roederer chose to make Cristal in, which it does only in good years; how it is drinking now is a question for the sommelier.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is Brut: dry, precise and silky.

wines.name: Krug Rosé Brut NV
wines.serviceNote: Bin 31481 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 750 ml, $865. The celebration tier for the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the bottle and say Krug Rosé, kroog roh-ZAY. Serve it at 48 to 52°F in a white-wine glass from an ice bucket, half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease it out with a quiet sigh. Pour the guests first and the host last. Say: “Krug Rosé: powerful, spicy and very long.”

Offer Krug Rosé for a big celebration at brunch with the shrimp and grits, to a guest who asks for the best rosé Champagne we have, or at dinner with the duck. For a vintage rosé at a lower price, the Billecart-Salmon Elisabeth Salmon is the alternative. Say: “Krug Rosé is powerful and spicy, red berries and blood orange, and it has the body for shrimp, tasso and Creole sauce.”

Krug Rosé is the most powerful pink Champagne on our list, $865 among the grandes marques, and the celebration bottle for the New Orleans shrimp and grits.

Krug is the Reims house that makes only prestige Champagne. Its rosé is built the way the Grande Cuvée is: wines from several years, each first fermented in small oak casks, then colored with a little red wine made from Pinot Noir. The blend includes Chardonnay and Meunier too.

In the glass it is a pale salmon copper with fine bubbles. It tastes powerful and spicy rather than sweet or pretty: red berries, blood orange, rose hip and toasted brioche, dry, with a very long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who wants the grandest rosé. Its red fruit and power stand up to Louisiana shrimp, smoky tasso and the fried pimento cheese grit cake, and it is glorious with the duck.

Asked: How is it different from Krug Grande Cuvée?

Answer: It is made the same careful way, but with a little red Pinot Noir wine for color, so it carries red fruit and spice.

Asked: Is it sweet because it is pink?

Answer: No, it is Brut: dry and powerful.

Asked: Which edition is it?

Answer: Krug numbers its rosé by edition too; I will check the number on our bottle with the sommelier.

Do not confuse it with the Krug Grande Cuvée, the white: this is the rosé, bin 31481, $865. Serve it warmer than the house bubbles. The edition number on the current bottle is a question for the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Dom Pérignon P2 2006 is the long-aged release of the most famous prestige Champagne, $1260 on our list among the grandes marques.

Dom Pérignon is the prestige Champagne of Moët & Chandon in Épernay, named for the Benedictine monk at the abbey of Hautvillers who helped shape the making of Champagne. It is always a vintage, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. The house releases each vintage at more than one plénitude, a peak in its life: P2, the second plénitude, is the same wine kept on its lees for many more years before it is disgorged.

In the glass it is a deep gold with creamy bubbles. The 2006 tastes deep and smoky: toasted brioche, candied citrus, hazelnut and a little smoke, with a very long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who knows Dom Pérignon and wants its rarest form. It is grand with the oysters, the turtle soup and the lobster.

Asked: What does P2 mean?

Answer: The second plénitude: the same vintage released years later, after much longer aging on its lees.

Asked: Who was Dom Pérignon?

Answer: A Benedictine monk at the abbey of Hautvillers who helped shape how Champagne is made; Moët & Chandon’s prestige wine carries his name.

Asked: Is it worth the extra age?

Answer: It tastes deeper and smokier than the first release; the sommelier can describe how the 2006 is showing.

The list prints it oddly as Dom Pérignon " P2" Brut, bin 34108, 2006, $1260. It is not the standard Dom Pérignon release, so say P2 clearly. Confirm with the sommelier that the bottle is in the cellar before you describe it at length. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Salon ‘Le Mesnil’ Blanc de Blancs Brut 2013
wines.serviceNote: Bin 32684 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 750 ml, $2080. A famous name; no dish tier. Opens slowly in the glass. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the bottle with care and say Salon Le Mesnil, 2013, sah-LOHN. Serve it at 48 to 52°F in a white-wine glass from an ice bucket, half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease it out with a quiet sigh. Host last. Say: “Salon 2013: all Chardonnay from Le Mesnil, give it time.”

Offer Salon only when a guest asks for it, asks for the rarest Champagne we have, or is clearly a collector; it is not a bottle to push. A milestone anniversary is the moment. Bring in the sommelier for the table. Say: “Salon 2013: one village, one grape, one great year, all Chardonnay from Le Mesnil, taut, chalky and endless.”

Salon Le Mesnil 2013 is one of the rarest Champagnes in the world, $2080 on our list among the grandes marques, and a name collectors ask for.

Salon makes one wine only: a Blanc de Blancs from Chardonnay grown in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, a Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs, from a single year. It is made only in the years the house judges exceptional, a handful in a decade; in other years the grapes go to its sister house, Delamotte. The 2013 was aged for about a decade before release.

In the glass it is pale gold with very fine bubbles. It tastes taut and chalky: lemon peel, white flowers and hazelnut, with a stony, very long finish that keeps unfolding.

It is on the list for the guest who knows exactly what it is. It opens slowly, so serve it in a wine glass and let it breathe. It is grand with the raw oysters and the crab claws.

Asked: Why is Salon so rare?

Answer: It is made from one village and one grape, only in exceptional years, a handful in a decade.

Asked: What happens in the other years?

Answer: The grapes go to its sister house, Delamotte.

Asked: Should we drink it now?

Answer: It is young for Salon and opens slowly; I will ask the sommelier how the 2013 is showing tonight.

The list prints bin 32684 for this Salon 2013 at $2080 and also for Pétrus 1989 at $14000, so ring it by name and vintage, never by bin alone, and tell the sommelier about the clash. Confirm with the sommelier that it is in the cellar and let the sommelier lead the service if they are free. Serve it in a white-wine glass, a touch warmer than other Champagnes, and pour slowly. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 is the gentlest priced half-bottle on our list, $25 for 375 ml, filed under Burgundy red, Beaujolais, and the half-bottle for the New Orleans shrimp and grits.

Louis Jadot is a great Burgundy house based in Beaune, and our by-the-glass list pours its Beaune Premier Cru. Beaujolais-Villages is the appellation for the villages in the granite hills of northern Beaujolais, at the southern end of Burgundy. The grape is Gamay.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is a bright ruby. It tastes light and juicy, red cherry and raspberry with a little pepper, soft tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list as the easy red for brunch. Spice makes tannin taste harsh, so a soft, fruity red with a slight chill keeps the Creole sauce and the tasso in balance.

Asked: Is Beaujolais a Burgundy?

Answer: Beaujolais is the southern end of Burgundy; its grape is Gamay rather than Pinot Noir.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: No, it is light and juicy, with soft tannin. We serve it slightly cool.

Asked: How much is in a half-bottle?

Answer: 375 ml, two or three glasses, which suits one red drinker at a table of white or bubbles.

It is a half-bottle, bin 32721, 2021, $25, printed as Louis Jadot Villages under Beaujolais; do not confuse it with the Louis Jadot Beaune Premier Cru we pour by the glass or the Jadot Meursault half-bottle. Serve it slightly cool. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Tribaut-Schloesser Origine is a grower Brut in a half-bottle, $50 for 375 ml, filed under Grower Producers, Vallée de la Marne, and a half-bottle to suggest with the Creole spiced nuts.

Tribaut-Schloesser is a family Champagne house in Romery, in the hills north of Épernay, founded in 1929. Origine is its Brut, Meunier-led with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from several villages, and a part of the reserve wine in it is aged in oak.

Asked: Is it real Champagne?

Answer: Yes, from a family house in Romery, in the hills north of Épernay.

Asked: What is Meunier?

Answer: One of the three main Champagne grapes, a cousin of Pinot Noir, fruity and soft; it leads this blend.

Asked: How much is in it?

Answer: A 375 ml half-bottle, two or three glasses, so two guests can each have a toast and a refill.

It is a half-bottle, bin 32361, $50, printed as Tribaut-Schloesser "Origine" Brut. The Bubbles happy hour pours its own rosé bottles at their own prices, so do not quote a Bubbles price for this one. Huet Le Haut-Lieu Sec 2019 is a dry Vouvray in a half-bottle, $50 for 375 ml, filed under Loire white, Vouvray and Touraine, and the half-bottle for the Louisiana oysters.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire near Tours, and Le Haut-Lieu is the vineyard where the estate began. Sec means dry. It is all Chenin Blanc, and the 2019 has had a few years in bottle.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is a deeper gold than a young white. It tastes of quince, pear, beeswax and chamomile, dry and textured, with the bright acidity Chenin keeps as it ages.

Answer: Not for Chenin Blanc: it ages well, gaining honey and beeswax while keeping its bright acidity.

Domaine Huet is one of the great estates of Vouvray, on the Loire near Tours, and Le Mont is one of its three vineyards, with Le Haut-Lieu and the Clos du Bourg. It grows only Chenin Blanc. Demi-sec means half dry: the wine keeps some natural sweetness, balanced by Chenin’s high acidity.

A guest who enjoyed the Jadot Beaune by the glass will like it. Say: “A half-bottle of Bouchard Clos de la Mousse: Premier Cru Beaune, red cherry and violet, gentle with the short rib.”

Bouchard Père & Fils Clos de la Mousse 2022 is a Beaune Premier Cru in a half-bottle, $110 for 375 ml, filed under Burgundy red, Beaune Premier Cru, and the half-bottle for the Eggs Owen.

Bouchard Père & Fils is one of the great houses of Beaune, the wine town at the heart of the Côte de Beaune. The Clos de la Mousse is a small Premier Cru vineyard enclosed by a wall, and Bouchard owns all of it. Our by-the-glass list pours another Beaune Premier Cru, from Louis Jadot.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is a clear ruby. It tastes of red cherry, raspberry and violet with a little spice, silky tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list as a gentle red Burgundy for brunch. The Eggs Owen carries red wine-braised short rib débris and marchand de vin sauce, and this red echoes the braise without weighing the plate down.

Asked: What does Clos mean?

Answer: A vineyard enclosed by a wall. The Clos de la Mousse is a small walled Premier Cru in Beaune that Bouchard owns entirely.

Asked: Is it a light red?

Asked: How does it compare with the Beaune by the glass?

Answer: Both are Beaune Premier Cru; this one comes from a single walled vineyard, in a half-bottle.

kept.a: Present the half-bottle and say Ridge Estate Cabernet, from the Santa Cruz Mountains. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a large Bordeaux glass; decant only if the guest asks. Offer the Ridge Estate half to a couple sharing the Chateaubriand when one or both want a red but not a full bottle, or to a guest at lunch with the hanger steak. A Cabernet lover who knows Monte Bello will light up. Say: “A half-bottle of Ridge Estate Cabernet from the Santa Cruz Mountains: blackcurrant and cedar, structured for the Chateaubriand.”

Ridge Estate Cabernet Sauvignon 2020 is a mountain Cabernet in a half-bottle, $110 for 375 ml, filed under United States Cabernet Sauvignon, Central Coast, and the half-bottle for the Roasted Chateaubriand.

Ridge Vineyards is famous for Monte Bello, the Cabernet from its vineyards high on a ridge in the Santa Cruz Mountains south of San Francisco. The Estate Cabernet comes from the same mountain vineyards. Whether it carries some Merlot or other grapes in this vintage is a question for the sommelier; Ridge prints its ingredients on the back label.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is deep purple. It tastes of blackcurrant, cedar and graphite with a savory herb note, firm tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for beef. Protein and fat soften tannin, so it tastes rounder with the Chateaubriand and the sauce Foyot.

Asked: Is it like Napa Cabernet?

Answer: It is more structured and savory than plush; mountain fruit gives cedar and graphite rather than jammy fruit.

Asked: Should it be decanted?

Answer: It does not need it; swirling in a large glass opens it, but we can decant if you like.

Asked: Is this Monte Bello?

Answer: No, Monte Bello is Ridge’s top wine; this Estate Cabernet comes from the same mountain vineyards.

Ridge has three half-bottles on our list: this Estate Cabernet, bin 32942, 2020, $110; the Lytton Springs; and the sweet Essence. Check the bin. Do not call it Monte Bello. The grape blend in 2020 is a lineup question for the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: Bin 32752 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 375 ml half-bottle, $115. The half-bottle for the Louisiana BBQ Lobster. The dinner tasting itself pours the Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé with the lobster. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the half-bottle and say Louis Jadot Meursault, mur-SOH. Serve it at 50 to 54°F in a white Burgundy bowl, with only a brief rest in the ice bucket; too cold hides its richness. Pour as the lobster lands, the guest first. Say: “Jadot Meursault: rich and round, hazelnut and toast.”

Offer the Jadot Meursault half to a guest ordering the BBQ lobster from the dinner tasting who wants more than the tasting pour, or to anyone who asks for Meursault in a half. It suits the pecan fish and the poussin too. For a full bottle of Meursault with the lobster, the Dupont-Fahn Les Tillets is the sweet spot. Say: “A half-bottle of Jadot Meursault: rich, round white Burgundy with hazelnut and toast, made for lobster and butter.”

Louis Jadot Meursault 2022 is a village white Burgundy in a half-bottle, $115 for 375 ml, filed under Burgundy white, Meursault, and the half-bottle for the Louisiana BBQ lobster.

Louis Jadot is a great Burgundy house in Beaune, and Meursault is the village of the Côte de Beaune best known for rich, nutty white Burgundy. This is Jadot’s village wine, all Chardonnay, aged in barrel; for how long is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is gold. It tastes of ripe lemon, hazelnut and toast, with a buttery roundness and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for the lobster course. A rich wine meets a rich plate: its roundness matches the lobster and its butter, and its acidity freshens the white bean stew and the ’nduja. The dinner tasting pours its own white with this course.

Asked: What makes Meursault different?

Answer: It is the village known for the richest, nuttiest white Burgundy, Chardonnay with a buttery roundness.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: It is barrel aged, which gives toast and hazelnut, balanced by fresh acidity.

Asked: Is this the wine on the tasting?

Answer: No, the dinner tasting pours a Mâcon-Igé from Fichet with the lobster; this half is an extra if you would like Meursault.

It is a half-bottle, bin 32752, 2022, $115, printed as Louis Jadot under Meursault. The lobster pour was once disputed: the printed dinner tasting pairs Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé 2024, so never tell a tasting guest this is their included wine. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: Bin 32921 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 375 ml half-bottle, $120. The half-bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, and a first pick for the Fried Pickles. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the half-bottle and say Veuve Fourny Blanc de Blancs, vuhv foor-NEE. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in a tulip or white-wine glass from an ice bucket, half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease it out with a quiet sigh. Host last. Say: “Veuve Fourny: bone dry Chardonnay Champagne for the oysters.”

Offer the Veuve Fourny half to two guests sharing the Grand Isle oysters at dinner or the fried pickles at the Roost Bar who want Champagne but not a full bottle. A guest who likes their bubbles very dry will love it. For a full bottle with the oysters, the Larmandier-Bernier Longitude from the same village is the sweet spot. Say: “A half-bottle of Veuve Fourny: bone dry grower Champagne, all Chardonnay, made for raw oysters.”

Veuve Fourny et Fils Blanc de Blancs Extra Brut is a grower Champagne in a half-bottle, $120 for 375 ml, filed under Grower Producers, Côtes de Blancs, the half-bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel oysters and a first pick for the fried pickles.

Veuve Fourny et Fils is a family grower in Vertus, a Premier Cru village at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs, the chalk slope where Champagne’s Chardonnay grows. This is a Blanc de Blancs, all Chardonnay, and Extra Brut, with very little sugar added.

The guest sees a half-bottle, opened at the table, two or three glasses. In the glass it is pale with fine bubbles. It tastes of lemon, green apple and chalk, bone dry, with a saline finish.

It is on the list as the oyster Champagne for two. Its chalk and salt mirror the brine and the mignonette, and its acidity matches the vinegar in the pickles.

Asked: Is this Veuve Clicquot?

Answer: No. Veuve means widow, and both houses were run by one, but Veuve Fourny is a family grower in Vertus.

Asked: What is Extra Brut?

Answer: Drier than Brut: very little sugar added, so it is bone dry.

Asked: What is Blanc de Blancs?

Answer: A Champagne made only from Chardonnay, crisp and citrusy.

Do not confuse Veuve Fourny with Veuve Clicquot, and do not confuse this white half, bin 32921, $120, with the Veuve Fourny rosé half beside it. It is Extra Brut, as is our house Champagne. Ask the guest about their preferred style; these labels alone do not rank the two bottles by dryness. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: La Cigarrera Manzanilla Sanlúcar de Barrameda NV (375 ml)
wines.serviceNote: Bin 14861 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 375 ml half-bottle, $120. The half-bottle for the Turtle Soup. The paste spells the bodega Cigarerra; the label reads La Cigarrera. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the half-bottle and say La Cigarrera Manzanilla, mahn-thah-NEE-yah. Serve it well chilled, 45 to 48°F, in a white-wine glass, 3 oz each, as the soup is sauced with sherry at the table. Keep the bottle iced. Host last. Say: “Bone dry Manzanilla: salty and nutty, for the turtle soup.”

Offer the Manzanilla to a guest ordering the turtle soup who is curious about the sherry in it, or to a table starting with oysters and spiced nuts. It is the sommelier’s pairing that surprises people. Pour small, 3 oz. For a nutty white with the same soup, the Laureau Savennières is the value bottle. Say: “The turtle soup is finished with sherry, so try a dry Manzanilla with it: salty, nutty and light.”

La Cigarrera Manzanilla is a bone dry sherry in a half-bottle, $120 for 375 ml, filed under Fortified Wines, Spain, and the half-bottle for the turtle soup.

Manzanilla is the sherry of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the seaside town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir river in southern Spain, and La Cigarrera is a family bodega there. It is made from the Palomino grape and aged under flor, a living layer of yeast on top of the wine that keeps it pale and fresh and gives it a salty, bready tang. It is fortified, but light.

The guest sees a half-bottle and small pours. In the glass it is pale straw. It tastes bone dry: green apple, chamomile, almond and bread dough, with a salty sea breeze.

It is on the list for the soup. Our turtle soup is finished with aged sherry, so a dry sherry beside it repeats that flavor and cuts the richness.

Asked: Is sherry sweet?

Answer: Not this one. Manzanilla is bone dry; the sweet sherries are a different style.

Asked: What is flor?

Answer: A layer of yeast that grows on the wine in the barrel, keeping it pale and fresh and giving a salty, bready taste.

Asked: Is it strong?

Answer: It is fortified, so a little stronger than wine; we pour small glasses of about 3 oz.

It is a half-bottle, bin 14861, $120; the paste spells the bodega Cigarerra, but the label reads La Cigarrera. Serve it well chilled in small pours. Once open, Manzanilla fades within days, so date the bottle and tell the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Dow’s Vintage Port 2000 (375 ml)
wines.serviceNote: Bin 192843 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 375 ml half-bottle, $120. The half-bottle for The Snickers. Vintage Port throws sediment: stand it upright and decant or pour slowly. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the half-bottle and say Dow’s Vintage Port, 2000. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a small Port or dessert glass, 3 oz each, poured slowly or from a decanter so the sediment stays behind. Host last. Say: “Dow’s 2000: blackberry and dark chocolate, sip it slowly.”

Offer the Dow’s half when a table orders The Snickers, the bread pudding or the cheese board and wants something rich to sip, or to a guest celebrating a year 2000 birthday or anniversary. For an aged tawny with nuts and coffee, the Niepoort Colheita is beside it. Say: “Dow’s 2000 Vintage Port, a half-bottle: blackberry and dark chocolate, made for The Snickers.”

Dow’s 2000 Vintage Port is a fortified dessert wine in a half-bottle, $120 for 375 ml, filed under Fortified Wines, Portugal, and the half-bottle for The Snickers.

Dow’s is one of the great Port houses of the Douro valley in northern Portugal, run by the Symington family, and its style is known for being on the drier side of Port. Vintage Port is made only in the best years, which the houses declare, and 2000 was a declared year. It is aged briefly in cask and then in bottle, where it throws a sediment. The grapes are a blend of Douro varieties; which ones is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half-bottle and small pours. In the glass it is deep garnet. It tastes of blackberry, plum, dark chocolate and licorice, sweet and fortified, its tannin softened by age.

It is on the list for chocolate. A dessert wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert, so it carries The Snickers.

Asked: What makes it vintage Port?

Answer: It comes from one declared year, here 2000, and ages mostly in bottle, unlike a tawny that ages in cask.

Asked: Why is there sediment?

Asked: How much should we pour?

Answer: Small glasses of about 3 oz; the half-bottle serves a table of four.

Offer the Colheita at brunch with the Café Brûlot coffee cake, after dinner with the bread pudding or Bananas Foster, or to a guest celebrating a 1997 birthday or anniversary. For a vintage Port with chocolate, the Dow’s 2000 half is beside it. Say: “Niepoort Colheita 1997: a tawny Port from one harvest, walnut and caramel, made for pecans and coffee.”

Niepoort Colheita 1997 is a single harvest tawny Port in a half-bottle, $120 for 375 ml, filed under Fortified Wines, Portugal, and the half-bottle for the Café Brûlot coffee cake.

Niepoort is a family Port house of Dutch origin, based in Porto and the Douro valley in northern Portugal and known for aged tawnies. Colheita means harvest: a tawny Port from a single year, here 1997, aged for many years in old casks, where it slowly turns amber and nutty. The label carries the bottling date as well as the harvest.

The guest sees a half-bottle and small pours. In the glass it is amber. It tastes of walnut, caramel, dried orange peel, coffee and spice, sweet and silky, with a long, nutty finish.

It is on the list for nuts and coffee. Its flavors are the coffee cake’s own: chicory coffee, bittersweet chocolate, pecans and spiced citrus glaze.

Asked: What is a Colheita?

Answer: A tawny Port from a single harvest, aged for many years in cask before bottling; ours is from 1997.

Asked: How is it different from vintage Port?

Answer: Vintage Port ages mostly in bottle and stays dark and fruity; a Colheita ages in cask and turns amber, nutty and silky.

Asked: Does it need decanting?

Answer: No, a tawny has no sediment, so we pour it straight from the bottle.

It is a half-bottle, bin 192423, 1997, $120. Do not confuse it with the Dow’s 2000 vintage Port, which needs decanting; the Colheita does not. Serve it a touch cool. Offer the Veuve Fourny rosé half to a couple starting dinner with the steak tartare cannoli, or with the crab claws, who want something pink and festive before a red. Veuve Fourny et Fils is a family grower in Vertus, a Premier Cru village at the southern end of the Côte des Blancs, better known for its Chardonnay. Its rosé carries the Premier Cru rating of the village; the blend and how it is colored are questions for the sommelier.

Offer the Gouges half to a guest on the dinner tasting who wants more red with the duck than the tasting pour, or to a couple ordering beef or the duck who want two glasses of red Burgundy. A guest who likes a savory, earthy red will love it. Say: “A half-bottle of Henri Gouges Nuits-Saint-Georges: savory red Burgundy, dark cherry and earth for the duck.”

Domaine Henri Gouges Nuits-Saint-Georges 2021 is a red Burgundy in a half-bottle, $130 for 375 ml, filed under Burgundy red, Nuits-Saint-Georges, and the half-bottle for the Roasted Rohan duck breast.

Domaine Henri Gouges is a family domaine in Nuits-Saint-Georges, the town that gives the Côte de Nuits its name, and one of the reference names of the village. This is its village wine, all Pinot Noir; which parcels go into it is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a half-bottle, two or three glasses. In the glass it is deep ruby. It tastes of dark cherry, plum and earth with a savory, iron note, firm tannin for Burgundy and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for the duck. Duck is rich, and Pinot Noir’s acidity cuts its fat while its fruit meets the cane syrup-glazed peaches; its earthiness suits the candied hazelnuts.

Asked: How is it different from the Beaune?

Answer: Nuits-Saint-Georges is in the Côte de Nuits, to the north: sturdier, darker and more savory than a Beaune.

Asked: Is it a light red?

Answer: Medium, with firm tannin for a Burgundy, but still fresh.

Asked: Does it go with the peaches on the duck?

Answer: Yes, its dark fruit meets the cane syrup peaches and its acidity cuts the richness of the duck.

It is a half-bottle, bin 32844, 2021, $130, printed as Domaine Henri Gouges under Nuits-Saint-Georges. The duck course was once disputed: the printed dinner tasting describes Roasted Rohan duck breast with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts. The tasting brings its own pour; this half is an extra. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Present the half-bottle and say Dönnhoff Oberhäuser Brücke Auslese, DURN-hoff, BROO-kuh. Serve it at 45 to 50°F in a small white or dessert glass, 2 to 3 oz each, as the tart lands. Offer the Brücke half when a table orders the lemon tart or the trifle and wants a dessert wine, or to a Riesling lover. Point out that a young Auslese is bright, not heavy. For a grander sweet wine with the tart, a half of Château d’Yquem 2016 is the celebration choice. Say: “Dönnhoff’s Brücke Auslese is sweet and racy, lemon curd and honey, and it matches the lemon tart bite for bite.”

Dönnhoff Oberhäuser Brücke Auslese Goldkapsel 2023 is a sweet Nahe Riesling in a half-bottle, $135 for 375 ml, filed under German Riesling, Nahe, and the half-bottle for the lemon tart.

Dönnhoff is a family estate in Oberhausen on the Nahe, a river valley west of the Rhine. The Brücke is a tiny vineyard beside the old bridge over the Nahe, and the Dönnhoff family are its only owners. Auslese means selected harvest, sweet and ripe, and the gold capsule marks an Auslese of richer, more selected fruit.

The guest sees a half-bottle, about four small dessert pours. In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of lemon curd, peach and honey with a little spice, sweet and concentrated, held up by piercing acidity.

Asked: What does Goldkapsel mean?

Answer: Gold capsule: a sign the grower used richer, more selected fruit for this Auslese.

Asked: Will it be too sweet?

Answer: Its acidity is as bright as the lemon, so it tastes lively rather than heavy.

Asked: How much do we pour?

Answer: Small pours of 2 to 3 oz; the half-bottle gives about four.

There are two Dönnhoff Auslese halves side by side: this Oberhäuser Brücke, bin 32821, $135, and the Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle, bin 32843, $145. Check the vineyard name on the label. Pour small, and recork and chill what is left. The list spells it Dönhoff; the estate is Dönnhoff, with two n’s, so write and say Dönnhoff. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Château Suduiraut is in the village of Preignac, next door to Château d’Yquem, and was ranked Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 classification of Sauternes. Sauternes is made from Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc left on the vine until noble rot, a beneficial mold, shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugar and flavor; they are picked by hand in several passes.

Asked: How much do we pour?

Answer: Small pours of 2 to 3 oz; the half-bottle gives about four.

Château d’Yquem 2015 is the most famous sweet wine in the world, in a half-bottle, $450 for 375 ml, filed under Dessert Wines, France, and the celebration choice for the Framboise French toast.

Château d’Yquem, in Sauternes, is the only estate ranked Premier Cru Supérieur, above every other Sauternes, in the 1855 classification. Its pickers pass through the vineyard many times each harvest, taking only the berries that noble rot has shriveled, and in poor years no Yquem is made at all. It is Sémillon-led with Sauvignon Blanc.

The guest sees a half-bottle, about four small pours. In the glass it is deep gold. The 2015 tastes of apricot, candied orange, saffron, honey and vanilla, luminous and luscious, with fresh acidity and a very long finish.

It is on the list for the grand celebration. With the French toast, its richness meets the mascarpone and the raspberry coulis.

Asked: Why is Yquem so famous?

Answer: It is the only Sauternes ranked above all others in 1855, and it is picked berry by berry; in poor years none is made.

Asked: Is it too sweet for breakfast?

Answer: It is rich, but its acidity keeps it fresh; with French toast and berries it is a celebration.

Asked: What is the difference between the 2015 and the 2016?

Answer: Both are on our list as halves at the same price; the sommelier can describe how each is drinking.

kept.a: Present the magnum with both hands and say Mas de Valériole Vé, from the Camargue. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass from a large ice bucket. Pour with one hand under the base and one at the shoulder, the guests first and the host last. Say: “A magnum of Vé: pale, dry and fresh, for the whole table.”

Offer the Vé magnum to a party of six or more in the courtyard or at the Roost Bar who are ordering rosé by the glass anyway, or to a birthday table that wants a big bottle without a big check. For a rosé with more depth for a smaller table, the Tempier Bandol is the sweet spot. Say: “For the whole table, a magnum of Vé rosé from the Camargue: pale, dry and salty fresh.”

Mas de Valériole Vé 2025 is a Mediterranean rosé in a magnum, $85 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Rosé, and the gentlest priced big bottle on our list.

Mas de Valériole is a family estate in the Camargue, the delta south of Arles where the Rhône meets the sea, and its vineyards are cooled by the steady Mediterranean wind. Vé is a Provençal expression meaning look at that. The rosé blends Caladoc, a cross of Grenache and Malbec, with Merlot and Marselan, pressed straight off the skins and kept fresh in steel tanks.

The guest sees a magnum, twice the size of a standard bottle, about ten to twelve glasses. In the glass it is very pale pink. It tastes of raspberry and ripe citrus with a salty, sea breeze finish, light and dry.

It is on the list for a party that is sharing. A magnum of rosé on the table says summer, and it suits the tomato tostada, the crab claws and the Roost Bar snacks.

Asked: How much is in a magnum?

Answer: Two standard bottles, 1.5 liters, about ten to twelve glasses.

Asked: What does Vé mean?

Answer: It is a Provençal expression meaning look at that, a nod to the estate’s home in the Camargue near Arles.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is dry and pale, with raspberry and citrus and a salty finish.

It is a magnum, bin 1569, 2025, $85, under Large Formats, Rosé. A magnum takes twice as long to chill, so put it on ice the moment it is ordered and keep it in a large bucket. Carry and pour it with both hands. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer the Pierre Péters magnum to a party of six or more celebrating at dinner, especially if they order oysters or crab, or to a table drinking glasses of Champagne who would enjoy one big bottle. For the house’s own anniversary magnum, the Billecart-Salmon Sous Bois is beside it. Say: “For the table, a magnum of Pierre Péters: Grand Cru Chardonnay from Le Mesnil, chalky, creamy and festive.”

Pierre Péters Cuvée de Réserve is a grower Grand Cru Blanc de Blancs in a magnum, $190 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Champagne.

Pierre Péters is a family grower in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, a Grand Cru village of the Côte des Blancs famous for chalk and Chardonnay; Salon comes from the same village. Cuvée de Réserve is all Chardonnay from Grand Cru vineyards, and its reserve wine is drawn from a perpetual reserve, a store of older wines topped up with each new harvest.

The guest sees a magnum, two bottles in one, about ten to twelve glasses. In the glass it is pale gold with a fine, creamy mousse. It tastes of lemon, white flowers and chalk, crisp and precise.

It is on the list for a celebration that wants grower Champagne for everyone. A magnum ages more slowly than a standard bottle, so Champagne from it tastes fresher and finer. It suits the oysters, the crab claws and the redfish.

Asked: Why is Champagne better from a magnum?

Answer: There is less air for the amount of wine, so it ages more slowly and tastes fresher and finer.

Asked: What is a perpetual reserve?

Answer: A store of older wines the grower tops up each year and draws from for every blend, which adds depth.

Asked: How many glasses?

Answer: About ten to twelve; a magnum is two standard bottles.

It is a magnum, bin 12494, $190, under Large Formats, Champagne. Chill it well ahead, in a large bucket. The larger cork pushes harder: keep your thumb on it and the bottle pointed away from guests. Carry and pour it with two hands. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Present the magnum with both hands and say Jean Foillard, Morgon Côte du Py, fwah-YAR. Say: “Foillard’s Côte du Py: dark cherry and violet, a touch cool.”

Offer the Foillard magnum to a party of six or more ordering a mix of fish and meat, to guests who follow natural or grower wine, or to a table that wants red but nothing heavy. Mention that it is served a touch cool. Say: “A magnum of Foillard’s Morgon Côte du Py: cult Beaujolais, dark cherry and violet, and it suits nearly everything on the table.”

Jean Foillard Morgon Côte du Py 2023 is a cru Beaujolais in a magnum, $250 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Red, France.

Jean Foillard is a grower in Morgon, one of the ten crus of Beaujolais, and one of the four growers, with Marcel Lapierre, Guy Breton and Jean-Paul Thévenet, who led the region back to traditional methods: whole bunches, native yeasts and a light hand in the cellar. The Côte du Py is the famous hill above Morgon, of old volcanic schist, and its Gamay is deeper and more structured than most Beaujolais.

The guest sees a magnum, about ten to twelve glasses. In the glass it is a deep, bright ruby. It tastes of dark cherry, raspberry and violet with a mineral, earthy depth, silky tannin and lively acidity.

It is on the list as the red for a table ordering a bit of everything. It is light enough for the redfish and deep enough for the duck.

Asked: Is this like Beaujolais Nouveau?

Answer: No. Morgon is one of the ten crus, the top villages, and the Côte du Py is its finest hill; this is serious, age-worthy Gamay.

Asked: Why serve a red cool?

Answer: Gamay tastes brighter and fresher slightly cool, around 55 to 58°F.

Asked: Who is Jean Foillard?

Answer: A Morgon grower and one of the four who led Beaujolais back to traditional, low intervention winemaking.

It is a magnum, bin 11371, 2023, $250, under Large Formats, Red. Serve it slightly cool, never warm; a magnum takes longer to chill. Wines made this way can vary bottle to bottle, so taste it at the table edge if the sommelier allows; any question about what is or is not added goes to the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer the Duckhorn magnum to a party of six or more ordering steaks or the Chateaubriand, or to a business dinner that wants one big, familiar Napa red. For a grander magnum with age, the Cos d’Estournel 2015 is the celebration choice. Say: “For the table, a magnum of Duckhorn Napa Cabernet: ripe blackcurrant and cocoa, made for steak.”

Duckhorn Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon 2022 is a Napa red in a magnum, $255 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Red, United States.

Duckhorn Vineyards is a Napa Valley winery best known for Merlot, which is on our list in a half-bottle with its Sauvignon Blanc. Its Napa Valley Cabernet is blended from vineyards across the valley and aged in oak; the exact blend is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a magnum, two bottles in one, about ten to twelve glasses. In the glass it is deep purple. It tastes of blackcurrant, black cherry and cocoa with a little cedar, ripe and polished, with firm but rounded tannin.

It is on the list for a party that is ordering beef. Protein and fat soften tannin, so it suits the Chateaubriand, the Creole hanger steak and the filet, and a big bottle of a name people know makes a table feel looked after.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: Full-bodied, but polished and rounded rather than harsh, and with steak the tannin feels softer still.

Asked: Should it be decanted?

Answer: A young magnum opens up with a decant; we can do that at the side stand if you like.

Asked: How many glasses?

Answer: About ten to twelve; a magnum is two bottles.

It is a magnum, bin 108222, 2022, $255, under Large Formats, Red. Duckhorn also appears as a Merlot half and a Sauvignon Blanc half; check the bin. Decanting a magnum needs a large decanter; ask the sommelier which to use. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Present the magnum with both hands and say Château Cos d’Estournel 2015, koss dess-toor-NELL. Decant it at the side stand off its sediment, then serve at 62 to 65°F in large Bordeaux glasses. Pour the guests first, the host last. Say: “Cos d’Estournel 2015: blackcurrant, cedar and spice.”

Offer the Cos magnum to a party celebrating with the Chateaubriand or steaks, or to a Bordeaux collector at a big table. Bring in the sommelier to decant. For a younger, friendlier big red, the Duckhorn Cabernet magnum is the alternative. Say: “For the table, a magnum of Cos d’Estournel 2015: Second Growth Saint-Estèphe, blackcurrant and cedar, decanted for you.”

Château Cos d’Estournel 2015 is a Second Growth Saint-Estèphe in a magnum, $600 for 1.5 L, under Large Formats, Red, France.

Cos d’Estournel is in Saint-Estèphe, in the Médoc on Bordeaux’s Left Bank, and was ranked a Second Growth in the 1855 classification. Its founder traded with India and built the château’s famous pagoda towers. The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot; the 2015 blend is a question for the sommelier.

The guest sees a magnum, two bottles in one, decanted at the side stand. In the glass it is deep purple garnet. It tastes of blackcurrant, plum, cedar and cocoa with a touch of exotic spice, powerful and polished, with fine tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list as a grand Bordeaux for a party. A magnum ages slowly and gracefully, and it suits the Chateaubriand and the filet.

Asked: What is a Second Growth?

Answer: The second of five tiers in the 1855 classification of the Médoc; Cos d’Estournel is among the most famous.

Asked: Why the towers on the label?

Answer: The founder traded with India and built pagoda towers on the château; they are on the label.

Asked: Will it need time?

Answer: It is decanted at the side stand; the sommelier can say how long the 2015 wants.

It is a magnum, bin 33553, 2015, $600. The list prints the same bin and price on the Saint-Estèphe page with no size, so ask the sommelier whether that is this magnum or a 750 ml bottle. Stand it upright as soon as it is ordered and ask the sommelier to decant it off its sediment, ideally well ahead. Use two hands to carry and pour. Do not confuse Cos with Château Cos Labory, also in Saint-Estèphe. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer the Prüm magnum to a large party celebrating who orders several desserts to share, especially the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, or to a German wine lover at a birthday. For a smaller table, the JJ Prüm Kabinett or the Keller PIUS half is the lighter choice. Say: “For the whole table’s desserts, a magnum of JJ Prüm Auslese: honeyed pineapple and racy acidity, a true celebration.”

J.J. Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Auslese Goldkapsel 2015 is a sweet Mosel Riesling in a magnum, $615 for 1.5 L, printed under Large Formats, White, Germany, as Riesling GKA, and the celebration choice for the Pineapple Tarte Tatin.

Joh. Jos. Prüm is the most famous estate of Wehlen on the Mosel, run by the Prüm family, and the Wehlener Sonnenuhr is its great steep vineyard of blue slate, named for the sundial built into the slope. GKA stands for Goldkapsel Auslese: a sweet, selected harvest, and the gold capsule marks richer fruit.

The guest sees a magnum, enough for about twenty small dessert pours. In the glass it is gold. It tastes of honeyed pineapple, apricot, lime and slate, sweet and racy, light in alcohol, and Prüm’s wines are known for aging for decades.

Answer: Goldkapsel Auslese: a sweet, selected harvest Riesling, and the gold capsule marks a richer selection.

Asked: What is the Sonnenuhr?

Answer: The sundial: a sundial is built into the steep Wehlen vineyard, which gives it its name.

Asked: How many does a magnum pour?

Answer: About twenty small dessert pours of 2 to 3 oz.

It is a magnum, bin 12135, 2015, $615, printed as J.J. Prum "Wehlener Sonnenuhr" Riesling GKA Mosel. Do not confuse it with the JJ Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett 2020, a lighter wine in a standard bottle. Pour small; recork and chill what is left. kept.a: Let the sommelier lead. Present it in its cradle and say Billecart-Salmon Réserve, in a Nebuchadnezzar. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in tulip or white-wine glasses, after hours on ice. Two people open it, cork and cage held firmly, and pour from the cradle. Say: “Twenty bottles of Billecart-Salmon in one. Cheers to you all.”

Mention the Nebuchadnezzar only to an event planner, a very large party or a host who wants a showpiece, and hand them to the manager and the sommelier to arrange it. Never promise it for tonight without checking. Say: “For a party this size, we have a Nebuchadnezzar of Billecart-Salmon: twenty bottles of Champagne in one, opened for you.”

Billecart-Salmon Réserve in a Nebuchadnezzar is the largest bottle on our list, $4900 for 15 L, printed under Champagne, Grande Marques.

A Nebuchadnezzar holds fifteen liters, the same as twenty standard bottles, and ours is filled with Billecart-Salmon Réserve, the house Brut of the family house in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, founded in 1818: Meunier, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with reserve wines, in a fresh, delicate style.

The guest sees a bottle taller than a child, opened and poured as a performance. It pours a hundred glasses or more. In the glass it is pale gold with fine bubbles and tastes of pear, citrus and a light brioche.

It is on the list for a private event, a wedding party or a very large celebration. It needs planning: it is ordered ahead, chilled for hours in a large tub of ice and water, and opened and poured by the sommelier with a second person, often from a cradle. The same wine comes in a 750 ml bottle and a magnum.

wines.serviceNote: Bin 22411 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 750 ml, $80. The value tier for the Redfish Véronique. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the bottle and say Louis Michel Chablis, mee-SHELL shah-BLEE. Serve it at 48 to 52°F in a white-wine glass or small white Burgundy bowl, with the bottle in the ice bucket between pours. Pour the guests first, the host last. Say: “Louis Michel Chablis: crisp lemon and chalk, no oak.”

Offer the Louis Michel to a guest at dinner ordering the redfish Véronique or the crab claws, or to anyone who asks for Chablis or a white with no oak. Raw oysters love it too. For a richer white Burgundy with the redfish, Leflaive’s Mâcon-Verzé is the sweet spot. Say: “Louis Michel Chablis has no oak at all: crisp lemon and chalk, and it loves the lemon beurre blanc.”

Louis Michel Chablis 2022 is the village Chablis on our list, $80, filed under Burgundy white, Chablis, and the value bottle for the redfish Véronique.

Domaine Louis Michel is a family estate in Chablis, the northernmost part of Burgundy, where the cool climate and the chalky clay soils give Chardonnay a lean, mineral style. The estate is known for making every wine in steel tanks with no oak at all, so the wine tastes of the place rather than the barrel. Our list also carries its Premier Cru Montmains in a half-bottle.

In the glass it is pale with a green tint. It tastes of green apple, lemon and white flowers, crisp and precise, with a chalky, oyster-shell finish.

It is on the list as the classic fish white at a value price. Its acidity matches the preserved lemon and the hibiscus-pickled grapes of the redfish, and its texture holds up to the beurre blanc.

Asked: Is Chablis a Chardonnay?

Answer: Yes, all Chablis is Chardonnay, from the northern tip of Burgundy, crisper and leaner than most.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: Not at all; Louis Michel makes everything in steel tanks.

Asked: Is it the same as the half-bottle?

Answer: The half-bottle is Louis Michel’s Premier Cru Montmains; this is the village Chablis, lighter and a little simpler.

It is the full bottle of village Chablis, bin 22411, 2022, $80, printed simply as Louis Michel under Chablis. The Montmains half-bottle is the Premier Cru, and the paste prints a shared bin for it. Do not confuse Chablis with Chardonnay from California. The list also prints bin 22411 for Domaine Justin Boxler Sommerberg 2017 at $125, an Alsace Riesling, so ring it by name and vintage and tell the sommelier about the clash. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: Bin 22762 on the Binwise list read 3 October 2026, 750 ml, $90. The value tier for the Louisiana Crab Claws. Confirm at lineup that it is in stock.

kept.a: Present the bottle and say Roc des Boutires, Pouilly-Fuissé, poo-YEE fwee-SAY. Serve it at 50 to 54°F in a white Burgundy bowl, with only a brief rest in the ice bucket. Pour as the claws land, guests first and the host last. Say: “Pouilly-Fuissé from one small parcel: round and fresh.”

Offer the Roc des Boutires to a table at dinner sharing the crab claws, or to a guest who asks for Pouilly-Fuissé or a white Burgundy at a fair price. It also suits the pecan fish at lunch. For a Premier Cru with the claws, the Paul Pillot Saint-Aubin is the sweet spot. Say: “The Roc des Boutires is Pouilly-Fuissé from a single small parcel: round, fresh Chardonnay, made for brown butter.”

Domaine du Roc des Boutires En Bertilionne 2020 is a single parcel Pouilly-Fuissé, $90, filed under Burgundy white, Mâconnais, and the value bottle for the Louisiana crab claws.

Pouilly-Fuissé is the best known appellation of the Mâconnais, in southern Burgundy, where vineyards spread beneath the great limestone rock of Solutré. Domaine du Roc des Boutires has been owned since 2016 by the Parinet family, who also own Château du Moulin-à-Vent in Beaujolais. En Bertilionne is a small east-facing parcel of older Chardonnay vines in the heart of Pouilly, facing the rock.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of ripe lemon, white flowers and hay, round and textured, with a saline, pithy finish, and the 2020 has a few years of bottle age.

It is on the list as white Burgundy with real character under $100. With the crab claws, its roundness meets the brown butter vinaigrette and its acidity keeps the sweet crab fresh.

Asked: Is Pouilly-Fuissé the same as Pouilly-Fumé?

Answer: No. Pouilly-Fuissé is Chardonnay from southern Burgundy; Pouilly-Fumé is Sauvignon Blanc from the Loire.

Asked: What is En Bertilionne?

Answer: The name of the small vineyard parcel the grapes come from, in the heart of the village of Pouilly.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Domaine Dupont-Fahn is a family estate in Tailly, just south of Meursault, now run by Raymond Dupont-Fahn. Les Tillets is a lieu-dit, a named vineyard, near the top of the village slope, one of the highest in Meursault, stony limestone named for its linden trees. It is not classed Premier Cru, but its altitude gives the wine an unusual freshness.

In the glass it is gold. It tastes of lemon, hazelnut and toast, rich and nutty in the Meursault way, with a stony, electric freshness running through it.

It is on the list as Meursault at a sweet spot price. With the BBQ lobster, its richness matches the sweet meat and the butter, and the freshness keeps the white bean stew and the nduja lively.

Asked: Is it a Premier Cru?

Answer: No, it is classed as village Meursault, though its height gives it real freshness.

Asked: Is it buttery?

Answer: Rich and nutty like Meursault, with a stony freshness that keeps it lively.

Domaine Paul Pillot is a family estate in Chassagne-Montrachet, in the Côte de Beaune. Saint-Aubin is the hillside village tucked behind Puligny and Chassagne, and its best slopes are rated Premier Cru; Le Charmois is one of them, close to the boundary with Puligny. White Burgundy lovers know Saint-Aubin as the place to find the Puligny style at a gentler price.

François Carillon Puligny-Montrachet 2022 is a village Puligny, $275, filed under Burgundy white, Puligny-Montrachet, and the celebration bottle for the Louisiana crab claws.

Puligny-Montrachet, in the Côte de Beaune, is the village many consider the purest expression of white Burgundy, home to Le Montrachet and Chevalier-Montrachet. The Carillon family has farmed vines there for centuries; in 2010 the estate was divided between two brothers, and François Carillon set up his own domaine.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of citrus, white peach, toasted hazelnut and a little smoke, elegant and precise, with Puligny’s fine, chalky tension and a long finish.

It is on the list as Puligny from a classic grower family. With the crab claws, its toasty, nutty depth mirrors the brown butter vinaigrette and lifts the fines herbes, while its tension keeps the sweet crab fresh.

Asked: What makes Puligny special?

Answer: It is the village many consider the purest white Burgundy, elegant and chalky, and home to Le Montrachet.

Asked: Who is François Carillon?

Answer: A grower from a family that has farmed Puligny for centuries; he set up his own domaine in 2010.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: It is toasty and nutty but elegant; how long it spends in barrel is a question for the sommelier.

It is bin 34233, 2022, $275, printed simply as François Carillon under Puligny-Montrachet. Do not confuse it with Domaine Jacques Carillon, the other brother’s estate, or with the Leflaive Puligny. Serve it cool, not cold. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Domaine Leflaive Puligny-Montrachet 2016 is a village Puligny from the village’s most famous domaine, $340, filed under Burgundy white, Puligny-Montrachet, and the celebration bottle for the redfish Véronique.

Domaine Leflaive is a family estate in Puligny-Montrachet whose wines set the standard for the village, and its holdings run up to the Grand Cru Chevalier-Montrachet, which is also on our list. Our glass of Mâcon-Verzé on the Coravin comes from the same domaine. The 2016 village Puligny has spent years in bottle.

Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat Les Preuses 2015 is a Chablis Grand Cru with bottle age, $350, filed under Chablis Grand Cru, and the celebration bottle for the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

Dauvissat is a family domaine in Chablis and, with Raveneau, one of the two great reference estates of the region. Les Preuses is one of the seven Grand Cru slopes rising above the town of Chablis. Dauvissat ages its wines partly in old oak barrels, which adds texture without the taste of new wood.

In the glass it is gold with a green glint. The 2015 tastes of lemon peel, white flowers and oyster shell with a touch of honey from age, steely and precise, with deep, saline length.

It is on the list as the grandest form of the classic pairing. Chablis and oysters share a briny, mineral character, and with the Grand Isle oysters its steel meets the brine while its depth stands up to the Fresno chili mignonette.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Asked: Is 2015 old for Chablis?

Answer: Not for Grand Cru; it is beginning to show honey and depth while staying precise.

Domaine des Comtes Lafon Clos de la Baronne 2022 is a Meursault from a walled vineyard, $425, filed under Burgundy white, Meursault, and the celebration bottle for the crab and corn omelette.

Domaine des Comtes Lafon is one of the great estates of Meursault, run by the Lafon family; their Mâconnais estate makes the Mâcon Milly-Lamartine also on our list. The Clos de la Baronne is a vineyard enclosed by a wall that the domaine owns entirely, classed as village Meursault.

Domaine Leflaive Sous le Dos d’Ane 2017 is a Meursault Premier Cru from the great Puligny estate, $435, filed under Meursault Premier Cru, and the celebration bottle for the Louisiana BBQ lobster.

Sous le Dos d’Ane means under the donkey’s back, for the shape of the hill. It is a Premier Cru of Meursault lying right on the boundary with Puligny-Montrachet, and Domaine Leflaive, the most famous estate of Puligny, farms it. kept.a: Present the bottle and say Domaine Roulot, Meursault, roo-LOH. Serve it at 50 to 54°F in a white Burgundy bowl, letting it open in the glass. Pour the guests first, the host last. Say: “Roulot Meursault: taut, precise and stony.”

Offer the Roulot to a guest who names it, who asks for the most sought after Meursault we have, or who says they love white Burgundy but not buttery Chardonnay. Let the sommelier join the table if they are free. For the classic rich Meursault, the Dupont-Fahn is the sweet spot. Domaine Roulot Meursault 2022 is a village Meursault from a cult estate, $500, filed under Burgundy white, Meursault, and an anchor among the great names on our list.

Domaine Roulot is a family estate in Meursault, run by Jean-Marc Roulot. His taut, precise wines changed how many people think of Meursault, a village long known for rich, buttery white Burgundy. Even the village wine is allocated and hard to find.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes taut and precise rather than buttery: lemon, green apple and white flowers with a stony, saline finish, and the village’s depth underneath.

It is on the list because collectors ask for it and because it shows the other face of Meursault. It suits pure seafood, the crab claws, the redfish and the oysters, and its precision makes it lovely with the lobster.

Asked: Why is Roulot so sought after?

Answer: Jean-Marc Roulot makes Meursault taut and precise rather than buttery, and there is very little of it.

Asked: Is it a Premier Cru?

Answer: This is the village Meursault; Roulot’s Premier Crus are even rarer.

Asked: Will it be too lean?

Answer: It is precise, but the depth of Meursault is underneath; it opens in the glass.

Domaine Coche-Dury Bourgogne Blanc 2022 is the regional white of the most sought after white Burgundy estate, $690, filed under Burgundy white, Bourgogne.

Domaine Coche-Dury is a family estate in Meursault, now run by Raphaël Coche after his father, Jean-François Coche-Dury. Its wines are among the scarcest and most collected in the world. Bourgogne Blanc is the regional appellation, the humblest label in Burgundy, but Coche-Dury makes it with the same care as its Grand Cru, which is why the bottle is priced far above any other Bourgogne.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes flinty and reductive: lemon, hazelnut and a struck-match note, taut and long.

It is on the list for the collector who wants a taste of the estate. Pour it with simple, pure seafood, the crab claws, the redfish or the oysters, so nothing hides it.

Château d’Esclans Whispering Angel 2024 is the best known Provence rosé on our list, $50, filed under Rosé, France, and the value bottle for the Creole tomato tostada.

Château d’Esclans is an estate in the hills of Provence, inland from the Riviera, and Whispering Angel is the pale rosé that helped make Provence rosé fashionable in America. wines.name: Stein ‘Weihwasser’ Riesling Feinherb 2023
