Domaine Jean-Louis Chave's Hermitage 2013 is one of the famous bottles on our Rhône pages: bin 24442, $490.

Hermitage, air-mee-TAHZH, is a single granite hill above the Rhône at Tain, and its Syrah is among the most long-lived red wines in France. The Chave family, SHAHV, from Mauves across the river, is the grower most associated with the hill. Their Hermitage is blended from several plots, each with its own soil and character, which is what gives it its completeness.

At thirteen years it is a deep, dark ruby. It tastes of blackberry, cassis, violet, smoke and iron, deep and firm, with a very long finish, still young for its kind.

It is here because collectors ask for Chave by name, and bottles are hard to find. It suits the Chateaubriand, lamb and venison, and it wants a long decant from the sommelier. The list carries Chave in more than one vintage, so name the 2013.

Asked: What is Hermitage?

Answer: A single granite hill above the Rhône, home of some of the longest-lived Syrah in the world.

Asked: Who is Chave?

Answer: The family grower most associated with the hill; they blend several plots into one wine.

Asked: Is the 2013 ready?

Answer: It is young for Hermitage; the sommelier will decant it well ahead.

E. Guigal's La Mouline Côte-Rôtie 2012 is one of the famous bottles on our Rhône pages: bin 27243, $1100.

Guigal, ghee-GAL, is the family house in Ampuis that brought Côte-Rôtie to the world. Its three single-vineyard wines, La Mouline, La Landonne and La Turque, are known to collectors as the La La's. La Mouline, lah moo-LEEN, is a terraced amphitheater on the Côte Blonde; the Syrah is co-fermented with a little Viognier, then aged a long time in new oak.

At fourteen years it is a medium, glowing ruby. It is the most perfumed and silky of the three: violet, raspberry and blackberry, bacon and spice, with a long, fine finish.

It is here because collectors ask for the La La's by name, and our list carries all three in several vintages. It suits lamb, duck and squab, and the sommelier decants it.

Asked: What are the La La's?

Asked: How is La Mouline different?

Answer: It is the most perfumed and silky of the three, with a little Viognier in with the Syrah.

Asked: Is there white in a red wine?

Answer: A little Viognier is fermented with the Syrah, which lifts the perfume; the wine is red.

Guigal on every one, so ring it in by bin 27243 and check the label reads La Mouline 2012. Rostaing also makes a La Landonne. Let the sommelier decant it. Château Rayas Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2011 is the cult bottle on our Rhône pages: bin 22458, $1200.

Rayas, rah-YAHS, is the Reynaud family's estate in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Its parcels are sandy and set among woods, cooler than most of the appellation, and its Châteauneuf is made from Grenache alone, in an old-fashioned cellar that rarely receives visitors. Where most Châteauneuf blends many varieties and leans dark and warm, Rayas is pale and fine.

At fifteen years it is a translucent, garnet-edged red. It tastes of strawberry, raspberry and kirsch, rose, spice and earth, silky and perfumed, closer to a great Burgundy in feel than to its neighbors.

It is here because collectors ask for Rayas by name, and bottles are scarce. It suits duck, squab and lamb, and it often shows best poured straight, as the sommelier decides. The list carries Rayas in three vintages, so name the 2011.

Asked: Why is Rayas so pale?

Answer: It is all Grenache grown in sand, which gives a translucent, perfumed wine rather than a dark one.

Asked: How is it different from other Châteauneuf?

Answer: No blend, cooler sandy parcels among woods, and an old-fashioned cellar: it is silky and fine rather than warm and dark.

Asked: Should it be decanted?

Answer: The sommelier will decide; it is often poured straight.

The list prints Rayas 2009 at $1060, 2011 at $1200 and 2012 at $1300, and its Côtes du Rhône, La Pialade, at $210 and $270, so ring it in by bin 22458 and check the label reads Château Rayas 2011. A pale color is normal for Rayas; do not apologize for it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: López de Heredia ‘Viña Cubillo’ Rioja Crianza 2016
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 1379, 750ml, $70. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say López de Heredia, Viña Cubillo, Rioja Crianza, 2016. Serve it at 60 to 63°F in a Bordeaux glass, with no decanting. Pour a taste for the host, then the guests, the host last, and leave the bottle on the table. Say: “Viña Cubillo: ten-year-old Rioja from Haro, mellow and savory.”

Bring it up at the Roost when a table orders the burger and wants a red bottle to share, or when a guest asks for something Spanish or old-school. It suits a guest who likes savory, not fruity, reds. For a step up in Rioja, the La Rioja Alta 904 Gran Reserva is the grand version. Say: “Viña Cubillo is ten-year-old Rioja from a family bodega in Haro, mellow and savory, and lovely with the burger.”

López de Heredia’s Viña Cubillo Crianza 2016 is a first pick for the Roost Burger and the Spanish anchor under $100: bin 1379, $70.

R. López de Heredia is one of the oldest bodegas in Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta, and still family run. They work the old way: grapes picked by hand, fermented in old wooden vats, then aged about three years in old American oak barrels from their own cooperage, and longer in bottle before release. Viña Cubillo is their youngest red, mostly Tempranillo with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo.

In the glass it is a light garnet. It tastes of dried cherry, strawberry, leather and gentle spice, light in tannin, with lively acidity.

It is on the list because it gives real age and character for very little: a Crianza that drinks like a much older wine. With the burger, its soft tannin and savory fruit meet short rib, bacon and cheese.

Asked: What does Crianza mean?

Answer: A Rioja aged in oak and bottle before release. López de Heredia ages theirs far longer than the rule asks, about three years in barrel.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: No, it is light to medium bodied, with soft tannin and fresh acidity.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: Not in the sweet, vanilla way; the barrels are old, so the oak shows as mellow, savory spice.

The list spells it Lopez de Heredia; say LOH-peth deh eh-REH-dee-ah. Cubillo is the house’s youngest red; Tondonia is their older wine, a different label. Whether it is poured at the Roost as well as in the dining room is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Fèlsina Chianti Classico 2022 is our anchor for Italian red under $100: bin 14062, $90.

Fattoria di Fèlsina, FEL-see-nah, farms vineyards at Castelnuovo Berardenga, on the warm southern edge of the Chianti Classico zone, northeast of Siena. Chianti Classico is the historic heart of Chianti, between Florence and Siena, and Sangiovese is its grape. Fèlsina’s Chianti Classico is all Sangiovese, fermented in steel and aged about a year in medium-size Slavonian oak casks, so the fruit leads.

At four years it is a bright ruby. It tastes of sour cherry, violet and dried herbs with a touch of earth, with firm acidity and fine, dusty tannin.

It is on the list because it is the easiest Italian bottle to put on any table. The acidity loves tomato, mushrooms, roast chicken and pork, and the price is gentle. For a deeper, single vineyard Fèlsina, the Rancia Riserva is the next step.

Asked: Is this the Chianti in the straw bottle?

Answer: No, that was the old everyday Chianti. Chianti Classico is the historic heart of the region, and Fèlsina is one of its top estates.

Asked: What grape is it?

Answer: Sangiovese, all of it, the grape of Tuscany.

Asked: Is it light or full?

Answer: Medium bodied, with bright acidity and fine tannin, so it never feels heavy.

Two Fèlsina wines share the page: this Chianti Classico at $90 and the Rancia Chianti Classico Riserva at $165, so ring it by name and bin 14062. Some importers call this bottling Berardenga; the label wording is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Decant thirty minutes ahead if the table can wait, or pour and let it open. A taste for the host first, the guests, the host last. Say: “Produttori del Barbaresco: Nebbiolo from the village growers, cherry, rose and tar.”

Offer it to a guest who asks for Italian red with steak, who knows Barolo, or who wants something more serious than Chianti under $100. When the guest wants a single vineyard, step up to the Asili. Say: “The Produttori del Barbaresco is classic Nebbiolo from the village growers: cherry, rose and tar, and lovely with beef.”

The Produttori del Barbaresco Barbaresco 2020 is our anchor for Nebbiolo under $100: bin 16122, $95.

Barbaresco is a small village in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, in northwest Italy, and its wine is made from Nebbiolo. The Produttori del Barbaresco is the village cooperative: some fifty grower families who bring their grapes to one cellar. This classic Barbaresco is blended from many of their vineyards and aged in large oak casks. In the best years they also bottle single vineyard wines, such as the Asili.

Nebbiolo is pale in the glass and firm on the tongue. Expect red cherry, rose, dried herbs and tar, with high acidity and grippy tannin.

It is on the list because it is the benchmark: true Barbaresco from the people who farm it, at a price that lets a guest try Nebbiolo with dinner. With beef, mushrooms or a butter sauce, the tannin softens and the perfume rises.

Asked: What is the difference between Barbaresco and Barolo?

Answer: Both are Nebbiolo from Piedmont, from neighboring villages; Barbaresco is often a touch softer and more perfumed.

Asked: Why is it so pale if it is firm?

Answer: Nebbiolo has light color but plenty of tannin and acidity; the color fools people.

Asked: Is a cooperative wine any good?

Answer: This one sets the standard for the whole village, grown by its own families.

The Produttori has five wines on the page: this Barbaresco at $95 and four single vineyards, Asili, Montefico, Ovello and Rabajà, each at $185. Ring it by bin 16122. The list prints Cantina Produttori Barbaresco; it is the same producer. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

CVNE Imperial Reserva 2018 is our Spanish anchor just over $100, between the Cubillo and the 904: bin 10422, $110.

CVNE, said KOO-nay, stands for Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España, a historic house in the railway station quarter of Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta. Its Imperial label is kept for Reserva and Gran Reserva. A Reserva is aged in oak barrels and then in bottle before release, so it arrives ready to drink. This one is mostly Tempranillo, with a little Graciano and Mazuelo; the exact mix in 2018 is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is deep ruby with a touch of brick. It tastes of red and black cherry, plum, sweet spice and leather, medium to full in body, with polished tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list as classic Rioja at its most polished: a little richer than the Cubillo and much gentler in price than the 904.

Asked: What does Reserva mean?

Answer: A Rioja aged in oak barrels and then in bottle before release, longer than a Crianza.

Asked: What grape is it?

Answer: Mostly Tempranillo, with a little Graciano and Mazuelo; the sommelier can give the 2018 mix.

wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 16433, 750ml, $165. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Fèlsina, Rancia, Chianti Classico Riserva, 2019. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a large Bordeaux glass, decanted thirty to forty-five minutes ahead. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Fèlsina Rancia Riserva: single vineyard Sangiovese, dark cherry and herbs.”

Bring it up for a guest who likes Italian reds and wants more than a Chianti Classico, for a table having lamb or beef, or for a Sangiovese lover celebrating. From the Fèlsina Chianti Classico at $90, it is the natural step up. Say: “Rancia is Fèlsina’s great single vineyard Riserva: deep Sangiovese, dark cherry and herbs, made for lamb and beef.”

Fèlsina Rancia Chianti Classico Riserva 2019 is an Italian anchor in the sweet spot: bin 16433, $165.

Rancia, RAHN-chah, is the most famous vineyard of Fattoria di Fèlsina, at Castelnuovo Berardenga in the warm southern corner of Chianti Classico, near Siena. Fèlsina bottles it on its own as a Riserva, which means longer aging before release. It is all Sangiovese, aged in oak barrels and then in bottle.

At seven years it is a deep ruby beginning to show garnet. It tastes of dark cherry and plum with dried herbs, leather and spice, firm but fine in tannin, with the long, savory acidity Sangiovese is loved for.

It is on the list as the serious face of Chianti Classico, a single vineyard wine that ages for decades, and the natural step up from Fèlsina’s Chianti Classico at $90. With roast lamb, wild mushrooms or the Chateaubriand, it opens beautifully.

Asked: What does Riserva mean?

Answer: Longer aging before release; in Chianti Classico a Riserva has more time in barrel and bottle.

Asked: Is it all Sangiovese?

Answer: Yes, all Sangiovese, from the single Rancia vineyard.

Asili, AH-zee-lee, is one of the most celebrated vineyards in the village of Barbaresco, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont. The Produttori del Barbaresco, the village cooperative of some fifty grower families, bottles its members’ best single vineyards on their own only in the great years, usually as Riservas, and aged in large oak casks. Asili is often the most perfumed of them.

In the glass it is a pale, bright garnet. It smells of rose petal and red cherry and tastes of cherry, orange peel and spice, with silky but firm tannin and lifting acidity that carries a long finish.

It is on the list because it is great cru Barbaresco at a fair price, and the natural step up from the Produttori’s classic Barbaresco at $95. With the Chateaubriand, mushrooms or truffle, it sings.

Asked: Is it like Pinot Noir?

Asked: Is it a Riserva?

Il Poggione Brunello di Montalcino 2018 is an Italian anchor in the sweet spot: bin 17832, $198.

Brunello di Montalcino is Sangiovese from the hill town of Montalcino in southern Tuscany, one of Italy’s great reds. The rules ask for long aging, years in barrel and bottle, before release. Il Poggione, eel poh-JOH-neh, is the Franceschi family’s estate at Sant’Angelo in Colle, in the warm south of the zone, and a historic name in Brunello. It ages the wine in large oak casks in the traditional way.

At eight years it is a deep garnet. It tastes of dark cherry and plum with dried herbs, leather and a little balsamic warmth, with firm tannin and bright acidity that keep it fresh.

It is on the list as the classic Brunello: generous, traditional and fairly priced. With the Chateaubriand, roast lamb or an aged cheese, the tannin softens and the fruit comes forward.

Asked: What is the difference between Brunello and Chianti?

Answer: Both are Sangiovese, but Brunello comes from Montalcino and ages much longer, so it is deeper and firmer.

Asked: Does it need decanting?

Answer: Forty-five minutes to an hour helps it open; I can do that now.

Asked: Is it all Sangiovese?

Answer: Yes, Brunello is made only from Sangiovese.

Il Poggione is not Il Marroneto, another Brunello on the same page. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Flor de Pingus 2022 is our Spanish anchor in the sweet spot, from one of Spain’s cult estates: bin 16161, $215.

Dominio de Pingus was created by the Danish winemaker Peter Sisseck at La Horra, in Ribera del Duero, on the high plateau of Castilla y León, north of Madrid. Its top wine, Pingus, is made in tiny amounts; Flor de Pingus is the estate’s second wine, from younger and other vineyards, with the same care. The grape is Tinto Fino, the local name for Tempranillo, farmed biodynamically and aged in French oak.

At four years it is a deep, inky purple. It tastes of blackberry, black cherry, licorice and graphite, with ripe, dense tannin and a fresh line from the altitude.

It is on the list for the guest who wants Spanish power rather than Rioja’s mellow age, and for big meat: the Chateaubriand, grilled steak or lamb.

Asked: Is this Pingus?

Answer: It is the estate’s second wine; Pingus itself is made in tiny amounts. Flor de Pingus has the same maker and style.

Asked: How is it different from Rioja?

Answer: Same grape, Tempranillo, but Ribera del Duero is higher and hotter by day, so the wine is darker and more powerful.

Asked: Is it ready to drink?

Answer: Yes, with an hour in the decanter.

Do not call it Pingus; it is Flor de Pingus, the second wine. Ribera del Duero is not Rioja. It is young, so decant about an hour ahead, and mention the decant when the guest orders. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

La Rioja Alta Gran Reserva 904 2015 is the sweet spot bottle with the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at lunch and an anchor of our Spanish reds: bin 179221, $250.

La Rioja Alta is a historic house in the railway station quarter of Haro, the wine town of Rioja Alta, and one of the keepers of traditional Rioja. A Gran Reserva is the longest aged level: the 904 is Tempranillo with a little Graciano, aged about four years in American oak barrels made in the house’s own cooperage, then years more in bottle before release.

In the glass it is a garnet turning brick at the rim. It tastes of dried cherry, strawberry, tobacco, vanilla, leather and sweet spice, silky in texture with mellow tannin and a long, savory finish.

It is on the list as grand Rioja at its most classic. With the hanger steak, its gentle tannin and spice meet the Creole seasoning, smoked potato pavé and béarnaise.

Asked: Why 904?

Answer: It is the name of the house’s historic Gran Reserva label; the sommelier can tell the story.

Asked: Is it still fresh at eleven years?

Answer: Yes, Gran Reserva is made to be drunk at this age: silky, savory and lively.

Its bin 179221 is a long number; read it twice when ringing. The list prints it as La Rioja Alta "904" Gran Reserva. It is $250, at the top of the sweet spot, so mention the price when you suggest it. An older Rioja can show sediment; pour gently. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it to a guest who asks for Barolo or traditional Italian wine, to a celebration over the Chateaubriand, or to a Burgundy lover who wants something firmer. With nine vintages on the list, bring the sommelier for a guest who wants an older year. Bartolo Mascarello Barolo 2017 is our Piedmont anchor in the celebration tier: bin 184221, $340.

Barolo is Nebbiolo from a handful of villages in the Langhe hills of Piedmont, and Bartolo Mascarello is one of its most revered names: a small family cellar in the village of Barolo, now run by Maria Teresa Mascarello. They are traditionalists. Where most estates bottle single vineyards, they blend Nebbiolo from four vineyards in Barolo and La Morra, which is why the list prints La Morra beside the name. The wine ferments with long skin contact and ages in large old oak casks, never new barrels.

In the glass it is pale garnet. It tastes of sour cherry, rose, tar, licorice and dried herbs, with high acidity and firm, fine tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list for the Barolo lover, and with nine vintages printed, for the guest who wants to choose a year.

Asked: Why is La Morra on the label?

Answer: One of the four vineyards blended into the wine is in La Morra, the village next to Barolo.

Asked: Is it ready to drink?

Answer: It drinks with an hour of air; Barolo also ages for decades, and older vintages are on the list.

Asked: What makes it traditional?

Answer: Blending vineyards, long skin contact and large old casks rather than new oak.

Nine vintages of the same label are printed, from 2011 to 2021, at prices from $260 to $850; the 2016 is $850 and sits right beside this $340 bottle. Ring it by vintage and bin 184221, always. Which vintages are in tonight is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say Gaja, Barbaresco, 2012. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a large Burgundy bowl, decanted forty-five minutes ahead and leaving any sediment behind. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Gaja Barbaresco 2012: aged Nebbiolo, rose, cherry and tobacco.”

Offer it to a guest who asks for Gaja by name, wants a famous Italian bottle, or is celebrating over the Chateaubriand. A fourteen-year-old Barbaresco ready to drink is rare. For a younger, gentler Barbaresco, the Produttori’s is the value. Say: “Gaja Barbaresco 2012 is fourteen-year-old Nebbiolo from the family that made Barbaresco famous: rose, cherry and tobacco.”

Gaja Barbaresco 2012 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 16332, $380.

Gaja, GUY-ah, is the family winery in the village of Barbaresco, in the Langhe hills of Piedmont. Angelo Gaja made it one of the most famous names in Italian wine, and his family runs it today. This is their flagship Barbaresco, all Nebbiolo from the family’s own vineyards in the village, made in a polished, precise style. The list prints it simply as Gaja, on the Barbaresco page.

At fourteen years it is a garnet with an orange rim. It tastes of red cherry, rose, dried orange peel, tobacco and spice, with refined tannin and fresh acidity that carry a long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the name and the guest who wants a great Italian bottle with age already on it. With the Chateaubriand or anything earthy and buttery, it is at its best.

Asked: Why is Gaja so famous?

Answer: Angelo Gaja brought Barbaresco to the world’s great tables, and the family’s wines are among Italy’s most sought after.

Asked: Is it ready to drink?

Answer: Yes, at fourteen years it has opened up; we decant it to leave any sediment.

Asked: Is it Barolo?

Answer: No, Barbaresco, the neighboring village; same grape, Nebbiolo.

The list prints only Gaja 2012 on the Barbaresco page. Gaja Barbaresco 2020 also appears at $400, once as a 750ml bottle and once as a 375ml half at the same price and bin, so check which before quoting it. Ca’Marcanda and Pieve Santa Restituta are Gaja’s Tuscan estates, different wines. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Biondi Santi Brunello 2012: the original Brunello, cherry, rose and leather.”

Offer it to a guest who asks for Brunello at its most historic, to an Italian wine lover celebrating, or to the table that enjoyed our Rare by the glass, since the same family owns both. For a younger, generous Brunello, Il Poggione is the gentler price. Say: “Biondi Santi is where Brunello was born: aged Sangiovese, cherry, rose and leather, from the family that owns our Rare.”

Biondi Santi Brunello di Montalcino 2012 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 18542, $425.

Biondi Santi, bee-OHN-dee SAHN-tee, is the family credited with creating Brunello di Montalcino in the nineteenth century, at their estate Tenuta Greppo outside the Tuscan hill town of Montalcino. Since 2016 the estate has been owned by the EPI group of the Descours family, the same owners as Piper-Heidsieck and Rare, both poured here. The annata is the regular Brunello, as opposed to the Riserva: all Sangiovese, aged years in large Slavonian oak casks before release.

At fourteen years it is a garnet with an orange rim. It is elegant rather than powerful: sour cherry, dried rose, leather, tobacco and earth, with high acidity and fine, firm tannin.

It is on the list as the original Brunello, the bottle for a guest who loves history in the glass. With roast lamb, mushrooms or aged cheese, it opens slowly and beautifully.

Asked: What does Annata mean?

Answer: The regular Brunello of the year, as opposed to the Riserva, which ages longer.

Asked: Did they really invent Brunello?

Answer: The Biondi Santi family is credited with creating Brunello di Montalcino at Tenuta Greppo in the nineteenth century.

Asked: Is it ready?

Answer: At fourteen years it drinks well with forty-five minutes of air.

Biondi Santi has six wines printed: the Annata 2012 at $425 and 2013 at $455, Riservas 1999, 2011 and 2015 from $1200 to $3480, and a Rosso di Montalcino 2019 at $255. Ring this one by vintage and bin 18542. Which Riservas are in tonight is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Tenuta San Guido ‘Sassicaia’ Bolgheri Sassicaia 2018
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 32686, 750ml, $515. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Sassicaia, Tenuta San Guido, 2018. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a large Bordeaux glass, decanted about an hour ahead. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Sassicaia: the first Super Tuscan, Cabernet from the coast.”

Offer it to a guest who asks for Sassicaia or a Super Tuscan, to a Bordeaux lover who wants Italy, and to a table celebrating over the Chateaubriand. For the same family’s style at a third of the price, there is Guidalberto at $150. Say: “Sassicaia is the first Super Tuscan: coastal Cabernet, blackcurrant, cedar and herbs, elegant enough for the Chateaubriand.”

Sassicaia 2018 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 32686, $515.

Sassicaia, sahs-see-KAI-ah, is made at Tenuta San Guido, the Incisa della Rocchetta family estate at Bolgheri on the Tuscan coast. The family planted Cabernet on stony ground there when Italian law and opinion said great wine came only from native grapes, and Sassicaia became the first of the Super Tuscans. It is now the only Italian estate with an appellation of its own, Bolgheri Sassicaia. The wine is Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc, aged in French oak barrels.

At eight years it is deep ruby. It is elegant rather than heavy: blackcurrant, cedar, graphite, Mediterranean herbs and violet, with fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the legend and for a celebration with the Chateaubriand or lamb. The same estate’s Guidalberto is the gentler priced way into the style.

Asked: What is a Super Tuscan?

Answer: A Tuscan red made outside the old rules, often with Cabernet or Merlot; Sassicaia was the first.

Asked: Is it like Bordeaux?

Answer: The same grapes, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc, with a sunnier, herbal Tuscan accent.

Asked: Should we drink it now?

Answer: The 2018 drinks well with an hour in the decanter, and will keep for many years.

Tenuta San Guido has two wines here: Sassicaia at $515 and Guidalberto at $150. Ring Sassicaia by name and bin 32686. It is not Ornellaia or Masseto, Bolgheri neighbors on the same page. Decant time is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it to a guest who asks for Tignanello or a Super Tuscan with age, to a Sangiovese lover celebrating, or as an Italian alternative to an older Bordeaux. Mention that it is sixteen years old and ready. For the coastal Cabernet style, Sassicaia is the other legend. Say: “Tignanello 2010 is a founding Super Tuscan with sixteen years of age: dried cherry, cedar and tobacco.”

Antinori’s Tignanello 2010 is a famous name in our celebration tier, sixteen years old: bin 17913, $720.

The Antinori family has made wine in Florence for centuries. Tignanello comes from the vineyard of that name on their estate in the Chianti Classico hills, and it was one of the wines that began the Super Tuscans: Sangiovese blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc and aged in small oak barrels, at a time when the rules allowed neither. It carries the regional Toscana label for that reason.

At sixteen years the color is garnet turning brick. It tastes of dried cherry, plum, cedar, tobacco and leather, with polished tannin and the lively acidity of Sangiovese.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the name and wants a great Tuscan with age already on it, and for a slow celebration with roast lamb, aged cheese or the Chateaubriand.

Asked: What makes it a Super Tuscan?

Answer: Sangiovese blended with Cabernet and aged in small barrels, outside the old Chianti rules; Tignanello was one of the first.

Asked: Is it still good at sixteen?

Answer: It is in a lovely place now; the sommelier will check the bottle and decant it off any sediment.

Asked: Is it Chianti?

Answer: It comes from the Chianti Classico hills, but carries the Toscana label.

The list prints it as Marchesi Antinori "Tignanello" Toscana Rosso 2010. Antinori’s Solaia magnum at $2230 sits on the same page; do not confuse the two. A sixteen-year-old bottle can carry sediment, so the sommelier checks it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it to a guest who asks for Vega Sicilia, wants Spain’s greatest red, or is celebrating with the Chateaubriand. A Bordeaux or Napa collector often loves it. For the estate’s younger wine, Valbuena 5° is on the list too. Say: “Vega Sicilia Único is Spain’s most famous red, aged a decade before release: cedar, dark cherry and spice.”

Vega Sicilia Único 2009 is a famous name in our celebration tier, Spain’s most famous red: bin 287122, $850.

Vega Sicilia, BEH-gah see-SEE-lee-ah, is the historic estate at Valbuena de Duero, in Ribera del Duero on the high plateau of Castilla y León, owned by the Álvarez family. Único is its flagship. It is Tinto Fino, the local Tempranillo, with Cabernet Sauvignon, and its patience is legendary: about ten years of aging in barrels of different sizes and in bottle before the estate releases it.

At seventeen years it is deep garnet. It is layered and fresh: dark cherry, plum, cedar, tobacco and sweet spice, with fine tannin and lively acidity that carry a very long finish.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the name and the guest who wants Spain at its grandest, with the Chateaubriand, roast lamb or aged cheese.

Asked: Why is it aged so long?

Answer: It is the estate’s tradition: about ten years in barrel and bottle, so it arrives ready to drink.

Asked: What grapes are in it?

Answer: Tinto Fino, the local Tempranillo, with Cabernet Sauvignon; the sommelier can give the 2009 blend.

Asked: What is Valbuena?

Answer: The estate’s younger red, released at five years, which is why it is called Valbuena 5°.

Vega Sicilia has several wines printed: Único 2009 at $850, Único Reserva Especial at $1040 and Valbuena 5° 2013 at $420 and 2014 at $450. Ring Único by bin 287122, and read the long number twice. The 2009 blend is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Say: “Masseto is Italy’s legendary Merlot from one clay hill in Bolgheri: plum, chocolate and truffle, velvet and long.”

Masseto 2011 is a famous name in our celebration tier, Italy’s most famous Merlot: bin 27143, $1080.

Masseto, mahs-SEH-toh, comes from a single hill of blue clay at Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast. It was first bottled by Tenuta dell’Ornellaia, which is why the list prints it under that name, and it is now run as an estate of its own by the Frescobaldi family. The clay holds water and keeps the vines cool, which gives Merlot a depth it rarely finds. The wine is aged in new French oak.

At fifteen years it is deep garnet. It is opulent: plum, black cherry, chocolate, truffle and spice, with velvet tannin and a fresh, long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and for the grand celebration. With the Chateaubriand and its sauce Foyot, truffle or mushrooms, its richness meets its match.

Asked: Is Masseto all Merlot?

Answer: Yes, Merlot from a single hill of blue clay in Bolgheri.

Asked: Is it the same as Ornellaia?

Answer: It was born at Ornellaia and now has its own estate; Ornellaia is a different wine, a Bordeaux blend.

Asked: How does fifteen-year-old Masseto taste?

Answer: Opulent and velvety, plum and chocolate with truffle coming in; the sommelier checks each bottle.

Masseto is printed in four vintages: 2011 at $1080, 2015 at $1225, 2016 at $1300 and 2020 at $1045. The 2020 costs less than the 2011, so ring by vintage and bin 27143, never by price. Condition of the 2011 is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Chappellet, shap-uh-LAY, was founded by Donn and Molly Chappellet on Pritchard Hill, on the eastern hills of the Napa Valley, in 1967, and the family still runs it. Their top wines come from the steep, rocky estate. Mountain Cuvée is the friendlier blend: led by Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot and smaller amounts of the other Bordeaux grapes, from the estate and other Napa vineyards. The mix changes every year, and the 2024 blend is a question for the sommelier.

It is deep purple and young. It tastes of ripe black cherry, cassis, mocha and a little spice, with soft, supple tannin, so it drinks well now.

It is on the list as the easiest way into Napa red: a family name with real pedigree at a price that suits a burger at the Roost or a weekday steak.

Asked: Is it too young?

Asked: Where is Pritchard Hill?

Answer: In the eastern hills of the Napa Valley; Chappellet was one of the first to plant there.

Duckhorn’s 2022 Napa Valley Cabernet is the value bottle with the Roasted Chateaubriand and a Napa anchor under $100: bin 1876, $90.

Duckhorn Vineyards is a St. Helena winery, in the heart of the Napa Valley, founded by Dan and Margaret Duckhorn. It made its name with Merlot, and its Three Palms Merlot is on our list too. Their Napa Valley Cabernet is mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with small amounts of the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in French oak.

At four years it is deep ruby, still youthful. It tastes of blackberry, cassis, cocoa and cedar with a touch of vanilla, ripe and generous, with firm but polished tannin.

It is on the list as classic Napa at a friendly price. With the Chateaubriand, the structure stands up to the tenderloin, and the ripe fruit loves the buttery sauce Foyot and the glazed squash. It is a natural choice for a couple sharing the Chateaubriand who want a bottle rather than glasses.

Asked: Isn’t Duckhorn known for Merlot?

Answer: It made its name with Merlot, but the Napa Cabernet is just as classic. The Three Palms Merlot is on the list too.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: Full bodied but polished; the tannin is firm but smooth.

Asked: Does it need decanting?

Answer: Twenty to thirty minutes helps, but it drinks well poured straight.

kept.a: Show the label and say Frog’s Leap, Estate, Rutherford, 2021. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a Bordeaux glass, decanted about thirty minutes ahead. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Frog’s Leap Estate: dry-farmed Rutherford Cabernet, currant and dusty earth.”

Offer it to a guest who wants Napa Cabernet but says they find it heavy or oaky, to a Bordeaux lover trying California, or with lamb and mushrooms. The farming story is easy to tell. Say: “Frog’s Leap is dry-farmed, organic Rutherford Cabernet: currant, cherry and dusty earth, fresh rather than heavy.”

Frog’s Leap Estate Rutherford Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 is a Napa anchor in the sweet spot: bin 109222, $165.

Frog’s Leap is John Williams’s winery in Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley. It is known for two things: farming organically, and dry farming, which means the vines get no irrigation and send their roots deep for water. The result is wine that tastes fresher and less heavy than much of Napa. The Estate Cabernet comes from Frog’s Leap’s own Rutherford vineyards.

At five years it is a bright, deep ruby. It tastes of red and black currant and cherry, with the dusty earth Rutherford is known for and a note of dried herbs, fresh acidity and fine, firm tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who finds big Napa too much, and for food: lamb, mushrooms, steak and the Chateaubriand. Older vintages, including a 1991, are on the list too.

Asked: What does dry farmed mean?

Answer: The vines are not irrigated, so their roots go deep for water; it gives fresher, more concentrated fruit.

Asked: Is it organic?

Answer: The vineyards are farmed organically; for anything about what is in the bottle, I will check with the sommelier.

Asked: Is it a big Napa Cabernet?

Answer: Medium to full, but restrained and fresh for Napa.

Frog’s Leap is printed several times: Estate Rutherford 2021 at $165, 2020 at $200, and two 1991 bottles, at $410 on the Cabernet page and $300 on the Merlot page. Ring by vintage and bin 109222. Frog’s Leap also has a white Napa Valley at $70 and $95. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Caymus Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon 2023 is a first pick for the Roost Burger, and the Napa name many guests ask for: bin 1726, $180.

Caymus, KAY-mus, is the Wagner family’s winery in Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley, run by Chuck Wagner and his family. It is known for a ripe, plush style of Cabernet Sauvignon: the grapes are picked ripe and the wine is aged in oak and made to be soft and generous young. The family also makes the Special Selection, our celebration Caymus.

At three years it is deep purple, almost opaque. It tastes of black cherry, cassis, cocoa, vanilla and sweet spice, full bodied, with soft, velvety tannin.

It is on the list because guests love it and ask for it. With the burger, its ripe fruit meets the tomato jam and the sweetness of the short rib, and its body handles the bacon, cheese and special sauce.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is dry; the ripe fruit and soft tannin can make it taste rich and round.

Asked: What is the difference from the Special Selection?

Answer: Special Selection is the family’s top Cabernet, made from their best lots; this is their Napa Valley Cabernet.

Asked: Does it need decanting?

Answer: No, it is soft and open young; it is ready to pour.

Two Caymus Cabernets are on the list: this Napa Valley at $180 and the Special Selection 2018 at $480. Ring by name and bin 1726. Do not call it sweet; it is a dry wine with ripe fruit. Whether it is poured at the Roost is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 18231, 750ml, $360. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Present the label: say Inglenook Rubicon, Rutherford, 2010. Stand the bottle upright ahead of service, decant only to leave the sediment, and give it no more than about thirty minutes of air. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in large Bordeaux glasses, a taste for the host first, the host served last. Say: “The 2010 Rubicon, the whole bottle: sixteen years old and silky.”

Offer the bottle when a table is on its second round of Rubicon glasses, when a couple orders the Chateaubriand and wants an aged Napa bottle, or when a guest asks for Inglenook by name. Do the arithmetic gently: five glasses is about the bottle. Say: “You are enjoying the Rubicon: the whole 2010 bottle is $360, sixteen years old and silky, and lovely with the Chateaubriand.”

Inglenook Rubicon 2010, sold as a whole bottle, is a Napa anchor in the celebration tier: bin 18231, $360. It is the same wine we pour by the glass at $70.

Inglenook is one of the historic estates of Rutherford, in the middle of the Napa Valley, restored under Francis Ford Coppola’s family. Rubicon is its flagship, a Cabernet Sauvignon based blend. Our wine is the 2010, sixteen years old, a Napa legend with real age on it.

In the glass it is deep garnet. Age has softened the tannins, so it is powerful but silky: blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth.

It is on the list as a bottle for the table that has tasted the glass and wants more, and for a couple sharing the Roasted Chateaubriand with its sauce Foyot. At $70 a glass, a table having five glasses or more is better served by the bottle, which is when to mention it. Older Rubicon vintages, 2005 and 2009, are printed too.

Asked: Is the bottle the same as the glass?

Answer: Yes, the same 2010 Rubicon; the bottle is $360 and the glass is $70.

Asked: Who owns Inglenook?

Answer: Francis Ford Coppola’s family restored the historic estate; the sommelier can tell the full story.

Asked: Will there be sediment?

Answer: It can have some at sixteen years; we stand it upright and decant it off the sediment.

The glass and the bottle share bin 18231: ring the bottle as the bottle, never as a glass. Rubicon 2005 at $355 and 2009 at $360 sit beside it, so name the vintage. Never decant it for more than about thirty minutes. The glass pour’s own card covers glass service. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say Silver Oak, Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, 2020. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a Bordeaux glass, decanted twenty to thirty minutes ahead if the table can wait. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Silver Oak Napa Valley: ripe Cabernet, blackberry and vanilla.”

Offer it when a table at the Roost is celebrating over burgers, when a guest asks for Silver Oak by name, or for any steak where the guest wants a famous, smooth Napa Cabernet. The Alexander Valley bottling at $180 is the gentler price. Say: “Silver Oak is ripe Napa Cabernet aged in American oak: blackberry and vanilla, smooth and full with the burger.”

Silver Oak Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon 2020 is a first pick for the Roost Burger: bin 1588, $360.

Silver Oak Cellars was founded by Justin Meyer and Ray Duncan and is run by the Duncan family. It makes only Cabernet Sauvignon, in two bottlings, Napa Valley and Alexander Valley, and its signature is American oak: the wine is aged only in American oak barrels and then rested in bottle before release. American oak gives vanilla, dill and sweet spice in a way French oak does not, and guests often recognize it.

At six years it is deep ruby. It tastes of blackberry and black cherry with vanilla, dill and sweet spice, full bodied, smooth, with polished tannin.

It is on the list because it is a name people love to toast with. With the burger’s double short rib patties, bacon and cheese, it has the weight and ripeness to match; with a steak it is just as happy.

Asked: Why American oak?

Answer: It is Silver Oak’s signature: aging only in American oak gives vanilla, dill and sweet spice.

Asked: What is the difference between the Napa and the Alexander Valley?

Answer: Two Cabernets from two valleys; the Napa is fuller and firmer, the Alexander Valley softer and gentler priced.

Asked: Is it ready to drink?

Answer: Yes, it is rested in bottle before release; twenty minutes of air helps.

Two Silver Oak Cabernets are printed: Napa Valley 2020 at $360 and Alexander Valley 2021 at $180. Ring by valley, vintage and bin 1588. Whether it is poured at the Roost as well as the dining room is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Ridge Monte Bello 2012: mountain Cabernet, blackcurrant and cedar.”

Offer it to a Bordeaux lover who wants an American wine, to a guest who asks for something historic from California, or with lamb or the Chateaubriand. Ridge’s Lytton Springs and Three Valleys are the gentler priced ways into the house. Say: “Ridge Monte Bello is California’s great mountain Cabernet: blackcurrant, cedar and graphite, fourteen years old and fresh.”

Ridge Monte Bello 2012 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 16131, $410.

Ridge Vineyards makes Monte Bello from its vineyard high on a limestone ridge in the Santa Cruz Mountains, south of San Francisco, a world away from Napa. Paul Draper, its longtime winemaker, made it one of America’s great wines. It is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc, aged in American oak; the exact mix changes by year. Monte Bello stood beside the great Bordeaux at the Judgment of Paris tasting in 1976 and won the rematch thirty years later.

At fourteen years it is deep garnet. It is savory and fresh: blackcurrant, cedar, graphite, mint and earth, with fine, firm tannin and bright acidity.

It is on the list for the guest who knows the story and the one who loves Bordeaux and wants America’s answer, with lamb or the Chateaubriand.

Asked: Is this from Napa?

Answer: No, from the Santa Cruz Mountains, south of San Francisco, on a high limestone ridge.

Asked: What was the Judgment of Paris?

Answer: A 1976 blind tasting where California wines stood against top Bordeaux and Burgundy; Monte Bello was there and won the rematch in 2006.

Asked: What grapes?

Answer: Mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc.

Ridge has several wines on the list: Monte Bello at $410, the Estate Cabernet at $110, Lytton Springs at $120 and Three Valleys at $60. Ring Monte Bello by name and bin 16131. The 2012 blend is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it to a guest who asks for Insignia or a great Napa blend, to a table celebrating over the Chateaubriand, or as an American answer to a Bordeaux first growth. For a party, the 2015 magnum is on the list too. Say: “Insignia was Napa’s first proprietary Bordeaux blend: thirteen years old, blackcurrant, cocoa and cedar, rich and polished.”

Joseph Phelps Insignia 2013 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 18727, $440.

Joseph Phelps Vineyards is in St. Helena, in the Napa Valley, and Insignia is its flagship. First made in 1974, it was California’s first proprietary Bordeaux-style blend: a wine named for itself rather than for a grape, chosen each year from the estate’s best lots. It is led by Cabernet Sauvignon with the other Bordeaux grapes and aged in new French oak; the 2013 blend is a question for the sommelier.

At thirteen years it is deep garnet. It is rich and polished: blackcurrant, black cherry, cocoa, cedar and violet, full in body with fine, firm tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and the celebration. With the Chateaubriand, prime steak or lamb, its depth and polish make an occasion of the meal. A magnum of the 2015 is on the list for a bigger table.

Asked: What does proprietary blend mean?

Answer: A wine named by the estate rather than the grape, blended from the best lots each year; Insignia was the first in California.

Asked: Is it all Cabernet?

Answer: Cabernet Sauvignon leads, with other Bordeaux grapes; the sommelier can give the 2013 blend.

Asked: Is 2013 ready?

Answer: Yes, with forty-five minutes in a decanter it is open and rich.

Insignia is printed as a 2013 bottle at $440 and as a 2015 magnum at $950; ring by size and vintage. Joseph Phelps is not Joseph Drouhin or Joseph Voillot, Burgundy names in the same list. The 2013 blend is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Caymus Vineyards is the Wagner family winery in Rutherford, in the Napa Valley, known for a ripe, plush style of Cabernet Sauvignon. Special Selection is its top wine. It is made only in some years, from the family’s best lots, and aged longer in oak than the Napa Valley Cabernet. The list prints it as Special Selection; you may also hear Special Select.

At eight years it is a deep, near-opaque ruby. It is opulent: black cherry, blackberry, cocoa, vanilla and sweet spice, very full in body, with velvety tannin and a long, rich finish.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Caymus and wants the grandest version, and for a celebration with the Chateaubriand for two or a prime steak. The Napa Valley Caymus is the sweet spot sibling.

Answer: Fuller, deeper and longer; the same plush style at its grandest.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is dry; the ripe fruit and velvet texture make it taste rich.

He farms the historic Napanook vineyard at Yountville, in the Napa Valley, and makes the wine with a Bordeaux sensibility: restraint, freshness and structure over sheer ripeness. It is Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot; the 2014 mix is a question for the sommelier.

At twelve years it is deep garnet. It is savory rather than sweet: blackcurrant, graphite, tobacco, dried herbs and earth, with firm, fine tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list for the Bordeaux lover who wants Napa, and for a quiet celebration over the Chateaubriand or lamb. An older Dominus, the 2001, is printed too.

Answer: Napa grown, but made in a restrained, savory Bordeaux style.

Heitz Cellar Martha’s Vineyard 2009 is a famous name in our celebration tier: bin 17761, $540.

Heitz Cellar was founded in St. Helena, in the Napa Valley, by Joe and Alice Heitz. Their Martha’s Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon comes from a vineyard in Oakville planted by Tom and Martha May, and it was one of the first Napa wines bottled under a vineyard’s name. It is famous for a signature note of mint and eucalyptus that guests who know it look for.

At seventeen years it is garnet with a brick rim. It tastes of blackcurrant, cedar, mint, eucalyptus and earth, the tannins softened, fresh and long.

It is on the list as Napa history in a glass: with many vintages printed back to 1997, it is a collector’s bottle and a celebration bottle. With lamb, herbs or the Chateaubriand, the mint and cedar sing.

Asked: Where does the mint come from?

Answer: It is the vineyard’s signature; people have tasted mint and eucalyptus in Martha’s Vineyard for decades.

Asked: Who is Martha?

Answer: Martha May, who planted the vineyard in Oakville with her husband Tom.

Asked: Do you have other vintages?

Answer: Many, back to 1997, and magnums; I will ask the sommelier what is in tonight.

Martha’s Vineyard is printed in many vintages from 1997 to 2009 and in magnums of 2004, 2009 and 2010. The 2009 bottle is $540 and the 2009 magnum $985: ring by size, vintage and bin 17761. Heitz Lot C-91 and Linda Falls are different wines. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it to a guest who asks for Opus One, to a table celebrating a milestone over the Chateaubriand, or to a Bordeaux lover curious about Napa. Mention that the 2010 has sixteen years of age. For more Opus, the sommelier can show other vintages and magnums. Say: “Opus One 2010 is the Napa icon from Mondavi and Rothschild: sixteen years old, silky, cedar and cocoa.”

Opus One 2010 is a famous name in our celebration tier, sixteen years old: bin 145112, $775.

Opus One began as a partnership between Robert Mondavi, the Napa pioneer, and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild in Bordeaux. The idea was one wine joining Napa fruit and Bordeaux craft, made at its own winery in Oakville, in the heart of the Napa Valley. It is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak.

At sixteen years it is deep garnet. It tastes of blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, tobacco and cocoa, with silky tannin and a long finish; the age has made it seamless.

It is on the list because guests ask for it by name and dream of it with a great steak. With the Chateaubriand for two, prime steak or lamb, it makes the occasion. Several vintages and magnums are printed, so the sommelier can help a guest choose.

Asked: Who makes Opus One?

Answer: It began as a partnership of Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Mouton Rothschild, with its own winery in Oakville.

Asked: What is Overture?

Answer: Opus One’s second wine; it is on the list too.

Asked: Is the 2010 ready?

Answer: Yes, at sixteen years it is silky; a short decant leaves any sediment behind.

Opus One is printed many ways: this 2010 at $775, 2003 at $800, 2005 at $900, 2007 at $915, magnums, Overture from $345, and on the half-bottle page 2011 at $270 to 2016 at $280, likely halves. Ring by vintage, size and bin 145112. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: The sommelier presents and opens it. Show the label and say Harlan Estate, Oakville, 2006. Stood upright ahead, it is decanted just before pouring, leaving the sediment. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in large Bordeaux glasses, small pours, the host last. Say: “Harlan Estate 2006: Napa’s cult Cabernet, twenty years old.”

Offer it only when a guest asks for Harlan or for the greatest Napa on the list, or is marking a milestone and wants the best. Bring the sommelier in at once; with ten vintages, the right year may be a birthday. Say: “Harlan Estate is one of Napa’s cult wines: twenty-year-old hillside Cabernet, blackcurrant, cedar and violet.”

Harlan Estate 2006 is a famous name in our celebration tier, twenty years old: bin 16665, $1250.

Harlan Estate was founded by Bill Harlan on the western hills above Oakville, in the Napa Valley, with a clear ambition: to make a first growth of California. It is one of Napa’s cult wines, made in very small amounts and sold mostly to a mailing list. It is a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with the other Bordeaux grapes, aged in new French oak.

At twenty years it is deep garnet with a bricking rim. It tastes of blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, graphite, tobacco and violet, dense yet silky, with a very long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and the once in a lifetime occasion. The list prints ten vintages from 2003 to 2015, a rare vertical, so the sommelier can guide a guest to the year that matters to them.

Asked: What makes Harlan a cult wine?

Answer: Tiny production from hillside vineyards above Oakville, sold mostly to a mailing list, and a reputation among Napa’s very best.

Asked: Do you have other vintages?

Answer: Ten, from 2003 to 2015; the sommelier can walk you through them.

Asked: Is 2006 ready?

Answer: At twenty years it is in a beautiful place; the sommelier will decant it off the sediment.

Ten Harlan vintages are printed from $1200 to $2300; 2003 and 2006 are both $1250. Ring by vintage and bin 16665, never by price. Harlan is not Calera’s Mt. Harlan wines on the same list. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Screaming Eagle Second Flight 2012 is a famous name on our list for a grand celebration: bin 181131, $1400.

Screaming Eagle is the most famous of Napa’s cult wines: a tiny estate in Oakville whose wine is sold almost entirely to a long-closed mailing list. Second Flight is its second wine, renamed The Flight, and it is rare in its own right. The 2012 is a Bordeaux blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc; the exact proportions are a question for the sommelier.

At fourteen years it is deep garnet. It tastes of cassis, plum, black olive, spice and earth, plush yet savory, with fine tannin and a long finish.

It is on the list for the collector who wants a Screaming Eagle experience, filed with the other red blends rather than the Cabernets. With the Chateaubriand at a grand occasion, it is a story as much as a wine.

Asked: Is this Screaming Eagle?

Answer: It is Screaming Eagle’s second wine, Second Flight, now called The Flight.

Asked: What grapes?

Answer: The 2012 blends Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc; how much of each is a question for the sommelier.

Asked: Where is the vineyard?

Answer: In Oakville, in the heart of the Napa Valley; the estate wine itself is not on our list.

It is filed on the list with the other red blends, not with the Napa Cabernets, so look there. Do not present it as the Screaming Eagle estate wine. Its long bin 181131 is worth reading twice. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Ridge ‘Three Valleys’ Sonoma County 2023
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 15142, 750ml, $60. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Ridge, Three Valleys, 2023. Serve it a touch cool, 58 to 62°F, in a Bordeaux glass, with no decanting. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last, and leave the bottle on the table. Say: “Ridge Three Valleys: juicy Sonoma Zinfandel, blackberry and pepper.”

Offer it at dinner when a guest orders the Creole Hanger Steak and wants a bottle under $100, to a guest who loves Zinfandel, or to a table that likes spice. For the classic Ridge Zinfandel, Lytton Springs is the sweet spot step. Say: “Ridge Three Valleys is a juicy Sonoma Zinfandel blend, blackberry and pepper, and it loves the chili crisp.”

Ridge Three Valleys 2023 is the value bottle with the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner: bin 15142, $60.

Ridge Vineyards is one of California’s great Zinfandel houses, best known for Monte Bello in the Santa Cruz Mountains and Lytton Springs in Sonoma. Three Valleys is their Sonoma County blend, built on Zinfandel with Petite Sirah and other old field grapes drawn from several valleys there, and aged in oak. The exact 2023 mix is a question for the sommelier.

It is a young, deep purple. It tastes of blackberry, raspberry and black pepper with a little sweet spice, juicy and round, with soft tannin and bright acidity.

It is on the list as the friendliest way into Ridge, and it earns its place with spice. The chili crisp and Creole seasoning on the hanger steak make a firm, tannic red taste bitter; Zinfandel’s ripe fruit and soft tannin stay calm and juicy beside them.

Asked: Is Zinfandel a sweet wine?

Answer: Not this one; red Zinfandel is dry. The sweet pink wine called White Zinfandel is a different style.

Asked: Why Zinfandel with the hanger steak?

Answer: Its ripe fruit and soft tannin stay smooth with heat; a firm red would taste bitter beside the chili crisp.

Asked: What is in the blend?

Answer: Mostly Zinfandel, with Petite Sirah and other old field grapes; the sommelier can give the 2023 mix.

Ridge has several bottles on the list: Three Valleys at $60, Lytton Springs at $120, the Estate Cabernet at $110 and Monte Bello at $410. Ring this one by name and bin 15142. The 2023 blend is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say Ken Wright Cellars, Willamette Valley Pinot Noir, 2024. Serve it at 58 to 62°F in a Burgundy bowl, with no decanting. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Ken Wright Willamette Pinot: bright cherry and forest floor.”

Offer it at dinner with the Blackened Tofu, to a guest who wants Pinot Noir under $100, or to a table eating mushrooms, salmon or chicken. For one of Ken Wright’s single vineyards, the Canary Hill or Freedom Hill at $150 is the step up. Say: “Ken Wright’s Willamette Pinot is bright and earthy, cherry and forest floor, and gentle with the blackening spice.”

Ken Wright Cellars Willamette Valley Pinot Noir 2024 is the value bottle with the Blackened Tofu and our Oregon anchor under $100: bin 148412, $72.

Ken Wright Cellars is in Carlton, in the Willamette Valley of Oregon, the state’s heartland for Pinot Noir. Ken Wright is known for bottling single vineyard Pinot Noirs, several of which are on our list. This wine is his valley-wide blend, drawn from those vineyard sources and made to drink young.

It is a bright ruby. It tastes of red cherry, raspberry, forest floor and a little spice, light to medium in body, silky, with low tannin and fresh acidity.

It is on the list as the friendly Oregon Pinot, and it is the value pairing for the Blackened Tofu. The earthy forest floor note meets the preserved shiitakes and rice grits, and the low tannin stays calm with the blackening spice, where a tannic red would turn bitter.

Asked: How does Oregon Pinot compare with Burgundy?

Answer: Same grape and a cool climate, so similar freshness; Oregon often shows a little more ripe red fruit.

Asked: Is it light?

Answer: Light to medium in body, silky, with low tannin.

Asked: Do you have a single vineyard Ken Wright?

Answer: Canary Hill and Freedom Hill are on the list at $150, and Carter Vineyard as a half-bottle; I will check what is in tonight.

Ken Wright has many bottles printed: this valley blend at $72, single vineyards such as Canary Hill and Freedom Hill at $150, magnums at $300, and half-bottles. Ring this one by name and bin 148412. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 13362, 750ml, $80. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Piedrasassi, Bien Nacido Vineyard Syrah, 2021. Serve it at 60 to 63°F in a large Burgundy or Syrah glass, decanted about twenty minutes ahead. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Piedrasassi Bien Nacido: savory Syrah, black cherry, pepper and smoke.”

Offer it to a guest who likes Northern Rhône Syrah or peppery reds, who wants an interesting bottle under $100, or with lamb, hanger steak or the burger. The same maker’s Rim Rock Syrah sits beside it at the same price. Say: “Piedrasassi is cool-climate California Syrah in the Rhône style: black cherry, pepper and smoke, savory and fresh.”

Piedrasassi Bien Nacido Vineyard Syrah 2021 is an anchor among our other reds under $100: bin 13362, $80.

Piedrasassi, pee-ay-drah-SAH-see, is the Syrah label of Sashi Moorman and Melissa Sorongon, made in Lompoc on the Central Coast of California. This wine comes from the Bien Nacido Vineyard in the Santa Maria Valley, a cool valley open to Pacific fog, where some of the oldest Syrah vines on the Central Coast grow. They make it in the style of the Northern Rhône in France, for savor and freshness rather than ripeness.

At five years it is a deep purple-ruby. It tastes of black cherry, black pepper, smoked meat, olive and herbs, medium in body, with fine tannin and lively acidity.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Rhône wine and the guest who wants something different from Cabernet. With grilled lamb, hanger steak or the burger, the pepper and smoke come alive.

Asked: Is it like Australian Shiraz?

Answer: Same grape, Syrah, but this is cool-climate and savory, closer to the Northern Rhône than to a ripe Shiraz.

Asked: Where is Bien Nacido?

Answer: A famous vineyard in the Santa Maria Valley of Santa Barbara County, cooled by Pacific fog.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: Medium bodied, with fine tannin and fresh acidity.

Two Piedrasassi Syrahs share the page at $80: Bien Nacido from the Santa Maria Valley and Rim Rock from the Arroyo Grande Valley. Ring by vineyard and bin 13362. How the vineyard is farmed today is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Ridge ‘Lytton Springs’ Dry Creek Valley 2022
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 16719, 750ml, $120. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Ridge, Lytton Springs, 2022. Serve it at 60 to 63°F in a Bordeaux glass, decanted about twenty minutes ahead if the table can wait. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Ridge Lytton Springs: old-vine Zinfandel, blackberry, pepper and clove.”

Offer it at dinner with the Creole Hanger Steak when a guest wants something better than the value bottle, to a Zinfandel lover, or with grilled lamb. From the Three Valleys at $60, it is the natural step up in the Ridge family. Say: “Lytton Springs is old-vine Dry Creek Zinfandel, brambly and peppery, and it meets the Creole spice and Madeira glaze.”

Ridge Lytton Springs 2022 is the sweet spot bottle with the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner: bin 16719, $120.

Lytton Springs is Ridge Vineyards’ estate in the Dry Creek Valley of Sonoma County. Its oldest vines were planted as a field blend, the old California way: Zinfandel growing side by side with Petite Sirah, Carignane and other grapes, picked and fermented together. Because Zinfandel is not always enough of the mix to name it on the label, Ridge calls the wine simply Lytton Springs. It is aged in American oak.

At four years it is a deep purple. It tastes of blackberry, black cherry, black pepper and clove, brambly and spiced, medium-full in body with firm but ripe tannin.

It is on the list as Ridge’s classic Zinfandel, and it is the sweet spot pairing for the dinner hanger steak: the spice meets the Creole seasoning, the ripe fruit loves the Madeira glaze on the broccolini, and it stands up to the chili crisp.

Asked: Is it Zinfandel?

Answer: Mostly Zinfandel, with Petite Sirah and Carignane from an old field blend; that is why the label says only Lytton Springs.

Asked: Is it a big wine?

Answer: Medium-full with ripe tannin, spicy rather than heavy.

Asked: What makes it go with the steak?

Answer: Its pepper and clove meet the Creole seasoning, and the ripe fruit loves the Madeira glaze.

Ridge has several bottles printed: Lytton Springs at $120, Three Valleys at $60, the Estate Cabernet at $110 and Monte Bello at $410. Ring by name and bin 16719. The list files it under Zinfandel; the label may not say Zinfandel. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Penfolds ‘Bin 389’ Cabernet Shiraz 2019
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 121322, 750ml, $145. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Penfolds, Bin 389, Cabernet Shiraz, 2019. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in a Bordeaux glass, decanted thirty to forty-five minutes ahead. A taste for the host first, then the guests, the host last. Say: “Penfolds Bin 389: Cabernet and Shiraz, blackcurrant, plum and mocha.”

Offer it to a guest who loves big Napa Cabernet or Australian Shiraz, to a table having steak or lamb, or to a guest who asks about Grange but wants a gentler price. For the real thing, Grange 2004 is on the list. Say: “Penfolds Bin 389 is Australia’s classic Cabernet Shiraz, called Baby Grange: blackcurrant, plum and mocha, rich and firm.”

Penfolds Bin 389 Cabernet Shiraz 2019 is an anchor among our other reds in the sweet spot: bin 121322, $145.

Penfolds is South Australia’s most famous wine house, the maker of Grange, and its wines carry bin numbers from the cellar. Bin 389 is its Cabernet Shiraz, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz that Australia made its own. It is aged in American oak, including barrels that held Grange in an earlier year, which is why it is often called Baby Grange. The list prints Barossa Valley; the label usually says South Australia, which is a question for the sommelier.

At seven years it is a deep purple-red. It tastes of blackcurrant and plum with mocha, licorice and spice, full bodied with solid tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who loves big, rich reds and the Penfolds name, at a far gentler price than Grange, and for steak, lamb or the burger.

Asked: Why is it called Baby Grange?

Answer: It is aged partly in barrels that earlier held Penfolds Grange, and shares some of its richness.

Asked: What does the bin number mean?

Answer: Penfolds names wines by the cellar bin where the first one was kept.

Asked: Is it ready?

Answer: At seven years it is opening; thirty to forty-five minutes in a decanter helps.

Do not confuse the bin number on the label, Bin 389, with our list bin, 121322. The list prints Barossa Valley; the label region is a lineup question. Grange sits on the same page at much higher prices. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it to a guest who asks for Kosta Browne or California Pinot, wants a rich, smooth red that is not Cabernet, or is having fish, pork or mushrooms. The founders’ tip money story is a lovely one to share. Say: “Kosta Browne was started by two restaurant workers with their tips; this Sonoma Coast Pinot is rich, silky and spiced.”

Kosta Browne Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir 2021 is an anchor among our other reds in the sweet spot: bin 14612, $230.

Kosta Browne was founded in Sebastopol, in Sonoma County, by Dan Kosta and Michael Browne, two restaurant workers who started making wine with tip money they had saved. It grew into one of California’s most sought-after Pinot Noir houses, which servers enjoy telling. This bottling is from cool vineyards on the Sonoma Coast, near the Pacific, made in a rich, polished style with French oak.

At five years it is a deep ruby. It tastes of black cherry, raspberry, cola and baking spice, ripe and silky, medium-full in body with smooth tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Pinot Noir but wants more richness than Burgundy, and for duck, pork, salmon or mushrooms. A server’s story with a server’s favorite wine.

Asked: Is it like Burgundy?

Answer: Same grape, Pinot Noir, but richer and riper, with more black cherry and spice.

Asked: Is the story true about the tips?

Answer: Yes, Dan Kosta and Michael Browne started it with tip money saved from restaurant work.

Asked: Will it go with fish?

Answer: With salmon or richer fish, yes; it is soft enough in tannin.

Kosta Browne is printed many ways: Sonoma Coast 2021 at $230 and 2020 at $240, and on the half-bottle page a Russian River at $120 and Gap’s Crown at $165. Ring by vintage and bin 14612; the 2020 costs more than the 2021. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Duckhorn ‘Three Palms Vineyard’ Napa Valley Merlot 2020
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 141234, 750ml, $240. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

Offer it to a guest who asks for Merlot, to a table that wants a plush red that is not Cabernet, or with duck, pork or the hanger steaks. For a party, magnums and a double magnum are on the list. Say: “Three Palms is the single vineyard Merlot that made Duckhorn famous: black cherry, plum and cocoa, plush and firm.”

Duckhorn Three Palms Vineyard Merlot 2020 is an anchor among our other reds in the sweet spot: bin 141234, $240.

Duckhorn Vineyards, the St. Helena winery founded by Dan and Margaret Duckhorn, made its name with Merlot, and Three Palms is the vineyard most tied to that story. It lies on a rocky alluvial fan on the valley floor near Calistoga, at the warm north end of the Napa Valley, and is named for three palm trees on the property. The stones drain well and keep the vines lean, which gives the wine concentration.

At six years it is a deep ruby-purple. It tastes of black cherry, plum, cocoa and cedar with a little herb, full and plush in body, with firm, velvety tannin.

It is on the list for the guest who loves Merlot and wants its grandest Napa expression, and for duck, roast pork, mushrooms or steak.

Asked: Why is it called Three Palms?

Answer: The vineyard near Calistoga is named for three palm trees on the property.

Asked: Is Merlot softer than Cabernet?

Answer: Usually rounder, but Three Palms is full and firm, with velvety tannin.

Asked: Do you have a bigger bottle?

Answer: A 2016 magnum and a 2015 double magnum are on the list; I will check they are in tonight.

Duckhorn appears many times: this Three Palms 2020 at $240, a 2016 magnum at $435 and a 2015 double magnum at $870, the Napa Cabernet at $90 and a Merlot half-bottle. Ring by name, size and bin 141234. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Château Musar Bekaa Valley 2003
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 33512, 750ml, $285. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Château Musar, Bekaa Valley, 2003. Stand the bottle upright ahead of service and decant it about thirty minutes before pouring, leaving the sediment. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in large Bordeaux glasses, a taste for the host first, the host last. Say: “Château Musar 2003: Lebanon’s great red, dried cherry, fig and spice.”

Offer it to a guest who wants something different and historic, an older red with character, or to a table having lamb or cheese. Tell them it is unlike Bordeaux: wilder and more savory. For a younger, gentler start, Musar’s Hochar is $90. Say: “Château Musar 2003 is Lebanon’s legendary red: twenty-three years old, dried cherry, fig, spice and leather.”

Château Musar 2003 is an anchor among our other reds in the celebration tier: bin 33512, $285.

Château Musar was founded in Lebanon by Gaston Hochar and made world famous by his son Serge Hochar, who kept making wine through years of war. The grapes grow high in the Bekaa Valley, and the wine is made and aged north of Beirut. The red is a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault and Carignan, aged in oak and then in bottle for years before release; its style is famously individual, with a wild, savory edge that collectors love.

At twenty-three years it is a garnet with an amber rim. It tastes of dried cherry, fig, spice, leather and incense, silky, with lively acidity.

It is on the list for the adventurous guest and the collector, and with five vintages printed it makes a story. With lamb, game or a cheese course, it is at home.

Asked: Is Lebanese wine any good?

Answer: Lebanon has made wine for thousands of years, and Château Musar is among the world’s most collected reds.

Asked: What does it taste like?

Answer: Silky and savory, with dried cherry, fig, leather and spice, a little wild; unlike a Bordeaux.

Asked: Why is it so old?

Answer: Musar ages its wine for years before release, and it keeps for decades.

Musar is printed in five wines: 1994 at $400, 1995 at $450, 1997 at $285, 2003 at $285 and the younger Hochar 2020 at $90. The 1997 and 2003 share a price, so ring by vintage and bin 33512. Warn a first-time guest that the style is wild and savory. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Penfolds ‘Grange’ Shiraz 2004
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 11723, 750ml, $650. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: The sommelier presents it. Show the label and say Penfolds Grange, 2004. Stand the bottle upright ahead of service and decant it forty-five minutes before pouring, leaving the sediment. Serve it at 60 to 64°F in large Bordeaux glasses, a taste for the host first, the host last. Say: “Penfolds Grange 2004: Australia’s great Shiraz, blackberry and mocha.”

Offer it to a guest who asks for Grange, a lover of big Shiraz or Napa, or a table celebrating over the Chateaubriand. Mention that the 2004 has twenty-two years of age, which younger vintages cannot offer. For a taste of the house at a gentler price, there is Bin 389. Say: “Grange 2004 is Australia’s most famous red: twenty-two-year-old Shiraz, blackberry, mocha and licorice.”

Penfolds Grange 2004 is a famous name in our celebration tier, twenty-two years old: bin 11723, $650.

Grange is Australia’s most famous wine. Max Schubert, Penfolds’ chief winemaker, created it in the 1950s after a visit to Bordeaux, determined to make an Australian red that could age for decades. It is Shiraz, with a little Cabernet Sauvignon in most years, blended from old vineyards across South Australia and aged in new American oak. The list prints Barossa Valley; the label usually says South Australia, a question for the sommelier.

At twenty-two years it is a deep garnet. It tastes of blackberry, plum, mocha, licorice, leather and spice, dense and powerful, the ripe tannin softening into a long finish.

It is on the list for the collector and for the guest who wants the grandest Australian red, with the Chateaubriand, prime steak or lamb. Three younger vintages are printed too.

Asked: Why is Grange so famous?

Answer: Max Schubert created it in the 1950s to rival the great Bordeaux, and it became Australia’s most collected red.

Asked: Is it all Shiraz?

Answer: Mostly Shiraz, usually with a little Cabernet Sauvignon.

Asked: Do you have other vintages?

wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 192345, 750ml, $60. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Castello Banfi, Florus, Moscadello di Montalcino, 2011. Serve it at 46 to 50°F in a small white wine or dessert glass, from an ice bucket with water. Small pours, the guests first and the host last. Say: “Florus: late harvest Moscato from Montalcino, honey and orange blossom.”

Offer it when a table orders the Blackberry Trifle or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin and wants a sweet bottle to share, or when a guest wants a dessert wine at a friendly price. Two or three guests can share a bottle over dessert. For more depth with the tarte Tatin, the Kracher Auslese is the step up. Say: “Florus is Montalcino’s old sweet wine, late harvest Moscato: honey, apricot and orange blossom with the fruit.”

Castello Banfi Florus 2011 is the value bottle with two desserts, the Blackberry Trifle and the Pineapple Tarte Tatin: bin 192345, $60.

Long before Brunello made Montalcino famous, the Tuscan hill town was known for a sweet wine called Moscadello, made from Moscato Bianco. Castello Banfi, the large estate founded there by the Mariani family, American wine importers, revived it with Florus: a late harvest wine from grapes left on the vine to ripen and concentrate, partly aged in oak.

At fifteen years it is golden amber. It tastes of honey, apricot, candied orange and orange blossom, with a little nuttiness from age and fresh acidity to keep it lively.

It is on the list as the gentlest priced dessert bottle, and it works twice. It is sweeter than the lemon curd and blackberry in the trifle, so it never tastes thin, and its honeyed, tropical fruit meets the charred pineapple and sweet anglaise of the tarte Tatin.

Asked: Is it like Moscato d’Asti?

Answer: Same grape family, but this is still, late harvested and richer, from Montalcino in Tuscany.

Asked: How sweet is it?

Answer: Properly sweet, with fresh acidity so it does not cloy.

Asked: Is it still good at fifteen?

Answer: Late harvest wines age well; I will check with the sommelier how this bottle is showing.

Florus is not Brunello, even though Banfi makes both in Montalcino. At fifteen years a late harvest Moscato deepens to amber; how it is showing is a lineup question. Banfi is not Castello di Ama or Castello di Volpaia on the same pages. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.
