wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 27501, 750ml, $85. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Hexamer, Rheingrafenberg, Riesling Spätlese, 2010. Serve it at 46 to 50°F in a small white wine glass, from an ice bucket with water. Pour after the flambé settles, small pours, the host last. Say: “Hexamer Spätlese: aged Riesling, honey and baked apple, with a bright finish.”

Offer it when a table orders the Bananas Foster and wants a sweet wine, especially a table watching it flambéed. Two or three guests can share the bottle. It suits a guest who likes Riesling or wants something less heavy than Port. For a grand step, the old Rivesaltes or the Gilette are on the list. Say: “The Hexamer is sixteen-year-old Riesling Spätlese, honey and baked apple, with bright acidity that cuts the butter.”

Hexamer Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg Riesling Spätlese 2010 is the value bottle with the World Famous Bananas Foster: bin 27501, $85.

Weingut Hexamer is a family estate at Meddersheim on the Nahe, a small Riesling region of Germany between the Mosel and the Rhine. Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg names the village and the vineyard, its best known. Spätlese means late harvest: riper Riesling picked later, here made sweet.

At sixteen years it is a deep gold. The fruit has turned to honey, baked apple and apricot, with a little petrol and spice, the marks of aged Riesling, and the acidity is still bright and racy.

It is on the list because aged German Riesling is one of the great matches for caramel and fruit, at a friendly price. With the Bananas Foster, flambéed tableside in brown sugar, butter and rum, it is sweet enough to stand up to the caramel, and its acidity cuts through the butter so the dessert tastes lighter.

Asked: What does Spätlese mean?

Answer: Late harvest: riper Riesling picked later; this one is made sweet.

Asked: Why does it smell a little like petrol?

Answer: That is a normal note of aged Riesling, loved by Riesling fans.

Asked: Is it too sweet for Bananas Foster?

Answer: No, it needs to be as sweet as the dessert, and its acidity keeps it fresh.

Hexamer has three wines on the list: this Spätlese at $85, a Rheingrafenberg Trocken, which is dry, at $90, and an Altenberg Kabinett at $60. Ring by name and bin 27501, and never offer the Trocken with dessert. The Bananas Foster is flambéed tableside for a minimum of two. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 19341, 750ml, $90. The value tier for the Baked Apple and the New Orleans Bread Pudding. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Domaine des Baumard, Clos Sainte Catherine, Coteaux du Layon, 2006. Serve it at 46 to 50°F in a small white wine or dessert glass, from an ice bucket with water. Small pours, the host last. Say: “Baumard Clos Sainte Catherine: sweet Loire Chenin, quince, honey and apple.”

Offer it to a table on the breakfast tasting when the Baked Apple arrives and they want a sweet bottle to share, with the New Orleans Bread Pudding at dessert, or to a guest who loves Loire wines. For a richer step with the same grape, the Huet Moelleux is the sweet spot. Say: “The Baumard is twenty-year-old sweet Chenin from the Loire: quince, honey and baked apple, bright enough for the glaze.”

Domaine des Baumard Clos Sainte Catherine 2006 is the value bottle with the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting and with the New Orleans Bread Pudding: bin 19341, $90.

Domaine des Baumard, boh-MAR, is a family estate at Rochefort-sur-Loire, in Anjou in the Loire Valley. The Coteaux du Layon is the stretch of slopes along the Layon river where Chenin Blanc is left to ripen late for sweet wine. The Clos Sainte Catherine is Baumard’s walled vineyard there.

At twenty years it is a deep gold. It tastes of quince, baked apple, honey, apricot and a little ginger, sweet, with the lively acidity Chenin keeps for decades.

It is on the list because Chenin Blanc is the natural partner for apple, and this one has age at a friendly price. With the Baked Apple, its fruit echoes the apple and its sweetness matches the brown sugar glaze, while the acidity lifts the crème fraîche and the oat and pecan crumble. With the bread pudding, it is as sweet as the whiskey caramel, its honey meets the pralines, and its acidity keeps the custard from feeling heavy.

Asked: What is Coteaux du Layon?

Answer: Slopes along the Layon river in the Loire, where Chenin Blanc ripens late for sweet wine.

Asked: Is it too sweet for breakfast?

Answer: It is sweet, but its acidity keeps it light; a small glass with the Baked Apple is lovely.

Asked: Is twenty years old a problem?

Answer: Not for sweet Chenin, which ages for decades and stays fresh.

Whether a bottle can be poured with the breakfast tasting is a lineup question. Clos Sainte Catherine is sweet; other Baumard wines may be dry, so read the label. Its bin 19341 is close to other dessert bins; ring by name. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say Dr. Hermann, Ürziger Würzgarten, Kranklei, Spätlese, 2018. Serve it at 46 to 50°F in a small white wine glass, from an ice bucket with water. Small pours, the host last. Say: “Dr. Hermann Spätlese: sweet Mosel Riesling, peach and lime.”

Offer it with the Framboise French Toast at breakfast and lunch, or with the Lemon Tart at any meal, to a guest who wants a sweet wine that is not heavy. It suits a Riesling lover and a guest who finds Port too rich. For the tart, the Climens is the sweet spot step. Say: “The Dr. Hermann is sweet Mosel Riesling, peach and lime, one of the few wines that loves lemon.”

Dr. Hermann’s Kranklei Goldkapsel Spätlese 2018 is the value bottle with two desserts, the Framboise French Toast and the Lemon Tart: bin 28461, $95.

Weingut Dr. Hermann is a family estate at Erden on the Mosel. This wine comes from the Kranklei, a parcel of the Ürziger Würzgarten, the spice garden of Ürzig, a steep vineyard of red slate above the river. Spätlese means late harvest, and the Goldkapsel, the gold capsule on the bottle, marks a richer selection within it. The list spells it Urziger Wurtzgarten; the label says Ürziger Würzgarten.

At eight years it is a pale gold. It tastes of white peach, apricot, lime, spice and slate, light in body and sweet, with electric acidity.

It is on the list because sweet Mosel Riesling is one of the few wines that survives lemon. With the Lemon Tart it stays bright against yuzu and meringue, and with the French toast it cuts the mascarpone and meets the raspberry coulis.

Asked: What does Goldkapsel mean?

Answer: The gold capsule marks a richer, riper selection within the Spätlese.

Asked: Why Riesling with the Lemon Tart?

Answer: Its acidity is high enough to survive the lemon and yuzu; most dessert wines taste flat beside citrus.

Asked: Is it heavy?

Answer: No, it is light in body and fresh, even though it is sweet.

The list spells it Urziger Wurtzgarten; say URTS-ig-er VURTS-gar-ten. Dr. Hermann has other wines printed: an Erdener Herzlei Goldkapsel Spätlese at $110 and the Erdener Prälat Auslese half-bottle at $80, which is our glass list’s dessert Riesling. Ring by vineyard and bin 28461. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 33431, 750ml, $135. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Domaine Huet, Le Mont, Vouvray Moelleux, 2009, and point to the word moelleux. Serve it at 46 to 50°F in a small white wine glass, from an ice bucket with water. Small pours, the host last. Say: “Huet Le Mont Moelleux: honeyed Vouvray, quince and baked apple.”

Offer it to a table on the breakfast tasting celebrating something, when the Baked Apple arrives, or to a guest who loves Loire wine or Chenin Blanc. It is the step up from the Baumard; the Huet demi-sec half-bottle is the lighter choice. Say: “Huet Le Mont Moelleux is golden, honeyed Vouvray that tastes like the baked apple itself.”

Domaine Huet Le Mont Moelleux 2009 is the sweet spot bottle with the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting: bin 33431, $135.

Domaine Huet, oo-ETT, is the great estate of Vouvray, in the Touraine of the Loire Valley, and is farmed biodynamically. It makes Chenin Blanc from three famous vineyards, and Le Mont is one of them. Each year Huet decides how sweet each vineyard’s wine will be: sec is dry, demi-sec gently sweet, and moelleux, mwah-LUH, properly sweet.

At seventeen years it is golden. It tastes of honeyed quince, baked apple, chamomile and beeswax, sweet and rich, with Chenin’s fresh acidity and a long, mineral finish.

It is on the list as one of the world’s great sweet Chenin Blanc wines with age on it. With the Baked Apple, it tastes like the apple itself; it is as sweet as the brown sugar glaze, and its acidity lifts the crème fraîche and the crumble.

Asked: What does moelleux mean?

Answer: Sweet; Huet makes each vineyard dry, gently sweet or sweet depending on the year.

Asked: What grape is Vouvray?

Answer: Chenin Blanc, the Loire’s great white grape.

Asked: Is it too sweet for breakfast?

Answer: It is sweet, but its acidity keeps it fresh; a small glass with the Baked Apple is lovely, and it is a fine way to celebrate.

Huet Le Mont comes in three styles on the list: sec, demi-sec and this moelleux; only the moelleux and demi-sec go with dessert. The same moelleux is printed twice, on the Loire page and under dessert wines, both bin 33431 at $135. Ring by style and vintage. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it when a table orders the Pineapple Tarte Tatin and wants something special, or to a guest curious about Austrian wine. It suits a guest who likes tropical fruit and a creamy texture. Kracher Cuvée Auslese 2017 is the sweet spot bottle with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin: bin 19234, $190.

Kracher, KRAH-ker, is the most famous sweet wine house in Austria, at Illmitz on the eastern shore of the Neusiedlersee in Burgenland. The lake is wide and shallow, and its autumn mists help the grapes ripen and concentrate. Alois Kracher made the estate’s name around the world, and his son Gerhard runs it today. The Cuvée Auslese blends Welschriesling with Chardonnay, fermented and kept in steel to stay fresh; how much of each grape went into the 2017 is a question for the sommelier.

In the glass it is bright gold. It tastes of pear, quince, mandarin, passion fruit and orange blossom honey, creamy, sweet, with fresh acidity.

It is on the list for its tropical richness: with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin it echoes the charred pineapple and the sweet condensed milk anglaise.

Asked: What does Auslese mean?

Answer: A selection of very ripe grapes, here made into a sweet wine.

Asked: What grapes?

Answer: Welschriesling and Chardonnay, a Kracher signature blend.

Asked: Is it like Sauternes?

Answer: Both are sweet and golden, but this is fresher and more tropical, kept in steel rather than oak, so the fruit stays bright beside the pineapple.

Bin 19234 is printed for this Kracher and for two other dessert wines, a Calera Viognier Doux half at $90 and a Vin Santo half at $120; ring it by name and tell the sommelier about the clash. This wine is usually bottled in halves, so the size is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say Château Climens, Barsac, 2010. Serve it at 48 to 52°F in a small white wine glass, from an ice bucket with water. Small pours, the guests first and the host last. Say: “Château Climens: all Sémillon Barsac, candied lemon and honey.”

Offer it with the Lemon Tart when a guest wants something grander than the Riesling, to a lover of Sauternes, or for a celebration dessert. Bring up the noble rot story; guests enjoy it. Say: “Château Climens is the great Barsac, all Sémillon: candied lemon and honey, fresh enough for the Lemon Tart.”

Château Climens 2010 is the sweet spot bottle with the Lemon Tart: bin 192821, $200.

Barsac is the village next to Sauternes in Bordeaux, on lower, limestone ground, and its sweet wines are known for a lifted freshness. Château Climens, klee-MAHNS, is a first growth of Barsac in the 1855 classification of sweet wines, farmed biodynamically. Unusually, it makes its wine from Sémillon alone. The grapes are picked by hand in several passes once noble rot has shriveled and concentrated them, and the wine is aged in oak.

At sixteen years it is deep gold. It tastes of candied lemon, apricot, pineapple, honey and saffron, sweet and rich, but with a freshness that keeps it lively.

It is on the list as one of the great sweet wines of Bordeaux, and it suits the Lemon Tart because its citrus meets the yuzu and lemon jelly, and its honey loves the toasted meringue.

Asked: What is noble rot?

Answer: A mold that shrivels ripe grapes in misty autumns, concentrating their sugar and flavor; it makes Sauternes and Barsac.

Asked: Is Barsac the same as Sauternes?

Answer: Barsac is a village inside the Sauternes area that may use either name; its wines tend to be a little fresher.

Asked: Why only Sémillon?

Answer: It is Climens’s way; most neighbors add Sauvignon Blanc.

Climens is Barsac, not Sauternes; say Barsac. The Suduiraut Sauternes 2010 at $230 is the nearest mix-up, the same year and close in price. The list prints Premier Cru Classé; that is correct for Climens. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say Inniskillin, Cabernet Franc Icewine, 2015. Serve it at 46 to 50°F in a small dessert glass, from an ice bucket with water. Small pours, the guests first and the host last. Say: “Inniskillin red icewine: frozen Cabernet Franc, strawberry and raspberry.”

Offer it with the Blackberry Trifle when a table wants something memorable, to a guest who has never tried icewine, or to a celebration that loves a story. Explain the frozen grapes; guests love it. Say: “Inniskillin’s red icewine is made from Cabernet Franc frozen on the vine: strawberry and raspberry, sweet and bright.”

Inniskillin Cabernet Franc Icewine 2015 is the sweet spot bottle with the Blackberry Trifle: bin 192231, $225.

Icewine is made from grapes left on the vine into winter, picked while frozen and pressed while still frozen. The water stays behind as ice, and only a few drops of very sweet, concentrated juice come out. Inniskillin, in-ih-SKIL-in, founded by Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser on the Niagara Peninsula of Ontario, made Canadian icewine famous around the world. Most icewine is white; this is a rare red, from Cabernet Franc. The list spells Peninsula with a double n.

It is pale ruby. It tastes of strawberry, raspberry, red cherry and rhubarb with candied fruit, intensely sweet with vivid acidity.

It is on the list as a conversation piece and a great match for berries. With the Blackberry Trifle, its red berry fruit echoes the blackberry curd, and its acidity stays fresh beside the lemon curd and coconut.

Asked: Is it really made from frozen grapes?

Answer: Yes, picked and pressed while frozen in the Canadian winter, so only the sweetest juice comes out.

Asked: Why is it pink?

Answer: It is made from a red grape, Cabernet Franc, so it has a pale ruby color.

Asked: Why is it so expensive?

Answer: Frozen grapes give tiny amounts of juice, and picking in the winter cold is hard work.

Icewine is usually bottled in small sizes, often 375ml; the list prints 750ml, so the size is a lineup question before you quote it. The list spells Peninsula with a double n. It is very sweet: small pours. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Trimbach, TRIM-bahk, is a great family house at Ribeauvillé in Alsace, the French region on the Rhine border with Germany. It is best known for bone dry Riesling, but in the finest years it also makes Vendanges Tardives, vahn-DAHNZH tar-DEEV, late harvest wines from grapes left long on the vine to ripen and concentrate. The list files this one under Gewurztraminer, the most perfumed grape of Alsace, and spells it Vendages Tardives.

At nineteen years it is deep gold. It tastes of lychee, rose, candied ginger, cinnamon, baked apple and honey, rich, sweet and full, with a gently fresh finish.

It is on the list for a celebration dessert and for the guest who loves aromatic wines. With the Baked Apple, its warm spice and ripe fruit echo the oat, pecan and raisin crumble and the brown sugar glaze.

Asked: What does Vendanges Tardives mean?

Answer: Late harvest: the grapes stay on the vine long after the normal harvest to ripen and concentrate.

Asked: What does Gewurztraminer taste like?

Answer: Very perfumed: lychee, rose and spice; late harvest makes it rich and sweet.

Asked: Isn’t Trimbach known for dry wines?

Answer: Yes, for dry Riesling; the Vendanges Tardives are their rare sweet wines.

The list spells it Vendages Tardives and names no grape; it sits on the Gewurztraminer page, and the grape is a lineup question. Another Trimbach Vendanges Tardive, the 2000 at $145, is printed; ring by vintage and bin 29958. Trimbach’s dry wines nearby are not for dessert. wines.name: Giuseppe Quintarelli Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997
wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 19321, 750ml, $500. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: Show the label and say Giuseppe Quintarelli, Recioto della Valpolicella, 1997. Stand it upright ahead and decant it just before pouring, leaving the sediment. Serve it at 60 to 63°F in small red wine glasses, small pours, the host last. Say: “Quintarelli Recioto 1997: sweet red from dried grapes, cherry and fig.”

Offer it to a guest who loves Italian wine and is celebrating, to a collector who knows the Quintarelli name, or with the Blackberry Trifle for a table that wants something unforgettable. Explain that it is a sweet red, which surprises many guests. Say: “Quintarelli’s Recioto is sweet red wine from dried grapes, by a Valpolicella legend: dark cherry, fig and chocolate.”

Giuseppe Quintarelli Recioto della Valpolicella 1997 is the celebration bottle with the Blackberry Trifle: bin 19321, $500.

Giuseppe Quintarelli was the great traditionalist of Valpolicella, working in the hills above Negrar, near Verona, and his family carries on the estate. Its Amarone and Recioto, made from dried grapes, are among Italy’s most sought after wines. Recioto, reh-CHOH-toh, is the region’s old sweet red: Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella and other local grapes are laid out to dry for months, pressed, and fermented until the wine is rich but still sweet.

At twenty-nine years it is a deep garnet. It tastes of dark cherry, blackberry, fig, raisin, chocolate and spice, sweet and velvety, with fresh acidity.

It is on the list as a true rarity, a sweet red from a legend. With the Blackberry Trifle, its dark berry fruit echoes the blackberry curd, and it is wonderful with chocolate or blue cheese.

Asked: Is it like Amarone?

Asked: A sweet red wine?

Offer it to a table celebrating as the Bananas Foster is flambéed, to a guest born in or marking 1989, or to a Sauternes lover who wants something rare. The concrete vat story is a good one. For a younger Sauternes with the bread pudding, Suduiraut is the sweet spot. Say: “Gilette Crème de Tête 1989 is Sauternes aged for decades before release: caramel and crème brûlée with the flambé.”

Château Gilette Crème de Tête 1989 is the celebration bottle with the World Famous Bananas Foster: bin 19112, $515.

Château Gilette, zhee-LET, is a tiny estate at Preignac, in Sauternes, run by the Médeville family. It does something no other Sauternes estate does: it holds its wine for many years in small concrete vats, protected from air, and bottles and releases it only when it is ready, often two decades after the harvest. Crème de Tête, the cream of the top, is its best selection, Sémillon with a little Sauvignon Blanc. It was not ranked in 1855, and needs no ranking.

At thirty-seven years it is amber gold. It tastes of crème brûlée, caramel, dried apricot, orange peel and saffron, sweet, with a surprising freshness.

It is on the list as one of the great old Sauternes, and with the Bananas Foster, flambéed in butter, brown sugar and rum, its caramel depth is a match made at the table.

Asked: Why was it aged so long?

Answer: Gilette holds its wine for many years in small concrete vats and releases it only when ready; it is the estate’s tradition.

Asked: What does Crème de Tête mean?

Answer: The cream of the top: the estate’s best selection.

Asked: Will it still be sweet at thirty-seven?

Answer: Yes, sweet and rich, with caramel and apricot and a fresh finish.

Gilette is not Yquem or Suduiraut, though all three are near Preignac. It is not a classified growth; never call it a first growth. Pour it after the Bananas Foster flambé, never near the flame. Its release date is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Château d’Yquem, ee-KEM, in Sauternes, is the most famous sweet wine in the world. In the 1855 classification it was the only estate ranked Premier Cru Supérieur, above every other Sauternes, and today it is owned by LVMH. It is Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc. The pickers go through the vineyard many times, taking grapes one by one as noble rot concentrates them, and the wine is aged in new oak; in a poor year, no Yquem is made at all.

At nineteen years it is deep gold. It tastes of apricot, honey, candied orange, pineapple, vanilla and saffron, rich and sweet, with fresh acidity and an endless finish.

It is on the list as the legend, for the grandest celebration. With the bread pudding, it matches the custard and whiskey caramel in richness, and its acidity keeps every bite lively.

Asked: Why is Yquem so famous?

Offer it as an aperitif to a guest who likes sherry or nutty flavors, or with the cheese board at the Roost Bar. For the bread pudding, offer the Baumard Coteaux du Layon instead: the dessert wants a sweeter wine. Barbadillo Pale Cream is our gentlest priced sweet wine and a first pick for the cheese board: bin 29801, $50.

Sherry comes from the southwest corner of Spain, around Jerez and the seaside town of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where Bodegas Barbadillo, a family house best known for manzanilla, makes its wines. Most sherry starts dry, from the Palomino grape. A pale cream is a light, pale sherry made in the fino style and then gently sweetened, so it keeps a fresh, nutty edge.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of apricot, honey, almond and vanilla with a faint salty, nutty note, medium sweet and silky, with a soft, long finish.

It is on the list as the friendly sweet sherry: lovely chilled before dinner, and with the cheese board its salty, nutty edge meets the cheese. It is too lightly sweet for the bread pudding, which wants a sweeter wine.

Asked: Isn’t sherry dry?

Answer: Most sherry starts dry; a pale cream is a light, pale sherry that has been gently sweetened.

Asked: Do I drink it cold?

Answer: Yes, chilled, which keeps it fresh and nutty; it is lovely as an aperitif before the meal.

Asked: Is it strong?

Answer: Sherry is fortified, so it is a little stronger than table wine; small pours are the custom.

It is non-vintage; the list prints NV. Pale Cream is sweet; Barbadillo’s manzanilla, if the guest asks for it, is dry and a different wine. Serve it chilled, never at room temperature. How long an open bottle keeps is a lineup question. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer it with the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake at breakfast and lunch or The Snickers at any meal, to a guest who loves Port, or to a table that wants a sweet red to share. For a grander Port with the coffee cake, the Niepoort 1987 is the celebration. Say: “Feist LBV is twenty-year-old Port, black cherry and cocoa, sweet and supple with the chocolate.”

Feist Late Bottled Vintage Port 2006 is the value bottle with two desserts, the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and The Snickers: bin 193212, $60.

Port is the sweet fortified red of the Douro Valley in northern Portugal: grape spirit is added during fermentation, which stops it while the wine is still sweet. A Late Bottled Vintage, or LBV, comes from a single year and is aged several years in wood before bottling, so it is ready sooner than a vintage Port. Feist is an old Port house founded by two German cousins, today part of the Sogevinus group, known mostly for ruby and tawny Ports.

At twenty years this 2006 is unusually mature for an LBV. It tastes of black cherry, plum, raisin, cocoa and spice, sweet, with softened tannin.

It is on the list as the friendly Port for chocolate. Its cocoa and dark fruit meet the chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate of the coffee cake and the milk chocolate and caramel of The Snickers.

Asked: What is Late Bottled Vintage?

Answer: Port from a single year, aged several years in wood before bottling, so it drinks sooner than vintage Port.

Asked: Is it very sweet?

Answer: Sweet, but the dark fruit and softened tannin keep it balanced with chocolate.

Asked: Will it keep once open?

Answer: Port keeps longer than table wine once open; the sommelier sets the house rule.

LBV is not vintage Port; do not call it a vintage Port. The list prints Feist Late Bottled Vintage 2006; whether it is unfiltered and needs decanting is a lineup question. It pairs with two desserts, so it may already be open. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Rivesaltes, reev-SALT, is a vin doux naturel from Roussillon, in the far south of France near Perpignan and the Spanish border. Grenache and Grenache Gris are fermented, and grape spirit is added partway to stop the fermentation, leaving the wine sweet. The old wines are then aged for decades in old casks, where air slowly turns them amber and nutty. Riveyrac wines come from the cooperative cellar of Salses-le-Château, one of the oldest in the area.

At fifty-one years it is amber. It tastes of caramel, walnut, quince, marmalade, coffee and spice, sweet, with a delicate acidity that keeps it lively.

It is on the list as a half century of history at a sweet spot price. With the Bananas Foster, flambéed in butter, brown sugar and rum, its caramel and nut notes taste like the sauce itself.

Asked: What is a vin doux naturel?

Answer: A French sweet wine whose fermentation is stopped with grape spirit, keeping the grape’s sweetness, like a French cousin of Port.

Asked: Fifty-one years old, is it still good?

Answer: Cask-aged sweet wines like this last for decades; it is meant to taste of caramel and nuts.

Asked: Why is it brown?

Answer: Decades in old casks with a little air turn it amber.

Asked: What is Madeira?

Answer: The fortified wine of a Portuguese island, aged warm, so it tastes of caramel and coffee and keeps for months.

Answer: The grape of the sweetest Madeira style, also called Malmsey.

Asked: What is a single cask?

Taylor Fladgate is one of the great Port houses of the Douro Valley in Portugal, and its declared vintage Ports are among the most prized of all, built around its estate, Quinta de Vargellas. Vintage Port is made only in the finest years, which the house declares; it is bottled young and ages for decades in bottle, where it throws a crust. 1977 was a declared vintage.

At forty-nine years it is a garnet turning tawny. It tastes of dried cherry, plum, violet, fig and spice with a touch of cedar, sweet but refined, the tannin softened into a long, elegant finish.

It is on the list as a classic old vintage Port for a grand celebration. With the Cherries Jubilee, flambéed tableside, its dried cherry and spice match the black cherries and Luxardo sauce.

Answer: It is made only in declared years, the finest, and ages for decades in bottle.

Asked: How do you open such an old bottle?

Answer: Gently, with a two-prong opener or port tongs, then decanted off the crust.

wines.serviceNote: On the Binwise bottle list of 3 October 2026: bin 29088, 750ml, $3200. Confirm at lineup that it is in the cellar tonight; anything the label or the sommelier says about allergens goes to the sommelier.

kept.a: The sommelier presents it. Show the label and say Henriques & Henriques, Founder’s Solera, 1894. Serve it at 55 to 60°F in small port or Madeira glasses; it needs no decanting. Small pours, the host last, and the bottle keeps for months. Say: “Founder’s Solera 1894: Madeira from the nineteenth century, toffee and spice.”

Offer it only when a guest asks for the oldest wine on the list, loves Madeira, or is marking an extraordinary occasion. Call the sommelier over before the guest decides. Explain the solera simply. Say: “This Madeira comes from a solera begun in 1894: toffee, dried fruit and spice, with a finish that lasts minutes.”

Henriques & Henriques Founder’s Solera 1894 is a famous name in our celebration tier and the oldest date on our list: bin 29088, $3200.

Madeira is the fortified wine of a Portuguese island in the Atlantic. It is aged warm, which gives it caramel and dried fruit and makes it nearly immortal; a bottle a century old can still be vivid, and an open one keeps for months. Henriques & Henriques is a historic Madeira house on the island. Its Founder’s Solera was begun in 1894: in a solera, wine is drawn from the casks and they are refreshed with other wine over the years, so 1894 marks the start, not a single harvest.

In the glass it is dark amber with a green rim. It tastes of dried fruit, toffee, dark chocolate, spice, honey and old wood, sweet, with piercing acidity and a finish that lasts minutes.

It is on the list as history in a glass, for the guest who wants to taste the nineteenth century.

Asked: Is the wine from 1894?

Answer: The solera was begun in 1894; wine has been drawn off and the casks refreshed over the years, so it holds wine from that time onward.

Asked: How can a wine last so long?

Answer: Madeira is aged warm and fortified, which makes it nearly indestructible.

Asked: What grape is it?

Answer: The list prints Verdelho; I will confirm with the sommelier.

Never present 1894 as a vintage; it is the year the solera began. The list prints Verdelho, while the producer describes the Founder’s Solera as Malvasia, so the grape is a lineup question. At $3200, the sommelier handles it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.serviceNote: Dairy. Alcohol. It opens the Traditional Breakfast tasting. Offer it at the greeting, it’s the first sale of the morning.

kept.a: Offer the milk punch at the greeting, before the menus are even open: it is the first sale of the morning and the classic way to start. Every guest on the Traditional Breakfast gets one; for the others, it sets the mood. Next rounds are the Bloody Bull at $13 or, with dessert, the Irish Coffee at $12. Say: “Can I start you with a Brandy Milk Punch? It's our classic New Orleans eye opener: brandy, cream, vanilla and nutmeg.”
No house recipe page for the Brandy Milk Punch is published; quote the four menu ingredients only: brandy, heavy cream, vanilla bean, nutmeg.

The Brandy Milk Punch is a Brennan's signature drink, $12 at breakfast and lunch, and the eye opener that begins the Traditional Breakfast.

In New Orleans a proper breakfast starts with an eye opener, and the milk punch is the classic. The menu prints four things: brandy, heavy cream, vanilla bean and nutmeg. The bar shakes the brandy with the cream and real vanilla bean, serves it cold, and finishes it with nutmeg on top. No house recipe is published, so the server quotes those four and no measures.

The guest gets a cold, pale, creamy drink with the nutmeg dusted over it. It tastes creamy, smooth and a little sweet, gently boozy: think of a lighter, boozier eggnog without the egg.

It is the first sale of the morning, offered at the greeting, and the opening course of the $80 tasting, before the baked apple. For a guest who skips it, the Café Glacé de la Maison takes its place without alcohol.

Asked: What is an eye opener?

Answer: The New Orleans tradition of a drink to start breakfast. The Brandy Milk Punch is the classic one.

Asked: What is in it?

Answer: Brandy, heavy cream, vanilla bean and nutmeg, shaken and served cold. The house does not publish measures, so that is all I quote.

Asked: Is it like eggnog?

Answer: A lighter, boozier eggnog without the egg: creamy, smooth and a little sweet.

On the Traditional Breakfast the milk punch is included as course one: never charge it, and pour it at the greeting so the tasting starts on time. Quote only the four menu ingredients; no house recipe is published. Watch the table's intake across the tasting, and offer the Café Glacé de la Maison to a guest who skips alcohol. Do not confuse it with the Prisoner of Love on the fall list, a gin drink made with clarified heavy cream. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

The Bloody Bull is a Brennan's signature drink, $13 at breakfast and lunch, and the drink poured with the soup course on the Traditional Breakfast.

It is a Bloody Mary with beef bouillon stirred in: vodka, our housemade Bloody Mary mix and bouillon, a clear, savory beef broth. The guide calls it a Brennan's breakfast classic, and that is how a server says it. Where it was first made is not something we tell as fact: a guest who asks gets a manager's answer, never a claim that it was invented here.

The guest gets a deep red, savory drink. It tastes savory, rich and meaty, almost like a spicy, chilled consommé, with the spice of the house mix.

It is wonderful with the turtle soup, which is why the tasting pairs them. For a guest who would rather not have beef, the Brennan's Bloody Mary at $11, with pickled okra and spicy beans, is the classic alternative.

Asked: What makes it a Bull?

Answer: Beef bouillon, a clear, savory beef broth, stirred into a Bloody Mary with our housemade mix and vodka.

Asked: Was it invented here?

Asked: Is it spicy?

It carries beef: say so plainly, and offer the Brennan's Bloody Mary to a guest who skips beef, asking the bar about the mix. cocktails.name: Classic Sazerac
cocktails.serviceNote: Spirit-forward and strong, served without ice (confirm the glass and the bar’s build). Upsells: Thompson’s Dream ($20, Willett 4-year rye, Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, St. George absinthe rinse) and Origin Story ($40, Dudognon Cognac, barrel-aged Peychaud’s, Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe). Herbsaint is ERB-saint.

kept.a: Offer the Sazerac to whiskey drinkers, to anyone who asks for a New Orleans cocktail, and before dinner. Then climb the ladder: Thompson's Dream at $20 for a richer rye, Origin Story at $40 for the Cognac original. Say: “The Sazerac is New Orleans' official cocktail: Sazerac rye and Peychaud's bitters, in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint.” For a curious guest, describe all three rungs and let them choose.

The Classic Sazerac is a Brennan's signature drink, $13 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and New Orleans' own cocktail.

The Louisiana Legislature named it the official cocktail of New Orleans in 2008: the city's, not the state's. Ours is Sazerac rye whiskey stirred with Peychaud's, PAY-shoze, the bright red New Orleans bitters with anise and cherry notes, and served without ice in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint, ERB-sant, the anise liqueur created in New Orleans in 1934. The rinse gives its aroma without much of its flavor. Sugar and lemon peel are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, amber, iceless drink with an anise perfume. It tastes spirit-forward, spicy and aromatic, and strong.

It is the first rung of the house's Sazerac ladder: $13, then Thompson's Dream at $20 with Willett rye, then Origin Story at $40 with Cognac and absinthe, the way the first Sazeracs were made. It suits the guest before dinner or with the steak.

Asked: Is it really the official cocktail?

Answer: Yes, of the city of New Orleans, named by the Louisiana Legislature in 2008; the city's, not the state's.

Asked: What is Herbsaint?

Answer: ERB-sant: an anise liqueur created in New Orleans in 1934. It is only a rinse in the glass, for aroma.

Asked: Can I have it on the rocks?

Answer: It is served without ice. I will check with the bar before promising it on the rocks.

kept.q: What is the classic Sazerac build, and is it ours?
kept.a: The Classic Sazerac at Brennan's is Sazerac rye stirred with Peychaud's bitters, served without ice in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint (ERB-saint), $13; confirm sugar and lemon peel with the bar. The Sazerac Company's own recipe is a sugar cube, three dashes of Peychaud's, an ounce and a half of Sazerac Rye, a quarter ounce of Herbsaint and a lemon peel, built across two glasses and served neat in a chilled rocks glass; the IBA version is Cognac based with absinthe. Give those as the classic, never as the house build. If a guest asks for it on the rocks, check with the bar before promising it. Two luxury versions: Thompson's Dream with Willett rye, and Origin Story with Cognac and absinthe; the price ladder is $13, $20 and $40.

It is strong and served without ice: confirm the glass and the bar's build, sugar and lemon peel included, at lineup. Give the Sazerac Company's recipe only as the classic, never as our house build. Never say America's first cocktail. Say Herbsaint without the H. Pronounce Peychaud's PAY-shoze, and confirm the pharmacy story at lineup before telling it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.q: What story can I tell at the table?
kept.a: Three short ones, each true. First, the bitters: Antoine Peychaud kept his apothecary at what is now 437 Royal Street, the same block as ours at 417, as the Sazerac Company tells it; the house has not said it wants that told, so check at lineup first. Second, the bottles: Sazerac rye, Peychaud's and Herbsaint are all Sazerac Company brands, one New Orleans family in one glass. Third, the name Herbsaint comes from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood; it was created in 1934 to stand in for absinthe, banned from 1912 until 2007. If a guest tells you Peychaud served it in an egg cup and so gave us the word cocktail, smile: the word was in print in 1806. Never call it America's first cocktail.

cocktails.name: Brennan’s Irish Coffee
cocktails.serviceNote: Dairy; caffeine; alcohol. On both the breakfast/lunch menu and the dessert menu. Pair with dessert as an upsell.

kept.a: The bar builds the Irish Coffee; you present it. Carry it level so the cream cap stays whole, set it down with the handle toward the guest's right hand, and name it as it lands. Do not stir it: the point is to sip the hot coffee through the cool cream. If the table is having Bananas Foster, bring it just before the flambé, never set down beside the flame. Say: “Here's our Irish Coffee: sip it through the cream, don't stir it.”

Offer the Irish Coffee as dessert arrives, above all with Bananas Foster or the bread pudding, and to a guest lingering after a meal. Next rounds: Ralph's Coffee at $8.00 for a gentler coffee with nut liqueurs, the Espresso Martini at $16.00, or our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory at $11 without whiskey. Say: “With the Foster, our Irish Coffee is lovely: chicory coffee, brown sugar and Tullamore D.E.W. under whipped cream.”

Brennan's Irish Coffee is a signature drink, $12 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: an Irish coffee with a New Orleans accent.

It starts with our dark roast coffee with chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, roasted chicory root blended in the New Orleans way, which adds a roasty, almost chocolatey depth. It is sweetened with brown sugar, spiked with Tullamore D.E.W. Irish whiskey, whose initials are those of Daniel E. Williams, the distillery's manager who became its owner, and topped with whipped cream.

The guest gets a warm coffee under a cool white cap of cream, and sips the hot coffee through it. It tastes warm, sweet and smooth, roasty from the chicory.

It is the dessert upsell, on the breakfast and lunch menu and on the dessert menu: the natural partner for Bananas Foster or the bread pudding. For a guest who wants coffee without whiskey, our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory is the same roast on its own.

Asked: What makes it Brennan's?

Answer: Our dark roast coffee with chicory, the New Orleans tradition, sweetened with brown sugar.

Asked: What whiskey is in it?

Answer: Tullamore D.E.W. Irish whiskey; the initials are those of Daniel E. Williams, the distillery's manager who became its owner.

Asked: Can I have it without alcohol?

Answer: Our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory is the same roast without the whiskey.

It is served hot with a cream cap: carry it level and set it down with the handle toward the guest. It carries caffeine and whiskey. For a guest avoiding alcohol, offer the plain coffee with chicory, which still carries caffeine; for a guest avoiding caffeine, offer the Revive Cold-Pressed Juice, or say “I will ask the bar about decaf.” Fire it with dessert so it arrives with the Foster, not after. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.q: Where does Irish coffee come from?
kept.a: Irish coffee is credited to Joe Sheridan, the chef at the Foynes flying boat terminal in County Limerick, in the winter of 1942 to 1943, warming passengers off a flight turned back by weather. The Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco recreated it in 1952, and it pours Tullamore D.E.W., the whiskey in ours. Our accent is the chicory coffee and the brown sugar. Tell it in two sentences as the glass lands.

cocktails.name: Flamingo

kept.a: In the Roost, offer the Flamingo to anyone celebrating, a couple toasting, or a guest who loves Champagne but wants a cocktail. From the dining room, invite them to the bar: it is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge. Next rounds in the Roost: the Spoonbill at $36.00 or the Birdcage at $31.00. Say: “For a celebration, the Flamingo is Chopin vodka and Monkey 47 gin with dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger Champagne.”

The Flamingo is one of the three luxury cocktails poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, at $28.00, and the Roost's celebration drink.

It pairs Chopin, SHOH-pan, a Polish potato vodka, smooth and round, with Monkey 47, a Black Forest gin bottled at 47 percent with a big botanical lift, then dragonfruit, fresh lemon and Taittinger La Française Champagne, from one of the great Champagne houses. The page prints those five parts; measures, glass and garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a bright, festive glass with fine bubbles. It tastes bright, fruity and dry: citrus and gin botanicals under fine Champagne bubbles, celebratory from the first sip.

It is the drink for an anniversary or a birthday when the guest wants a cocktail rather than a glass of Rare, and a fine reason to start or end the evening in the Roost. Because it is poured only there, a dining room server mentions it as an invitation to the Roost Bar, never as a drink to bring to the table.

Asked: Can I have it at my table in the dining room?

Answer: The Flamingo is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge; it is a lovely reason to visit the bar before or after dinner.

Asked: Which Champagne is in it?

Answer: Taittinger La Française, from one of the great Champagne houses.

Asked: What is Monkey 47?

Answer: A gin from Germany's Black Forest made with 47 botanicals and bottled at 47 percent: that is the 47.

It is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge: never promise it at a dining room table. Say Taittinger as teh-tan-ZHAY (TAT-in-jer is often heard) and Chopin as SHOH-pan. Confirm at lineup that it is still on the luxury page, and its measures, glass and garnish. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Birdcage

kept.a: In the Roost, offer the Birdcage to an Old Fashioned or bourbon drinker, and as a nightcap after dinner. From the dining room, invite a whiskey lover to the Roost for it. Next rounds in the Roost: the Spoonbill at $36.00 or the Flamingo at $28.00. Say: “Our Birdcage is a smoked Old Fashioned on Rabbit Hole Dareringer bourbon, with Angostura, orange and cherry: rich, smoky and smooth.”

The Birdcage is one of the three luxury cocktails poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, at $31.00: our smoked Old Fashioned.

It is built on Rabbit Hole Dareringer, DAIR-ring-er, a Kentucky straight bourbon from Louisville finished in PX sherry casks, so it carries dried fruit and a little extra richness. It is made with Angostura bitters, the classic aromatic bitters of an Old Fashioned, orange and cherry, then smoked, so the first thing the guest meets is the aroma. How the bar smokes it, and the glass and garnish, are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, amber drink, wrapped in smoke. It tastes of rich bourbon with dried fruit from the sherry cask, bitters, orange and cherry, under the smoke: rich, smoky and smooth.

It is the Old Fashioned drinker's step up and a slow nightcap for the guest who moves to the Roost after dinner. From the dining room it is an invitation to the bar, never an upsell at the table.

Asked: How is it smoked?

Answer: The page does not say, so I will check with the bar and tell you how they do it tonight.

Asked: What is Dareringer?

Answer: Rabbit Hole Dareringer, a Kentucky straight bourbon from Louisville finished in PX sherry casks, so it carries dried fruit and richness.

Asked: Is it a strong drink?

Answer: It is an Old Fashioned, spirit-forward and made for slow sipping.

It is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge: never offer it at a dining room table. How it is smoked, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. It is spirit-forward: pace a guest who has had several drinks. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: In the Roost, offer the Spoonbill to a martini or gin drinker, and at the start of a celebration. From the dining room, a Prisoner of Love drinker is the guest to invite up for it. Next rounds in the Roost: the Flamingo at $28.00 or the Birdcage at $31.00. Say: “The Spoonbill is Hendrick's gin with a Corsican quinquina and chive oil, served with a spoon of caviar.”

The Spoonbill is the grandest of the three luxury cocktails poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, at $36.00.

It is Hendrick's, HEN-dricks, a Scottish gin with cucumber and rose, with Cap Corse Mattei Blanc, kap KORS mah-TAY, a Corsican quinquina, kan-kee-NAH: a wine aperitif with a gentle bitterness from the same bark that gives tonic water its bite. Chive oil adds a savory, green note, and the drink comes with a spoon of caviar. Which caviar, how much and the glass are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a cool, pale drink and the little spoon of caviar beside it. It tastes of cool cucumber and rose from the gin, a gentle bitter wine note, savory green chive, then the salt of the caviar.

It is a martini drinker's treat, and the caviar makes it a moment, so it suits the start of a celebration. It is poured only in the Roost; from the dining room, it is the grand gin drink to invite a guest up for.

Asked: What is a quinquina?

Answer: Kan-kee-NAH: a wine aperitif with a gentle bitterness, from the same bark that gives tonic water its bite. Ours is Cap Corse Mattei Blanc, from Corsica.

Asked: Which caviar comes with it?

Answer: The page says a spoon of caviar; I will check with the bar which caviar and how much.

Asked: Is it like a martini?

Answer: A savory cousin: gin and an aperitif wine, with chive oil and the caviar alongside.

It is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge: never offer it at a dining room table. Which caviar, how much, and the glass are lineup questions for the bar; do not describe the caviar until you know. Say Cap Corse Mattei as kap KORS mah-TAY. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Thompson’s Dream

kept.a: Offer Thompson's Dream to a guest ordering a second Sazerac, and to a rye lover who wants more spice. It sits between the Classic at $13 and Origin Story at $40. Next rounds: Origin Story, or Rumors are Flying at $20.00, our barrel-aged rye with tart cherry. Say: “If you loved the Sazerac, Thompson's Dream is the next rung: Willett rye, Creole bitters and a St. George absinthe rinse.”

Thompson's Dream is the middle rung of our Sazerac ladder, $20 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: our Sazerac stepped up.

The guide prints it inside the Classic Sazerac's service note with its build and price. It is Willett 4-year rye, WILL-it, from a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, founded in 1936, which runs spicier and stronger than the classic's rye; Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, made in Munich as a tribute to the New Orleans style; and a glass rinsed with St. George absinthe, the first American absinthe made legally after the old ban. No measures, glass or garnish are printed; the build follows the Classic, confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, iceless, amber drink like the Classic, with a greener perfume. It tastes of louder rye spice and more heat, with a more herbal rinse.

The name is the house's own; no Willett bottling carries it, so a server says it is probably named for Thompson Willett, the distillery's founder. It is the drink to offer whenever a guest orders a second Sazerac.

Asked: Who is Thompson?

Answer: The name is the house's own. It is probably named for Thompson Willett, who founded the Willett distillery in Bardstown; I would not say more until the bar confirms it.

Asked: How is it different from the Classic Sazerac?

Answer: Willett 4-year rye instead of Sazerac rye, Bitter Truth Creole Bitters instead of Peychaud's, and a St. George absinthe rinse instead of Herbsaint: spicier and bolder.

Asked: What is St. George absinthe?

Answer: A Californian absinthe, the first American one made legally after the old ban.

Say probably named for Thompson Willett, never as a fact, until the bar confirms it. No measures, glass or garnish are printed: confirm them, the Willett bottling and its proof at lineup; the current menu lists it under Sazerac Selections. The Birdcage is a Roost Bar drink, never an upsell at the table. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Origin Story

kept.a: Offer Origin Story at the top of the Sazerac conversation, to a Cognac lover, at the Chateaubriand table, and after the dinner tasting. Tell the story: it is the way the drink began. Next rounds: Thompson's Dream at $20, or the Irish Coffee at $12 to close. Say: “Origin Story is the Sazerac the way it began, on Cognac: Dudognon, barrel-aged Peychaud's and Jade absinthe.”

Origin Story is the top of our Sazerac ladder, $40 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, the highest cocktail price the guide prints.

It is the Sazerac the way it began. The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's; rye took over once phylloxera made Cognac scarce in the 1870s and 1880s. So it is built on Dudognon, doo-doh-NYOHN, a family Cognac estate in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first growth, with Peychaud's bitters rested in a barrel and Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe, created by a New Orleans native as a tribute to the city's old absinthe houses. Which Dudognon, and who ages the bitters, are lineup questions.

The guest gets a short, iceless, deep amber drink. It tastes rounder than the Classic: grape, dried fruit and oak, a softer bitters note and a floral wormwood aroma.

It is the drink for the Chateaubriand table, for a guest celebrating, and for the curious drinker who wants to taste where the Sazerac started.

Asked: Why Cognac?

Answer: The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's. Rye took over once phylloxera made Cognac scarce in the 1870s and 1880s.

Asked: What is Dudognon?

Answer: Doo-doh-NYOHN: a family Cognac estate in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first growth.

Asked: What makes the bitters barrel-aged?

Answer: The Peychaud's is rested in a barrel. Who ages it and in what cask is a lineup question, so I will check with the bar.

Say the way it began, never the way it was first made. Which Dudognon expression, who barrel-ages the Peychaud's, and the measures are lineup questions; the current menu lists it under Sazerac Selections, misspelled Orgin Story, so say Origin Story. At $40, name the price when you offer it. The Birdcage is a Roost Bar drink, never an upsell at the table. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Brennan’s Bloody Mary

kept.a: Offer the Bloody Mary to a guest who wants a savory eye opener but no beef, and to anyone who orders a Bloody Mary by name. For a guest who wants it richer, the Bloody Bull at $13.00; for a sweeter start, the Brandy Milk Punch at $12.00; without alcohol, the Revive cold-pressed juice at $10.00. Say: “Our Bloody Mary is vodka and our housemade mix with pickled okra and spicy beans: savory, tangy and bright.”

Brennan's Bloody Mary is one of the classic eye openers, $11.00 at breakfast and lunch, the morning drinks New Orleans is known for.

The menu prints four parts: our housemade Bloody Mary mix, vodka, pickled okra and spicy beans. The Bloody Bull's menu line prints a housemade Bloody Mary mix too, with beef bouillon added; whether it is the same batch is a question for the bar, with which vodka, how hot the mix runs today and the glass.

The guest gets a red, savory drink with the pickled okra and spicy beans standing in it. It tastes savory, tangy and spicy, with a pickled crunch.

It is the eye opener for a guest who skips the beef in the Bloody Bull, our other Bloody classic, which is the same idea with beef bouillon stirred in for a richer, meatier drink. For a guest who wants a morning drink without alcohol, the Revive cold-pressed juice takes its place.

Asked: How is it different from the Bloody Bull?

Answer: The Bloody Bull has beef bouillon stirred into its housemade mix; the Bloody Mary does not, and it comes with pickled okra and spicy beans.

Asked: How spicy is it?

Answer: That depends on the mix; I will check with the bar how it is running today.

Asked: Which vodka do you use?

Answer: The menu prints vodka without naming it, so I will check with the bar.

The menu prints the mix as housemade, but not the vodka or the heat: those are lineup questions for the bar. It is the alternative for a guest who skips beef; for any guest asking exactly what is in the mix, the bar answers, not the server. It is poured at breakfast and lunch only. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Brennan’s Champagne Cocktail

kept.a: Present the Champagne Cocktail the moment it leaves the bar, while the bubbles are still rising from the sugar cube: carry it by the stem or the base and set it down at the guest's right. Name it as it lands, and for a celebration toast the occasion in a word. If the bar finishes it at the table, stand back and let the guest watch the fizz climb from the cube. Say: “Here's our Champagne Cocktail: watch the bubbles rise from the sugar. Congratulations.”

Offer the Champagne Cocktail at Bubbles to anyone celebrating, to a couple in the courtyard, and on a Friday before the sabering. For a lighter round, the Riviera at $12.00 or the Chandon Garden Spritz at $15.00; in the Roost, the step up is the Flamingo at $28.00 or the Spoonbill at $36.00. Say: “Our Champagne Cocktail is the classic: Champagne over a sugar cube and Angostura bitters, festive and dry; on Fridays at five, stay for the sabering.”

Brennan's Champagne Cocktail is the house's bubbly classic at Bubbles at Brennan's, $20.00, our afternoon Champagne service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, where it now sits beside four newer bubbly cocktails.

The menu prints three parts: Champagne, Angostura bitters, ang-guh-STOO-ruh, and a demerara sugar cube. That is the classic build, printed back in 1862: the cube is soaked in bitters, set in the glass, and the Champagne poured over it. Which Champagne, the glass and any garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a glass of Champagne with a steady stream of bubbles rising from the cube. It tastes dry and festive, with a soft spice from the bitters and a faint sweetness as the sugar dissolves.

It is the drink to offer anyone celebrating and a couple in the courtyard, and the grandest of the Bubbles cocktails. Champagne is sabered on Fridays at 5 pm, as the menu prints, and the hours are confirmed on shift.

Asked: What is in it?

Answer: Champagne poured over a demerara sugar cube with Angostura bitters, the classic build. Which Champagne we are pouring tonight, I will check with the bar.

Asked: When is the sabering?

Answer: Fridays at 5 pm, as the menu prints; I confirm it with the host stand each Friday.

Asked: When is Bubbles?

Answer: The menu prints Monday to Friday, 2 to 6 pm, in the Roost Bar and the courtyard; the hours are confirmed on shift.

Which Champagne is poured and the glass are not printed: confirm them with the bar before you name a house. The Bubbles hours are disputed between the menu and an older listing: confirm on shift, and check the courtyard is not privately booked. Do not confuse it with the Chandon Garden Spritz, which is sparkling wine, not Champagne. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Riviera

kept.a: Present the Riviera the moment it leaves the bar, while it is still sparkling: carry it by the stem or the base, set it down at the guest's right and name it as it lands. In the courtyard, keep the tray out of the direct sun. If the bar tops it at the table, let the guest see the wine go in. Say: “Here's your Riviera: Lillet, sparkling wine and lemon, light and bright.”

Offer the Riviera to a guest settling into the courtyard or the Roost at Bubbles, to a light drinker, and as the first round before the Friday sabering. Next rounds: the Chandon Garden Spritz at $15.00 for something bittersweet, Brennan's Champagne Cocktail at $20.00, or the OBX at $12.00 for gin and peach. Say: “The Riviera is Lillet Blanc, sparkling wine and lemon: light, floral and lovely in the afternoon.”

The Riviera is one of the bubbly cocktails at Bubbles at Brennan's, our afternoon Champagne service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, at $12.00.

The menu prints Lillet Blanc, sparkling wine and lemon, though it spells the aperitif Lilet; the bottle is Lillet, lee-LAY BLAHN, a light French aperitif wine, floral and citrusy. Which sparkling wine, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a pale, sparkling drink. It tastes light and bright: the Lillet's floral, citrusy notes, lifted by the bubbles and the lemon.

It is the easy afternoon drink, gentler than a spirit cocktail and a little more interesting than a plain glass of bubbles. The name calls up the sunny Mediterranean coast, and it suits the courtyard. The same Lillet appears on the fall list in To Each His Own, with Calvados and quince.

Asked: What is Lillet?

Answer: Lee-LAY: a light French aperitif wine, floral and citrusy.

Asked: Is it strong?

Answer: No, it is the gentle one: an aperitif wine with sparkling wine and lemon.

Asked: When is Bubbles?

Answer: The menu prints Monday to Friday, 2 to 6 pm, in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, with Champagne sabering on Fridays at 5 pm; I confirm the hours on shift.

The menu spells it Lilet; say and write Lillet. The Bodrum is the creamy drink among the bubbly cocktails at Bubbles at Brennan's, our afternoon service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, at $12.00. It carries the name of a seaside resort town, and the menu says no more about it.

The menu prints rum, pistachio, cream, lime and sparkling water. Which rum, how the pistachio goes in, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a creamy drink with a light sparkle. It tastes nutty and smooth from the pistachio and cream, with rum underneath and lime keeping it bright; the sparkling water lightens it.

It is the drink for a rum lover, and for a guest who wants something different at Bubbles rather than another glass of wine. It is the one bubbly cocktail made with sparkling water rather than sparkling wine, so it is a good choice for a guest who does not care for wine.

Asked: What does it taste like?

Answer: Creamy and nutty from the pistachio and cream, bright with lime, with a light fizz from the sparkling water.

Answer: The menu does not name it; I will check with the bar.

Asked: What is Bodrum?

It carries pistachio and cream, as printed: read the service note and confirm at lineup before answering any question about nuts or cream. kept.a: Bring the OBX straight from the bar while the Bigaro is still lively: hold it low on the stem or by the base, place it at the guest's right, and say the three letters as it lands. Out in the courtyard, shade the tray on a bright afternoon. If the bar finishes it at the table, step back so the guest can watch the sparkling wine go in. Say: “Your OBX: Gentilly gin, peach and lemon, under a gently sweet Italian sparkle.”

Offer the OBX at Bubbles to a gin drinker, to a guest who likes peach, and to a table in the courtyard on a warm afternoon. Next rounds: the Riviera at $12.00 for something lighter, the Chandon Garden Spritz at $15.00 for bittersweet orange, or in the Roost the Spoonbill at $36.00. Say: “The OBX is Gentilly gin with peach and lemon, topped with a gently sweet Italian sparkling wine.”

The OBX is the gin drink among the bubbly cocktails at Bubbles at Brennan's, our afternoon service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, at $12.00. OBX is the common shorthand for the barrier islands of North Carolina, a beach name for a courtyard drink.

The menu prints Gentilly Gin, peach, lemon and Elio Perrone Bigaro, EL-yoh peh-ROH-neh bee-gah-ROH, a softly sparkling pink wine from Piedmont, Brachetto and Moscato, gently sweet and low in alcohol. Who makes the Gentilly gin, how the peach goes in, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a sparkling, fruity drink. It tastes of ripe peach and lemon over the gin, with the soft sweetness and fizz of the Bigaro.

It is the drink for a gin lover at Bubbles, and for a guest who likes fruit in a glass of bubbles. A guest who loves it and wants to go grander can follow it with our Champagne Cocktail or, in the Roost, the Spoonbill, our luxury gin drink.

Asked: What does OBX mean?

Answer: It is the common shorthand for the barrier islands of North Carolina; the menu says no more about the name.

Asked: What is Bigaro?

Answer: Bee-gah-ROH: an Italian sparkling wine from Elio Perrone in Piedmont, gently sweet. I will ask the sommelier for more if you are curious.

Asked: Who makes the gin?

Answer: The menu prints Gentilly Gin without the distiller; I will check with the bar.

Say the letters, oh-bee-EX. The Bigaro is gently sweet, so tell a guest who wants a dry drink and offer the Riviera instead. Who makes the Gentilly gin, the measures and the glass are lineup questions for the bar, and the Bubbles hours are confirmed on shift. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Chandon Garden Spritz

kept.a: Set the Garden Spritz down as soon as the bar hands it over, while it is still lively: carry it by the base or the stem and give the name as it reaches the guest's right side. If the bar tops it at the table, hold the tray steady and let the guest watch the bubbles meet the orange. Say: “Your Chandon Garden Spritz: Chandon Brut and bitter orange, bright and bittersweet. Enjoy the afternoon.”

Offer the Chandon Garden Spritz at Bubbles to a guest who loves a spritz or an aperitivo, before dinner, and with the Cheese Board. Next rounds: Brennan's Champagne Cocktail at $20.00, the Riviera at $12.00 for something lighter, or in the Roost the Flamingo at $28.00. Say: “Our Chandon Garden Spritz is Chandon Brut with a bitter orange liqueur: bittersweet, bright and very refreshing.”

The Chandon Garden Spritz is the spritz among the bubbly cocktails at Bubbles at Brennan's, our afternoon service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, at $15.00, between the Riviera and the Champagne Cocktail in price.

The menu prints two parts: a bitter orange liqueur and Chandon Brut sparkling wine, Chandon said shahn-DOHN. Brut means dry. Which orange liqueur, whether the bar builds it or pours it ready made, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a sparkling aperitivo. It tastes bittersweet: orange peel and a gentle bitterness under dry, fine bubbles.

It is the drink for a guest who loves an aperitivo spritz, and a good way to open the appetite before dinner. It sits between the light Riviera at $12.00 and Brennan's Champagne Cocktail at $20.00, the house's own bubbly classic, and the menu calls the Chandon sparkling wine, never Champagne.

Asked: Is it bitter?

Answer: Bittersweet: the orange liqueur brings a gentle bitterness and the dry sparkling wine keeps it bright.

Asked: Which orange liqueur is it?

Answer: The menu prints a bitter orange liqueur without naming it; I will check with the bar.

Asked: Is the Chandon a Champagne?

Answer: No: Chandon is sparkling wine, not Champagne; call it sparkling wine. Chandon sells a ready made Garden Spritz from Mendoza, Argentina; whether ours is that bottle or the bar's build on Chandon Brut, as the menu prints it, I will check with the bar.

Call it sparkling wine, as the menu does, never Champagne. Which orange liqueur, whether it is built at the bar, the measures and the glass are lineup questions, and the Bubbles hours are confirmed on shift. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory

kept.a: Pour the coffee at the table from the right, with the cup on its saucer and the handle toward the guest. Fill to about a finger below the rim so cream has room, offer cream and sugar before you leave, and come back to top up before the cup is empty. With the Foster, pour after the flame has died, never across the cart. Say: “Here's our New Orleans coffee with chicory. Cream or sugar?”

Offer our coffee with chicory with every dessert, above all the flambés, and to any guest who wants the New Orleans way. It is the spirit-free partner the guide names for six sweet plates. Next rounds: the Café Glacé de la Maison if they want it cold, or the Congregation single origin for a cup without chicory. Say: “With the Foster, our New Orleans coffee with chicory is the classic: dark and smooth, with a gentle bitterness.”

Our New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory is $11 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, priced in the guide's eye openers and coffee list, where one $11 stands before all three coffees.

New Orleans coffee means coffee with chicory. Chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, is a roasted root; the city's habit is usually traced to Civil War blockade shortages, and it stuck because it adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness without any caffeine of its own. The breakfast tasting pours Brennan's private blend from Congregation Coffee, a roaster in Algiers Point, across the river.

The guest gets a hot, dark cup, served the way they take it. It tastes dark, roasty and smooth, with a gentle bitterness.

That bitterness is exactly what balances dessert, which is why the guide makes it the zero-proof pick with six sweet plates: the Framboise French Toast, the coffee cake, Bananas Foster, Cherries Jubilee, the bread pudding and The Snickers. It closes the Traditional Breakfast beside the Foster.

Asked: What is chicory?

Answer: CHICK-uh-ree: a roasted root blended into the coffee, the New Orleans way. It adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness.

Asked: Does chicory have caffeine?

Answer: The chicory itself has none; the coffee does.

Asked: Why chicory in New Orleans?

Answer: The habit is usually traced to wartime shortages in the 1860s, when coffee ran short, and it stuck.

One $11 is printed before all three coffees: confirm at lineup that each is $11, and that the chicory coffee is the Brennan's private blend from Congregation at every meal. On the Traditional Breakfast the coffee with the Foster is included: do not charge it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Café Glacé de la Maison

kept.a: The bar builds the Café Glacé; you present it. Carry it level so the orange flower foam stays whole, set it down at the guest's right, and name it as it lands. Suggest the first sip through the foam, so the guest gets the orange flower and the cold coffee together. Say: “Here's our Café Glacé: take the first sip through the foam.”

Offer the Café Glacé to a guest skipping the milk punch, with the baked apple, the turtle soup or the duck confit waffle, and on a warm day. Next rounds: our hot coffee with chicory, or the Personality at $16.00, our spirit-free sparkling rosé drink. Say: “Our Café Glacé de la Maison is chicory cold brew with cardamom and clove, under an orange flower foam: cold, roasty and fragrant.”

The Café Glacé de la Maison is our house iced coffee, $11 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, priced and built in the guide's eye openers and coffee list.

Café glacé, ka-FAY gla-SAY, is French for iced coffee. Ours starts with chicory cold brew, so it is smooth and roasty, sweetened with a syrup of cardamom and clove, the clove a nod to the city's flamed café brûlot, and topped with an orange flower foam.

The guest gets a cold coffee under a pale, fragrant foam. It tastes cold, roasty and lightly sweet, with warm spice and a floral orange lift.

It is the guide's zero-proof pick with the baked apple, the turtle soup and the duck confit waffle, and the cold choice with the coffee cake. It is also the drink for anyone skipping the milk punch at breakfast, and a refreshing, spirit-free choice on a warm courtyard day.

Asked: What is in it?

Answer: Chicory cold brew, a cardamom and clove syrup, and an orange flower foam on top.

Asked: Is there alcohol in it?

Answer: No. It is iced coffee, spirit-free, which makes it the drink for anyone skipping the milk punch.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Lightly: the cardamom and clove syrup sweetens it, and the chicory cold brew keeps it roasty and smooth.

It carries caffeine from the cold brew: offer it with that in mind late in the day. One $11 is printed before all three coffees: confirm each price at lineup. Serve it promptly so the foam holds. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Revive Cold-Pressed Juice

kept.a: Offer the juice to a guest who wants no alcohol and no caffeine, to a light breakfast eater, to a child, and to a guest who turns down the coffee. Next rounds: the Personality at $16.00 or Oh! What It Seemed to Be at $16.00 for something more like a cocktail. Say: “We also pour Revive, a cold-pressed juice of strawberry, apple and pineapple: fresh and bright, with no alcohol.”

Revive Cold-Pressed Juice sits on the breakfast and lunch menu at $10.00, under Cold Pressed Juices, locally made and fresh squeezed, and is used in no pairing.

The menu prints its fruit: strawberry, apple and pineapple. Cold pressing squeezes the fruit without heat, which keeps the juice bright and lively. Who presses it for us, and whether another juice joins it, are questions for the bar.

The guest gets a glass of cold juice. It tastes fresh, sweet and fruity: strawberry first, with apple and the tang of pineapple.

It is the drink for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine, and for anyone who would like something light with breakfast. It suits a child or a guest who is not drinking and does not want coffee, and it gives a breakfast table a fresh option beside the eye openers.

Answer: Strawberry, apple and pineapple, as the menu prints it, pressed locally and served cold.

Asked: What does cold-pressed mean?

Answer: The fruit is squeezed without heat, which keeps the juice bright and lively.

Asked: Is there caffeine in it?

Answer: No, and no alcohol: it is simply cold-pressed fruit juice, a fresh start to breakfast and a good choice for a child at the table.

The menu prints one juice, Revive, with strawberry, apple and pineapple: name those, and ask the bar before promising any other. kept.a: Offer For Sentimental Reasons at the start of brunch or dinner, to a table celebrating, and to a guest who would otherwise order a glass of sparkling wine. Say: “For Sentimental Reasons is pear and warm allspice topped with sparkling wine: fizzy, fruity and a lovely way to start.”

For Sentimental Reasons is the first drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $15.00, the lowest price on that list. The list celebrates 80 years of Brennan's, which opened in 1946, and each drink carries the title of a song from that year.

The menu prints three parts: allspice dram, a liqueur that tastes of warm baking spice, then pear purée, topped with sparkling wine. Which sparkling wine, which allspice dram, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a sparkling drink with the soft body the purée gives. It tastes fizzy and fruity, ripe pear first, with a gentle spice on the finish.

It is the lightest way into the fall list: a brunch drink, a toast for a celebration, and the one to offer a guest who usually orders a glass of bubbles. Its spirit-free neighbor on the menu is the Personality, a sparkling rosé drink.

Asked: What is allspice dram?

Answer: A liqueur flavored with allspice, the berry that tastes like clove, cinnamon and nutmeg together. Which one our bar pours, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Why are the drinks named for songs?

Answer: The fall list is Billboard Songs from 1946, the year Brennan's opened, for our 80 years. Each drink carries the title of a song from that year.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Fruity rather than sugary: the pear gives softness and the bubbles keep it bright.

Say the full name, For Sentimental Reasons, when you ring it, so the bar never has to guess between song titles. Which sparkling wine, which allspice dram, the measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar; describe only the three printed parts until then. It is a sparkling drink: carry it straight from the bar so it keeps its fizz. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Offer the Prisoner of Love to a gin drinker, to a tea lover, and to a guest who wants something silky and fragrant before dinner or as a gentle nightcap. Next rounds: Five Minutes More at $20.00 for a bolder herbal drink, For Sentimental Reasons at $15.00 for bubbles, or the Personality at $16.00 without alcohol. Say: “Prisoner of Love is gin with Earl Grey tea and orange flower water, made silky with clarified cream.”

Prisoner of Love is the gin drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $16.00. Like every drink on the list, it carries the title of a song from 1946, the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints gin, Earl Grey tea, clarified heavy cream and orange flower water. Clarifying is the old milk punch technique, where the milk is curdled and strained off clear; it leaves a silky texture without the weight of cream. Which gin, how our bar clarifies the cream, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a fragrant, silky drink. It tastes of the bergamot in the tea and a floral orange note over the gin.

It is the drink for a gin lover who wants something gentler than a martini, and a good talking point for anyone curious about cocktail history: milk punch is an old New Orleans habit, and our Brandy Milk Punch, the cold, creamy kind, opens the Traditional Breakfast.

Asked: What is clarified heavy cream?

Answer: Cream used the old milk punch way: it is curdled and strained off clear, so the drink keeps a silky texture without being heavy. How our bar does it, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Is it creamy like a milk punch?

Answer: The menu prints clarified heavy cream: in the old method the solids are strained out, so it drinks smooth rather than thick. How our bar makes it, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Which gin is it?

Answer: The menu does not name it; I will check with the bar.

Do not describe it as a cream drink: the cream is clarified, and a guest expecting a milk punch may be surprised. Do not confuse it with the Brandy Milk Punch, our breakfast eye opener. Which gin, how the cream is clarified, the measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: To Each His Own

kept.a: Offer To Each His Own to a brandy or Cognac drinker, to a guest who loves apple desserts, and as a fall aperitif before dinner. Next rounds: Origin Story at $40.00 for the Sazerac on Cognac, For Sentimental Reasons at $15.00 for something sparkling, or the Apple Crumble at $15.00 with dessert. Say: “To Each His Own is Calvados, an apple brandy, with Lillet Blanc and quince: fall orchard fruit in a glass.”

To Each His Own is the orchard drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $18.00, named like the others for a song of the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints three parts. Daron Fine Calvados, dah-ROHN KAL-vuh-dohs, is apple brandy from northern France; Fine is the youngest grade of Calvados, fresh and fruity. Lillet Blanc, lee-LAY BLAHN, is a light French aperitif wine, floral and citrusy. The quince liqueur brings a fruit between an apple and a pear, very fragrant. Which quince liqueur, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a smooth, spirit-forward drink. It tastes of baked apple and perfumed quince, softened and lifted by the Lillet.

It is the drink for a brandy lover, and the most seasonal flavor on the fall list. For the next brandy round, our Origin Story is the Sazerac on Cognac.

Asked: What is Calvados?

Answer: KAL-vuh-dohs: apple brandy from northern France. Ours is Daron Fine.

Asked: What is quince?

Answer: A fragrant fruit somewhere between an apple and a pear, often cooked into preserves. Which quince liqueur we pour, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Is it strong?

Answer: It is spirit-forward, brandy with an aperitif wine and a liqueur, so it is a drink to sip slowly.

Say Calvados, not Cognac: both are French brandy, but Calvados is apple brandy. The same Lillet Blanc goes into the Riviera at Bubbles, so name the drink clearly when you ring it. Which quince liqueur, the measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.
