kept.a: Offer Old Buttermilk Sky to a margarita or whiskey sour drinker, and to a guest who wants a fall flavor in a lighter, silky drink. Next rounds: Five Minutes More at $20.00 for an herbal citrus drink, Rumors are Flying at $20.00 for whiskey, or Oh! What It Seemed to Be at $16.00, its spirit-free twin. Say: “Old Buttermilk Sky is a tequila sour with fig and cinnamon, silky from the egg white and bright with lemon.”

Old Buttermilk Sky is the tequila sour on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $18.00, named for one of the songs of the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints Volcán Reposado Tequila, vol-KAHN reh-poh-SAH-doh, a tequila rested in oak, rounder than an unaged one; then fig liqueur, lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white. Egg white is the classic way to give a sour its silky body. Which fig liqueur, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a sour with a silky texture. It tastes warm and fruity, ripe fig and cinnamon over the rested tequila, with lemon keeping it bright.

It is the drink for a margarita or whiskey sour lover who wants something for fall. Its spirit-free twin on the menu, Oh! What It Seemed to Be, follows the same pattern on Lyre's non-alcoholic agave spirit with fig syrup, so a table can share the idea whether or not they drink.

Asked: What does reposado mean?

Answer: Rested: a tequila aged in oak for a while, so it is rounder and softer than an unaged one.

Asked: Could the bar leave out the egg white?

Answer: I will read the service note and check with the bar before I promise it.

Asked: Who sang Old Buttermilk Sky?

Answer: It was one of the songs of 1946; I will check at lineup and come back to you.

cocktails.name: Five Minutes More

kept.a: Offer Five Minutes More to a guest who asks for something herbal, to a vodka drinker who wants more flavor, and to an adventurous table. Next rounds: Old Buttermilk Sky at $18.00 for a silky sour, the Prisoner of Love at $16.00 for a gentler gin drink, or the Espresso Martini at $16.00 after dinner. Say: “Five Minutes More is mandarin vodka with Green Chartreuse, Licor 43 and lemon: bright, herbal and a little sweet.”

Five Minutes More is the herbal drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $20.00, the top price on the list beside Rumors are Flying. Its name is the title of a song from 1946, the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints four parts: Cathead Mandarin Vodka, a mandarin flavored vodka; Green Chartreuse, shar-TROOZ, a French herbal liqueur, intense and green; Licor 43, lee-KOR kwah-REN-tah ee TRESS, a Spanish liqueur with vanilla and citrus; and lemon. The measures, the method, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a bright, citrusy drink. It tastes of mandarin and lemon first, then the deep green herbs of the Chartreuse, with a soft vanilla sweetness from the Licor 43 on the finish.

It is the drink for a guest who loves herbal liqueurs, and for a vodka drinker who wants more character than a vodka soda. It is strong and layered, so it sips slowly.

Asked: What is Green Chartreuse?

Answer: Shar-TROOZ: a French herbal liqueur made by Carthusian monks in the Alps from a secret recipe of 130 plants, bottled at 55 percent.

Asked: What is Licor 43?

Answer: Lee-KOR kwah-REN-tah ee TRESS: a Spanish liqueur from Cartagena named for its 43 ingredients; vanilla and citrus lead.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Balanced: the lemon keeps it bright and the liqueurs give it a gentle sweetness. If you prefer it drier, I will ask the bar.

Name both liqueurs clearly: Green Chartreuse and Licor 43 are the talking points, and the Chartreuse is high in alcohol, so let the guest know it is a strong drink. The measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Personality is one of the two spirit-free drinks on our current menu, under Temperance, 1946, at $16.00. Like the Billboard Songs from 1946 cocktails beside it, it carries the title of a song from the year Brennan's opened.

The guest gets a pink, sparkling drink. It tastes fizzy and bright, red fruit and tart cherry, with a gentle warmth from the brown sugar.

It is the drink that lets a guest who is not drinking join the toast, at brunch or at a birthday. It shares its tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup with Rumors are Flying, the rye drink on the fall list, so a couple can order the same idea with and without spirit.

The guest gets a creamy, fizzy drink with ice cream in it. It tastes sweet and nostalgic: vanilla, root beer spice and the rich caramel note of the Amarula.

It is the playful close to a meal, dessert and drink in one, and a natural for a birthday table or anyone who grew up on floats.

The menu prints seven parts: bourbon, apple cider, butterscotch schnapps, maple, cinnamon, lemon and black walnut bitters. It is the dessert for a bourbon drinker, and for anyone who wants the flavor of a fall pie without ordering a plate. With a coffee after dinner it makes a full dessert course on its own.

Asked: Is it served hot?

Answer: The menu does not say; I will check with the bar how they serve it tonight.

Asked: Is it very sweet?

Answer: It is a dessert drink, but the lemon and the black walnut bitters keep the butterscotch and maple in balance.

Asked: Which bourbon is it?

kept.a: Offer the Banane au Chocolat to a chocolate lover, to a guest who loved the Bananas Foster, and to a table that wants one more sweet thing without another plate. Next rounds: the Espresso Martini at $16.00, Floating in South Africa at $15.00, or Brennan's Irish Coffee at $12.00. Say: “Banane au Chocolat is banana and chocolate liqueurs with Pedro Ximénez sherry: rich, silky and sweet, the Foster you can sip.”

Banane au Chocolat, bah-NAHN oh shoh-koh-LAH, is the banana and chocolate drink among our three dessert cocktails, at $16.00, the top price of the three. The name is French for banana with chocolate.

The menu prints three parts: crème de banana and crème de cocoa, two classic dessert liqueurs, and Pedro Ximénez sherry, PAY-droh hee-MEH-nez, the sweetest style of sherry, dark and syrupy, tasting of raisins and figs. Which liqueurs, which sherry, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a dark, silky dessert drink. It tastes of ripe banana and chocolate, with the sherry's dried fruit depth underneath.

It is the drink for a chocolate lover and a fine companion to the house's banana story: Bananas Foster was invented at Brennan's in 1951. A guest who loves the Foster but cannot manage another dessert can sip this instead.

Asked: What is Pedro Ximénez?

Answer: PAY-droh hee-MEH-nez: the sweetest style of Spanish sherry, dark and syrupy, made from the grape of the same name.

Asked: Is it very sweet?

Answer: Yes, it is a true dessert drink, rich and silky; a coffee alongside balances it well.

Asked: Does it taste like Bananas Foster?

Answer: It shares the banana and the richness, with chocolate and sherry in place of the rum and butter.

Say it bah-NAHN oh shoh-koh-LAH, and do not mix it up with Floating in South Africa, the dessert drink with ice cream: this one has none. Which liqueurs and which sherry, the measures and the glass are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Offer the Espresso Martini as dessert menus go down, to a vodka drinker, and to a table that wants coffee and a nightcap at once. Next rounds: Ralph's Coffee at $8.00 for something gentler, Brennan's Irish Coffee at $12.00, or the Banane au Chocolat at $16.00 for chocolate. Say: “Our Espresso Martini has a New Orleans accent: vodka with chicory, Frangelico and Kahlua, roasty and smooth.”

Our Espresso Martini is the first of the two coffee cocktails on the dessert menu, at $16.00: the modern classic with a New Orleans accent.

The menu prints chicory, vodka, Frangelico and Kahlua. Chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, is the roasted root New Orleans blends into its coffee, which adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness. Frangelico, fran-JEL-ih-koh, is an Italian hazelnut liqueur, and Kahlua, kuh-LOO-uh, a coffee liqueur. Whether the chicory comes as our chicory coffee or another way, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a dark coffee cocktail. It tastes roasty and smooth: chicory and coffee liqueur, toasted hazelnut, and clean vodka underneath.

It is the drink for a guest who wants dessert and a coffee in one glass, and for a vodka drinker at the end of a meal. Ralph's Coffee, beside it on the menu, carries the Frangelico too, in coffee under whipped cream.

Asked: Is there espresso in it?

Answer: The menu prints chicory with the vodka, Frangelico and Kahlua; I will check with the bar whether it is made with our chicory coffee or espresso.

Asked: Will it keep me awake?

Answer: That depends on the coffee in it, so I will check with the bar. Chicory itself carries no caffeine.

Asked: What is Frangelico?

Answer: Fran-JEL-ih-koh: an Italian hazelnut liqueur.

Do not promise caffeine or no caffeine: chicory carries none, and the bar knows what else is in the glass. The menu calls it an Espresso Martini but prints chicory, so confirm the coffee at lineup. Frangelico is a hazelnut liqueur: read the service note and confirm at lineup before answering ingredient questions. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: The bar builds Ralph's Coffee and you present it. Carry it level so the cream cap stays whole, turn any handle toward the guest's right hand, and say the name as you set it down so it is never taken for the Irish Coffee. Ask the guest not to stir: the coffee is meant to be sipped through the cream. At a Bananas Foster table, bring it just before the flame, never beside it. Say: “Here's Ralph's Coffee: hazelnut and walnut in our chicory coffee. Sip it through the cream.”

Offer Ralph's Coffee as dessert arrives, with Bananas Foster or the bread pudding, and to a guest who wants a coffee with a little something but not a whiskey drink. Next rounds: Brennan's Irish Coffee at $12.00 with whiskey, the Espresso Martini at $16.00, or our New Orleans Style Coffee at $11.00 on its own. Say: “Ralph's Coffee is our chicory coffee with hazelnut and walnut liqueurs under whipped cream: nutty and comforting.”

Ralph's Coffee is the second coffee cocktail on our dessert menu, at $8.00, the lowest cocktail price on the menu.

The menu prints dark roast coffee with chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, the same coffee that goes into Brennan's Irish Coffee, then Frangelico, fran-JEL-ih-koh, an Italian hazelnut liqueur, and Nocello, noh-CHEL-oh, an Italian walnut liqueur, under whipped cream. The measures and the glass are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a coffee under a white cap of cream, and sips the coffee through it. It tastes roasty and nutty, hazelnut and walnut in the chicory coffee, with the cool cream on top.

It is the gentle choice beside the Irish Coffee: no whiskey and no brown sugar, the nut liqueurs instead. The menu does not say who it is named for, so a server tells no story about the name until a manager gives one. With Bananas Foster or the bread pudding, it is the easiest way to keep a table lingering.

Asked: Who is Ralph?

Answer: The menu does not say; I will check with a manager before I tell you a story about the name.

Asked: How is it different from the Irish Coffee?

Answer: Same chicory coffee and whipped cream, but with hazelnut and walnut liqueurs in place of Irish whiskey and brown sugar.

Asked: What is Nocello?

Answer: Noh-CHEL-oh: an Italian walnut liqueur.

Do not mix it up with Brennan's Irish Coffee: both are chicory coffee under whipped cream, so name the drink as you ring it and as it lands. toGuest.value: Eggs Hussarde is New Orleans’ answer to Eggs Benedict, with a red wine sauce as well as hollandaise.
Eggs Sardou is the New Orleans egg dish with artichokes and creamed spinach.
Marchand de vin is a savory red wine and mushroom sauce; it gives the eggs a deep, rich note.
Hollandaise is the buttery, lemony egg-yolk sauce you know from Eggs Benedict.
Béarnaise is a rich butter sauce with tarragon, the classic sauce for steak.
Choron is a béarnaise with tomato, tangy and herbal.
Sauce Foyot is béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze.
Débris is meltingly tender, slow-cooked meat in its own gravy.
Véronique means fish with grapes, ours are pickled with hibiscus.
En papillote means in paper; here we use a banana leaf instead, so the fish steams in its own juices and stays moist.
Beurre blanc is a silky white wine and butter sauce.
Poussin à la moutarde means young chicken with mustard.
’Nduja is a spicy, spreadable Italian sausage that melts into the beans.
Persillade is a fresh parsley-and-garlic topping, ours has pumpkin seeds for crunch.
Mignonette is the classic raw bar sauce for oysters, vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper; ours has preserved Fresno chili.
The egg yolk is cured and grated over the top, like bottarga, it adds a rich, salty finish.
Brabant potatoes are New Orleans’ crispy cubed potatoes.

Milk punch comes two ways: ours at breakfast is the New Orleans kind, brandy, cream, vanilla and nutmeg, shaken and cold; the older English kind curdles milk and strains it clear, the technique behind the clarified cream in the Prisoner of Love.
A Bloody Bull is a Bloody Mary with beef broth, savory and rich.
Chicory is a roasted root we blend into our coffee, the New Orleans way.
Café brûlot is New Orleans’ spiced, flamed coffee, the cake borrows its flavors.

say.value: TAH-so (TASS-oh is also heard; confirm the house habit)

toGuest.value: Tasso is Cajun spiced, cured and smoked pork, used to season the sauce.
Popcorn rice is a Louisiana rice with a nutty, toasty aroma.
Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down caramelized tart, ours is pineapple.

say.value: ERB-sant (ERB-saint also heard); never sound the H

toGuest.value: Herbsaint is the anise liqueur created in New Orleans in 1934, its name from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood; it is only a rinse in the Sazerac glass, for aroma.
Framboise is French for raspberry; the French toast is finished with raspberry coulis and local raspberries.
Fines herbes is the classic French mix of delicate herbs, parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, on the crab claws.
Mimolette is a bright orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and a little sweet as it ages, dyed with annatto; it makes the fondue on the shells and cheese.
Pralines are the New Orleans pecan and brown sugar candies crumbled over the bread pudding.
Rösti is the Swiss grated potato cake under the petite filet on the breakfast tasting.
Mascarpone is a rich Italian cream cheese, whipped into a light mousse for the French toast.
Shiitake are the savory Japanese mushrooms, preserved, on the blackened tofu.
Burrata is fresh mozzarella with a creamy center, on the Creole tomato tostada.
Grana Padano is a hard, nutty Italian cheese like Parmesan, on the Caesar and the shells and cheese.
Castelvetrano olives are the bright green, mild and buttery Sicilian olives in the papillote.
Gremolata is a fresh chopped topping; ours is Marcona almond with lemon and basil on the crab and corn omelette.
Harissa is the North African chili paste that seasons the smoked cauliflower.
Yuzu is a fragrant Japanese citrus; its mousse is the heart of the lemon tart.
Chateaubriand is the thick center cut of the beef tenderloin, roasted for two.
Confit is meat cured and cooked slowly in its own fat until tender; the duck leg on the waffle.
Pavé means paving stone; the smoked potato pavé is layered potato pressed and cut into a neat block.
Andouille is the smoky Louisiana pork sausage in the gumbo.
Gumbo is the Louisiana stew built on a dark roux; ours is seafood with andouille over popcorn rice.
Luxardo is the Italian family house famous for maraschino cherries and the liqueur, founded in 1821 and in Italy since 1947; its sauce dresses the Cherries Jubilee.

Peychaud's is the bright red New Orleans bitters with anise and cherry notes in the Sazerac; the story puts Antoine Peychaud's pharmacy a few doors up Royal Street, so confirm it at lineup before telling it.
The Sazerac is New Orleans' official cocktail: ours is rye stirred with Peychaud's in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint, and the first Sazeracs were made on Cognac, as our Origin Story is.
Crème fraîche is a slightly tangy cultured cream, sweetened on the baked apple and whipped on the coffee cake.
Financiers are small, buttery almond cakes; the blackberry ones give the trifle its texture.
A bavarois, or Bavarian, is a set cream; the Snickers starts with a Bavarian milk chocolate.
Paul Blangé was the house's first chef, who led the kitchen until the 1970s and created Bananas Foster and Eggs Hussarde.
Escoffier was the great French chef who wrote down sauce Foyot and is credited with Cherries Jubilee for Queen Victoria's jubilee.
The guéridon is the cart the Bananas Foster is made on at your table.
Fresno is a red Californian chili from the 1950s, about the heat of a jalapeño but fruitier; preserved in the mignonette it gives a gentle warmth, not real heat.
Creole is New Orleans city cooking, French and Spanish at the root with more butter, cream and sauces; Cajun is the country cooking of Acadiana, one pot, dark roux and spicier. Brennan's is Creole.

say.value: PEE-pair HIDE-seek (PIE-per HIDE-seek is common and fine)

toGuest.value: Piper-Heidsieck is the Champagne house behind our house bubbles, bottled under the Brennan's name as an Extra Brut, very dry.
Rare is the prestige vintage Champagne that began at Piper-Heidsieck and is now its own house; we pour it by the glass from a bottle kept fresh under a Coravin Sparkling stopper.
Pierre Sparr is an Alsace house; its sparkling rosé is all Pinot Noir, made like Champagne, dry with bright berry fruit.
Charles Lafitte is the crisp, dry Champagne poured on both tasting menus, a house with roots to 1834 in the Vranken-Pommery group.
C.H. Berres is an old Mosel family estate at Ürzig; its Old Vines Riesling is our off-dry glass for spice and for the duck waffle.
Pazo das Bruxas, the manor of the witches, is Familia Torres's Albariño from Spain's Atlantic coast, citrusy with a salty edge.
Albariño is the crisp, saline white grape of Rías Baixas in Galicia, made for seafood.
Durand is the family behind our Loire Sauvignon Blanc, crisp and herbal, the wine that loves artichokes; the current menu prints it as Famille Durand.

say.value: GAY-nee (worth an ear check with the sommelier)

toGuest.value: Gainey is a Santa Barbara County estate; its Chardonnay is creamy but fresh, our first pick for the butter sauces.
Domaine Leflaive is one of Burgundy's great white wine estates, famous for Puligny-Montrachet; we pour its Mâcon by the glass by Coravin.
Mâcon-Verzé is the village appellation in southern Burgundy where Leflaive makes this Chardonnay.
Domaine Fichet is a family estate at Igé in the Mâconnais; its Château London is a named vineyard parcel, no castle and nothing to do with England.
Mâcon-Igé is the village appellation of the Fichet Chardonnay poured with the lobster on the dinner tasting.
Minuty is a Provence estate; its Prestige rosé is pale, dry and refreshing, lovely with tomatoes and shrimp.
Damien Martin runs his family's domaine at Davayé in the Mâconnais; his Bourgogne Pinot Noir is our light, silky red by the glass.
Louis Jadot is the Burgundy house whose Beaune Premier Cru is poured with the redfish on the dinner tasting; Beaune has no Grand Cru, so Premier Cru is its top tier.
Beaune is the wine capital of Burgundy and the village behind the Jadot Premier Cru on the tasting.
Beaumes-de-Venise is a Southern Rhône village famous for sweet Muscat; the Durban we pour is its dry red, ripe Grenache with Syrah.
Domaine de Durban is the Beaumes-de-Venise estate behind our ripe, soft Southern Rhône red.
Domaine de Châteaumar makes the Cuvée Vincent Côtes du Rhône poured with the filet at breakfast: old vine Syrah from beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, juicy and soft.
Moulin d'Issan is the Bordeaux from the Château d'Issan team in Margaux, a Cabernet Sauvignon blend, cassis and cedar for the steak.
Rubicon is Inglenook's flagship Napa Cabernet from Rutherford; our 2010 has sixteen years of age, powerful but silky, $70 the glass.
Paul Hobbs is the Napa winemaker whose Coombsville Cabernet is poured with the duck on the dinner tasting.
Coombsville is one of Napa's cooler corners, near the town of Napa, so its Cabernet keeps its freshness.
Dr. Hermann is the Mosel estate behind our sweet Erdener Prälat Auslese, the $80 half-bottle for dessert.
Erdener Prälat is one of the Mosel's famous steep vineyards, the source of our Auslese.
Auslese means selected harvest, a tier above late harvest Spätlese: sweet, honeyed Riesling with bright acidity.
La Tour Vieille is the Banyuls estate whose Reserva, fig, caramel and coffee, is the dessert pour on the dinner tasting.
Banyuls is a sweet fortified red from the schist terraces of Roussillon, at least half Grenache, the classic with chocolate.
Coravin lets us pour a single glass and keep the bottle fresh: a needle through the cork for the Leflaive, a sparkling stopper on the opened bottle for the Rare.
Extra Brut means 0 to 6 grams of sugar per liter in the finished Champagne. Our house Champagne is Extra Brut, a very dry style.
Creekstone Farms is Black Angus beef from a Kansas producer; the breakfast hanger is USDA Prime.
Vital Farms is pasture raised eggs; every hen gets over a hundred square feet of grass.
Rohan is a special cross bred for the D'Artagnan company and raised in New York's Hudson Valley for tender, rosy meat.
