explain.value:
Brennan's began in 1946, when Owen Brennan, an Irish-American New Orleanian, opened the Vieux Carré restaurant on Bourbon Street, across from the Old Absinthe House he already ran. The house legend says a rival teased him that an Irishman's cooking stopped at boiled potatoes, and he set out to prove otherwise with French and Creole cooking.

A lease dispute in 1954 pushed him to plan a move to Royal Street. Owen died in November 1955, before the new house opened; his sister Ella and the family finished the move, and the restaurant opened at 417 Royal Street in 1956.

At the table this is the eighty-year story behind every signature plate: the Hussarde, the turtle soup and the Foster all belong to the family's first decade.

value.front: When and where did Brennan’s first open?
value.back: In 1946, on Bourbon Street, as Owen Brennan’s Vieux Carré restaurant. Owen died in 1955; the family moved the house to 417 Royal Street in 1956.

explain.value:
The pink house at 417 Royal Street was built in 1795, after the great fire, and soon passed to Don José Faurie. It later became the Banque de la Louisiane, the first bank in Louisiana, and the bank's initials, LB, still sit in the ironwork at the center of the balcony railing.

From 1841 to 1891 the Morphy family owned it, and Paul Morphy, the chess prodigy many called the unofficial world champion, lived there until his death in 1884.

Brennan's has served here since 1956. Guests often ask how old the building is while they wait for the first course, so point them to the balcony monogram on the way out: it is the easiest way to make the history real.

value.front: What was 417 Royal Street before it was Brennan’s?
value.back: Built in 1795, it became Louisiana’s first bank, the Banque de la Louisiane, whose LB monogram survives in the balcony, then the Morphy family home.

explain.value:
Owen Brennan noticed that most New Orleans restaurants served only lunch and dinner. Taking his cue from the popular novel Dinner at Antoine's, he asked why not Breakfast at Brennan's, and built a long, celebratory morning meal: an eye opener, a soup, an egg dish, a flamed dessert.

That idea is still the shape of the day. Breakfast and lunch runs Monday to Friday 9 to 2 and Saturday and Sunday 8 to 2, and the Traditional Breakfast at $80 walks a guest through the whole ritual with its drinks included.

When a guest asks what to order, sell the morning as a sequence, not a single plate: something to start, an egg dish, and the Foster to finish.

value.front: Why is Brennan’s famous for breakfast?
value.back: Owen Brennan built a long, celebratory breakfast when others served only lunch and dinner: eye opener, soup, an egg dish and a flamed dessert.

explain.value:
2026 is Brennan's eightieth year, and the house marks it with two tasting menus at $80 through the year. The Traditional Breakfast includes tasting portions and every listed drink: a Brandy Milk Punch, the Baked Apple, turtle soup or gumbo with a Bloody Bull, Eggs Hussarde with Champagne, the Petite Filet with a red, and Bananas Foster at the table.

The dinner tasting runs from Grand Isle Jewel oysters through the BBQ lobster, Redfish Véronique and the Rohan duck to The Snickers, with a $120 wine pairing.

Read the printed card at lineup: the guide and the live pages disagree on some pours and on the duck course, so quote only what is in your hand that day.

value.front: What does the $80 Traditional Breakfast include?
value.back: Tasting portions of every course and all its listed drinks: milk punch, Baked Apple, soup with a Bloody Bull, Hussarde with Champagne, filet with red, Bananas Foster.

explain.value:
Brennan's closed in June 2013 after a foreclosure and a family dispute. Ralph Brennan, a cousin of the former owners, and his partner Terry White bought the building at auction, later acquired the name, and restored the house from top to bottom before reopening in November 2014, with interiors by Richard Keith Langham.

The restoration brought the courtyard and the Chanteclair Room back to life and found ten turtles living in the courtyard, now part of the house's lore.

If a returning guest notices a plate has changed, this is the reason: the menu was refreshed at the reopening and has kept moving since. Keep the answer short and kind: a cousin bought it and brought it back.

value.front: Why did Brennan’s close, and who reopened it?
value.back: It closed in 2013 after a foreclosure and family dispute; Ralph Brennan, a cousin, and partner Terry White bought it and reopened in November 2014.

explain.value:
During the 2014 restoration the builders found turtles living in the courtyard, and the house adopted them. Ten turtles live there now, named for sauces: five for Escoffier's mother sauces, Béchamel, Velouté, Espagnole, Tomate and Hollandaise, and five for New Orleans sauces, Rémoulade, Ravigote, Bordelaise, Mignonette and Cocktail. Cocktail is the only male.

Each spring the house holds a turtle parade to the fountain, which it calls the slowest second line on earth.

Guests ordering the turtle soup sometimes look nervously at the fountain. Say it before they ask, with a smile: the soup is not the turtles, and the courtyard ten are family.

value.front: Is the turtle soup made from the courtyard turtles?
value.back: No. The ten courtyard turtles, named for five French mother sauces and five New Orleans sauces, are house pets; the soup uses farm-raised turtle.

explain.value:
Creole cooking is the city's: the food of New Orleans households and restaurants, French in technique, shaped by Spanish, West African, Caribbean, German and Italian cooks, rich in butter, cream and tomato. Cajun cooking is the country food of the Acadians, French settlers who came from Canada to the bayous and prairies west of the city: smoked meats, dark roux and rice.

The two share the trinity, roux and gumbo, and the line between them blurs in every kitchen.

Brennan's is a Creole house that borrows Cajun pantry staples, tasso, andouille and rice dressing. When a guest asks, say Creole is the city, Cajun the country, and our menu is the city with country seasoning.

value.front: What is the difference between Creole and Cajun cooking?
value.back: Creole is the city’s cooking, French technique with butter, cream and tomato; Cajun is the Acadian country cooking of smoked meats, dark roux and rice.

explain.value:
Auguste Escoffier, the chef who codified French restaurant cooking in Le Guide Culinaire, organized sauces into families. The mother sauces are espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate and hollandaise; every other classical sauce is a daughter, built by adding to one of them.

Brennan's menus read like a lesson in the hollandaise family: plain hollandaise on the Hussarde and Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, Choron on the Sardou, Foyot on the Chateaubriand. The marchand de vin and bordelaise come from the brown side.

The guide's own advice is that the sauce usually matters more than the protein, for the guest and for the wine. Learn the sauce on each plate first and the rest of the description follows.

value.front: Name the five French mother sauces.
value.back: Espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate and hollandaise. Our egg dishes and steaks use the hollandaise family: hollandaise, béarnaise, Choron and Foyot.

explain.value:
Brennan's prints a children's breakfast and a children's dinner, each at one set price of $25.00 for guests ten and under. The breakfast price covers fruit, the plate, ice cream and a drink; the dinner price covers salami and cheese, the plate, ice cream and a drink.

The plates are simple on purpose: eggs, French toast, grilled cheese, popcorn shrimp, fried Gulf shrimp, buttered noodles and sautéed Gulf fish, with Brabant potatoes, fries or vegetables.

Tell the parents the whole price at once so there is no surprise, offer the fruit or salami course straight away so the child eats while the adults order, and confirm any cooking style or preference with the kitchen on the ticket.

value.front: What does the $25.00 children’s price include?
value.back: For ten and under: at breakfast fruit, the plate, ice cream and a drink; at dinner salami and cheese, the plate, ice cream and a drink.

components.name: The Roost Bar and Bubbles at Brennan’s

explain.value:
The Roost is the house bar, and birds run through its design: a painted glass mural of birds and birdcages hung over the bar, a nod to Chanticleer, the rooster Owen Brennan chose to stand for early-morning vitality. Bubbles at Brennan's is the afternoon program there, with sparkling wine, bubbly cocktails and a short list of snacks.

The guide gives the hours as Monday to Friday 2 to 6, with a Champagne sabering on Fridays at 5; an older listing differs, so confirm the days on shift.

The snacks run from Creole spiced nuts at $6 to the Roost Burger at $17. Suggest a snack the moment a drink lands: salt and crunch sell the second glass.

value.front: When is Bubbles at Brennan’s, and what happens on Fridays?
value.back: Per the guide, Monday to Friday 2 to 6 in the Roost Bar and courtyard, with Champagne sabering Fridays at 5; confirm the hours on shift.

explain.value:
Hollandaise is a warm emulsion of egg yolks and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a reduction of vinegar. The yolks are whisked over gentle heat until they thicken, then melted or clarified butter goes in slowly; lecithin in the yolk holds fat and water together in a smooth, pale yellow sauce.

The name means Dutch sauce, though no clear Dutch link has been found. Escoffier counted it among his five mother sauces, and béarnaise, Choron and Foyot are its daughters.

It is fragile: too hot and it scrambles, too cool and it splits. On the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen it is the rich, lemony layer over the egg, the classic half of their two-sauce finish.

value.front: What is hollandaise, and which of our dishes carry it?
value.back: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter sharpened with lemon or vinegar reduction; the mother of béarnaise. It tops the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen.

explain.value:
Marchand de vin means wine merchant. In classical French cooking it is shallots reduced in red wine with a brown stock or demi-glace. New Orleans made its own version: onion and plenty of garlic in place of the shallot, often ham and mushrooms, beef stock and red wine, frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce. Antoine's made it famous in the city.

The guide's best wording is a savory red wine and mushroom sauce; calling it a bare reduction undersells it.

On the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen it is the dark, winey half of the two sauces, under the egg. Whether tonight's sauce carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef before you promise either.

value.front: What is marchand de vin sauce?
value.back: The wine merchant’s sauce: a savory red wine and mushroom brown sauce, New Orleans style, under the egg on the Hussarde and Owen. Confirm ham with the chef.

explain.value:
Béarnaise is hollandaise built on a reduction of white wine vinegar, shallot, tarragon and chervil, finished with fresh tarragon. It is credited to the chef Collinet, who is said to have made it in 1836 for the opening of the Pavillon Henri IV at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris, and named it for Béarn, the home region of King Henri IV.

The vinegar and tarragon give it a sharper, herbal edge than plain hollandaise, which is why it is the classic sauce for grilled beef.

On the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak it is printed as French béarnaise, with a Vital Farms egg alongside. It is also the base for the Choron on the Sardou and the Foyot on the Chateaubriand.

value.front: What makes béarnaise different from hollandaise?
value.back: It is hollandaise built on a vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction, so it is sharper and herbal; the classic steak sauce, on our breakfast hanger.

explain.value:
Sauce Choron is béarnaise finished with tomato. It is named for Alexandre Étienne Choron, chef de cuisine at the celebrated Voisin restaurant on the rue Saint-Honoré in Paris, who is also remembered for the extraordinary Christmas menu he served during the Siege of Paris.

The tomato is cooked down to a thick paste before it is folded in, so it colors the sauce a soft coral and adds a gentle sweetness without thinning the emulsion.

Brennan's puts Choron on the Eggs Sardou in place of the usual hollandaise. The guide's words for it are tangy and herbal, and that is how to say it to a guest: béarnaise with tomato, brighter than hollandaise.

value.front: What is Choron sauce, and where do we serve it?
value.back: Béarnaise with tomato folded in, tangy and herbal, named for the Paris chef Alexandre Choron. It replaces hollandaise on our Eggs Sardou.

explain.value:
Sauce Foyot, also called sauce Valois, is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in. Glace de viande is brown stock reduced until it is thick and syrupy; a spoonful turns pale, sharp béarnaise tawny, deeper and more savory.

It takes its name from the Restaurant Foyot on the rue de Tournon in Paris, opposite the Senate, named for Nicolas Foyot, who had cooked for King Louis-Philippe. Several dishes there carried the house name.

On the Roasted Chateaubriand it does a necessary job: tenderloin is the leanest, mildest cut on the animal, so a rich, savory sauce brings the depth the meat lacks. Say it as béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze.

value.front: What is sauce Foyot?
value.back: Béarnaise enriched with glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, so it is deeper and more savory. It goes with our Roasted Chateaubriand.

explain.value:
Beurre blanc, white butter, is a warm sauce of cold butter whisked into a sharp reduction of white wine, vinegar and shallot. There are no egg yolks: the butter alone, added piece by piece over low heat, makes a light, silky emulsion that tastes of cream and acid.

It is a Loire sauce, credited by tradition to Clémence Lefeuvre, who served river fish at an inn east of Nantes; the legend says she made a béarnaise and forgot the yolks and tarragon.

On the Redfish Véronique it is a preserved lemon beurre blanc, salty and perfumed, which suits a flaky fish. Say burr BLAHN, with no K at the end.

value.front: What is a beurre blanc?
value.back: A Loire sauce of cold butter whisked into a wine, vinegar and shallot reduction, no eggs. Ours is preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique.

explain.value:
Bordelaise means two different sauces, and the difference matters. In classical French cooking it is a red wine sauce with shallot, demi-glace and bone marrow, named for Bordeaux. In New Orleans restaurants the word usually means a garlic butter: butter and olive oil with garlic and parsley, spooned over fish or bread.

A pecan bordelaise on a crab-topped Gulf fish with cauliflower purée most likely belongs to the New Orleans family, with toasted pecans worked into the butter.

That is still a reading, not a recipe. The guide's own advice is to confirm with the kitchen which bordelaise it is before you pair wine, because a red wine sauce changes the bottle.

value.front: Which bordelaise is on the Pecan Gulf Fish?
value.back: In New Orleans bordelaise usually means garlic butter, here with pecans; the French one is a red wine sauce. Confirm with the kitchen before pairing wine.

explain.value:
A mustard cream sauce is the Burgundian bistro classic behind poulet à la moutarde: shallot softened in butter, a splash of white wine reduced, cream added and simmered, and mustard stirred in at the end. The mustard goes in off the heat, because boiling dulls its bite and can make it bitter.

The result is tangy, rich and pale gold, a sauce that loves crisp poultry.

On the Poussin à la Moutarde it meets something French cooks would not expect: a sweet tea-brined, fried Cornish hen. That pairing, Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce, is the whole idea of the dish and the line to give a guest.

value.front: What does à la moutarde mean on our poussin?
value.back: With mustard: a French bistro mustard cream sauce, shallot, wine and cream with mustard stirred in, over our sweet tea-brined fried Cornish hen.

explain.value:
Creole sauce is the New Orleans tomato sauce: the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper softened in fat with garlic, then tomatoes, stock, bay, thyme and a measure of cayenne, simmered until thick. It is the backbone of shrimp Creole and of many Creole fish and egg dishes.

It differs from an Italian tomato sauce in its trinity and its pepper, and from a Cajun gravy in its bright tomato.

On the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits it carries tasso, the spiced smoked pork, so the sauce is smoky as well as tangy. That tomato base is what makes our version Creole rather than the bacon and lemon pan gravy of the Carolina dish.

value.front: What is in a Creole sauce?
value.back: A New Orleans tomato sauce built on the holy trinity, onion, celery and bell pepper, with garlic and cayenne; ours carries tasso on the Shrimp & Grits.

explain.value:
New Orleans barbecue shrimp is never barbecued. The style was born at Pascal's Manale, Uptown, in 1954, by the family's account, when a regular described a buttery shrimp dish he had eaten in Chicago: head-on shrimp cooked in a pan sauce of butter, black pepper, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon.

The sauce is a pan emulsion, buttery and peppery, not smoky and not tomato. It breaks if it boils or sits.

Brennan's uses the name on two plates, the Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the dinner tasting. The house recipe is not published, so describe it as a buttery, peppery New Orleans BBQ sauce and send Worcestershire questions to the kitchen.

value.front: Is New Orleans BBQ sauce smoky or tomato-based?
value.back: Neither: it is a buttery, peppery pan sauce in the barbecue shrimp style from Pascal’s Manale. Send questions on its contents to the kitchen.

explain.value:
Mignonette is the classic raw bar sauce: finely chopped shallot in vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. Mignonnette is the French word for that cracked pepper, which is why the pepper is the ingredient the sauce is named for.

It is spooned onto an oyster by the guest at the table, never poured over in advance, because the acid starts to firm the oyster.

Ours is a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette with parsley on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters: the chilli, salted or pickled and diluted in vinegar, adds a fruity, gentle warmth to the clean, briny oyster. How the chilli is preserved is a good question to ask the chef.

value.front: What is a mignonette, and what is in ours?
value.back: Shallot, vinegar and cracked pepper for raw oysters; ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley, a gentle warmth, on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

explain.value:
Rémoulade is a cold, spiced sauce with two families. The French one is white: mayonnaise with mustard, chopped pickles, capers and herbs, close to tartar sauce. The New Orleans Creole one is pinker and hotter, built on Creole mustard with paprika, cayenne or hot sauce, with or without mayonnaise.

Rémoulade is one of the five New Orleans sauces the courtyard turtles are named for, a sign of how local it feels.

On the Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost it is a chive rémoulade, cool, tangy and herby against hot pastry. The menu does not print the full recipe, so if a guest asks which style, the kitchen has the answer.

value.front: What is rémoulade, and where is it on our menu?
value.back: A cold spiced sauce, French white or New Orleans pink with Creole mustard; a chive rémoulade comes with the Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost.

explain.value:
A gastrique is a French sweet and sour reduction: sugar cooked to caramel, then loosened with vinegar and reduced to a glossy syrup. It balances rich or fried food with acid and sweetness at once.

Crystal is the New Orleans hot sauce made by the family-owned Baumer Foods since 1923, from aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt. It is milder and more vinegary than many hot sauces, so it reads tangy before it reads hot.

On the Roost's Popcorn Shrimp the two meet: a Crystal hot sauce gastrique, sweet, tangy and gently spicy, for dipping crisp fried Louisiana shrimp. Describe it as a sweet and tangy hot sauce glaze.

value.front: What is the Crystal gastrique on the Popcorn Shrimp?
value.back: A sweet and sour reduction made with Crystal, the New Orleans aged cayenne hot sauce since 1923: sweet, tangy, gently spicy with fried shrimp.

value.where: Reserve, Louisiana (founded on Tchoupitoulas Street, New Orleans)
value.history:
In 1923 Alvin A. Baumer borrowed money from his future in-laws and bought Mill's Fruit Products, a small snow-cone syrup company on Tchoupitoulas Street. Tucked in a drawer was a recipe for a pepper sauce labeled Crystal Pure. Baumer renamed it Crystal Pure Louisiana Hot Sauce and began bottling it in the city.

For decades Baumer Foods was as much a maker of jellies, preserves and mustard as of hot sauce. From the 1940s it bottled Crystal on Tulane Avenue, where a neon sign of a chef stirring a steaming pot of strawberry jam became a local landmark. The flooding after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ruined that plant and forced the company to drop its historic preserves, jellies and mustard; it moved upriver to Reserve, Louisiana, at the Port of South Louisiana, 9 feet above sea level.

The recipe is short: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt, giving a reddish orange sauce with medium heat. The company is still family owned, led by Alvin "Al" Baumer Jr.
facts: In 1923 Alvin A. Baumer bought Mill's Fruit Products on Tchoupitoulas Street, with the Crystal recipe included.
Made from aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt.
Reddish orange with medium heat.
From the 1940s it was bottled on Tulane Avenue, under a neon sign of a chef stirring jam.
Flooding after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ended the Tulane Avenue plant; production moved upriver to Reserve, Louisiana.
Still family owned, led by Alvin "Al" Baumer Jr.
notes: Describe the gastrique as sweet, tangy and gently spicy; Crystal reads tangy before hot.
The menu prints only 'Crystal Gastrique'; how sweet or hot tonight's batch is, ask the kitchen.
Do not quote factory sizes or gallons shipped; the published figures disagree.
value.sayIt: The dip is a gastrique made with Crystal, New Orleans' own hot sauce since 1923: sweet, tangy, gently spicy.

explain.value:
Crème anglaise is the French pouring custard: milk or cream heated with sugar and vanilla, poured over egg yolks, and stirred gently until it coats the back of a spoon, never boiled or it curdles. It is the base of ice cream and of a Bavarian cream.

A sweetened condensed anglaise is the kitchen's twist: condensed milk, cooked down with sugar, brings a caramel, dulce de leche note to the custard.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin it is poured beside the charred pineapple and puff pastry, cool and silky against hot caramel. Say it to a guest as a pouring custard with a caramelized milk flavor.

value.front: What is the anglaise on the Pineapple Tarte Tatin?
value.back: Crème anglaise, a stirred vanilla pouring custard, made with sweetened condensed milk for a caramel note, poured beside the charred pineapple.

explain.value:
A roux is flour cooked in fat, stirred constantly, and used to thicken and flavor a sauce or soup. French kitchens cook it white or blond for béchamel and velouté. Louisiana cooks take it much further, to peanut butter, then chocolate or mahogany brown, which gives a toasty, nutty depth; the darker it gets, the more flavor and the less thickening power it has.

A dark roux is the Creole tradition for gumbo and turtle soup, and New Orleans marchand de vin is often roux-bound too. How dark our own kitchen takes each one is a question for the chef.

At the table, a roux is part of why a gumbo or a turtle soup tastes deep rather than brothy. Questions about flour in a dish go to the kitchen.

value.front: What is a roux, and how do Louisiana cooks take it?
value.back: Flour cooked in fat to thicken and flavor. Creole tradition takes it dark for gumbo and turtle soup: toasty depth, less thickening. How dark ours goes, ask the chef.

explain.value:
The holy trinity is onion, celery and green bell pepper, chopped and softened together at the start of a Cajun or Creole dish. It is Louisiana's version of the French mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot, which grew more easily in early Louisiana.

The name nods to the Catholic faith of the early settlers, and the phrase was most likely popularized by the chef Paul Prudhomme. Garlic is so often added that some cooks call it the pope.

The trinity is in our gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana rice dressing. It is the reason those dishes taste of Louisiana before a single spice goes in.

value.front: What is the holy trinity in Louisiana cooking?
value.back: Onion, celery and green bell pepper softened together: Louisiana’s mirepoix, with bell pepper for carrot. It starts our gumbo, turtle soup and Creole sauce.

explain.value:
Andouille is a coarse-grained, heavily smoked pork sausage, French in origin and remade in Louisiana. German and French butchers along the River Parishes shaped the local style: pork shoulder and fat seasoned with garlic, black and red pepper, stuffed and smoked low over pecan wood and sugar cane for hours. LaPlace calls itself the andouille capital of the world.

It is firm and smoky rather than juicy, made to season a pot rather than to eat alone.

In the Seafood Gumbo it gives the smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters. Say ahn-DOO-ee, and tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order.

value.front: What is andouille, and where is it on our menu?
value.back: A coarse, heavily smoked Louisiana pork sausage with garlic and pepper, smoked over pecan wood. It is the smoky backbone of our Seafood Gumbo.

value.who: LaPlace andouille, the Andouille Capital of the World
value.where: LaPlace, St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana
value.history:
Andouille in Louisiana is a River Parishes sausage. The Germans of the German Coast, upriver from New Orleans, brought a strong tradition of sausage making, with French, Acadian, Native American, Spanish and African influences alongside. The town that made it famous is LaPlace, which Governor Edwin Edwards proclaimed the Andouille Capital of the World in the 1970s.

Three LaPlace shops carry the name. Jacob's World Famous Andouille dates from 1928, when Nelson and Camille Jacob began selling smoked andouille from their Milesville home; Aaron Lion is its fourth-generation owner. Wayne Jacob's Smokehouse, no relation to Jacob's, opened in 1950, and Bailey's sits next door to Jacob's. Locals say Jacob's is the smokiest, Wayne Jacob's has the spice and the girth, and Bailey's sits in between. LaPlace andouille is, as one writer put it, thick as a wrist, brown as tobacco and steeped in pecan wood smoke.

The town has held an Andouille Festival every October since the first, on 28 and 29 October 1972. Brennan's prints andouille in its Seafood Gumbo, as in its published gumbo recipe, and names no maker.

Say ahn-DOO-ee.

explain.value:
Tasso is south Louisiana's seasoning meat: strips of pork shoulder cured in salt and sugar, coated thickly in cayenne, garlic and other spices, then hot-smoked until firm. It is sometimes called Cajun ham, but it comes from the shoulder, not the leg, and it is far too spicy and smoky to slice and eat like ham.

Cooks dice it small and cook it into a dish, so a little spreads smoke, salt and heat through the whole pot: jambalaya, red beans, gumbo and cream sauces.

On the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits it seasons the Creole sauce. Both TAH-so and TASS-oh are heard in Louisiana; follow the house habit.

value.front: What is tasso?
value.back: Spiced, cured, hot-smoked pork shoulder used in small amounts as a seasoning meat; called Cajun ham though not leg. It seasons our Shrimp & Grits sauce.

value.who: Tasso, the Cajun smokehouse seasoning meat
value.history:
Tasso belongs to the boucherie, the communal hog butchering of Acadiana, where neighbors killed a pig together and shared every part. The boucherie gave the Cajun larder boudin, cracklin', andouille and tasso, and tasso was traditionally made from the last lean pieces: a seasoning meat, not a meal.

It is often called a ham, but the name misleads. Tasso is cut from the shoulder, not the hind leg. The shoulder is sliced across the grain into pieces about three inches thick, cured briefly in salt and sugar for only three or four hours, rinsed, rubbed with cayenne and garlic, and hot-smoked until cooked through. The smokehouse has its own Acadian French word, boucanière.

Cooks rarely eat tasso on its own. They dice it into jambalaya, stews and braised vegetables, where a little carries smoke, salt and heat through the pot. At Brennan's it seasons the Creole sauce of the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. The menu names no maker, so who smokes it is a question for the kitchen.
facts: Tasso is a smoked, spiced, cured south Louisiana meat cut from the hog's shoulder, not the leg.
The shoulder is cut about three inches thick and cured only three or four hours.
After curing it is rubbed with cayenne and garlic and hot-smoked until cooked through.
At a boucherie, tasso was made from the last lean pieces; it is a seasoning meat.
The boucherie gave the Cajun larder boudin, cracklin', andouille and tasso.
Boucanière is the Acadian French word for smokehouse.
notes: Call it a seasoning meat; if a guest says Cajun ham, explain it is shoulder, not leg.
Tasso is pork; flag it for guests who avoid pork before they order the Shrimp & Grits.
The menu names no maker; ask before claiming it is smoked in-house or bought from a named smokehouse.
TAH-so and TASS-oh are both heard; follow the house habit.
value.sayIt: Tasso is Cajun smoked pork shoulder, spiced with cayenne and garlic, used a little at a time to season our Creole sauce.
askKitchen: Is our tasso smoked in-house, and if not, who makes it?

explain.value:
Louisiana is one of the largest shrimp producers in the country, and the Gulf's brown and white shrimp, caught in the bays and passes of the coast, are the backbone of New Orleans cooking. Brown shrimp come mostly in early summer and taste a little more of iodine and the sea; white shrimp come later in the year and are sweeter and milder.

They are cooked briefly, a couple of minutes at most, or they turn tight and rubbery.

Shrimp appear on our menus in the gumbo, the Shrimp & Grits, the Roost's Popcorn Shrimp and two children's plates. When a guest asks where they come from, the menu's words are Louisiana or Gulf shrimp.

value.front: What do we mean by Louisiana or Gulf shrimp?
value.back: Wild brown and white shrimp from the Gulf coast, the backbone of New Orleans cooking; cooked briefly. In our gumbo, Shrimp & Grits and Popcorn Shrimp.

value.history:
Shrimp is Louisiana's most valuable commercial fishery and the state is first in the nation for shrimp landings: in 2012 nearly 102 million pounds came ashore, worth more than $146 million at the dock. About 5,500 licensed shrimpers work two species, the brown shrimp of the spring season, roughly May to July, and the white shrimp of the autumn season, from mid-August to mid-December. The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission opens and closes each area on its biologists' advice.

The fishery is old and many-voiced. By the 1880s the marshes south of New Orleans were dotted with villages on stilts where shrimp were dried on raised platforms for Asia, the Philippines and Hawaii; at the peak, between 1900 and 1915, there were at least 95. Most of the merchants were Chinese, and the fishermen were Filipino, Chinese, Japanese, Italian, Croatian, Isleño, Creole, Cajun, African American and Native American. Manila Village, built over the oyster reefs of Barataria Bay by Filipino fishermen led by Quintin de la Cruz, even had its own post office.

Today almost 90 percent of the shrimp eaten in America is imported, which is what makes the word Louisiana on a menu worth saying.
facts: Louisiana is first in the nation for commercial shrimp landings; in 2012 nearly 102 million pounds were landed.
Two species carry the fishery: brown shrimp, Farfantepenaeus aztecus, and white shrimp, Litopenaeus setiferus.
Brown shrimp season generally runs May to July; white shrimp season mid-August to mid-December.
Shrimp is Louisiana's most valuable commercial fishery, with about 5,500 licensed commercial shrimpers.
At the peak of shrimp drying, 1900 to 1915, the marshes held at least 95 platform communities.
Manila Village in Barataria Bay was founded by Filipino fishermen led by Quintin de la Cruz.
Almost 90 percent of the shrimp eaten in the United States is imported, which is why Louisiana on a menu matters.
Louisiana's Act 372 of 2019 requires a menu notice when a restaurant serves imported shrimp or crawfish.
notes: Use the menu's words: Louisiana shrimp on the Shrimp & Grits and the Roost Popcorn Shrimp, Gulf shrimp on the children's fried shrimp.
If asked brown or white, the honest answer depends on the season and the boat; ask the kitchen rather than guess.
Never say all our shrimp are Louisiana: the children's breakfast popcorn shrimp prints no origin.
A good story at the table: the Filipino and Chinese shrimp-drying villages of the marsh, more than a century ago.
value.sayIt: It's wild Louisiana shrimp, from the state that lands more shrimp than any other in the country.
askKitchen: Are tonight's shrimp brown or white, and from which supplier?
Is the children's breakfast popcorn shrimp the same Louisiana shrimp?

components.name: Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat

explain.value:
Louisiana's crab is the blue crab, caught in the brackish marshes and bays of the coast. Picked crabmeat is sold by grade: jumbo lump is the two large muscles that drive the swimming legs, lump is large body pieces just below it, backfin is smaller flakes, and claw meat is darker and stronger. Cocktail claws are claws with the shell cracked away and the pincer left as a handle.

Lump is sweet, delicate and already cooked, so it is warmed gently, never cooked again.

Our menus use it on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the Crab & Corn Omelette, the en papillote and in the gumbo, with warm claws as a dinner starter. Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.

value.front: What is lump crabmeat?
value.back: Large pieces of sweet, cooked body meat from the Louisiana blue crab, the grade just below jumbo lump; warmed gently. On the Pecan Gulf Fish and omelette.

value.history:
Louisiana runs the largest commercial blue crab fishery in the Gulf and in the United States, supplying about a quarter of all the blue crab caught in the country. In 2018 it landed 30.6% of the nation's blue crabs, and its 2024 harvest was 40 million pounds. The crab is trapped in the brackish marshes and bays where fresh river water meets the Gulf.

Most of that catch is cooked and picked by hand, and the meat is sold by grade. New Orleans seafood counters sell three: jumbo lump, backfin lump and claw. Lump is prized for its large, sweet white pieces that hold their shape on a plate, while claw meat, darker and sweeter, is what many home cooks put in stuffed crabs.

Brennan's prints Louisiana lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Crab & Corn Omelette, Louisiana crab on the Gulf Fish en Papillote, and serves warm Louisiana Crab Claws as a starter. No picking house or crabber is named.
facts: Louisiana's commercial blue crab fishery is the largest in the Gulf and in the United States.
Louisiana supplies about a quarter of the blue crab harvested in the United States.
Louisiana landed 30.6% of all US blue crabs in 2018; its 2024 harvest was 40 million pounds.
New Orleans seafood counters sell picked crabmeat in three grades: jumbo lump, backfin lump and claw.
The menu prints Louisiana lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Crab & Corn Omelette.
notes: Say Louisiana lump crab, as printed; it is the sweet, large-piece grade, already cooked and only warmed.
Louisiana catches more blue crab than any other state, which is a fair thing to say with pride.
Do not name a picking house or claim jumbo lump; the menu prints lump.
Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: That's Louisiana lump crab, sweet hand-picked blue crab from the state that catches more of it than any other.
askKitchen: Which picking house supplies our lump and claws?

explain.value:
Louisiana oysters are the Eastern oyster of the Gulf coast, grown in the warm, brackish water where the Mississippi meets the sea. Most come from private leases, beds a family works on state water bottoms, with a small share from the state's public reefs; a growing number are farmed in cages off the bottom. They are larger, milder and less salty than many northern oysters, which is why New Orleans cooks them as often as it eats them raw.

Cooked oysters want only seconds: they are done when the edges curl, and a moment longer shrinks them.

On our menus oysters come cooked in New Orleans BBQ sauce at breakfast and lunch, in the gumbo, and as the smoky dressing on the Creole Caesar. How many come per order is a lineup question.

value.front: How do Louisiana oysters differ from northern oysters?
value.back: Gulf oysters from brackish Mississippi water: larger, milder and less salty, so New Orleans cooks them as often as it eats them raw. Edges curl when done.

value.who: Louisiana oyster leases and public reefs
value.where: Louisiana coast, from the Mississippi delta west to Vermilion Bay
value.history:
Louisiana leads the nation in oysters. Between 2003 and 2022 it landed about a third of all oysters in the United States, and in 2022 it produced more than seven million pounds of oyster meat.

Oystermen have long dredged from two kinds of water bottom: about 1.7 million acres of public reefs, which the state opens each season, and about 400,403 acres of private leases, beds that families rent from the state and tend themselves. For years the split was roughly even. Since about 2007, freshwater pouring onto the main public grounds east of the Mississippi has weakened those reefs, and private leases now give more than nine oysters in ten; in 2023 public reefs gave only 7.3% of landings.

The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission sets the public season each year from its biologists' stock assessment, usually opening in September, with market oysters for sale following. Gulf water is less salty than the Atlantic, partly thanks to the Mississippi, which is why Louisiana oysters are plump, mild and a little sweet.
facts: From 2003 through 2022 Louisiana landed 32.3% of the nation's oysters, more than any other state.
Louisiana has about 1.7 million acres of public oyster reefs and about 400,403 acres of private leases.
In 2023 private leases gave 92.7% of Louisiana's commercial oyster landings and public reefs 7.3%.
Since about 2007 freshwater has weakened the main public grounds east of the Mississippi River.
The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission sets the public season yearly from LDWF biologists' stock assessment.
Gulf oysters grow in less salty water than Atlantic ones, so they are milder, plumper and slightly sweet.
notes: Say Louisiana oysters, grown on the state's private leases and public reefs; do not name a bay, reef or family unless the kitchen tells you.
Guests from the East Coast often ask why these are cooked: Gulf oysters are large and mild, so New Orleans cooks them as often as it eats them raw.
If a guest wants a briny raw oyster, steer them to the Grand Isle Jewels.
Never promise the oysters in a cooked dish are local on a given night; the menu prints Louisiana, the source behind it is the kitchen's.
value.sayIt: These are Louisiana oysters, big and mild from the Gulf, cooked in our New Orleans BBQ sauce.
askKitchen: Where are tonight's cooked oysters from, and how many come per order?

explain.value:
When the menu says Gulf fish, it means the day's catch from the Gulf waters along the coast rather than a fixed species. Kitchens in New Orleans buy what the boats bring: drum, sheepshead, snapper, grouper, triggerfish, speckled trout and others, each with its own texture, from flaky and delicate to firm and meaty.

The preparation is built to suit a range of fish, so the sauce and garnish stay the same while the fillet changes.

That makes one habit essential: know today's fish and how it is cooked before service. It is on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the Gulf Fish en Papillote and the children's sautéed Gulf fish, and every guest will ask what it is tonight.

value.front: What should you know before selling a Gulf fish dish?
value.back: Gulf fish means the day’s catch, not one species: drum, snapper, trout and others. Learn tonight’s fish and preparation at lineup before you sell it.

value.history:
Gulf fish on a New Orleans menu means the day's catch, not one species. The city's appetite runs to fish such as true American red snapper and black drum, which sell far above the national average here, and sheepshead, an estuarine fish of Louisiana's coast that is nearly all sold to restaurants and markets in the state.

Louisiana has worked to widen that list. In 1981 the legislature created the Louisiana Seafood Promotion and Marketing Board to promote the state's commercial catch, with particular attention to underused species.

Brennan's owner has a public record on Gulf seafood. After the 2010 BP oil spill Ralph Brennan testified before Congress about the damage to the Gulf seafood industry, and he advocates sustainable, local seafood sourcing in each of his restaurants. In New Orleans the Audubon Nature Institute runs GULF, a sustainable seafood program founded in 2012 that works with restaurants and fisheries.
facts: Gulf fish means the day's catch from Gulf waters, not a fixed species.
True American red snapper and black drum sell far above average in the New Orleans area.
Nearly all commercially caught Louisiana sheepshead is sold to restaurants or markets in the state.
Louisiana created its Seafood Promotion and Marketing Board in 1981, with a focus on underused species.
Ralph Brennan testified before Congress on the Gulf seafood industry after the 2010 BP oil spill.
Audubon Nature Institute's GULF sustainable seafood program was founded in 2012.
notes: Learn tonight's fish at lineup; every table will ask what the Gulf fish is.
You may say our owner, Ralph Brennan, is a public advocate for local Gulf seafood; do not claim any certification or partnership.
Never guess a species. If the kitchen has not said, offer to ask.
Redfish on the Véronique is its own fish with its own story; do not call it the Gulf fish of the day.
value.sayIt: Gulf fish is the day's catch from the Gulf; let me tell you exactly which fish the kitchen has tonight and how it's cooked.
askKitchen: What is tonight's Gulf fish on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the en Papillote and the children's plate?
Is it from a Louisiana boat, and from which supplier?

explain.value:
Redfish, or red drum, is a Gulf fish with a black spot near the tail and firm, mild, slightly sweet white flesh that holds together in the pan. It became a national craze around 1980 when the chef Paul Prudhomme blackened it at K-Paul's in New Orleans, and demand grew so fast that Louisiana banned commercial redfish fishing later that decade to protect the stock.

So restaurant redfish today is usually farm-raised or comes from other sources; where ours comes from is a question for the chef.

On the Redfish Véronique it stands in for the sole of the French classic: firm enough for a beurre blanc and pickled grapes, mild enough to let them speak.

value.front: What is redfish, and why is its source a question?
value.back: Red drum, a firm, mild Gulf fish. The blackening craze of the 1980s led Louisiana to ban commercial catch, so ask the chef where ours comes from.

value.where: Gulf of Mexico; farmed redfish mainly in Texas
value.history:
Redfish, the red drum, was an important commercial and restaurant fish in Louisiana until 1988. Its fall began one March evening in 1980, when Paul Prudhomme served blackened redfish at K-Paul's in New Orleans; from 1983 he took it on pop-ups to New York and San Francisco, where people queued for hours. Kitchens all over the country copied it, and the Gulf was fished hard: 12.7 million pounds of red drum in a single year.

The stock fell, and Louisiana's Wildlife and Fisheries Commission closed the commercial redfish fishery in the late 1980s; sources give 1987 and 1988. In 1988 anglers were limited to five fish a day with only one over 27 inches, and there has been no commercial redfish fishing in Louisiana since.

The collapse also spurred red drum hatcheries and farms, partly to restock the Gulf, and Texas has led the nation in red drum farms. Louisiana law lets licensed dealers sell farm-raised red drum, or red drum legally caught and sold commercially outside the state, so the redfish on a Louisiana menu today is one or the other.
facts: Paul Prudhomme served blackened redfish at K-Paul's in March 1980 and set off a national craze.
In one year 12.7 million pounds of red drum were harvested from the Gulf.

Red drum farming grew from the 1980s collapse; in one national count Texas led with eight red drum farms.
notes: Redfish is the red drum: firm, mild, slightly sweet, with a black spot near the tail.
Never say ours is wild Louisiana redfish: Louisiana has had no commercial redfish fishery since the late 1980s.
The story guests enjoy: Prudhomme's blackening craze nearly fished redfish out, and the rules since brought it back.
Where ours comes from, farmed or another state's catch, is a chef question.
value.sayIt: Redfish is the red drum, firm and mild; it is the fish Paul Prudhomme made famous, and here it stands in for the classic sole.
askKitchen: Is our redfish farm-raised, and from where?

Creole tomatoes are Louisiana's summer tomatoes. Growers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes, below New Orleans, traditionally sold their vine-ripened tomatoes as Creole, crediting the rich river soil, and in the early 1900s tomatoes from the River Parishes upstream were called Creole too. The LSU AgCenter released a variety named Creole in 1969, but today the word is used for tomatoes grown in Louisiana.

They are prized for being picked ripe: juicy, sweet and sharp, with a soft skin, so they do not travel far.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada they are served raw with heirloom tomatoes, burrata and smoked tomato water. The dish follows the season, so expect it to change when the tomatoes finish.

value.front: What is a Creole tomato?
value.back: A vine-ripened Louisiana tomato, long sold as Creole by St. Bernard and Plaquemines growers: juicy, sweet and sharp. Served raw on our seasonal Creole Tomato Tostada.

value.where: St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes, below New Orleans, and Louisiana generally
value.history:
Creole is a growers' word before it is a variety. Farmers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes traditionally sold their tomatoes as Creole, and said that ripening on the vine in rich alluvial river soil gave them a flavor no other Louisiana or American tomato had. In the early 1900s, before tomatoes carried variety names, fruit from St. Charles, St. John and St. James parishes was simply called Creole too.

The LSU AgCenter muddied the water in 1969, when researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety actually named Creole. It yielded poorly, less than six pounds a plant, was never common in St. Bernard or Plaquemines, and the AgCenter did not keep its seed. So a Creole tomato today is a Louisiana-grown tomato picked ripe, not one cultivar.

The city celebrates it every June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival, which began in 1985 to mark the start of the season and honors the farmers who grow them. The French Market itself has stood since 1791.
facts: St. Bernard and Plaquemines growers traditionally sold their tomatoes as Creole, crediting vine ripening and alluvial soil.
In the early 1900s tomatoes from St. Charles, St. John and St. James parishes were also simply called Creole.
LSU AgCenter researcher Teme Hernandez released a variety named Creole in 1969; its seed stock was not kept.
Hernandez's Creole yielded less than six pounds per plant and was never common in St. Bernard or Plaquemines.
The French Market's Creole Tomato Festival began in 1985 and is held every June.
The French Market in New Orleans has stood since 1791.
notes: Say Creole tomato means a Louisiana tomato picked ripe, not a single variety; the menu pairs them with Louisiana heirlooms.
Do not name a farm or a parish for tonight's tomatoes unless the kitchen tells you at lineup.
The tostada follows the summer season; if guests ask why it has gone, the tomatoes have finished.
Guests sometimes ask whether Creole tomatoes are a breed: the honest answer is that the word is older than the 1969 LSU variety and means local and vine-ripened.

explain.value:
Okra is the green seed pod of a plant in the mallow family, brought to the Americas from West and Central Africa. Sliced and simmered, it releases a silky thickness that thickens soups; fried or dried crisp, it loses that texture and turns nutty. The word gumbo itself most likely comes from a West African word for okra, ki ngombo.

Southern and Creole cooks fry it, pickle it and stew it with tomatoes.

On our menus it is crisp: a housemade okra tostada under the Creole tomatoes, and fried okra chips on the Shrimp & Grits. The menu does not list okra in the gumbo, so do not promise it there.

value.front: Where does okra come from, and how do we serve it?
value.back: A seed pod from West and Central Africa that gave gumbo its name. We serve it crisp: the okra tostada and the fried okra chips on the Shrimp & Grits.

explain.value:
Popcorn rice is a Louisiana aromatic long-grain rice that really does smell of popcorn as it cooks. The aroma comes from a compound called 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the same molecule that perfumes basmati and jasmine rice and fresh popcorn, and Louisiana aromatic rice carries it in large amounts.

It cooks up firmer and more separate than jasmine, which is what a gumbo wants: grains that hold their shape in the broth.

Our Seafood Gumbo is served over popcorn rice. If a guest notices the nutty, toasty smell, that is the rice, not the roux, and it is a nice detail to share when the bowl lands.

value.front: What is popcorn rice, and why does it smell like popcorn?
value.back: A Louisiana aromatic long grain carrying 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the popcorn and basmati aroma molecule. Firm, separate grains under our Seafood Gumbo.

value.who: Louisiana popcorn rice (the Della type, bred by the LSU AgCenter)
value.where: LSU Rice Research Station, Crowley, Louisiana; milled across south Louisiana
value.history:
Popcorn rice is Louisiana's own aromatic long grain. The Rice Research Station at Crowley opened in 1909 on a 60-acre farm, set up by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station with the USDA and now run by the LSU AgCenter, and it was the AgCenter that released Della, an aromatic long-grain rice bred for cooks who wanted a fluffy texture and a strong popcorn-like aroma. Della is tall, falls over easily and yields poorly, which is why it remains a speciality rather than a field staple. The aroma itself is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the molecule that also scents basmati, jasmine and fresh popcorn.

The best-known retail example comes from the Conrad Rice Mill in New Iberia, founded in 1912 by Philip Amalus Conrad and the oldest independently owned rice mill in the United States still working. Its Konriko brand, named in the 1950s, sells Wild Pecan Rice, a Della-type brown popcorn rice that smells of roasted nuts. Mike Davis bought the mill in February 1975 and turned it towards speciality rice.

Brennan's prints popcorn rice under its Seafood Gumbo and names no mill, so Konriko is the story of the style, not the kitchen's bag.
facts: The Rice Research Station at Crowley opened in 1909 on a 60-acre farm, a joint Louisiana and USDA project now run by the LSU AgCenter.
The LSU AgCenter released Della, an aromatic long grain with a strong popcorn-like aroma.
Della is tall, lodges easily and yields poorly, so it stays a speciality rice.
Popcorn rice owes its aroma to 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, shared with basmati and jasmine.
The Conrad Rice Mill in New Iberia, founded in 1912, is the oldest independently owned US rice mill still operating.
Konriko's Wild Pecan Rice is a Della-type brown popcorn rice with a roasted-nut aroma.
notes: There is no popcorn and no pecan in popcorn rice or Wild Pecan Rice; the names describe the aroma.
Do not name Konriko or any mill as ours unless the kitchen confirms it.
If a guest notices a toasty smell as the gumbo lands, that is the rice.
Do not give a year for Della's release; sources place it only in the early 1970s.
value.sayIt: The gumbo sits on Louisiana popcorn rice, an aromatic long grain bred at LSU that really smells of popcorn as it cooks.
askKitchen: Whose popcorn rice do we use under the gumbo?

explain.value:
Grits are dried corn ground coarse and simmered slowly in water or milk until creamy, the Southern answer to polenta. Stone-ground grits keep more of the corn's germ and flavor and take longer to cook than quick grits; hominy grits are made from corn treated with alkali.

They are a blank, comforting base that takes on butter, cheese and sauce.

We serve them two ways: Cheddar Grits as a breakfast side, and a fried pimento cheese grit cake, crisp outside and creamy inside, under the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. Whether ours are stone-ground, and whose corn, are good questions for the kitchen.

value.front: What are grits?
value.back: Coarse-ground dried corn simmered slowly until creamy, the Southern polenta. We serve Cheddar Grits as a side and a fried pimento cheese grit cake.

explain.value:
Pimento cheese is the South's best-loved spread: grated sharp cheddar bound with mayonnaise and chopped sweet red pimientos. It began in New York around the 1870s as soft Neufchâtel mixed with imported Spanish peppers, then moved south, where cooks remade it with cheddar and mayonnaise and claimed it as their own.

It is tangy, creamy and a little sweet, and it melts beautifully.

On the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits it is folded into the grits before they set, then the cake is fried, so the outside is crisp and the inside creamy and cheesy. That fried grit cake is what most surprises guests who expect a bowl.

value.front: What is pimento cheese, and how is it used on our Shrimp & Grits?
value.back: Cheddar, mayonnaise and sweet pimientos, a Southern spread born in New York. It is folded into our grits, which are set and fried into a crisp cake.

explain.value:
Creole seasoning is a dry blend built on paprika, cayenne and black pepper, with garlic and onion powder, dried thyme and oregano, and salt. It gives warmth, color and savor more than raw heat, and every kitchen keeps its own proportions.

Brennan's makes its own, and the menu names it on the dinner Creole Hanger Steak; the breakfast hanger, the potato on the Eggs Owen and the Roost's spiced nuts are seasoned in the same style.

What is in the house blend is not printed, so if a guest asks about a particular spice, or how hot it is, the kitchen has the answer. In general, describe it as warm and savory rather than fiery.

value.front: What is in Creole seasoning?
value.back: A dry blend of paprika, cayenne and black pepper with garlic, onion, thyme and oregano: warm rather than fiery. Ours is housemade; the kitchen has the recipe.

explain.value:
Blackening is a young Louisiana technique. The chef Paul Prudhomme created it at K-Paul's around 1980: a fillet dipped in melted butter, coated in a paprika-led spice blend, and laid in a dry cast-iron skillet heated past smoking. The spices toast to a dark, almost black crust in seconds while the inside stays moist.

Prudhomme used it because his small kitchen had no grill, and the hot pan imitated char. Blackened redfish became a national craze.

Our Blackened Tofu uses the method on local tofu. The butter in the classic method is why the guide asks you to check with the kitchen before calling the dish vegan.

value.front: What is blackening, and who made it famous?
value.back: A spice-coated food seared in a smoking-hot dry cast-iron pan to a dark crust; Paul Prudhomme’s technique from around 1980. Used on our Blackened Tofu.

explain.value:
Deep frying cooks food submerged in hot oil, usually around 175 to 190 C. A coating, flour, cornmeal, batter or crumb, dries and browns into a crust while the inside steams in its own moisture. Oil that is too cool makes food greasy; too hot burns the outside before the inside cooks. Fried food is drained on a rack and served at once.

Fried food sells itself at a bar, and our menus use it widely: popcorn shrimp, fried Gulf shrimp, fried pickles, fries, the fried grit cake and okra chips, crispy artichokes and the fried Cornish hen.

Questions about coatings, shared fryers or what oil is used go to the kitchen every time.

value.front: What makes fried food crisp rather than greasy?
value.back: Oil at the right heat, about 175 to 190 C, browns the coating fast while the inside steams; drained on a rack and served at once. Fryer questions go to the kitchen.

explain.value:
Brown butter, beurre noisette in French, is butter cooked past melting until its milk solids toast to the color of hazelnuts and it smells nutty and sweet. It must be stopped at that moment, often with lemon or vinegar, because a few seconds more and it burns bitter.

That nutty depth is why it appears across our menus in different forms.

On the Louisiana Crab Claws it becomes a warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid; the spinach in the Turtle Soup is wilted in brown butter; and the financiers in the Blackberry Trifle are made with it, which is what makes them taste buttery rather than cakey.

value.front: What is brown butter, and where do we use it?
value.back: Butter cooked until its milk solids toast nutty, beurre noisette, stopped with acid: the crab claws’ vinaigrette, the turtle soup’s spinach, the trifle’s financiers.

explain.value:
A poached egg is cooked out of its shell in water held just below a simmer, often with a splash of vinegar to help the white set. The fresher the egg, the tighter the white. After about three minutes the white is set and the yolk still runs; restaurant kitchens often poach ahead, hold the eggs in iced water and reheat them for a few seconds at service.

The runny yolk becomes part of the sauce when the guest cuts in.

Our poached eggs sit at the heart of the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Sardou. They come soft unless the guest asks otherwise, and the guide says to check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs.

value.front: How are the eggs on the Hussarde and Sardou cooked?
value.back: Soft poached: cooked out of the shell in water below a simmer until the white sets and the yolk runs. Check with the kitchen before promising firmer.

explain.value:
Eggs any style covers the short list a breakfast cook makes every day. Sunny side up is fried on one side only, white set and yolk liquid; over easy is flipped briefly; over medium and over hard cook the yolk further. Scrambled eggs are stirred as they set, soft or firm; a soft-boiled egg is simmered in its shell for about six minutes so the yolk stays runny.

The server's job is to ask and to write it exactly on the ticket.

Our menus print a soft-boiled egg on the Eggs Owen and a sunny-side-up egg on the Duck Confit Waffle and the breakfast hanger, and offer an Egg Any Style side and the children's eggs. Confirm the styles the kitchen offers at lineup.

value.front: What are the common egg styles to ask a guest?
value.back: Sunny side up, over easy, over medium, over hard, scrambled soft or firm, poached, soft-boiled. Write the style exactly on the ticket.

explain.value:
Leidenheimer is the bakery behind New Orleans French bread and the po-boy. George Leidenheimer, from Deidesheim in Germany, started it in 1896, moved it to Simon Bolivar Avenue in 1904, and soon switched from dense German loaves to the light, airy loaf with a thin, crackly crust that the city preferred.

That loaf shatters when you bite it and stays tender inside; it is the standard for po-boys across the city.

On the Creole Caesar it becomes Leidenheimer crisps, thin toasted slices that replace croutons. Telling a guest the crisps are made from the city's po-boy bread turns a garnish into a piece of New Orleans.

value.front: What is Leidenheimer, and where is it on our menu?
value.back: The New Orleans bakery since 1896 whose light, crackly French loaf is the po-boy standard. Toasted into the crisps on our Creole Caesar.

value.history:
George Leidenheimer came to New Orleans from Deidesheim in Germany and opened a bakery on Dryades Street in 1896. He began with the heavy, dense brown breads of home, but the city's customers of French descent preferred a light, airy loaf, so he turned to New Orleans French bread, with its crisp crust.

In 1904 the bakery moved to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes. Its bread is older than the po-boy itself, which dates to the late 1920s, yet it became the loaf most of the city's po-boy shops reach for, and Leidenheimer is now the largest and best-known po-boy bread maker in New Orleans. The dough is naturally fermented and hand-stretched to a 32-inch loaf, and the bakery also makes pistolets and muffuletta bread.

The family still runs it: Robert J. "Sandy" Whann IV, George Leidenheimer's great-grandson, is the fourth generation and runs it with his sister, Katherine. After Hurricane Katrina, when the city had no power or clean water, Whann kept the bread coming by sending his operations manager to bake in a friend's bakery in Chicago.
facts: Founded in 1896 by George Leidenheimer, an immigrant from Deidesheim, Germany, first on Dryades Street.
Moved in 1904 to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes.
He switched from dense German loaves to the light, crisp-crusted New Orleans French bread.
Its bread predates the po-boy, which dates to the late 1920s.
The dough is naturally fermented and hand-stretched to a 32-inch loaf.
Run by Sandy Whann, the fourth generation and George Leidenheimer's great-grandson.
After Hurricane Katrina it kept baking in a friend's bakery in Chicago.
notes: Say the crisps are made from Leidenheimer, the city's po-boy bread; that turns a garnish into a piece of New Orleans.
The menu prints the name; no source says more about how Brennan's buys or makes the crisps, so how they are cut and toasted is a kitchen answer.
Guests often ask whether the bakery is still family run: yes, the fourth generation.
Never claim Leidenheimer invented the po-boy; its bread is older than the sandwich.
value.sayIt: The crisps are made from Leidenheimer French bread, the po-boy loaf New Orleans has baked since 1896.
askKitchen: How are the Leidenheimer crisps made: sliced and toasted here, with butter or oil?

explain.value:
The pecan is a hickory native to the Mississippi valley and the South, the nut New Orleans cooks reach for first. It is rich, buttery and sweet, softer than an almond, and it toasts quickly, so it is roasted gently.

Louisiana cooks used pecans in place of the almonds of French recipes, which is how the praline became a pecan candy and how pecan butters came to dress fish.

Pecans appear across our menus: in the crumble on the Baked Apple, on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, in the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish and in the pralines on the bread pudding. Nut questions always go to the kitchen and the service note.

value.front: Why are pecans everywhere on a New Orleans menu?
value.back: The native Southern nut, rich and buttery; Louisiana cooks used it in place of French almonds. On our Baked Apple, coffee cake, Gulf fish and pralines.

value.where: Louisiana and the Mississippi valley; Oak Alley Plantation, St. James Parish, for the first grafted pecans
value.history:
Louisiana is one of the few states where the pecan is native. The state holds between 19,000 and 21,000 acres of native trees, and their nuts tend to be small, flavorful and high in oil, unlike the larger improved varieties bred since. The LSU AgCenter runs the only university research station in the country devoted solely to pecans.

The improved pecan itself began in Louisiana. In the winter of 1846 or 1847, Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley Plantation in St. James Parish, grafted pecan wood from a tree with large, thin-shelled nuts onto other trees. He grafted sixteen trees near the house, more were grafted later, and by the end of the Civil War in 1865 Oak Alley had 126 grafted trees in bearing. His nut, later named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, and grafting made the pecan an orchard crop.

In New Orleans kitchens the pecan stands where the almond stood in French recipes. It runs right through Brennan's menus: the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the oat and pecan crumble on the Baked Apple, the pecans on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and the pralines on the bread pudding.
facts: Louisiana is one of few states where pecans are native.
Louisiana has between 19,000 and 21,000 acres of native pecans.
Native pecans tend to be small, flavorful and high in oil compared with improved varieties.
The LSU AgCenter runs the only university research station in the United States devoted solely to pecans.
Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley, grafted pecans in 1846 or 1847; by 1865 the plantation had 126 grafted trees.
Antoine's pecan, named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia.
notes: Pecans appear in four dishes; nut questions always go to the kitchen and the service note, never a verdict from you.
Do not claim our pecans are Louisiana-grown or native unless the kitchen confirms the supplier.
Antoine's story is a powerful one for interested guests; tell it plainly and with respect.
Say pih-KAHN, the common Louisiana pronunciation.
value.sayIt: The pecan is native to Louisiana, and New Orleans cooks use it where French recipes used almonds, from the fish to the pralines.
askKitchen: Where do our pecans come from, and are they Louisiana or native pecans?

explain.value:
Crème fraîche is cream thickened and soured gently by lactic cultures, the French cousin of sour cream. It is richer and milder than sour cream, with a fresh, slightly nutty tang, and it does not split when warmed.

A spoonful brings cool, tangy richness against something warm, sweet or rich.

We use it three ways: sweetened beside the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting, whipped on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, and as the cool, silky layer in the Steak Tartare Cannoli. Say krem FRESH, and describe it to a guest as a slightly tangy cultured cream.

value.front: What is crème fraîche, and where do we use it?
value.back: A cultured French cream, richer and milder than sour cream with a gentle tang: sweetened on the Baked Apple, whipped on the coffee cake, in the tartare cannoli.

explain.value:
Collard greens are broad, sturdy leaves of the cabbage family, a pillar of Southern cooking. Traditionally they are simmered for a long time with smoked pork until silky, and the cooking liquid, the pot likker, is prized in its own right.

Cooked quickly or pickled, they keep a pleasant chew and a cabbagey bite.

Our menus use them two ways. On the Louisiana Oysters they are pickled, a sharp bite that cuts the rich BBQ sauce the way a mignonette would. On the Pecan Gulf Fish they are wilted, earthy greens beside the cauliflower purée. Neither is the long-simmered pot of a Sunday table, which is worth saying if a guest expects it.

value.front: How do we serve collard greens?
value.back: Pickled on the Louisiana Oysters for a sharp bite against the rich sauce, and wilted on the Pecan Gulf Fish, not the long-simmered Southern pot.

components.name: Baked apple with oat and pecan crumble

explain.value:
The Baked Apple starts with a whole apple, peeled, cored and trimmed flat so it stands. A crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon is packed on top, and the apple bakes until a skewer slides through with no resistance. The brown sugar melts into the apple's juices and caramelizes, which is where the glaze comes from.

It is the French baked apple meeting the British crumble, warm and soft under a little crunch.

It is the first plated course of the Traditional Breakfast, after the Brandy Milk Punch. Which apple the kitchen uses, and whether the tasting portion is whole or half, are good lineup questions.

value.front: How is the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting made?
value.back: A whole apple, peeled and cored, baked soft under an oat, pecan, raisin, brown sugar and cinnamon crumble that caramelizes into a glaze; served with sweetened crème fraîche.

explain.value:
Filet mignon is a small steak cut from the narrow end of the beef tenderloin, the muscle along the spine that does almost no work. That makes it the most tender cut on the animal and also one of the mildest, so it relies on its sauce and garnish for savor.

A petite filet is a small portion that cooks quickly: seared hard, finished gently and rested for a few minutes so the juices settle.

On the Traditional Breakfast it is the fourth course, with a crisp potato rösti, garlic spinach and a 4 oz pour of Côtes du Rhône. Take the guest's temperature when you take the tasting order, not when the course fires.

value.front: When do you take the temperature for the tasting’s Petite Filet?
value.back: With the tasting order, at the start. Filet mignon is the tender, mild narrow end of the tenderloin; ours comes with rösti, garlic spinach and Côtes du Rhône.

explain.value:
Rösti is the Swiss potato cake from the Bern region: potato grated, pressed into a hot pan with butter or fat, and cooked slowly on both sides into a thick, golden disc that is crisp outside and soft within. Raw grated potato gives the most crunch; restaurants often par-boil the potatoes, chill them and grate them the next day so the cake holds together.

The Bernese say it with a soft sh, which is why the guide's RUHSH-tee is right.

Under the Petite Filet Mignon on the breakfast tasting it does the job of the classic steak potato: crisp texture and starch to catch the meat's juices.

value.front: What is a rösti?
value.back: A Swiss grated potato cake from Bern, pressed in a hot buttered pan until crisp outside and soft within. It sits under our Petite Filet Mignon.

explain.value:
Garlic spinach is fresh spinach wilted quickly in a hot pan with oil or butter and sliced garlic, then squeezed of its water and seasoned at the last moment so it stays bright green rather than gray.

It is the simplest of the greens on our menus, light where the creamed spinach is rich.

On the Petite Filet Mignon it brings the savor that a mild filet lacks: garlic, iron and a little bitterness to balance the beef and the crisp rösti. If a guest asks how it differs from the Sardou's spinach, the answer is that this one is wilted with garlic, not creamed with Parmesan.

value.front: How does the filet’s garlic spinach differ from our creamed spinach?
value.back: It is wilted quickly with garlic, light and green; the creamed spinach on the Sardou and as a side is bound with cream and Parmesan.

explain.value:
Lobster on a New Orleans menu comes from the cold waters of the North Atlantic; the Gulf has spiny lobsters but no clawed lobster. The meat is sweet, firm and rich, and it toughens quickly if it boils, so kitchens usually blanch and shell it first, then finish it gently in a sauce.

New Orleans cooks have long dressed it in local styles, and here it wears the city's barbecue shrimp sauce.

On the dinner tasting's Louisiana BBQ Lobster it sits on a white bean stew with 'nduja. The guide asks you to confirm the night's BBQ sauce at lineup, because the house's version has changed over the years.

value.front: Where does the lobster on the BBQ Lobster come from?
value.back: Clawed lobster comes from the cold North Atlantic, not the Gulf. Ours is finished gently in New Orleans BBQ sauce over a white bean and ’nduja stew.

explain.value:
'Nduja is a soft, spicy pork sausage from Calabria, at the toe of Italy, made around the village of Spilinga. Pork trimmings and fatback are ground with a large share of sun-dried Calabrian chilli, stuffed, lightly smoked and cured. At room temperature it is soft enough to spread like a pâté.

Warmed, it melts into whatever it touches, carrying fat, salt and a slow red-pepper heat.

In the white bean stew under the Louisiana BBQ Lobster it plays the part andouille plays in red beans: a little pork melting into the beans, so every spoonful is rich and gently hot. Say en-DOO-yah, and warn guests who are shy of spice.

value.front: What is ’nduja?
value.back: A spreadable, chilli-hot pork sausage from Spilinga in Calabria. It melts into the white bean stew under our BBQ Lobster, giving a slow red-pepper heat.

value.where: Spilinga, province of Vibo Valentia, Calabria
value.history:
'Nduja comes from Spilinga, a hill town in the province of Vibo Valentia, at the toe of Italy. It was a poor family's sausage. After the winter slaughter the better cuts went to the landowners, and what was left, the fatty, less prized trimmings, was turned into something that would keep and feed a household.

The method is simple and bold: fatback, belly and shoulder trimmings minced very fine with dried Calabrian chilli, around a third of the weight, plus salt, packed into a natural casing, lightly smoked over local wood and aged for several months. The result is soft enough to spread like a pâté and melts into anything warm.

Where it came from is argued. One theory says the Aragonese brought it in the sixteenth century; another derives it from the French andouille, introduced when Joachim Murat ruled the Kingdom of Naples at the beginning of the nineteenth century. If that second theory is right, the 'nduja in our white beans and the andouille in our gumbo share a French ancestor, a pleasing thought for a New Orleans table, offered as a theory and no more.
facts: 'Nduja comes from Spilinga in the province of Vibo Valentia, Calabria.
It is fatty pork trimmings minced with dried Calabrian chilli, about a third of the weight.
It is cased, lightly smoked and aged for several months, and spreads like a pâté.
It began as a way to use the fatty cuts left after the better ones went to landowners.
One theory credits the Aragonese in the sixteenth century; another the French andouille under Joachim Murat.
notes: Say en-DOO-yah, and warn spice-shy guests: it carries a slow red-pepper heat.
The andouille link is a theory, a good one for New Orleans; say one theory is, never that it is fact.
No maker is printed; whether ours is Italian or American is a kitchen question.
Pork is in the beans; dietary questions go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: 'Nduja, en-DOO-yah, the spreadable chilli pork sausage of Spilinga in Calabria, melted into the white beans under the lobster.
askKitchen: Whose 'nduja do we use, and is it rendered into the beans or dolloped on top?

explain.value:
A white bean stew is dried white beans soaked and simmered slowly with aromatics and stock until they are creamy but still whole, the idea behind a French cassoulet or a pot of Louisiana beans. The beans drink up fat and flavor, so they make a soft bed for something rich.

Kept loose and spoonable, the stew catches the sauce from whatever sits on top.

Under the Louisiana BBQ Lobster it carries 'nduja, so the beans are creamy, porky and gently hot, and the buttery BBQ sauce runs into them. Whether the 'nduja is cooked into the beans or added as a finishing spoonful is a good question for the chef.

value.front: What sits under the Louisiana BBQ Lobster?
value.back: A creamy white bean stew with ’nduja, like a spicy Calabrian cousin of Louisiana beans; it catches the buttery BBQ sauce from the lobster.

explain.value:
Rohan is not a breed but a proprietary cross created for D'Artagnan, a specialty meat company. It brings together the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, and the birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York State's Catskills, without antibiotics, to about eleven weeks, longer than most commercial ducks.

The name honors the Rohan family of Brittany. The meat is rosy, tender and milder than wild duck, with a good layer of fat under the skin.

We use it twice: the roasted breast on the dinner tasting and the confit leg on the Duck Confit Waffle. Say a special cross raised in New York, and do not call it a breed.

value.front: What is a Rohan duck?
value.back: A proprietary Mallard and Pekin cross raised for D’Artagnan in New York’s Catskills: rosy, tender, mild meat. Our tasting breast and confit waffle leg.

value.where: Raised in New York's Catskills; D'Artagnan is based in Union, New Jersey
value.history:
The Rohan is D'Artagnan's own duck. D'Artagnan was founded in 1985 by Ariane Daguin and George Faison, who met working at a charcuterie shop in New York City. A farmer had the first domestically raised foie gras in the United States and needed someone to sell it, so the two started a company to do it, selling whole raw lobes to New York chefs. Daguin was born in Auch, in Gascony, the eldest child of the Michelin-starred chef André Daguin, and the company is named for the Gascon musketeer. It is based in Union, New Jersey.

D'Artagnan's blog introduced the Rohan in January 2012. It is a proprietary cross of several breeds, including the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, bred to approximate a style of duck found in Normandy and named for the family of dukes and princes of Rohan in Brittany. The birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York's Catskills, cage-free and never given antibiotics, hormones or steroids, to 11 weeks, five weeks longer than the average factory duck. Daguin says the extra time deepens the flavor and improves the meat-to-bone ratio.

The result is rosy, tender, mild meat with a rich, buttery depth. Brennan's prints Rohan on the duck breast of the dinner tasting and on the confit leg of the Duck Confit Waffle.
facts: The Rohan is a proprietary D'Artagnan cross of several breeds, including the heritage Mallard and the Pekin.
Raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York's Catskills to 11 weeks, five weeks longer than the average factory duck.
Raised cage-free, never given antibiotics, hormones or steroids.
Named for the family of dukes and princes of Rohan, in Brittany; bred to approximate a style of Normandy duck.
D'Artagnan was founded in 1985 by Ariane Daguin and George Faison to sell the first domestically raised US foie gras.
Ariane Daguin is the eldest child of André Daguin, the Michelin-starred Gascon chef famous for foie gras.
D'Artagnan has its headquarters and distribution center in Union, New Jersey.
notes: Say a special cross, not a breed; the guide's word breed is loose.
The menu prints Rohan, not D'Artagnan. If a guest asks, Rohan is D'Artagnan's duck, raised in New York's Catskills; whether we buy direct is not confirmed.
Never name a farm: no source names the farm that raises the Rohan, and Crescent Duck Farm on Long Island is a separate Pekin farm.
The tasting duck changes with the season: the pasted card has cane syrup peaches, the house website a hazelnut-crusted, 14-day dry-aged breast. Read tonight's card.
