Duck breast is served rosy; take the guest's preference to the kitchen rather than promising a temperature.
value.sayIt: Rohan is a special Mallard and Pekin cross raised in New York's Catskills, longer than most ducks, for rosy, tender meat.
askKitchen: Do we buy the Rohan direct from D'Artagnan or through a distributor?
Which duck course is on tonight: the cane syrup peaches or the hazelnut-crusted, dry-aged breast?
If the breast is dry-aged, for how long on the current course?

explain.value:
A duck breast carries a thick layer of fat under the skin, and the cook's job is to render most of it away while keeping the meat rosy. The skin is scored in a tight crosshatch, the breast goes skin-down into a cold or moderate pan, and the fat melts out slowly as the skin crisps. A short turn on the flesh side, a finish in the oven and a rest of a few minutes follow, then it is sliced across the grain.

Duck breast is served pink, like a steak; cooked through it turns gray and livery.

On the dinner tasting the Rohan breast comes with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts. The usual doneness is medium-rare to medium; confirm at lineup.

value.front: How is duck breast usually served, and why?
value.back: Pink, medium-rare to medium, after the fat is rendered from scored skin; cooked through it turns gray and livery. Confirm the kitchen’s temperature at lineup.

explain.value:
Cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles until thick, with nothing taken out. Molasses is what remains after sugar has been crystallized and removed, so cane syrup is sweeter, lighter and milder, with a buttery caramel taste rather than molasses's bitter edge. Steen's of Abbeville has made it since 1910, after a freeze threatened a cane crop.

It is a Louisiana pantry staple poured on biscuits, baked into cakes and used to glaze meat.

On the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast it glazes peaches, sweet and caramelized against rich duck. The menu does not name a brand, so say Louisiana cane syrup, a lighter cousin of molasses.

value.front: How does cane syrup differ from molasses?
value.back: Cane syrup is cane juice simply boiled down with nothing removed, so it is sweeter and lighter; molasses is what is left after sugar is taken out.

value.who: Louisiana cane syrup (Steen's of Abbeville is the best-known maker; the menu names none)
value.history:
Louisiana cane syrup is cane juice concentrated by long cooking in open kettles, with nothing taken out and nothing added. Slow Food lists traditional cane syrup on its Ark of Taste, the catalog of heritage foods worth saving.

The name most Louisianans reach for is Steen's. In 1910 an early freeze hit Charley Steen's cane crop near Abbeville. Rather than lose it, he built a small mill and turned the frozen cane into a few barrels of syrup. By 1930 Charley and Elizabeth Steen and their children had built a larger mill in the heart of Abbeville, on the banks of Bayou Vermilion, and from the 1950s the yellow can became a fixture of Cajun and Creole kitchens. The mill is still run by the Steen family and still cooks in open kettles, which is why the label reads 100% Pure Cane Syrup.

Brennan's menu prints cane syrup on the peaches of the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast but names no maker, so Steen's is the story of the style, not a claim about the kitchen's bottle.
facts: Cane syrup is cane juice concentrated by long cooking in open kettles.
Traditional cane syrup is listed on Slow Food's Ark of Taste.
Steen's began in 1910 when an early freeze hit Charley Steen's cane crop and he milled it into syrup.
By 1930 Charley and Elizabeth Steen built a larger mill in Abbeville on Bayou Vermilion.
Steen's still cooks in open kettles and adds nothing, hence 100% Pure Cane Syrup on the label.
Molasses is what remains after sugar is crystallized out; cane syrup has nothing removed.
notes: Say Louisiana cane syrup; never say Steen's is on the plate unless the kitchen confirms it.
Guests often ask if it is molasses: no, it is lighter and sweeter, cane juice simply boiled down.
The duck course has appeared in two versions on the house's own pages; describe the one printed tonight.
Steen's makes a good story for curious guests: a 1910 freeze turned into a Louisiana staple.
value.sayIt: The peaches are glazed in Louisiana cane syrup, cane juice simply boiled down, lighter and more buttery than molasses, against the rich duck.
askKitchen: Whose cane syrup glazes the peaches on the duck, Steen's or another maker?
Is tonight's duck the cane syrup peach version or the hazelnut-crusted version?

explain.value:
Candied hazelnuts are toasted hazelnuts coated in caramelized sugar, the same family as a French praline. Hazelnuts are sweet, buttery and slightly bitter in the skin, and toasting brings out their aroma.

The coating must stay dry and glassy; humid air turns it sticky within an hour, so they are made close to service.

On the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast they give crunch and a toasty sweetness against the soft duck and glazed peaches. The guide notes that the autumn version of the duck course may change to a hazelnut-crusted plate, so read the printed tasting card at lineup before describing it.

value.front: What gives crunch on the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast?
value.back: Candied hazelnuts, toasted nuts in a glassy caramel coating, a praline cousin; toasty and sweet against the duck and cane syrup peaches.

explain.value:
A trifle is an English layered pudding with centuries of history: sponge or biscuits soaked in sherry or juice, fruit, custard and whipped cream, built in a glass bowl so the layers show. It was a dish for gatherings and a way to use up cake.

Our Blackberry Trifle rebuilds it in French pastry terms. Fruit curds take the place of custard, small financiers replace the sponge, and a coconut chia pudding is the modern layer.

It is built in a glass so the guest sees the colors. Served as a starter on the breakfast and lunch menu, it suits the middle of the table while the eggs are cooking: tart rather than sugary.

value.front: What is a trifle, and how does ours differ?
value.back: An English layered pudding of sponge, fruit, custard and cream. Ours uses blackberry and lemon curds, coconut chia pudding and blackberry financiers.

explain.value:
A fruit curd is a cooked spread of fruit juice, sugar, egg yolks and butter, stirred over gentle heat until it thickens to coat a spoon, then chilled until set. Lemon curd is the British classic; blackberry curd uses the purée of the fruit, which gives a deep purple color and a tart, jammy taste.

Curds are richer and sharper than jam and silkier than custard.

In the Blackberry Trifle the two curds are the bright, tart layers, purple and yellow, that keep the dessert from tasting sugary. They are made ahead and set cold, so the trifle can be built quickly to order. The service note lists what the curds contain.

value.front: What is a fruit curd?
value.back: Fruit juice, sugar, egg yolks and butter cooked until thick and set cold: tart, rich and silky. Blackberry and lemon curds are the bright layers of our trifle.

explain.value:
Chia seeds come from a plant of the mint family native to Central America. Soaked in liquid for several hours, each seed swells and wraps itself in a soft gel, so a spoonful of seeds sets a whole bowl of milk into a pudding without cooking.

Made with coconut milk it is lightly sweet and tropical, with a texture like tapioca.

In the Blackberry Trifle it is the creamy, modern layer between the tart curds. The guide suggests mentioning the seedy texture before a guest orders, since some people love it and some do not; coconut is listed on the service note.

value.front: What is the chia pudding layer in the trifle?
value.back: Chia seeds soaked in coconut milk until they swell into a gel and set the milk: creamy, lightly sweet, tapioca-like. Mention the seedy texture.

explain.value:
A financier is a small French cake of ground almonds, egg whites, sugar, a little flour and brown butter, baked in a small mold. The standard account credits a Paris pâtissier named Lasne, whose shop stood near the stock exchange around 1890; he shaped them like little gold bars for the traders, and the name stuck.

The brown butter is what makes them taste rich and nutty, with crisp edges and a moist center.

In the Blackberry Trifle they are blackberry financier biscuits, the trifle's answer to sponge. The guide notes they are traditionally made with almond flour and asks you to confirm with the kitchen.

value.front: Why is a financier shaped like a gold bar?
value.back: A Paris pâtissier near the stock exchange shaped these almond and brown butter cakes like gold bars for traders around 1890. Ours sit in the trifle.

explain.value:
French toast is pain perdu, lost bread: stale bread rescued by soaking it in egg and milk, often with sugar and vanilla, and frying it in butter. In New Orleans it is an old Creole breakfast. The bread must be thick and slightly dry, or it soaks to mush; the pan must be moderate, so the custard center sets before the outside burns.

Brioche makes the richest version, soft and custardy inside with a caramelized crust.

Our Framboise French Toast uses housemade citrus brioche, sold as a starter to share, and the children's breakfast offers a vanilla French toast with berries and whipped cream.

value.front: What does pain perdu mean, and where is it on our menu?
value.back: Lost bread: stale bread soaked in egg and milk and fried in butter. Our Framboise French Toast uses citrus brioche; children get vanilla French toast.

explain.value:
Brioche is a French bread enriched with eggs, butter and a little sugar, so it bakes up golden, soft and almost cake-like, with a fine, tender crumb. The dough is slow and sticky to make, and the butter is worked in after the dough has built its stretch.

A citrus brioche adds orange or lemon zest for perfume.

The kitchen bakes its own for the Framboise French Toast, sliced thick so it can soak up custard without falling apart. That housemade detail is worth saying: it is why the French toast is rich and custardy inside rather than bready.

value.front: What kind of bread is in the Framboise French Toast?
value.back: Housemade citrus brioche, an egg and butter enriched French bread with zest, sliced thick so it soaks up custard and stays rich inside.

explain.value:
Mascarpone is a fresh cheese from Lombardy, made by setting cream with acid and draining it. It is rich, mild and spoonable, closer to clotted cream than to a cream cheese, and it is the cheese in tiramisu.

Whipped with a little sugar and cream, it becomes a light mousse that holds its shape on warm food.

On the Framboise French Toast the mascarpone mousse is the cool, creamy layer against the warm brioche and the sharp raspberries. The guide's description, a whipped Italian cream cheese, is a fair word for guests. Say mahs-kar-POH-neh, four syllables.

value.front: What is mascarpone?
value.back: A rich, mild fresh cheese from Lombardy made from cream, the cheese in tiramisu. Whipped into a mousse on our Framboise French Toast.

explain.value:
Framboise is French for raspberry, which is where the French Toast gets its name. A coulis is a smooth fruit sauce: berries cooked briefly or simply puréed with sugar and a little lemon, then pushed through a fine sieve so no seeds remain.

Raspberries are among the sharpest of the soft fruits, so the coulis cuts richness.

On the Framboise French Toast the raspberry comes twice, as a bright red coulis and as fresh local raspberries, against the brioche and the mascarpone mousse. Say frahm-BWAHZ for the name and koo-LEE for the sauce.

value.front: What do framboise and coulis mean?
value.back: Framboise is French for raspberry; a coulis is a smooth, sieved fruit sauce. Our French toast gets a raspberry coulis and fresh local raspberries.

explain.value:
Café brûlot is New Orleans' flaming after-dinner coffee. Antoine's credits Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, with café brûlot diabolique in the late nineteenth century: brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with cinnamon, clove and a long spiral of orange and lemon peel, then ladled into strong coffee at the table. Brûlot comes from brûler, to burn.

It is one of the city's great tableside rituals.

Brennan's borrows its flavors for the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. The drink itself is not on our list, so sell the cake as the coffee's flavors, not the flame.

value.front: What is café brûlot, and how does our coffee cake use it?
value.back: New Orleans’ flaming spiced coffee with brandy and citrus peel, from Antoine’s. Our coffee cake borrows its flavors: chicory coffee, chocolate, spiced citrus glaze.

explain.value:
Chicory is a plant whose root is roasted and ground and mixed with coffee. The French stretched coffee with it during the blockades of the Napoleonic wars, and New Orleans, a French city and a great coffee port, kept the habit, most famously when the Union blockade cut off coffee during the Civil War.

It stayed because people liked it: chicory adds a roasty, slightly bitter, chocolatey depth and a smooth body.

Our New Orleans style coffee is made with chicory, and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake bakes chicory coffee into a bittersweet chocolate cake, where it deepens the chocolate. Questions about caffeine go to the service note.

value.front: Why does New Orleans coffee contain chicory?
value.back: Roasted chicory root stretched coffee in French blockades and the Civil War, and New Orleans kept it for its roasty, chocolatey depth. It is in our coffee cake.

value.who: Roasted chicory root, the New Orleans coffee tradition
value.where: Grown mostly in France and Belgium; roasted and blended with coffee in New Orleans
value.history:
Chicory is the root of a blue-flowered perennial, dug, cut, dried, roasted and ground. In 1806 the British blockaded the French coast and Napoleon answered with his Continental System, an embargo on British trade that lasted until 1814. Imported coffee grew scarce, chicory became the French substitute, and the French kept their taste for it after the embargo ended. The habit reached New Orleans with its French colonial ties.

New Orleans was ready for it. By 1840 the port was the second largest coffee importer in the United States. During the Civil War, from 1861, the Union naval blockade cut the port off, and Louisianans stretched what coffee they had with chicory. Smithsonian calls it a cost-saving workaround that stuck around for tradition's sake: the rest of the South dropped it, New Orleans did not.

Today most commercial chicory is grown in France and Belgium. At Brennan's it is in the New Orleans Style Coffee, a blend of chicory and dark roast, in the private blend poured on the breakfast tasting, and baked into the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.
facts: Chicory is the roasted root of a blue-flowered perennial plant.
Napoleon's Continental System, an embargo on British trade from 21 November 1806, made imported coffee scarce, and chicory filled the gap.
The French kept drinking chicory in their coffee after the Continental System collapsed.
By 1840 New Orleans was the second largest coffee importer in the United States.
From 1861 the Union naval blockade cut off the port, and Louisianans stretched coffee with chicory.
Most commercial chicory is grown in France and Belgium.
Brennan's prints chicory in its New Orleans Style Coffee, the breakfast tasting coffee and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.
notes: Chicory is not coffee: it is a roasted root blended with coffee for body and a roasty, bitter-chocolate depth.

The breakfast tasting blend is roasted by Congregation, which has its own card; the menu names no roaster for the New Orleans Style Coffee, and where the chicory is grown is not public, so name no country for ours.
The Civil War story is true but not the whole story: the French habit came first.
Caffeine questions go to the service note and the kitchen; do not guess decaf options.
value.sayIt: Chicory is a roasted root, a French habit New Orleans kept through the Civil War blockade; it gives our coffee a roasty, chocolatey depth.
askKitchen: What proportion of chicory is in the New Orleans Style Coffee blend?
Is the coffee cake baked with the same Congregation chicory blend we pour?

explain.value:
Saltines are thin, crisp, lightly salted crackers, the cracker that sits on every Gulf Coast oyster bar beside the hot sauce and horseradish. Crushed, fried in butter or oil and seasoned, they become a crunchy crumble.

It is the raw bar's oyster cracker turned into a garnish.

On the Louisiana Oysters the fried saltine crumble gives crunch against the soft oysters and the rich BBQ sauce, and it is added at the last moment so it stays crisp. The guide lists saltines on the service note; questions go there and to the kitchen.

value.front: What is the crunchy topping on the Louisiana Oysters?
value.back: A fried saltine crumble: the Gulf oyster bar’s cracker, crushed and fried, added at the last moment for crunch against the oysters and BBQ sauce.

explain.value:
Burrata is a fresh cheese from Puglia in southern Italy: a pouch of mozzarella filled with stracciatella, shreds of curd soaked in cream. Cut open, the center spills out soft and milky.

It is best at room temperature and torn rather than sliced; cold burrata is firm and loses its sweetness.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada it is the creamy partner to the raw Louisiana tomatoes, the way mozzarella partners tomato in a caprese. The guide's line, mozzarella with a creamy center, is exactly right for a guest. Say boo-RAH-tah.

value.front: What is burrata?
value.back: A Puglian mozzarella pouch filled with cream-soaked curd, soft and milky inside, served at room temperature. The creamy partner on our Creole Tomato Tostada.

value.history:
Burrata is a fresh cheese of the Murgia in Puglia, made from cow's milk, rennet and cream: a pouch of mozzarella filled with shreds of curd soaked in cream. Its birthplace is the town of Andria, though the date is argued. Some place it about 1900, at the farm of the brothers Lorenzo and Vincenzo Bianchino; more recent records credit Lorenzo Bianchino of the Piana Padura farm with first making it in 1956.

The story told in Puglia is of a heavy February snowfall that kept Bianchino from the market. With milk that would not keep, he wrapped curd, scraps of mozzarella and the cream from the morning milking inside a skin of mozzarella, so nothing was wasted.

For decades it stayed a local fresh cheese that had to be eaten within days. In November 2016 Burrata di Andria became a protected geographical indication, an IGP, recognizing the town's claim.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada it does what mozzarella does in a caprese: a cool, milky foil for raw Louisiana tomatoes, torn and served at room temperature.
facts: Burrata is a fresh cow's milk cheese of the Murgia in Puglia, mozzarella filled with cream-soaked curd.
Its birthplace is Andria; some date it to about 1900 at the Bianchino brothers' farm.
More recent records credit Lorenzo Bianchino of the Piana Padura farm, in 1956.
The story says a February snowfall kept him from market, so he used up curd and cream.
Burrata di Andria became a protected geographical indication in November 2016.
notes: Say boo-RAH-tah: mozzarella with a creamy center, from Andria in Puglia.
Never call ours Burrata di Andria IGP or Italian unless the kitchen confirms it; good burrata is also made in America.
Tell the snowstorm story as a story; the date itself is argued.
No meat is printed on the dish; vegetarian and dairy questions still go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: Burrata, boo-RAH-tah, from Andria in Puglia: a pouch of mozzarella with a soft, creamy center, beside our Creole tomatoes.
askKitchen: Where is our burrata made, Italy or America?

components.name: Okra tostada and smoked tomato water

explain.value:
A tostada is a flat, crisp fried tortilla of the Mexican kitchen, used as a base for toppings. Ours is housemade with okra; the menu does not say whether it is made on masa or wheat, which matters for some guests, so ask the kitchen.

Tomato water is the clear juice that drips from salted, puréed tomatoes hung in cloth overnight: pale gold, intensely tomatoey and light. Smoking it adds a gentle campfire note.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada the tomato water goes on last, so the tostada stays crisp for the first bites. Tell the guest to eat it soon after it lands: the crunch fades within minutes.

value.front: What is smoked tomato water?
value.back: The clear juice of salted, puréed tomatoes strained overnight, then smoked: intensely tomatoey and light. Poured on last so our okra tostada stays crisp.

explain.value:
Fines herbes is the classical French mix of four soft herbs: parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, chopped finely and used fresh. Chervil tastes of mild anise and parsley, tarragon of stronger anise, chives of gentle onion.

They are added at the very end of cooking, because heat blackens tarragon and chervil and kills their perfume.

On the Louisiana Crab Claws they are tossed through the warm brown butter vinaigrette at the last moment, a fresh green lift against nutty butter and sweet crab. If a guest asks what the green flecks are, name the four herbs.

value.front: What are fines herbes?
value.back: The classic French four: parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, added fresh at the end. They finish the brown butter vinaigrette on our Louisiana Crab Claws.

explain.value:
Cocktail crab claws are blue crab claws with the shell cracked away from the meat and the pincer left on as a handle. They arrive already cooked and chilled, so the kitchen only warms them through; cooking them again tightens the meat onto the cartilage and makes it hard to pull.

Guests eat them with their fingers: hold the pincer, bite the meat and slide the cartilage out.

Our Louisiana Crab Claws are served warm in the brown butter vinaigrette, which surprises guests who expect cold claws, so say served warm aloud and bring napkins and a plate for the shells. Whether they can be served chilled on request is a question for the chef.

value.front: How do guests eat the Louisiana Crab Claws?
value.back: With fingers: hold the pincer, bite the meat, slide the cartilage out. Say they are served warm, and bring napkins and a plate for shells.

explain.value:
Grand Isle is the barrier island at the edge of the Louisiana coast. Grand Isle Jewels is a brand launched in April 2025 by JEDCO, the Jefferson Parish economic development commission, with the island's off-bottom oyster farmers.

Off-bottom farming raises oysters in cages that float or hang above the seafloor. The cages float just below the surface in an aquapark where ocean and estuary water mix, which keeps the oysters off the mud and gives them a briny, bright flavor, and the method is gentler on a storm-damaged coast than dredging wild reefs.

We serve them raw with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting. Know the count per order, and ask the chef whether to tell the farming story.

value.front: What are Grand Isle Jewel oysters?
value.back: Louisiana oysters farmed in floating cages off Grand Isle, a 2025 brand from JEDCO and the island’s eight growers: briny and bright. Served raw.

value.history:
Grand Isle is the barrier island at the southern edge of Jefferson Parish. Its oyster industry was about 150 years old when it failed in the 1980s.

The revival began in 2012, when Jules Melancon, a multigenerational oysterman, became the first permitted to farm oysters off-bottom there: seed grown in floating cages just below the surface instead of on the seabed. Others followed, working in the Grand Isle Aquapark, where ocean and estuary water mix and the salinity suits a briny oyster. Melancon died in 2023.

In April 2025 the Jefferson Parish Economic Development Commission, JEDCO, gathered eight of the island's growers under one regional brand, Grand Isle Jewels. The name nods to the island's pirate past and to Melancon himself. The brand sells to restaurants across the Southeast and Texas, and a distribution partnership with Inland Foods followed a market test of about 10,000 products.
facts: Grand Isle Jewels is a regional oyster brand launched by JEDCO, the Jefferson Parish Economic Development Commission, in April 2025.
Eight Grand Isle growers farm under the brand, in floating cages rather than on the seabed.
Jules Melancon brought off-bottom farming to Grand Isle in 2012; the brand's name honors him and the island's pirate past.
The island's oyster industry, about 150 years old, had failed in the 1980s before off-bottom farming revived it.
Seed oysters grow just below the surface in an aquapark chosen for temperature, water flow and salinity.
The growers describe the flavor as briny and bright, from the mix of ocean and estuary water.
Inland Foods tested about 10,000 Grand Isle Jewels products before expanding distribution across the Southeast and Texas.
notes: The menu prints Grand Isle Jewel; the brand is Grand Isle Jewels. Either is fine aloud.
Expect these to taste saltier and brighter than the cooked Louisiana Oysters: they are grown in briny water on purpose.
Do not name a single farm, or say the method was invented on Grand Isle; say the island revived its oysters by farming them off the bottom.
Raw shellfish questions go to the manager or the kitchen; point to the asterisk on the menu, never give a safety verdict yourself.
value.sayIt: These are Grand Isle Jewels, farmed in floating cages off Louisiana's barrier island: briny, bright and served raw.
askKitchen: How many oysters come per order, and which Grand Isle farm or farms are they from tonight?
Do we buy them from the growers or through a distributor?

explain.value:
Oysters on the half shell are shucked to order: the knife goes in at the hinge, the top shell comes off, and the adductor muscle is cut cleanly so the oyster sits loose in its cup with its liquor. They are bedded on crushed ice and reach the table cold.

The liquor, the salty juice in the shell, is part of the taste; a good shucker never pours it away.

The Grand Isle Jewel oysters are served this way. The guide flags a raw shellfish advisory on this dish: read the service note, and send every question about raw seafood to the kitchen or the manager rather than answering it yourself.

value.front: What should a server know when selling raw oysters?
value.back: They are shucked to order and served cold with their liquor. Read the raw shellfish advisory on the service note and send questions to the kitchen.

explain.value:
The Fresno chilli was released in 1952 by Clarence Brown Hamlin and named for Fresno, California. It looks like a jalapeño and sits in the same heat band, roughly 2,500 to 10,000 Scoville units, but it has thinner walls, ripens quickly to bright red and tastes fruitier. A fully red Fresno can be a little hotter than a green one.

Preserved, salted or pickled, it softens and spreads its warmth evenly through a liquid.

In the mignonette on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters it is diluted in vinegar, so it reads as a gentle, fruity warmth rather than real heat, which is why the guide calls it mild.

value.front: How hot is the Fresno chilli in our mignonette?
value.back: A jalapeño-level chilli from 1952, fruitier and thinner-walled; preserved and diluted in vinegar it reads as a gentle warmth on the Grand Isle oysters.

explain.value:
Steak tartare is raw beef, trimmed of every sinew and chopped finely by hand, then seasoned at the last moment. The Paris brasserie version mixes in shallot, capers, cornichons, mustard and a raw yolk, served with toast or fries.

Hand-cutting matters: ground beef turns pasty and gray, while a knife keeps a clean, silky texture.

In the Steak Tartare Cannoli the seasoned beef is piped into a crisp potato shell with crème fraîche and finished with grated cured egg yolk, two bites held in the hand. The guide carries a raw beef advisory on this dish; read the service note and send questions to the kitchen.

value.front: What is steak tartare?
value.back: Raw beef trimmed and finely hand-chopped, seasoned at the last moment. Ours is piped into a crisp potato cannoli; read the raw beef advisory on the service note.

explain.value:
A cannoli is a Sicilian pastry: a fried tube of dough filled with sweet ricotta. The Steak Tartare Cannoli borrows the shape and makes the shell from potato instead, a thin potato sheet wrapped around a mold and fried until it holds a crisp tube.

The shells are fried ahead and kept dry and warm; an hour in humid air and they soften.

Piped end to end with tartare and crème fraîche, the shell gives a crunch that replaces the toast or fries of a brasserie tartare. How the shell is made, and whether it shares a fryer, are questions for the kitchen, as the guide asks.

value.front: What is the cannoli shell on the Steak Tartare Cannoli made of?
value.back: Potato: a thin sheet fried crisp around a mold in the shape of a Sicilian cannoli, replacing the toast or fries of a brasserie tartare.

explain.value:
Bottarga is salted, pressed and dried fish roe, gray mullet in Sardinia and tuna in Sicily, grated over pasta like a savory cheese. Egg yolk bottarga borrows the idea: yolks are buried in salt and sugar for a day or more, rinsed and dried at low heat until firm enough to grate.

The result is rich, salty and deeply savory, a golden snow on the plate.

On the Steak Tartare Cannoli it is grated over the top in place of the raw yolk of a classic tartare. It is the only dish on the current menus with it, so do not describe cured yolk as a standing house preparation.

value.front: What is egg yolk bottarga?
value.back: Egg yolks cured in salt and sugar, dried firm and grated like bottarga, the cured fish roe: rich and salty, over our Steak Tartare Cannoli.

explain.value:
Turtle soup came to New Orleans in the French colonial era and became a Creole classic. Where the turtle soups of London and Philadelphia were clear consommés, Creole cooks made a dark, thick soup: turtle meat with a brown roux, the trinity, tomato, stock and Worcestershire, finished with sherry, lemon and chopped hard-boiled egg.

Many turtle soups, in restaurants and in cans, are stretched with veal or beef, and mock turtle has none at all. That is why our menu prints 100% turtle meat.

It is a Brennan's signature at both meals and the second course of the Traditional Breakfast. Say the word turtle plainly; many guests are trying it for the first time.

value.front: Why does our menu say 100% turtle meat?
value.back: Many turtle soups are stretched with veal or beef, and mock turtle has none. Ours is all turtle: a dark, roux-thickened Creole soup finished with sherry.

explain.value:
The turtle in our soup is snapping turtle, a freshwater turtle. The wild alligator snapper has been off limits to commercial trappers in Louisiana since 2004, so restaurants buy it from licensed turtle farms, or buy common snapping turtle, which licensed collectors may still sell. The meat is dark, firm and rich, somewhere between veal and dark chicken, with plenty of gelatine, which gives the soup its body.

It is chopped finely and simmered for a long time, so it is tender and spread through the soup rather than served in chunks.

When a guest hesitates, describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savory, like a deep beef stew. The current supplier is a question for the chef, not a guess.

value.front: Where does the turtle in our soup come from?
value.back: Snapping turtle from licensed farms or collectors; never the courtyard turtles. Whether ours is farm-raised, and from whom, is a question for the chef.

value.where: Louisiana, from licensed turtle farms and collectors
value.history:
Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s, and it is still on the menus of the old houses: Arnaud's, Commander's Palace, Mandina's, Felix's and Brennan's among them. At Brennan's the chefs use snappers, freshwater snapping turtles.

The rules on which snapper changed in 2004. The alligator snapping turtle, the great loggerhead once common in Louisiana markets, became off limits to commercial trappers when a Wildlife and Fisheries regulation took effect on 20 November 2004. Licensed turtle farmers may still sell alligator snappers hatched from their own breeding stock, and Commander's Palace uses farm-raised alligator snapper for a steady supply. The common snapping turtle could still be taken and sold by holders of a reptile and amphibian collection license, by a 2017 account, and most of the state's turtle trade involves farm-hatched animals.

For cooks, Brennan's own published turtle soup recipe notes that fresh or frozen turtle meat can be bought from specialty markets and seafood dealers in and around New Orleans. Brennan's menu prints 100% turtle meat, which means the meat in the soup is all turtle, not stretched with veal or beef. It does not say which snapper or which supplier.
facts: Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s.
Louisiana banned commercial trapping of the wild alligator snapping turtle from 20 November 2004.
Licensed Louisiana turtle farmers may still sell alligator snappers hatched from their breeding stock.
Commander's Palace buys farm-raised alligator snapping turtle for a steady supply.
Most of Louisiana's turtle trade involves animals hatched on farms.
Brennan's published recipe says turtle meat can be bought from seafood dealers in and around New Orleans.
Our menu prints 100% turtle meat: no veal or beef stretches the soup.
notes: Say 100% turtle meat, exactly as printed, and explain it means no veal or beef in the soup.
Do not say farm-raised or name a species or supplier until the chef tells you; both farmed and licensed wild snapping turtle are legal in Louisiana.
Never the courtyard turtles: they are red-eared sliders, pardoned house mascots, and the chefs use snappers. Smile when guests joke about it.
For a hesitant guest, describe the taste: rich, meaty and savory, like a deep, finely chopped stew.
value.sayIt: It's 100% turtle meat, snapping turtle, in a rich Creole soup finished with spinach, grated egg and aged Sherry.
askKitchen: Which turtle is in our soup, alligator snapper or common snapper, and is it farm-raised?
Who supplies it?

explain.value:
Sherry is the fortified wine of Jerez in southern Spain, aged in a solera of barrels where young wine is blended into older wine over years. The dry, aged styles, amontillado and oloroso, taste of walnuts, toffee and salted caramel, with a sharp, dry finish.

A spoonful of sherry stirred into a rich soup at the end lifts it, the way lemon lifts fish: the acidity and nutty aroma cut through fat and gelatin.

Aged sherry finishes our Turtle Soup, along with brown butter spinach and grated egg. Whether it is added in the kitchen, at the pass or at the table is a lineup question, and guests who avoid alcohol should be told it is there.

value.front: Why is sherry added to the turtle soup?
value.back: A dry, aged sherry, nutty and sharp, lifts the rich soup at the end the way lemon lifts fish. Tell guests who avoid alcohol it is there.

value.where: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María, Cádiz, Spain
value.history:
Sherry is the fortified wine of a triangle of towns in the province of Cádiz, in southern Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María. It is made mostly from the Palomino grape, in styles from pale, salty Manzanilla and fino to the darker Amontillado and oloroso, which age in contact with air and turn nutty and deep.

What makes Sherry is the way it ages, criaderas y solera. Barrels are stacked in tiers; wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest, which is topped up from the next oldest, and so on up to the youngest. Every bottle is a blend of many years, and the style stays the same from decade to decade. That aging was long reserved to the three towns.

In 1933 Jerez became the first denominación de origen recognized under Spain's new wine law, D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry, though Rioja, which set up its own in 1925, also claims to be first.

Brennan's has finished its turtle soup with sherry for a long time: its own published recipe calls for dry sherry and hard-boiled egg, and says the flavor is heightened by a touch of sherry. Tonight's menu prints aged Sherry, and which bottle the kitchen uses is a question for lineup.
facts: Sherry must come from the triangle of Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María.
D.O. Jerez-Xeres-Sherry, recognized in 1933, was the first under Spain's wine law; Rioja dates its own to 1925.
It ages by criaderas y solera, a tiered blend of young into old wine.
It is made mostly from Palomino, from Manzanilla and fino to Amontillado and oloroso.
Brennan's published turtle soup recipe calls for dry sherry and hard-boiled egg.
The wine list's Sherries are Barbadillo Pale Cream, Valdespino VOS Solera 1842 and La Cigarrera Manzanilla.
notes: Say aged Sherry, the nutty fortified wine of Jerez, lifts the soup at the end; do not name a bottle until the kitchen does.
Never say the soup uses a Sherry from the wine list; that is unconfirmed.
Tell guests who avoid alcohol that Sherry is in the soup; never promise it cooks off.
A guest who likes the note can be offered a glass of the list's Sherry alongside, checked with the sommelier.
value.sayIt: Finished with aged Sherry from Jerez in southern Spain, nutty and dry, which cuts the richness of the turtle soup.
askKitchen: Which Sherry finishes the Turtle Soup, and is it added in the kitchen, at the pass or at the table?

components.name: Brown butter spinach and grated egg

explain.value:
Our Turtle Soup is finished with two garnishes that go back to the old Creole recipes. Spinach is wilted in brown butter, so it is nutty and soft, and folded through the soup. Hard-boiled egg is grated finely over the top.

The egg adds richness and a soft texture; the body of the soup comes from the roux and the gelatin of the turtle and stock, not from the egg, whatever older notes say.

Together with the aged sherry they make the bright, nutty finish the guide describes. If a guest asks what the yellow and green flecks are, name them: grated egg and brown butter spinach.

value.front: What are the green and yellow flecks in the turtle soup?
value.back: Brown butter spinach, wilted and nutty, and finely grated hard-boiled egg, which adds richness; the body comes from the roux and the turtle’s gelatin.

explain.value:
Gumbo is the dish that tells Louisiana's history in one bowl. Its name most likely comes from a West African word for okra; its roux comes from French cooking, made darker in Louisiana; its filé, ground sassafras leaves, came from the Choctaw; and Spanish, German and Caribbean cooks all added to it.

There are countless gumbos: seafood, chicken and andouille, and the green gumbo z'herbes. A seafood gumbo uses a dark roux and a stock made from the seafood shells, with the seafood added at the end.

Ours is Shrimp, crab, oysters and andouille over popcorn rice, a signature at both meals and the alternative to turtle soup on the Traditional Breakfast.

value.front: What cultures came together in gumbo?
value.back: West African okra and its name, French roux, Choctaw filé, plus Spanish, German and Caribbean cooks. Ours is seafood with andouille over popcorn rice.

explain.value:
The Caesar salad was created in 1924 at Caesar Cardini's restaurant in Tijuana, just over the border, a draw for visitors escaping Prohibition. The story is that it was improvised at the table: romaine, a raw egg yolk, olive oil, Parmesan, Worcestershire, lime and toasted bread. Cardini relied on the anchovy in the Worcestershire rather than adding whole anchovies; those came later.

It became the most copied salad in the world, often made tableside.

Our Creole Caesar gives it a Gulf accent: gem lettuce, a smoked oyster dressing in the briny role of anchovy, Grana Padano and Leidenheimer crisps in place of croutons.

value.front: Where did the Caesar salad come from?
value.back: Caesar Cardini’s restaurant in Tijuana, 1924, improvised at the table. Our Creole Caesar swaps anchovy for a smoked oyster dressing and croutons for Leidenheimer crisps.

explain.value:
Little Gem is a small, sweet lettuce, a cross between romaine and butterhead: crisp, upright hearts with tender, slightly buttery leaves. It holds a thick dressing without wilting and is often served halved or quartered through the core so each wedge stays together.

It is milder and sweeter than a full romaine and keeps its crunch longer on the plate.

On the Creole Caesar it carries the smoked oyster dressing, the Grana Padano and the Leidenheimer crisps. If a guest asks why it is not romaine, the answer is that gem is the sweeter, crisper little cousin.

value.front: What lettuce is in the Creole Caesar?
value.back: Little Gem, a small, sweet cross of romaine and butterhead with crisp hearts that hold a thick dressing without wilting.

explain.value:
A Caesar dressing is an emulsion of egg yolk, garlic, lemon, Worcestershire, oil and cheese. Ours blends smoked oysters into it, so the oysters take the briny, savory role that anchovy usually plays, and add a gentle smoke.

It is the change that makes the salad a Gulf dish: the oyster is the most New Orleans of ingredients.

Because the dressing is made with oysters, the guide asks servers to treat the Creole Caesar as a shellfish dish: flag it on the ticket and check with the kitchen for any guest who asks about shellfish. Whether the dressing also carries anchovy is a question for the chef.

value.front: What makes the Creole Caesar dressing different?
value.back: Smoked oysters are blended into the Caesar emulsion in place of anchovy, briny and smoky. Flag it as shellfish on the ticket and check with the kitchen.

explain.value:
Grana Padano is a hard cheese from the Po Valley of northern Italy, made from partly skimmed cow's milk and aged for at least nine months, usually longer. It has protected status, and its origin story credits Cistercian monks in the Middle Ages. Grana means grainy, for its crumbly, crystalline texture.

It is milder, younger and sweeter than Parmigiano Reggiano, and it melts smoothly.

We use it twice: shaved over the Creole Caesar and finishing the Shells & Cheese. A guest who asks whether it is Parmesan can be told it is its milder Po Valley cousin.

value.front: Is Grana Padano the same as Parmesan?
value.back: No: it is a milder, younger hard cheese from the Po Valley, grainy and nutty. It is on our Creole Caesar and finishes the Shells & Cheese.

value.who: Grana Padano DOP, Consorzio di Tutela
value.history:
Grana Padano traces itself to 1135 and the Abbey of Chiaravalle, a few kilometers south of Milan. Bernard of Clairvaux had chosen to reclaim the marshland there, and his Cistercian monks drained and farmed it. With more milk than they could drink, they made a hard cheese that kept, which they called caseus vetus, old cheese. Ordinary people named it for its texture instead: grana, grainy, and Padano, from the Po Valley.

The Consorzio di Tutela, which protects the name, was founded on 18 June 1954, uniting producers, refiners and merchants, and the European Union made Grana Padano a DOP in 1996. Every wheel, 24 to 40 kg, ages at least nine months; at nine months inspectors test it with a hammer, a needle and a probe, and only a wheel that passes is fire-branded. Some age beyond 24 months.

It is now the world's best-selling protected cheese, over 5.2 million wheels in 2022. Its rules are its own: it may be made in 32 provinces across five northern regions, the cows may eat silage, and lysozyme, a protein from egg white, may be used as a preservative. With its nine-month minimum it is a younger, milder and different cheese from Parmigiano Reggiano, not a lesser copy of it.
facts: The Consorzio dates the cheese to 1135 at the Abbey of Chiaravalle, south of Milan.
The monks called it caseus vetus, old cheese; grana means grainy, Padano means of the Po Valley.
The Consorzio di Tutela was founded on 18 June 1954.
The European Union recognized Grana Padano as a DOP in 1996.
Every wheel ages at least nine months and is tested with hammer, needle and probe before fire-branding.
It is the world's best-selling PDO cheese: over 5.2 million wheels in 2022.
It may be made in 32 provinces across five northern regions of Italy.
Its rules allow silage in the feed and lysozyme, an egg-white protein, as a preservative.
notes: Say Grana Padano is the Po Valley's protected hard cheese, younger and milder than Parmigiano Reggiano; never call it Parmigiano.
The menu names no maker or age; do not claim a particular maker or a 24-month wheel.
Lysozyme, an egg-white protein, is allowed in Grana Padano, though not every wheel uses it: any egg question on the Caesar or Shells & Cheese goes to the kitchen.
The monks of Chiaravalle make a good one-line story: a cheese born of drained marshland and spare milk, in 1135.
value.sayIt: Grana Padano, the Po Valley's protected hard cheese, first made by Cistercian monks near Milan in 1135: nutty, grainy and a touch milder than Parmigiano.
askKitchen: Which Grana Padano do we buy, and how old is it?

explain.value:
Hussarde is French for hussar style, after the hussars, the light cavalry of Hungary. Eggs Hussarde is poached eggs on Canadian bacon over a toasted base, with marchand de vin beneath and hollandaise on top.

The dish is older than the restaurant: a recipe for poached eggs à la Hussarde was printed in 1895, credited to the chef Adolphe Gallier of the Hotel Brunswick in New York, and Escoffier gave a version in 1903. Brennan's made it famous from about 1950, and it became the house's signature egg dish.

So call it our signature and New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict, and never say it was invented here.

value.front: Was Eggs Hussarde invented at Brennan’s?
value.back: No: a poached eggs à la Hussarde recipe was printed in 1895, and Escoffier gave one. Brennan’s made it famous from about 1950; it is our signature.

explain.value:
An English muffin is a flat, round yeasted bread cooked on a griddle rather than baked, dusted with cornmeal, and split with a fork so its holes and craggy surface catch butter and sauce.

The classic Brennan's Hussarde was built on Holland rusks, dry, crisp toasts; the restaurant now bakes its own English muffins, a change a returning guest may notice.

The muffin is the base that soaks up both sauces without falling apart. On the Eggs Hussarde the stack goes muffin, coffee-cured Canadian bacon, marchand de vin, poached egg and hollandaise. Saying the muffins are made in house is a small detail guests remember.

value.front: What base does the Eggs Hussarde sit on now?
value.back: Housemade English muffins, griddled and split so they catch both sauces; the old house build used Holland rusks, which returning guests may remember.

explain.value:
Canadian bacon is cured, lightly smoked pork loin, lean and ham-like, sliced into rounds; it is the meat of Eggs Benedict. A coffee cure rubs the loin with salt, sugar and ground coffee before it is smoked or roasted, adding a roasty, slightly bitter depth to the sweet, salty pork.

The coffee echoes the city's chicory coffee and gives the lean meat more savor.

It is the meat layer of the Eggs Hussarde, between the English muffin and the marchand de vin. The guide confirms the coffee cure; how long it cures, and whether the kitchen makes it in house, are questions for the chef.

value.front: What is the meat on the Eggs Hussarde?
value.back: Coffee-cured Canadian bacon: lean cured pork loin rubbed with salt, sugar and ground coffee before smoking or roasting, roasty and sweet.

explain.value:
Eggs Sardou was created at Antoine's and named in honor of the French playwright Victorien Sardou on a visit to New Orleans; sources disagree on the year. Antoine's original was poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, finished with ham, anchovy and truffle, with no spinach.

Most later versions dropped the ham, anchovy and truffle for creamed spinach, and the creamed spinach version is the one Brennan's made its own.

Our Sardou varies the house classic again: crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach, poached eggs and Choron sauce in place of hollandaise. Never present it as a Brennan's invention; it is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style.

value.front: Where was Eggs Sardou created, and who is it named for?
value.back: At Antoine’s, named for the French playwright Victorien Sardou. Ours is the Brennan’s style: crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach and Choron.

explain.value:
The artichoke is the flower bud of a thistle. Its heart and the fleshy base of its leaves are tender and nutty once trimmed and cooked; the classic Sardou sits the eggs on artichoke bottoms, the cup-shaped base of the heart.

Ours are crispy: trimmed hearts, cooked until tender and then coated and fried, so they bring crunch against the soft eggs and creamy spinach.

The guide notes that crispy artichokes are likely breaded or floured before frying and asks servers to check with the kitchen on any question about the coating. It is the texture guests notice first on our Eggs Sardou.

value.front: How are the artichokes on our Eggs Sardou cooked?
value.back: Trimmed hearts cooked tender, then coated and fried crisp for crunch against the eggs and spinach. Check the coating with the kitchen.

explain.value:
Creamed spinach is spinach blanched, plunged into iced water, squeezed hard and chopped, then bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and a little nutmeg. Squeezing out the water is the step that keeps it rich rather than watery.

It is a New Orleans and steakhouse classic, and the base of the Brennan's Eggs Sardou.

We serve Parmesan creamed spinach under the eggs on the Sardou and offer creamed spinach as a breakfast and lunch side. Whether the side and the Sardou's spinach are the same preparation is worth confirming with the kitchen before you say so.

value.front: How is creamed spinach made?
value.back: Spinach blanched, squeezed dry and chopped, bound with cream or light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and nutmeg; under our Sardou and as a side.

explain.value:
Eggs Owen shares its name with Owen Brennan, who founded the restaurant in 1946, and guests often guess it was named for him. The menu does not say so, and the restaurant has not published that story, so the guide's instruction stands: confirm at lineup before you tell it.

What can be said is how the plate relates to its neighbors. It takes the Hussarde's two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin, and replaces the Canadian bacon and muffin with red wine-braised short rib débris and a Creole-spiced potato, topped with a soft-boiled egg.

It is the heartier choice at $32 against the Hussarde at $27: steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

value.front: Is Eggs Owen named for Owen Brennan?
value.back: The menu does not say, and the house has not published it: confirm at lineup before telling that story. It is the Hussarde’s sauces over short rib débris.

explain.value:
Débris is Louisiana French for scraps, and in New Orleans it means the shreds of meat that fall into the gravy as a roast cooks and is carved. Mother's Restaurant on Poydras Street, opened in 1938, made the word famous with its debris roast beef po-boy.

Ours is short rib braised slowly in red wine until it falls apart, then pulled into its own reduced braising liquid: the same idea, richer.

On the Eggs Owen it replaces the Hussarde's Canadian bacon, under hollandaise and marchand de vin. Say DAY-bree, the local way, and describe it as slow-cooked beef that falls apart into its own gravy.

value.front: What does débris mean on the Eggs Owen?
value.back: Louisiana French for scraps: meat that falls into its gravy, made famous by Mother’s. Ours is red wine-braised short rib, pulled into its own sauce.

explain.value:
Braising cooks a tough, well-worked cut slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot, so its connective tissue melts into gelatin. Short rib is ideal: marbled, sinewy and full of flavor.

The ribs are seared hard for color, the vegetables sweated, the pan deglazed with red wine and reduced, then stock added; the pot goes into a low oven for about three hours, until a fork turns the meat. The liquid is skimmed and reduced into a glossy sauce, and the meat is pulled back into it.

That is the short rib débris on the Eggs Owen: meltingly tender beef in a deep, winey gravy, which echoes the marchand de vin on the same plate.

value.front: Why is short rib braised rather than grilled?
value.back: It is tough and sinewy; slow, covered cooking in red wine and stock melts its connective tissue into gelatin, giving tender meat and a glossy sauce.

explain.value:
Confit comes from the French confire, to preserve, and it is the larder technique of Gascony in south-western France. Duck legs are rubbed with salt, garlic and herbs and left for up to a day and a half, rinsed, then cooked slowly submerged in duck fat at a bare tremble for hours, and stored under the fat.

To serve, the leg is crisped skin-side down, so the skin shatters and the meat pulls from the bone.

On the Duck Confit Waffle the Rohan duck leg is confit. The menu idiom says cooked in its own fat; kitchens use pooled duck fat, so describe the method in general and promise no house times.

value.front: What does confit mean?
value.back: From confire, to preserve: salted duck legs cooked slowly submerged in duck fat until tender, then crisped. Our Rohan duck leg on the waffle is confit.

explain.value:
A cornbread waffle uses a cornmeal batter, the Southern skillet cornbread, cooked in a waffle iron so it gets a crisp, deep-pocketed crust and a tender center. Chives make it savory rather than sweet.

The pockets catch sauce and syrup, which is the point.

On the Duck Confit Waffle it is the base under the Rohan duck leg, with foie gras butter, mustard maple syrup and a sunny-side-up egg: chicken and waffles made luxurious. The guide notes the waffle likely contains wheat flour as well as cornmeal, so check with the kitchen for any guest who asks.

value.front: What kind of waffle is on the Duck Confit Waffle?
value.back: A savory cornbread and chive waffle, cornmeal batter crisp in the iron with pockets for the foie gras butter and mustard maple syrup.

explain.value:
Foie gras is the fattened liver of a duck or goose, a French delicacy of the south-west with a rich, silky, buttery texture. Foie gras butter is foie gras puréed into soft butter, so a spoonful melts over hot food and spreads its richness through it.

It is a luxurious touch in small amounts rather than a main ingredient.

On the Duck Confit Waffle it melts into the cornbread waffle's pockets with the mustard maple syrup. Some guests avoid foie gras by choice; the guide asks you to check with the kitchen whether it can be left off before you promise it.

value.front: Can the foie gras butter come off the Duck Confit Waffle?
value.back: Ask the kitchen first. Foie gras butter is fattened duck or goose liver puréed into soft butter, melting into the waffle’s pockets.

explain.value:
Maple syrup is the sap of the sugar maple boiled down, with a woody caramel sweetness. Sharpened with mustard, Dijon or whole-grain, it becomes sweet, tangy and gently hot, the same balance a honey mustard strikes.

The mustard keeps the syrup from tasting like dessert, so it works with savory, fatty meat.

On the Duck Confit Waffle it ties the plate together: sweet against the salty, crisp duck, sharp against the foie gras butter and the egg yolk. It is the savory-sweet note the guide's description promises, so name it when you describe the dish.

value.front: What is the syrup on the Duck Confit Waffle?
value.back: Mustard maple syrup: maple sharpened with mustard, sweet and tangy, cutting the rich duck, foie gras butter and egg yolk.

explain.value:
Shrimp and grits began as a breakfast for shrimpers in the South Carolina Lowcountry: fresh shrimp cooked in bacon fat over hominy grits. Charleston recipes for it were printed by 1930, and it went national in 1985, when Craig Claiborne published Bill Neal's version from Crook's Corner in Chapel Hill, with cheese and bacon, in The New York Times.

Charleston's dish uses a bacon and lemon pan gravy. Ours is Creole instead.

Our New Orleans Shrimp & Grits is Louisiana shrimp with a fried pimento cheese grit cake, a tomato Creole sauce seasoned with tasso, and fried okra chips. That tomato and tasso is the difference to name.

value.front: How does our Shrimp & Grits differ from the Charleston dish?
value.back: Charleston’s is shrimp in a bacon and lemon gravy over grits. Ours is Creole: a tomato Creole sauce with tasso over a fried pimento cheese grit cake.

explain.value:
An omelette is beaten eggs cooked quickly in a hot buttered pan. The French omelette is stirred as it sets, then rolled into a smooth, pale cylinder with a soft, creamy center and barely any color. The American omelette is set flat, filled, and folded in half, firmer and lightly golden.

Either way the filling goes in warm, so the eggs are not overcooked waiting for it.

Our Crab & Corn Omelette is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata. Which style the kitchen makes is a fair question to ask at lineup, so you can describe it before it lands.

value.front: What is the difference between a French and an American omelette?
value.back: A French omelette is stirred and rolled, pale and creamy inside; an American one is set flat, filled and folded, firmer and golden. Ask which ours is.

explain.value:
Sweet corn is corn picked young, while its kernels are still full of sugar and milky juice. Roasting it, on the cob or in the pan, caramelizes some of that sugar and adds a toasty, slightly smoky note.

Corn and crab are a summer pairing all along the Gulf and the Atlantic coast, both naturally sweet.

In the Crab & Corn Omelette the roasted kernels add pops of sweetness and a little chew against the soft eggs and lump crab. Whether the corn is roasted on the cob, and whether it changes with the season, are good questions for the chef.

value.front: Why do crab and corn go together in our omelette?
value.back: Both are naturally sweet summer foods of the coast; roasting the corn adds a toasty note and chew against the soft eggs and lump crab.

explain.value:
Miso is a Japanese paste of soybeans fermented with salt and koji, a mold grown on rice or barley. White miso is mild and sweet; darker misos are saltier and stronger. Beaten into soft butter, it makes a compound butter that is salty, nutty and deeply savory.

It brings umami, the savory depth of aged cheese and cured ham, without tasting obviously Japanese.

On the Crab & Corn Omelette the house-made miso butter rounds out the sweet crab and corn. The guide names soy from the miso on this dish, so send dietary questions to the service note and the kitchen.

value.front: What is miso butter?
value.back: Miso, a fermented soybean paste, beaten into soft butter: salty, nutty and savory. It rounds out the sweet crab and corn on our omelette.

explain.value:
Marcona is a Spanish almond variety, shorter, rounder, softer and sweeter than the Californian almonds most guests know. In Spain they are blanched to remove the skin, fried in oil and salted, which makes them rich and tender with a gentle crunch.

They are one of the luxury snacks of Spain, eaten with sherry and cheese.

We use them twice: in the gremolata on the Crab & Corn Omelette, and with the sorghum, crab and olives in the Gulf Fish en Papillote, where they add a nutty crunch. Nut questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

value.front: What is a Marcona almond?
value.back: A round, sweet, tender Spanish almond, usually blanched, fried in oil and salted. In the omelette’s gremolata and the en papillote.

value.where: Alicante, Spain, and the Mediterranean coast from southern Catalonia to Valencia
value.history:
The Marcona is a Spanish almond variety native to the province of Alicante, and grown along the Mediterranean coast in southern Catalonia, Castellón and Valencia. It is called the queen of almonds. It is shorter, wider and rounder than the long almonds of commercial orchards, softer and sweeter, and it has almost none of the bitter edge an ordinary almond carries.

Its oldest work is in sweets. Marcona is the almond of turrón, the nougat of Alicante and Jijona, made in Jijona since at least the sixteenth century, and of marzipan. Jijona grinds the almond to a fine paste for its soft turrón; Alicante uses it whole and toasted in the hard one.

At the table, Marcona is the tapas almond: blanched to slip off the skin, roasted or fried in olive oil, and dusted with salt, so it eats rich and tender with a gentle crunch, and sits well beside Sherry and cheese.

At Brennan's it appears twice: in the gremolata on the Crab & Corn Omelette, and in the banana leaf of the Gulf Fish en Papillote, with olives, sorghum and crab.
facts: Marcona is a Spanish almond variety native to the province of Alicante.
It is shorter, wider and rounder than standard almonds, with almost no bitterness.
It is the traditional almond of turrón; Jijona turrón is recorded from at least the sixteenth century.
Jijona turrón grinds it to a paste; Alicante turrón uses it whole and toasted.
It is usually served blanched, roasted or fried in olive oil, and salted.
notes: Say Marcona as the round, sweet Spanish almond, the one Spain eats with Sherry.
No grower or packer is printed; do not name one.
Tree nut questions on the omelette or the en papillote go straight to the kitchen; never say a dish can be made without them unless the kitchen says so.
Whether ours are fried, roasted or raw is a lineup question.
value.sayIt: Marcona almonds, the round, sweet almond of Alicante in Spain, buttery and tender, the one Spain eats with Sherry.
askKitchen: Are our Marcona almonds bought fried and salted, or do we toast them?

explain.value:
Gremolata is the Milanese finish for osso buco: finely chopped parsley, garlic and lemon zest, scattered over a rich braise at the last moment so its sharp, fresh perfume wakes the dish up.

Modern kitchens vary it with other herbs, citrus and nuts, keeping the idea of a bright, raw topping.

On the Crab & Corn Omelette it is a Marcona almond gremolata, with basil and lemon on the plate as well, so it adds crunch as well as freshness against the buttery eggs. Describe it as a crunchy herb, citrus and almond topping.

value.front: What is a gremolata?
value.back: The Milanese parsley, garlic and lemon zest finish for osso buco. Ours adds Marcona almonds for crunch on the Crab & Corn Omelette.

explain.value:
Cauliflower is a brassica whose tight white head is mild and nutty, and it changes completely with the cooking. Simmered in milk and cream and blended, it becomes a velvety purée, lighter than potato. Roasted or smoked, it browns, sweetens and takes on a meaty depth.

Smoking it after blanching or roasting lets it absorb smoke without turning soft.

We use it both ways: a cauliflower purée under the Pecan Gulf Fish, and the Smoked Cauliflower side at dinner with preserved lemon and harissa. Whether the side is cooked with butter or oil is a question for the kitchen for any guest who asks.

value.front: How do we serve cauliflower?
value.back: Two ways: a velvety purée under the Pecan Gulf Fish, and smoked as a dinner side with preserved lemon and harissa.

explain.value:
Creekstone Farms is a Black Angus beef producer. John and Carol Stewart founded it in 1995 as a purebred Black Angus farm in Kentucky, and since 2003 it has processed its beef at a plant in Arkansas City, Kansas. Its beef is graded USDA Prime and Choice.

A Prime grade marks the most marbled beef, which is richer and more tender when cooked.

The menu names Creekstone on all three of its beef dishes: the Prime hanger at breakfast and lunch, the dinner hanger, and the tenderloin for the Roasted Chateaubriand. Say Black Angus from a Kansas producer, and Prime where the menu says so.

value.front: What is Creekstone Farms?
value.back: A Black Angus beef producer founded in 1995, processing in Arkansas City, Kansas. It supplies our hangers and the Chateaubriand tenderloin.

value.where: Arkansas City, Kansas (founded in Campbellsburg, Kentucky)
value.history:
Creekstone Farms began in 1995, when John and Carol Stewart set up a purebred Black Angus farm in Campbellsburg, Kentucky. Stewart was a cattle geneticist at heart: he developed his own Angus line, sold bulls, genetics and semen to ranchers, and at one point owned the highest-marbling bull in the breed.

In 2003 the company moved into processing, buying a processing plant in Arkansas City, Kansas, where it began processing its own Premium Black Angus cattle in May 2003. Its cattle-receiving facility was the first built from the ground up to the low-stress handling standards of Dr. Temple Grandin. After BSE was found in the US herd in December 2003, Creekstone asked in 2004 to test every animal it slaughtered, and when the USDA refused, it took the question to court.

Stewart announced his retirement in October 2006. Sun Capital Partners had owned the business since 2005, and in 2017 it sold Creekstone to the Japanese trading house Marubeni Corporation, which owns it today. The company still buys its cattle on verifiable Black Angus genetics rather than hide color, and its Natural Black Angus line carries the Certified Humane label.

At Brennan's the name is printed on three plates: both hanger steaks and the tenderloin of the Roasted Chateaubriand.
facts: Founded in 1995 by John and Carol Stewart as a purebred Black Angus farm in Campbellsburg, Kentucky.
Processes its beef at a plant in Arkansas City, Kansas, bought in 2003; processing began there in May 2003.
Its cattle-receiving facility was the first built from the ground up to Dr. Temple Grandin's handling standards.
Cattle are bought on verifiable Black Angus genetics, not on black hide color alone.
Owned by Japan's Marubeni Corporation since 2017, which bought it from Sun Capital Partners.
Its Natural Black Angus Beef has carried the Certified Humane Raised and Handled label since September 2015, verified by Humane Farm Animal Care.
In 2004 Creekstone asked to test every animal it slaughtered for BSE; the USDA refused and Creekstone went to court.
USDA Prime, printed on our breakfast hanger, is the top grade: young, well-fed cattle with abundant marbling.
notes: The menu prints Prime only on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. Do not call the dinner hanger or the Chateaubriand Prime unless the kitchen confirms it.
Do not say every Creekstone steak here is Certified Humane: the label covers the Natural Black Angus line, and which program the kitchen buys is not confirmed.
Guests ask whether the beef is local. The honest answer: it is Black Angus from Creekstone in Kansas, not a local farm.
If asked who owns it: Marubeni Corporation, the Japanese trading house, since 2017; John and Carol Stewart founded it in Kentucky in 1995.
The breakfast menu spells it Creekstone Farm; the company is Creekstone Farms.
Always take the guest's temperature on a hanger or the Chateaubriand; doneness is the guest's choice and the kitchen's craft.
value.sayIt: Creekstone Farms is Black Angus beef from Kansas, a company founded as an Angus farm in 1995 and built around careful, low-stress handling of its cattle.
askKitchen: Are the dinner hanger and the Chateaubriand tenderloin graded Prime or Choice?
Which Creekstone program do we buy: Natural Black Angus (Certified Humane) or Premium Black Angus?
Is the beef for the Steak Tartare Cannoli and the short rib débris of the Eggs Owen also Creekstone?

explain.value:
The hanger steak, onglet in France, hangs from the diaphragm near the kidneys. There is only one per animal, which is why butchers used to keep it for themselves and why it was long called the butcher's steak. A tough sinew runs down its center and is cut out, leaving two loose-grained lobes.

It is intensely beefy and best cooked hot and fast to medium-rare or medium, rested, and sliced across the grain; past medium it tightens and tastes of liver.

We serve two: the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at breakfast and lunch with béarnaise and an egg, and the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner with chilli crisp. Always take the temperature.

value.front: How should a hanger steak be cooked, and why?
value.back: Hot and fast to medium-rare or medium, sliced across the grain; past medium it tightens and tastes of liver. One per animal, the butcher’s steak.

explain.value:
Vital Farms began in 2007 near Austin, Texas, with twenty hens, and now works with hundreds of family farms. Its eggs are pasture-raised, which means each hen has at least 108 square feet of outdoor space on rotated pasture.

Hens that forage outdoors often lay eggs with deep orange yolks, and a sunny-side-up egg shows that color off.

The menu names Vital Farms on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, where a sunny-side-up egg sits beside the steak and the smoked potato pavé. A one-line guest answer is: pasture-raised eggs, every hen with over a hundred square feet of grass.

value.front: What does pasture-raised mean for our Vital Farms egg?
value.back: Each hen has at least 108 square feet of rotated outdoor pasture; Vital Farms began near Austin in 2007. The egg sits on our breakfast hanger.

value.history:
Vital Farms began in 2007, when Matt O'Hayer started with 20 hens on a 27-acre farm near Austin, Texas. The idea was eggs from hens that genuinely live outdoors, and the company built its standard around pasture: each hen has at least 108 square feet of rotated pasture, where it forages for grasses, succulents and wildflowers. That is the same figure the Certified Humane pasture standard sets, and the eggs carry that certification.

Rather than keep one great company flock, Vital Farms works with a network of small family farms, now numbering in the hundreds. In 2017 it opened its own egg washing and packing plant in Springfield, Missouri, which it calls Egg Central Station, and a second Egg Central Station is being built in Seymour, Indiana.

The company went public on Nasdaq as VITL in July 2020 and is a Certified B Corporation. It sells butter as well as eggs.

On our menu the name appears once: the sunny-side-up egg on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, where the runny yolk meets the béarnaise.
facts: Founded in 2007 by Matt O'Hayer and headquartered in Austin, Texas.
It began with 20 hens on a 27-acre farm.
Pasture-raised: at least 108 square feet of rotated outdoor pasture per hen, the Certified Humane pasture standard.
The eggs come from a network of hundreds of small family farms.
Its own packing plant, Egg Central Station, opened in Springfield, Missouri, in 2017.
Listed on Nasdaq as VITL since July 2020, and a Certified B Corporation.
notes: The menu names Vital Farms only on the breakfast hanger. Do not say the eggs on the Hussarde, Sardou, Owen or Duck Confit Waffle are Vital Farms until the kitchen confirms.
Guests ask what pasture-raised means: at least 108 square feet of rotated outdoor pasture per hen, so the hens forage on grass.
Do not promise a yolk color; it changes with the hens' diet and the season.
Any question about egg doneness or diet goes to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: The egg is Vital Farms, pasture-raised: every hen has at least 108 square feet of outdoor pasture.
askKitchen: Are all our eggs Vital Farms, or only the egg on the breakfast hanger?

explain.value:
Pavé is French for paving stone, after its neat rectangular shape. Potatoes are sliced paper-thin on a mandoline, layered with cream and butter in a lined tin, baked until tender, then pressed under a weight overnight and chilled. The block is cut into bricks and seared until each face is crisp, so you see dozens of fine layers.

It takes a day to make and seconds to finish, which is why kitchens love it.

On the breakfast hanger it is a smoked potato pavé. Whether the smoke is in the cream, the butter or the finished block is the kitchen's detail, so say it has a smoky note and leave the method to the chef.

value.front: What is a potato pavé?
value.back: Thin potato slices layered with cream and butter, baked, pressed overnight, cut into bricks and seared crisp: dozens of fine layers. Ours is smoked.

explain.value:
Chateaubriand is the thick center cut of the beef tenderloin, roasted or grilled whole and carved for two. The name is said to come from a chef called Montmireil, who around 1822 cooked it for the writer and diplomat François-René, Vicomte de Chateaubriand, traditionally between two lesser steaks that were thrown away. Escoffier later fixed the name to the cut itself.

Tenderloin is the tenderest and mildest muscle on the animal, so a rich sauce does the flavor's work.

Our Roasted Chateaubriand is Creekstone Farms tenderloin with glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, served for two at $120. A whole roast takes time: tell the table when you take the order.

value.front: What is a Chateaubriand?
value.back: The thick center cut of the tenderloin, roasted whole for two; said to be named for the Vicomte de Chateaubriand, whose chef cooked it around 1822.

explain.value:
Summer squash are the tender, thin-skinned squashes picked young, zucchini, yellow squash and pattypan among them, eaten skin and seeds and all. They are mild and sweet, and roasting browns their edges and concentrates them.

A glaze, usually butter with a little stock, honey or reduced juice, gives them a gloss and a touch of sweetness.

On the Roasted Chateaubriand they are the light, seasonal vegetable beside a rich roast and sauce Foyot. They change with the market, so expect a different vegetable when the season turns; the guide suggests Maggie's Mushrooms or Shells & Cheese as add-on sides for the table.

value.front: What vegetable comes with the Roasted Chateaubriand?
value.back: Roasted and glazed summer squash, tender young squash browned and glossed; a light seasonal partner to the rich roast and sauce Foyot.

explain.value:
À la Véronique means served with grapes. The classic is Sole Véronique, traditionally credited to Auguste Escoffier at the Carlton in London and named for André Messager's comic opera Véronique: poached sole in a creamy sauce with peeled green muscat grapes, glazed under the grill.

Dates and the chef's name vary between tellings, so frame it as a story.

Our Redfish Véronique makes three changes: Gulf redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and grapes pickled in hibiscus instead of fresh. It is also the third course of the dinner tasting, with a red Burgundy pour.

value.front: What does Véronique mean on a menu?
value.back: With grapes, after Sole Véronique, credited to Escoffier and named for an opera. Ours is redfish, hibiscus-pickled grapes and preserved lemon beurre blanc.

explain.value:
Pickled grapes are grapes steeped in a sweet and sour brine of vinegar, sugar and spice, which keeps their crunch and sweetness but gives them a sharp edge. Hibiscus, the dried flower behind many red teas, adds a ruby color and a tart, cranberry-like note.

The result is sweet, tart and floral, a bright counterpoint to rich fish and butter.

On the Redfish Véronique they stand in for the fresh muscat grapes of the French classic. If a guest is wary of fruit with fish, describe them as more like a sharp relish than a sweet fruit garnish.

value.front: What are the grapes on the Redfish Véronique?
value.back: Grapes pickled in a sweet and sour brine with hibiscus: ruby, tart and floral, a sharp relish against the fish and beurre blanc.

explain.value:
Preserved lemons are a North African staple: lemons cut, packed in salt and their own juice, and left for weeks until the rind turns soft, silky and edible. The sharp bitterness mellows into a salty, floral, almost perfumed lemon flavor.

Cooks use the rind, finely chopped, more than the flesh.

We use it twice at dinner: in the preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique, and with harissa on the Smoked Cauliflower. Describe it to a guest as lemon cured in salt, salty and perfumed rather than sour.

value.front: What is preserved lemon?
value.back: Lemon cured in salt and its own juice for weeks until the rind is soft: salty and perfumed. In the Véronique’s beurre blanc and on the Smoked Cauliflower.

explain.value:
Leeks are the mild, sweet member of the onion family. Braised slowly in butter and stock, they turn soft and silky, almost creamy, with none of an onion's bite.

Fingerling potatoes are small, finger-shaped waxy potatoes with thin skins; they hold their shape when cooked and taste buttery and slightly nutty.

Together on the Redfish Véronique they form the gentle base under the fish, with the hibiscus-pickled grapes and preserved lemon beurre blanc providing the brightness. They are the quiet, comforting part of the plate, which is worth saying to a guest who finds the grapes unusual.

value.front: What else is on the Redfish Véronique plate?
value.back: Braised leeks, soft and sweet, and fingerling potatoes, small waxy potatoes; the gentle base under the redfish, grapes and beurre blanc.

explain.value:
En papillote means in paper: food sealed in a parcel and baked, so it steams in its own juices and the aromas stay trapped until the parcel is opened. New Orleans knows it from Antoine's, where Jules Alciatore created pompano en papillote for a banquet honoring the Brazilian balloonist Alberto Santos-Dumont; the puffed paper suggested a balloon.

Our Gulf Fish en Papillote wraps the fish in banana leaf instead of paper. The leaf holds moisture just as well and adds a faint grassy, tea-like aroma.

Ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest to mind the steam when it is.

value.front: What does en papillote mean, and what is ours wrapped in?
value.back: In paper: sealed and baked so it steams in its own juices, made famous here by Antoine’s pompano. Ours is wrapped in banana leaf. Mind the steam.

explain.value:
Castelvetrano olives are the Nocellara del Belice variety from the Valle del Belice in western Sicily, named for the nearby town. They are picked young and cured briefly in lye, which removes bitterness quickly and keeps them a vivid bright green.

They are buttery, mild and almost sweet, with a crisp, meaty bite, the olive people who dislike olives often enjoy.

In the Gulf Fish en Papillote they cook with tomato, Louisiana crab, sorghum and Marcona almonds, giving the dish its bright, Mediterranean character. Warn guests that olives may come with stones unless the kitchen confirms they are pitted.

value.front: What are Castelvetrano olives?
value.back: Bright green Sicilian olives of the Nocellara del Belice variety, lye-cured so they are buttery, mild and crisp. In our Gulf Fish en Papillote.

value.who: Nocellara del Belice olives, Castelvetrano style
value.history:
What Americans call a Castelvetrano olive is, strictly, a way of preparing an olive. The variety is Nocellara del Belice, grown in the Valle del Belice in south-western Sicily, a dual-purpose olive pressed for oil and cured for the table. One of its table preparations is named for the comune of Castelvetrano in the valley, and olives treated that way are sold in the United States as Castelvetrano olives.
