The method explains the taste. The olives are picked young and green and washed in a lye and water solution, which strips their natural bitterness completely in a matter of weeks; they are then kept in brine without fermenting. Skipping fermentation keeps the vivid emerald color and leaves a mild, buttery, almost sweet olive with a crisp bite. The Sevillian method, by contrast, debitters partly and ferments, for a sharper olive.

In 1998 Nocellara del Belice was awarded a Protected Designation of Origin, and the variety now carries two: Nocellara del Belice DOP table olives and Valle del Belìce DOP extra virgin olive oil, which must be at least 70 percent Nocellara.
facts: The variety is Nocellara del Belice, from the Valle del Belice in south-western Sicily.
Castelvetrano names a preparation, after the comune of Castelvetrano in the valley.
Awarded a Protected Designation of Origin in 1998.
Two DOP names: Nocellara del Belice table olives and Valle del Belìce olive oil, at least 70 percent Nocellara.
Picked young and washed in lye, then brined without fermentation, keeping them bright green and mild.
The Sevillian method debitters only partly and ferments the olives.
notes: Say kah-stel-veh-TRAH-noh: the bright green Sicilian olive, buttery and mild, the one olive-shy guests often like.
Never call ours DOP unless the kitchen confirms the jar; the menu prints only Castelvetrano.
Warn that olives can carry stones unless the kitchen confirms they are pitted.
Guests sometimes ask whether the green means unripe: picked young, yes, and cured to remove bitterness.
value.sayIt: Castelvetrano olives, the bright green Nocellara del Belice of western Sicily, cured young so they stay mild and buttery.
askKitchen: Are the Castelvetrano olives pitted, and are they DOP Nocellara del Belice?

explain.value:
Sorghum is a cereal grass first grown in Africa and now farmed around the world, including across the American South, where its cane is also pressed for sorghum syrup. The whole grain is round and chewy, cooked like farro or barley, with a mild, nutty taste.

It holds its bite in liquid, so it soaks up juices without turning mushy.

In the Gulf Fish en Papillote the grain cooks inside the banana leaf with the fish, drinking up the tomato and crab juices. The guide notes that sorghum itself has no wheat but asks you to confirm the whole dish with the kitchen.

value.front: What is the grain in the Gulf Fish en Papillote?
value.back: Sorghum, an African cereal grain cooked like farro: round, chewy and nutty, soaking up the tomato and crab juices inside the banana leaf.

explain.value:
Poussin is French for a very young chicken. In Britain it means a bird under 28 days old, about a pound. The American equivalent is the Rock Cornish game hen, defined by the USDA as an immature chicken under five weeks and no more than 2 pounds: a little older and larger than a British poussin, and the nearest thing on an American menu.

Young birds are tender and mild, with a high ratio of crisp skin to meat.

Our menu says Poussin à la Moutarde and names the Cornish hen in the description, so there is no sleight of hand. It is a whole small bird and may have bones; say so to the guest.

value.front: What is a poussin, and what bird do we use?
value.back: French for a very young chicken; the menu names a Cornish hen, the American equivalent under five weeks and 2 pounds. A whole small bird, may have bones.

explain.value:
A brine is salted water that a bird soaks in before cooking; the salt seasons the meat throughout and helps it hold its juices. A sweet tea brine is a Southern fried chicken trick: strong black tea, sugar and salt. The tea's tannin and the sugar help the skin brown deeply, and the tea adds a faint, malty note.

After brining the bird is dried, coated and fried until the skin is crisp and the meat juicy.

On the Poussin à la Moutarde the sweet tea-brined Cornish hen is fried, then sauced with mustard cream, with turnips and shallots. How long it brines is a good question for the chef.

value.front: What does the sweet tea brine do for the poussin?
value.back: Salt seasons the bird and keeps it juicy; tea tannin and sugar help the skin brown deeply. A Southern fried chicken trick before frying.

explain.value:
Tofu is soybean milk curdled and pressed into blocks, as cheese is made from milk. Extra-firm tofu is pressed hardest, so it holds its shape in a hot pan and takes a crust.

Tien Dat is a local maker registered on the West Bank, in Marrero, across the river from the city. Its tofu is sold through the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, the member-owned co-op of Village de L'Est, the Vietnamese American community of New Orleans East, at the Crescent City Farmers Market.

Our menu names New Orleans Tien Dat tofu on the Blackened Tofu. Say it is made fresh across the river by a local Vietnamese maker; anything more, ask the kitchen.

value.front: Where does the tofu on the Blackened Tofu come from?
value.back: Tien Dat, a local maker on the West Bank whose extra-firm tofu is sold through VEGGI, the Vietnamese American co-op of New Orleans East.

value.where: West Bank, Jefferson Parish (Marrero and Harvey addresses); co-op in New Orleans East
value.history:
Tien Dat is a small local tofu maker, part of the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, whose extra firm tofu reaches the city through the co-op. Tien Dat Tofu LLC is registered on the West Bank, with addresses in Marrero and Harvey, across the river from the French Quarter. The tofu is made fresh in small batches, sold as extra firm and in flavored styles such as black mushroom, and lemongrass and red chilli.

VEGGI stands for the Village de L'Est Green Growers Initiative. Village de L'Est is the Vietnamese American community of New Orleans East, and the co-op was established there in 2011, across the street from Mary Queen of Vietnam Church, in the aftermath of the BP oil spill, when twelve growers and program developers chose through a community forum to build jobs in urban agriculture. It is owned and run by its members.

The co-op sells herbs, vegetables, chilli oil and more at the Crescent City Farmers Market, but it is best known for its freshly made tofu. Printing the name on the Blackened Tofu ties Brennan's plate to that community.
facts: Tien Dat Tofu LLC is a Louisiana company with West Bank addresses in Marrero and Harvey.
The tofu is sold through the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, made fresh in small batches.
VEGGI means Village de L'Est Green Growers Initiative, after the Vietnamese American community of New Orleans East.
The co-op was established in 2011, after the BP oil spill, and is member owned.
It sits across the street from Mary Queen of Vietnam Church.
Twelve growers and program developers formed it through a community forum.
The co-op is best known for its tofu and sells at the Crescent City Farmers Market.
notes: Say it is made locally by a Vietnamese American maker and sold through a New Orleans East co-op.
If a guest asks 'made in New Orleans?', the honest answer: the co-op is in New Orleans East; the maker's registered address is across the river on the West Bank.
No source names the person who makes it or describes the method; do not invent a family story.
Ingredient and dietary questions about the tofu and the blackening butter go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: The tofu is Tien Dat, made locally and sold through the VEGGI co-op, the Vietnamese American growers of New Orleans East.
askKitchen: Which Tien Dat style do we buy (plain extra firm?), and how does the house pronounce it?

explain.value:
Rice grits are broken grains of rice, the pieces that crack during milling, cooked slowly into a creamy porridge like corn grits but silkier. Two Brooks Farm in Sumner, Mississippi, in the Delta, started by Mike Wagner in 1992 and run with his children, grows rice and sells rice grits and flours among its products; ducks and geese winter on its flooded fields.

The farm is in Mississippi, not Louisiana, a detail guests sometimes test.

Under the Blackened Tofu the rice grits are the soft, creamy base for the spiced crust and the preserved shiitakes. Whether they are cooked with stock is a question for the kitchen.

value.front: What are rice grits, and where do ours come from?
value.back: Broken rice grains cooked creamy like grits; ours are from Two Brooks Farm in Sumner, in the Mississippi Delta, not Louisiana.

value.history:
Two Brooks Farm sits at Sumner in the Mississippi Delta. Mike Wagner started it in 1992, and he is a ninth-generation farmer: his family counts an unbroken line of ten generations back to 1742. The farm grows about 2,000 acres of rice and 1,000 of soybeans.

What sets it apart is the birds. The farm lies on the flyway, and after harvest ducks and geese settle on the flooded fields. Wagner noticed his soil changing where they gathered and began cutting back on fertiliser; the birds now supply much of it, and no fungicides or insecticides go on the rice.

From that long-grain rice the family built a line of 14 products, rice, grits and flour among them, with the Original Mississippi Midlands Brown Rice Grits one of Wagner's favorites. His son Lawrence and daughter Abbey, the next generation, have helped widen the range, and the products reach restaurants through US Foods. In 2022 Wagner was named Mississippi's winner of the Swisher Sweets/Sunbelt Ag Expo Southeastern Farmer of the Year award.
facts: At Sumner, Mississippi, in the Delta; started in 1992 by Mike Wagner.
Wagner is a ninth-generation farmer; the family traces ten generations back to 1742.
Ducks and geese winter on the fields and supply much of the fertiliser.
No fungicides or insecticides are used on the rice.
A line of 14 products, including rice, grits and flour.
Mississippi's state winner of the 2022 Swisher Sweets/Sunbelt Ag Expo Southeastern Farmer of the Year award.
Son Lawrence and daughter Abbey, the next generation, help run the farm.
notes: Two Brooks is in Mississippi, not Louisiana; guests sometimes test this.
The duck and geese story is true and memorable: the birds help fertilize the rice.
Whether the grits are cooked with stock or butter is a kitchen answer.
Do not call the rice organic; the sources say reduced fertiliser and no fungicides or insecticides, not certified organic.
value.sayIt: The rice grits come from Two Brooks Farm in the Mississippi Delta, a family rice farm where wintering ducks help fertilize the fields.
askKitchen: Which Two Brooks grits do we use, white or brown rice, and are they cooked with stock or butter?

explain.value:
Shiitake are mushrooms long cultivated on logs in Japan and China; the name joins shii, the tree they grew on, with take, mushroom. They are meaty and deeply savory, rich in the natural compounds that give umami.

Preserved shiitake are most likely cured in soy or pickled, which concentrates that savory depth; what the kitchen means by preserved is a question for the chef.

On the Blackened Tofu they bring the earthy, meaty note that makes the plate satisfying without meat, against the spiced crust and creamy rice grits. Say shee-TAH-keh, not shih-TAH-kee.

value.front: What do the preserved shiitakes add to the Blackened Tofu?
value.back: Deep, meaty, savory umami against the spiced crust and creamy rice grits. How the kitchen preserves them is a question for the chef.

explain.value:
Broccolini is a cross of broccoli and Chinese kale: long, tender stems with small florets, sweeter and milder than broccoli. Madeira is the fortified wine of the Portuguese island of Madeira, deliberately heated as it ages, so it tastes of caramel, toffee and walnut with a sharp acidity.

A Madeira glaze is the wine reduced with butter or stock until syrupy, sweet and savory at once.

On the dinner Creole Hanger Steak the glazed broccolini brings a sweet, nutty counterweight to the Creole spice and chilli crisp. Guests who avoid alcohol should know the glaze is made with wine.

value.front: What is the glaze on the Creole Hanger Steak’s broccolini?
value.back: Madeira, the heated, aged Portuguese fortified wine tasting of caramel and walnut, reduced to a sweet, savory glaze on tender broccolini.

value.history:
Madeira is a Portuguese island in the Atlantic, discovered by the navigators João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira in 1419. The first settlers planted vines, and by the 16th century the island had a wine trade, its casks shipped across the Atlantic.

Those voyages made the wine. Casks carried across the equator in hot holds came back changed, concentrated, darker and more stable, and the islanders learned to reproduce the voyage at home. The wine is fortified with grape spirit, then aged either by canteiro, casks warmed by the sun in lofts for years, or by estufagem, tanks heated to at most 50°C for at least 90 days, a method pioneered in 1794 by Pantaleão Fernandes. The four noble grapes name the styles, from dry Sercial and medium-dry Verdelho to Bual and sweet Malmsey, from Malvasia.

Because it has already been heated and aired, Madeira keeps, for decades and even after opening, which made it the wine of the American colonies; the signers are said to have toasted the Declaration of Independence with it in 1776, a story often told but thinly documented.

In the kitchen that same caramel, walnut and sharp acidity reduces into a glaze for the broccolini on the Creole Hanger Steak.
facts: The island was discovered by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira in 1419.
Heat in ships' holds crossing the equator improved the wine; makers learned to reproduce it.
Estufagem heats the wine to at most 50°C for at least 90 days, pioneered in 1794.
Canteiro ages casks warmed naturally by the sun for years.
Already heated and oxidized, Madeira keeps for decades, even after opening.
The four noble styles: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey, from dry to sweet.
The signers are said to have toasted the Declaration of Independence with Madeira in 1776; tell it as a story.
notes: Say the broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the Portuguese island wine that is heated as it ages, so it tastes of caramel and walnut.
Never say the glaze uses a bottle from the wine list; the cooking Madeira is not named.
Guests who avoid alcohol should know the glaze is made with wine; never promise it cooks off.
A guest who loves the note can be pointed to the list's Madeiras, Broadbent and Henriques & Henriques, through the sommelier.
value.sayIt: Broccolini glazed with Madeira, the Portuguese island wine aged in heat, beloved of the American colonies: caramel, walnut, bright acidity.
askKitchen: Which Madeira, and which style, goes into the broccolini glaze?

explain.value:
Persillade is a French finishing mix of finely chopped parsley and garlic, thrown over a dish at the last second so its fresh, sharp perfume hits the table. Pepita is Mexican Spanish for the hulled green pumpkin seed, toasted until it puffs and turns nutty.

Together they make a crunchy, garlicky, green topping.

On the Creole Hanger Steak the pepita persillade sits with a chilli crisp and Madeira-glazed broccolini: a French garnish, a Mexican seed and a Chinese condiment on a Creole-spiced steak. That mix of traditions is the modern Brennan's style and worth saying at the table.

value.front: What is a pepita persillade?
value.back: Persillade is chopped parsley and garlic; pepitas are toasted pumpkin seeds. Together a crunchy, garlicky topping on the dinner Creole Hanger Steak.

explain.value:
Chilli crisp is a Chinese condiment from Guizhou: dried chilli flakes fried slowly in oil with garlic and shallot, often with roasted beans and seeds, until crunchy. Lao Gan Ma made it famous around the world. It is a sauce you can chew, savory, crunchy and hot.

It brings real heat, more than anything else on the dinner menu.

On the Creole Hanger Steak it gives heat and crunch with the pepita persillade. The guide asks you to warn spice-shy guests and to offer it on the side if the kitchen agrees; questions about soy or sesame in it go to the kitchen.

value.front: What is chilli crisp, and how hot is it?
value.back: A Chinese condiment of chilli fried crisp in oil with garlic: crunchy, savory and genuinely hot. Warn spice-shy guests; ask the kitchen about serving it on the side.

explain.value:
Sautéing cooks food quickly in a little hot fat in a wide pan. For a fish fillet, the pan and fat are hot before it goes in, often skin or presentation side first; it is left alone to color, then turned once and finished gently so it stays moist and flakes at the touch. Many kitchens dust the fillet with flour first, the meunière way, for a golden crust.

Thin, delicate fish cook in two or three minutes; thicker fillets are finished in the oven.

The children's Sautéed Gulf Fish is cooked this way, and the Pecan Gulf Fish is likely pan-roasted or sautéed to order. Know today's fish and its preparation at lineup.

value.front: How is a fish fillet sautéed?
value.back: In a little hot fat in a wide pan, presentation side first, left to color, turned once and finished gently so it stays moist. Know tonight’s fish.

explain.value:
Southern breakfast sausage is fresh, not cured or smoked: coarsely ground pork shoulder with a good share of fat, seasoned with salt, black pepper and sage, often with red pepper flakes and a little brown sugar. Formed into patties, it is pan-fried until browned and crusty outside and juicy within.

Making it in house lets the kitchen set its own seasoning and grind.

Our Housemade Pork Sausage Patty is a $9 breakfast side, a savory partner to eggs, biscuits and grits. The spice list, and whether anything binds the meat, are questions for the kitchen if a guest asks.

value.front: What is in a Southern breakfast sausage patty?
value.back: Fresh, coarsely ground pork shoulder and fat seasoned with salt, pepper and sage, often red pepper; pan-fried crusty. Ours is made in house.

explain.value:
Bacon is pork belly cured with salt and usually smoked. Thick-cut slices are roughly twice the usual thickness, so they stay meaty in the middle while the edges crisp. They want a low, slow render, so the fat turns glassy and golden before the edges burn.

American bacon comes from the belly, streaky with fat, unlike the leaner back bacon of Britain.

Thick-cut bacon is a $9 breakfast side, comes with the children's eggs, and is on the Roost Burger. The breakfast menu names no brand; Nueske's appears only on the dinner succotash, so ask before saying the breakfast bacon is Nueske's.

value.front: What makes thick-cut bacon different?
value.back: Slices about twice the usual thickness, rendered slowly so they stay meaty in the middle and crisp at the edges. No brand is printed for the breakfast side.

explain.value:
A Southern biscuit is a quick bread: soft wheat flour, cold butter or lard rubbed in, and buttermilk, whose acid reacts with baking soda to make it rise. The dough is folded a few times to build flaky layers, cut and baked in a very hot oven.

Cold fat makes the layers; overworking the dough makes it tough.

Our Buttermilk Biscuit is a $5 breakfast side, tender and flaky with a gentle tang. The guide suggests it for mopping up the hollandaise or marchand de vin on the egg dishes, which is the easiest way to sell it.

value.front: How do you sell the $5 Buttermilk Biscuit?
value.back: As the thing for mopping up the hollandaise or marchand de vin: a flaky Southern quick bread, cold butter and buttermilk, baked hot.

explain.value:
Brabant potatoes are a New Orleans classic: potatoes cut into cubes, blanched or par-fried, then fried until golden and crisp and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley. They are sometimes called Louisiana fries and appear on the menus of the old Creole houses, Galatoire's and Antoine's among them.

The name is usually linked to the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands, though no one has proved the connection.

We serve them as a breakfast side and with two children's breakfast plates. The French say bra-BAHN; many locals say bruh-BANT. Confirm the house finish and fryer at lineup.

value.front: What are Brabant potatoes?
value.back: A New Orleans side: cubed potatoes fried golden and tossed in butter, garlic and parsley, sometimes called Louisiana fries. Say bra-BAHN or bruh-BANT.

explain.value:
Succotash is a Native American dish, older than any European kitchen in America. Its name comes from the Narragansett word msickquatash, boiled corn kernels, and the corn and beans at its heart were eaten in the north-east long before colonists arrived. The South adopted it later, with butter beans, corn and often pork.

So it is fair to call it a dish the South made its own, but not one the South invented.

Ours is a seasonal dinner side at $12: glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's applewood-smoked bacon. The vegetables change with the market, so learn tonight's mix at lineup.

value.front: Where does succotash come from?
value.back: A Native American corn and bean dish; the name is from the Narragansett msickquatash, boiled corn. Ours is glazed summer vegetables with Nueske’s bacon.

explain.value:
Nueske's is a family smokehouse in Wittenberg, Wisconsin. R.C. Nueske began selling the family's smoked hams, sausages and bacon in 1933, from recipes the family brought when it emigrated, driving them to the resorts of northern Wisconsin. The company is known above all for its applewood-smoked bacon, smoked over applewood for about 24 hours.

Applewood gives a sweet, rich, mellow smoke rather than the sharpness of hickory.

The menu names Nueske's on the dinner Succotash, where the bacon brings smoke and salt to the sweet glazed vegetables. The pronunciation is contested; NOO-skeez is common, so follow the house.

value.front: What is Nueske’s?
value.back: A Wisconsin family smokehouse since 1933, famous for bacon smoked over applewood for about 24 hours: sweet, mellow smoke. On our Succotash.

value.history:
The Nueske story starts with Wilhelm and Wilhelmina Nueske, who emigrated from Prussia to Wisconsin in 1887 and brought their family recipes and their way of smoking over applewood. Two generations later, in 1933, Robert Carl Nueske, known as R.C., then 19, left his grandparents, parents, two brothers and a sister to work the family farm at Wittenberg, traded his plough for a delivery truck, and sold the family's smoked bacon, hams and sausages to the resorts of northern Wisconsin.

In the 1940s he bought a butcher shop and designed and built six smokehouses. The method has barely changed since: the bacon is smoked for about a full day over embers of real Wisconsin applewood logs, which gives a sweet, rounded smoke.

The company is still family owned and run, now in its third generation, with Tanya Nueske as chief executive; she says the family smokes the way her grandfather did. Besides bacon it smokes hams, poultry and sausages.

At Brennan's the name is printed on one dish, the dinner Succotash, where the smoky bacon meets the sweet glazed summer vegetables.
facts: Wilhelm and Wilhelmina Nueske emigrated from Prussia to Wisconsin in 1887, bringing the family recipes.
R.C. Nueske began selling the family's applewood-smoked meats in 1933, at 19, to resorts in northern Wisconsin.
In the 1940s he bought a butcher shop and designed and built six smokehouses.
The bacon is smoked for about 24 hours over embers of real Wisconsin applewood logs.
Third-generation family owned and run in Wittenberg, Wisconsin, with Tanya Nueske as chief executive.
notes: Nueske's is printed only on the dinner Succotash. Do not say the breakfast Thick-Cut Bacon, the children's bacon or the Roost Burger bacon is Nueske's until the kitchen confirms.
Say about 24 hours of applewood smoke, not at least 24; accounts range from 20 to 24 hours.
The Succotash has bacon in it, so mention it when a guest orders vegetables expecting no meat; any dietary question goes to the kitchen.
The pronunciation is contested; follow the house.
value.sayIt: The bacon is Nueske's, a Wisconsin family smokehouse since 1933, smoked about a full day over real applewood.
askKitchen: Is the breakfast thick-cut bacon, and the bacon on the Roost Burger, also Nueske's?

explain.value:
Harissa is a North African chilli paste, most closely tied to Tunisia: dried red chillies soaked and pounded with garlic, olive oil and spices such as caraway, coriander and cumin. It is earthy and warm rather than sharp, with a slow heat.

Stirred into oil or yogurt it becomes a sauce; brushed on vegetables it roasts into a crust.

On the Smoked Cauliflower it partners preserved lemon, salt and perfume against the paste's warmth and the smoke of the cauliflower. The guide gives it moderate heat; warn guests who are shy of spice.

value.front: What is harissa?
value.back: A North African, especially Tunisian, paste of dried chilli, garlic, oil, caraway, coriander and cumin: earthy, moderate heat. On our Smoked Cauliflower.

explain.value:
Smoking flavors food with the smoke of smouldering wood. Hot smoking cooks and flavors together, as with bacon, tasso and andouille; cold smoking, below cooking temperature, flavors without cooking, as with smoked salmon or a smoked liquid. Different woods give different smoke: applewood sweet, hickory strong, pecan mellow.

A light touch of smoke adds savory depth; too much tastes acrid.

On our menus smoke turns up in many forms: the Smoked Cauliflower, the smoked tomato water on the tostada, the smoked potato pavé, the smoked oyster dressing on the Caesar, and the smoked meats, andouille, tasso and Nueske's bacon.

value.front: What is the difference between hot and cold smoking?
value.back: Hot smoking cooks and flavors at once, like bacon and andouille; cold smoking flavors without cooking, like a smoked liquid or salmon.

explain.value:
Mimolette is a round, bright orange cheese from Lille and French Flanders. The story goes that Louis XIV's minister Colbert, at odds with the Dutch, wanted a French cheese to replace Edam; the orange color, from annatto, set it apart. As it ages it turns hard, nutty, sweet and butterscotch-like.

Tiny cheese mites are encouraged on its rind, where they help it age and give the rind its pitted, moon-like look.

In the Shells & Cheese it is melted into a fondue with Abita Amber beer and finished with Grana Padano. Some guests love the mite story and some do not; read the table.

value.front: What is Mimolette?
value.back: A bright orange French cheese from Lille, said to be made to rival Dutch Edam; aged, it is nutty and butterscotch-sweet. Melted into our Shells & Cheese.

value.history:
Mimolette is the French answer to Dutch Edam. The story told in France is that Louis XIV, under the mercantilist policies of his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert, wanted a native cheese to replace the Edam the French were buying. Another telling has Colbert's embargo on foreign goods leaving the people of Flanders without their favorite Dutch-style cheese, so they made it themselves. Either way, it was made around Lille, and to tell it apart from Edam it was colored, first with carrot juice and later with annatto, the seed that gives its blazing orange.

As it ages, cheese mites, which the French call little affineurs, are allowed onto the rind. They eat into the crust, leaving the gray, pitted, moon-like surface, and help the cheese ripen. In 2013 the American FDA detained about a ton of Mimolette because the mites exceeded six per cubic inch; the restriction was lifted in 2014.

Today a large maker is the Normandy cooperative Isigny Sainte-Mère, which began making Mimolette, also called Boule de Lille, in 1951 with master cheesemakers recruited from the north, and sells it from young to extra-mature at 24 months.
facts: Traditionally made around Lille, said to be created under Colbert's policies to replace Dutch Edam.
It was colored first with carrot juice, later with annatto, to set it apart from Edam.
Cheese mites, the French little affineurs, work the rind and give its lunar surface.
In 2013 the FDA detained about a ton over mite levels above six per cubic inch; lifted in 2014.
It is also called Boule de Lille.
Isigny Sainte-Mère has made it since 1951, aged up to 24 months.
notes: Say mee-mo-LET: the orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and butterscotch-sweet as it ages.
The mite story delights some tables and puts others off; offer it only to the curious.
No maker or age is printed; never say Isigny Sainte-Mère or a particular age unless the kitchen confirms it.
The orange is annatto, a plant coloring, the same seed that turns some cheddar orange; dietary questions about the coloring go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: Mimolette, mee-mo-LET, the orange cheese of Lille, made in the seventeenth century to rival Dutch Edam, melted with Abita Amber.
askKitchen: Which Mimolette do we use, and how old is it?

explain.value:
Abita Brewing was founded in 1986 in Abita Springs, Louisiana, across Lake Pontchartrain from the city, by Jim Patton and Rush Cumming. Amber was its first beer and remains its flagship: a Munich-style lager of pale and caramel malts with German Perle hops, smooth, malty and lightly caramel.

A malty, low-bitterness beer is the right choice for cooking with cheese, because hops turn bitter as a sauce reduces.

In the Shells & Cheese it loosens the Mimolette fondue and adds a malty depth. The guide notes the beer's alcohol is mostly but not entirely cooked off, so tell guests who avoid alcohol.

value.front: Why is Abita Amber in the Shells & Cheese?
value.back: A malty, low-bitterness Louisiana lager, Abita’s first beer since 1986; it loosens the Mimolette fondue without turning bitter. Tell guests who avoid alcohol.

value.history:
Abita Brewing was founded in 1986 by Jim Patton and Rush Cumming in downtown Abita Springs, on the Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain. Its first beer went on sale on 4 July that year in New Orleans and Mandeville, and it is described as the first craft brewery to open in the South.

Amber was one of the brewery's original beers, and the one that put it on the map. Patton wrote the recipes for the flagships, Amber, Turbo Dog, Purple Haze and the root beer among them, before selling his share in 1997. Amber is a Munich-style lager of pale and caramel malts with German Perle hops: smooth, malty and lightly caramel, at 4.5 percent and a low 17 IBU.

At Brennan's the Amber goes into the Mimolette fondue of the Shells & Cheese, where its malt and low bitterness suit a cheese sauce, and the dessert list pours Abita Root Beer in the Amarula float.
facts: Founded in 1986 by Jim Patton and Rush Cumming in Abita Springs, Louisiana.
Its first beer went on sale on 4 July 1986.
Described as the first craft brewery to open in the South.
Amber, one of its original beers, is a Munich-style lager with pale and caramel malts and German Perle hops.
Amber is 4.5 percent alcohol with a low 17 IBU.
Brennan's prints Abita Amber in the Shells & Cheese and pours Abita Root Beer in the Amarula float.
notes: The low bitterness is why it suits a cheese sauce: hops turn bitter as a sauce reduces.
The guide says the beer's alcohol is mostly but not entirely cooked off; tell guests who avoid alcohol and let the kitchen answer anything further.
Do not quote well depths or water ages; those figures came from a retailer only.
Do not say Amber was Abita's very first beer; sources disagree, and some say Golden came first.
value.sayIt: The fondue is loosened with Abita Amber, brewed across the lake in Abita Springs since 1986, for a smooth, malty depth.

explain.value:
A fondue, from the French fondre, to melt, is cheese melted smoothly with a liquid, classically white wine in the Swiss pot. A beer cheese sauce uses beer instead, and a dry, aged cheese needs that liquid, and often a little starch, to melt smooth rather than turning stringy or oily.

Heat must stay gentle: boiled cheese splits.

Our Shells & Cheese folds pasta shells into a fondue of Mimolette and Abita Amber, finished with Grana Padano: rich, nutty and malty with a salty finish. It is a grown-up macaroni cheese, and an easy side to add to a steak for the table at $12.

value.front: What is the sauce in the Shells & Cheese?
value.back: A beer cheese fondue: Mimolette melted gently with Abita Amber, finished with Grana Padano, a rich, nutty, malty grown-up macaroni cheese.

explain.value:
The menu prints Maggie's Mushrooms with no description. The likely source is Mushroom Maggie's Farm in St Francisville, Louisiana, upriver from Baton Rouge, a family farm run by Maggie Long and Cyrus Lester that grows lion's mane, oyster, pink trumpet, shiitake and chestnut mushrooms for restaurants in Baton Rouge and New Orleans.

That link comes from a search, not from the house, so confirm it with the chef before you tell it.

Learn three things at lineup: tonight's varieties, how they are cooked, and whether the dish uses butter or stock. It is a $12 dinner side the guide suggests beside the Chateaubriand.

value.front: What should you learn about Maggie’s Mushrooms at lineup?
value.back: Tonight’s varieties, how they are cooked, butter or stock, and whether they come from Mushroom Maggie’s Farm in St Francisville; confirm with the chef.

value.who: Mushroom Maggie's Farm (to be confirmed by the chef)
value.history:
Mushroom Maggie's Farm is the best-known Louisiana grower called Maggie's, and the likely source of the side the menu prints simply as Maggie's Mushrooms. No public source names Brennan's as a customer, so treat the link as likely, not settled.

The farm is in St Francisville, upriver from Baton Rouge. Maggie Long and her husband Cyrus Lester have owned and run it since 2018. Their start was hard: in 2017, in the first week of official operations, a propane hose burst while they were steaming fruiting blocks, the barn burned down and Lester was left with burns over seventy percent of his skin. They started again from nothing and spent the next year rebuilding, so 2018 became the farm's first real year.

Today the farm grows 1,200 to 1,500 pounds of mushrooms a week, at least eight kinds, among them lion's mane, oyster, pink trumpet, shiitake and chestnut. It supplies about twenty top New Orleans restaurants and many closer to home, and Maggie Long often works directly with chefs as they plan their menus.
facts: In St Francisville, Louisiana, run since 2018 by Maggie Long and Cyrus Lester.
Grows 1,200 to 1,500 pounds of mushrooms a week.
At least eight kinds, including lion's mane, oyster, pink trumpet, shiitake and chestnut.
Supplies about twenty top New Orleans restaurants.
A 2017 fire in the first week of operations destroyed the barn and badly burned Cyrus Lester; they rebuilt for 2018.
notes: The menu prints only 'Maggie's Mushrooms'; no source confirms the farm supplies Brennan's.
Until the chef confirms it, say 'local mushrooms'; once confirmed, name the farm and St Francisville.
Learn tonight's varieties and how they are cooked at lineup; varieties change.
Butter, stock and whether the side is vegetarian are kitchen answers.
value.sayIt: Maggie's Mushrooms is our side of local speciality mushrooms; I'll tell you exactly which varieties the kitchen has tonight.
askKitchen: Are Maggie's Mushrooms from Mushroom Maggie's Farm in St Francisville?
Which varieties tonight, and how are they cooked (butter, stock)?

explain.value:
Rice dressing is a south Louisiana staple: cooked rice folded into a savory mix of ground meat browned with the holy trinity, garlic and seasoning, often with a little roux or gravy. It is the rice equivalent of a bread stuffing, which is why it is called dressing, and it appears on Sunday and holiday tables.

Its close cousin is dirty rice, and the line between them depends on who you ask: some say dressing is ground beef and pork and dirty rice carries chicken livers and gizzards, others say the reverse.

Ours is a $12 dinner side with no description printed, so confirm the meats with the kitchen before describing it.

value.front: How does rice dressing differ from dirty rice?
value.back: Both are rice with ground meat and the trinity; which carries livers depends on who you ask. Confirm the meats in ours with the kitchen.

value.where: The southwest Louisiana prairie, centered on Crowley, Acadia Parish
value.history:
South Louisiana Rice Dressing carries its place in its name. Rice growing on the southwest Louisiana prairie began in earnest in the early 1880s, and by 1890 a record crop of 80 million pounds made Louisiana the leading rice state, overtaking South Carolina. Crowley, the seat of Acadia Parish, became the center of the industry, its fields watered by canals and wells.

Between 1800 and 1920 the region changed from subsistence farming and open-range cattle country into the first mechanized commercial rice region in the world, and southwest Louisiana still holds nearly 500,000 acres of rice land.

That is why rice, not bread, is the stuffing of south Louisiana: rice dressing is cooked rice folded into browned meat and the holy trinity, a Sunday and holiday dish. Brennan's prints the side with no description and no rice brand, so the meats and the rice are questions for the kitchen.
facts: Rice growing in southwest Louisiana began in earnest in the early 1880s.
Louisiana's record 1890 crop of 80 million pounds made it the leading rice state, passing South Carolina.
Crowley, seat of Acadia Parish, became the center of southwestern Louisiana's rice industry.
Southwestern Louisiana became the first mechanized commercial rice region in the world by 1920.
Southwest Louisiana holds nearly 500,000 acres of rice land.
notes: The side prints no description; confirm the meats with the kitchen before describing it.
Do not claim the rice is from a named mill or parish without the kitchen's word.
Guests ask how it differs from dirty rice; the honest answer is that it depends who you ask.
Meat and dietary questions go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: Rice dressing is south Louisiana's stuffing, rice from the prairie rice country folded with browned meat and the trinity; I'll confirm tonight's meats.
askKitchen: Which meats go into the South Louisiana Rice Dressing, and is there liver?
Which rice is it made with?

explain.value:
Breakfast and lunch carries seven sides, each priced on its own: the Housemade Pork Sausage Patty and Thick-Cut Bacon at $9, the Buttermilk Biscuit at $5, an Egg Any Style at $3, and Cheddar Grits, Brabant Potatoes and Creamed Spinach at $7.

They exist to round out the egg dishes. A guest who orders the Eggs Sardou or the omelette and wants a little meat can add the sausage or bacon; a biscuit catches the hollandaise or marchand de vin.

Offer one side as you confirm the entrée, matched to the plate: something crisp beside a sauced dish, something rich beside a light one. Learn every side's service note before the first table.

value.front: Which breakfast sides are $9, and which is $5?
value.back: The Housemade Pork Sausage Patty and the Thick-Cut Bacon are $9; the Buttermilk Biscuit is $5. Grits, potatoes and creamed spinach are $7, an egg $3.

explain.value:
Dinner carries five sides at $12 each: Succotash with Nueske's bacon, Smoked Cauliflower with preserved lemon and harissa, Shells & Cheese, Maggie's Mushrooms and South Louisiana Rice Dressing. Two of them, the mushrooms and the rice dressing, print no description, so their preparation is learned at lineup.

Sides are shared at dinner, so sell them to the table rather than to one guest.

The guide's natural pairings: Maggie's Mushrooms or Shells & Cheese with the Roasted Chateaubriand, and the Smoked Cauliflower beside the Blackened Tofu for a guest eating without meat, once the kitchen confirms the butter and stock.

value.front: Which dinner sides does the guide suggest with the Chateaubriand?
value.back: Maggie’s Mushrooms or Shells & Cheese, each $12. Dinner sides are shared plates, so offer them to the whole table, not to one guest.

explain.value:
Bananas Foster was created at Brennan's in 1951, while the restaurant was still Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré on Bourbon Street. Owen asked for a new dessert for a dinner honoring his friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission. His sister Ella and chef Paul Blangé adapted the caramelized bananas their mother made at home, and named it for Foster.

Bananas made sense: New Orleans was the main port of entry for bananas from Central and South America.

2026 is its 75th year. It is $14, minimum two per order, made at the table, and the house calls it the most-ordered item on the menu.

value.front: Who created Bananas Foster, and who is it named for?
value.back: Ella Brennan and chef Paul Blangé, in 1951, at Owen Brennan’s request; named for Richard Foster, Owen’s friend and crime commission chairman.

components.name: Bananas, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon

explain.value:
Bananas Foster starts with a caramel made in the pan at the table: butter melted with brown sugar until it bubbles, dusted with cinnamon. The bananas, ripe but still firm, are halved and quartered and laid in the caramel, turned once so they soften without collapsing.

The caramel is kept at a blond, bubbling stage, because a darker caramel would harden into toffee on the cold ice cream.

The bananas and sauce are spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream, so warm and cold meet in every spoonful. Ripe but firm fruit is the cook's secret: soft bananas turn to mush in the flame.

value.front: What goes into the pan for Bananas Foster before the rum?
value.back: Butter and brown sugar melted to a bubbling blond caramel, cinnamon, then ripe but firm bananas turned once so they soften without collapsing.

explain.value:
The printed menu names rum, and the long-standing Brennan's recipe also uses banana liqueur, which loosens the caramel and deepens the banana flavor before the rum is lit. Dark rum gives molasses and spice notes and enough strength to catch the flame.

Follow the house procedure you are trained on rather than any recipe you find elsewhere, and do not quote quantities.

Flaming burns the alcohol vapor above the pan, not all the alcohol in it: a large share stays in the sauce. For a guest who avoids alcohol, the guide steers to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. Which rum the kitchen pours is a question for the chef.

value.front: Does the flame burn off all the alcohol in Bananas Foster?
value.back: No. Flaming burns the vapor, and much of the rum and banana liqueur stays in the sauce; steer guests who avoid alcohol to the Lemon Tart or Tarte Tatin.

explain.value:
Flambé means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so the alcohol vapor burns in a burst of blue and orange flame. It is theater and flavor at once, caramelizing the sauce's surface. At Brennan's it is done on a guéridon, the tableside cart.

The guide's steps are learned word for word: measure the spirit into a small vessel, never pour from the bottle near a flame, pull the pan off the flame to add it, tilt to ignite, keep a lid in reach, let the flame die before plating, and turn the burner off before leaving.

In a bright breakfast room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it clearly has died down.

value.front: What are the key safety rules for flambé at the table?
value.back: Measure the spirit first, never pour from the bottle near flame, add it off the flame, keep a lid in reach, let it burn out, turn the burner off.

explain.value:
Classic French-style vanilla ice cream is a crème anglaise, milk, cream, sugar and egg yolks infused with vanilla, chilled and churned so it freezes smooth and dense. Real vanilla comes from the cured pod of an orchid and gives tiny black seeds and a floral, warm perfume.

Very cold, rich and plain, it is the stage for a hot sauce.

The kitchen makes its own for both flamed desserts: Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee are spooned over it at the table, so the hot, boozy fruit meets cold vanilla. The guide notes the ice cream likely contains egg; confirm with the kitchen when a guest asks.

value.front: What do both flamed desserts sit on?
value.back: Housemade vanilla ice cream, a churned vanilla custard: the cold, plain stage for the hot Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee sauces.

explain.value:
Cherries Jubilee is older than Bananas Foster. It is generally credited to Auguste Escoffier, who made it for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be the Diamond Jubilee of 1897. His recipe was stoned cherries in a thickened syrup, served in small dishes with a spoonful of warmed kirsch lit at the table, and no ice cream; the ice cream is a later, largely American habit.

It belongs to the same flamed family as Bananas Foster and crêpes Suzette.

Ours is fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce, flamed at the table over housemade vanilla ice cream, $14. Brighter and fruitier than the Foster: for a table of two, have both.

value.front: Who is credited with Cherries Jubilee, and for what?
value.back: Auguste Escoffier, for one of Queen Victoria’s jubilees, usually said to be 1897. Ours is black cherries in Luxardo sauce, flamed over vanilla ice cream.

explain.value:
Cherries come in two broad families. Sweet cherries, dark red to near black, are the ones eaten fresh; sour or tart cherries are brighter red, sharper and usually cooked. The menu says fresh tart black cherries, which crosses the two, so which variety the kitchen uses is a fair question for the chef.

Cooked briefly in the pan, cherries soften and release a deep red juice that becomes the sauce.

On the Cherries Jubilee they are flamed at the table in a Luxardo sauce and spooned over vanilla ice cream. The guide notes cherries may contain pits; confirm with the kitchen before the guest takes a bite.

value.front: What should you confirm about the cherries in Cherries Jubilee?
value.back: Which variety, since tart cherries are usually red and black ones sweet, and whether any pits remain; ask the kitchen before serving.

explain.value:
Luxardo is the Italian family house famous for maraschino. Girolamo Luxardo founded the distillery in 1821 in Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, distilling a clear liqueur from the small, sour marasca cherry; after the Second World War destroyed the distillery, Giorgio Luxardo re-founded the firm at Torreglia, near Padua, in 1947, and the company grows its own marasca cherries there.

It also makes the dark candied cherries in syrup that bartenders prize.

The Cherries Jubilee's Luxardo sauce is cherry on cherry. The menu does not say whether it uses the liqueur or the cherries in syrup, so ask the chef which, and which spirit is lit.

value.front: What is Luxardo, and what does it bring to Cherries Jubilee?
value.back: The Italian house founded in 1821 in Zara, re-founded at Torreglia in 1947, famous for marasca cherry maraschino and candied cherries; its sauce is cherry on cherry.

value.where: Torreglia, near Padua, Italy (founded in Zara, Dalmatia)
value.history:
In 1817 Girolamo Luxardo moved to Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, as consular representative of the Kingdom of Sardinia. His wife, Maria Canevari, made rosolio maraschino at home, a cherry liqueur of the region, and in 1821 he founded a distillery to make it properly. Within eight years the Emperor recognized it as superior. Around 1905 the plant at Zara made the first Luxardo maraschino cherries, marasca cherries candied in their own syrup, and in 1913 Michelangelo Luxardo, the third generation, built a new distillery.

The war ended all of it. Allied bombing from November 1943 to October 1944 destroyed 80 percent of Zara, and the factory with it. Pietro Luxardo and his brother Nicolò, with Nicolò's wife, were killed by Tito's partisans. Giorgio Luxardo, the only survivor of the fourth generation, fled across the Adriatic; the family story says he carried a single cherry sapling.

With Nicolò III of the fifth generation he re-founded the firm briefly in Venice, then at Torreglia in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where the first marasca orchard was planted in 1947. It now has 20,000 trees, the company is still family owned, and it marked 200 years in 2021.
facts: Founded in 1821 by Girolamo Luxardo in Zara, then Habsburg Dalmatia.
His wife Maria Canevari made rosolio maraschino at home before the distillery.
The first Luxardo maraschino cherries were made at Zara around 1905.
Allied bombing in 1943 and 1944 destroyed the Zara factory.
Giorgio Luxardo, sole survivor of the fourth generation, re-founded the firm at Torreglia near Padua.
The first marasca orchard at Torreglia was planted in 1947; it now has 20,000 trees.
The firm is still family owned and marked 200 years in 2021.
Luxardo marasca also goes into Sangue Morlacco, its cherry liqueur.
notes: The Cherries Jubilee prints Luxardo by name, but it was not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026: confirm with a manager that it is served before offering it.
Never say which Luxardo product is in the sauce until the kitchen tells you: Maraschino, Sangue Morlacco or the cherries in syrup.
The single sapling is a family story; tell it as a story, not a record.
Alcohol questions go to the kitchen: flaming does not remove all the alcohol.
value.sayIt: Luxardo is the family cherry house founded in Zara in 1821 and replanted near Padua; its marasca cherry is the heart of this dessert.
askKitchen: Which Luxardo product goes into the sauce?
Which spirit is lit at the table?

explain.value:
Bread pudding is an old European way to use stale bread: soaked in sweet custard and baked until soft inside and golden on top. In New Orleans it became a staple, recorded in local cookbooks from at least 1885, because the city's light French bread stales fast and drinks custard without turning to paste.

The boozy sauce came later; restaurants revived the dessert from the 1970s with whiskey and bourbon sauces, and a warm whiskey sauce is now its signature.

Ours is $14: bread pudding with a whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream for tang and pralines for crunch. Tell guests who avoid alcohol that the caramel carries whiskey.

value.front: Why is bread pudding a New Orleans classic?
value.back: The city’s light French bread stales fast and soaks up custard; local cookbooks carry it from 1885. Ours has whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines.

explain.value:
A caramel sauce is sugar cooked until amber, then loosened with cream and butter into a pourable sauce. A whiskey caramel adds whiskey, which brings vanilla, oak and a warm, boozy edge that cuts the sweetness.

It holds better in service than the classic New Orleans whiskey sauce of butter, sugar and egg, which can split.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding it is the warm, boozy sauce against the soft pudding and the tangy buttermilk ice cream. Which whiskey the kitchen uses is a question for the chef, and the alcohol in it is worth mentioning to guests who avoid it.

value.front: What is the sauce on the New Orleans Bread Pudding?
value.back: A whiskey caramel: amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, with whiskey for vanilla, oak and warmth. Mention the alcohol to guests who avoid it.

explain.value:
Buttermilk is the tangy, slightly thick cultured milk of Southern baking. Churned into ice cream with cream and sugar, it gives a gently sour, refreshing ice cream, something like frozen yogurt but richer.

That tang is the point: it balances sweet, rich desserts the way crème fraîche does.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding it cools the warm pudding and cuts the sweetness of the whiskey caramel and pralines, so the dessert never feels heavy. Describe it to a guest as a tangy, Southern-style ice cream.

value.front: Why buttermilk ice cream with the bread pudding?
value.back: Its gentle tang, like a rich frozen yogurt, cools the warm pudding and cuts the sweetness of the whiskey caramel and pralines.

explain.value:
The praline takes its name from the seventeenth-century Maréchal du Plessis-Praslin, whose cook sugared almonds. The Ursuline nuns, who came to New Orleans in 1727, are credited by tradition with bringing the recipe; Louisiana cooks swapped in pecans and made a soft, creamy patty of brown sugar, butter and cream.

In the nineteenth century pralinières, women street vendors, many of them free women of color, sold them in the French Quarter.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding pralines add crunch and caramel sweetness. Say PRAH-leen; PRAY-leen marks a visitor.

value.front: Where do New Orleans pralines come from?
value.back: Named for the Maréchal du Plessis-Praslin’s sugared almonds; brought by tradition with the Ursulines in 1727 and remade with pecans. Say PRAH-leen.

value.who: The New Orleans praline and the pralinières
value.history:
The praline began as a French sugared almond, named for César, duc de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin, whose chef made it. Early in the eighteenth century the Ursuline nuns are credited with bringing the candy to New Orleans.

The New Orleans praline is a different thing, and it was made by the city's Black women. They took the almond sweet, used the pecans that grew all around them and added milk or cream, turning a hard sugared nut into the soft, creamy patty the city knows.

In the mid to late nineteenth century, women called pralinières sold them on the streets of the French Quarter. Free women of color and enslaved women alike made and sold them, and for Black women it was a way to earn their own money; some bought their own freedom and their families' with the proceeds. On Brennan's New Orleans Bread Pudding, pralines bring that history and a caramel crunch to the whiskey caramel and buttermilk ice cream.
facts: The praline is named for César, duc de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin, whose chef made sugared almonds.
The Ursuline nuns are credited with bringing the praline to New Orleans early in the eighteenth century.
The city's Black women made the pecan praline, adding milk or cream to thicken it.
Pralinières sold pralines on French Quarter streets in the mid to late nineteenth century.
Some pralinières bought their own and their families' freedom with their earnings.
notes: Locals say PRAH-leen; follow the house if a guest says it another way, and never correct them.
Whether our pralines are made in-house is not public; ask before saying housemade.
Nut and dairy questions go to the kitchen and the service note.
Credit the pralinières when a guest asks about the history; it is the true origin of the New Orleans style.
value.sayIt: New Orleans pralines are pecans, brown sugar and cream, a candy the city's pralinières sold in the French Quarter; they crown our bread pudding.
askKitchen: Are the pralines on the bread pudding made in-house, and if not, by whom?

components.name: The Snickers, a candy bar rebuilt

explain.value:
The Snickers is the pastry kitchen's take on the famous candy bar, taken apart and rebuilt as a plated dessert: a milk chocolate Bavarian cream for the chocolate, caramel custard for the caramel, nougat ice cream for the nougat, and roasted peanuts.

The name is a trademark, so say our Snickers lightly, as a wink rather than a claim.

It is $15 at both meals and closes the dinner tasting. The guide flags peanuts in capitals: confirm before ordering for every table. It is the dessert for the guest who wants chocolate, and the grown-up candy bar line sells it.

value.front: What is The Snickers on our dessert menu?
value.back: The candy bar rebuilt: milk chocolate Bavarian cream, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts. Confirm peanuts before ordering.

explain.value:
A Bavarian cream, bavarois in French, is a crème anglaise set with gelatin and lightened with whipped cream, then chilled in a mold. It sits between a mousse and a custard: light, silky and holding its shape. The great nineteenth-century chef Carême codified it.

Chocolate melted into the custard turns it into a chocolate Bavarian.

The Snickers's Bavarian milk chocolate almost certainly means a milk chocolate bavarois, not chocolate from Bavaria. The guide notes Bavarian creams are usually set with gelatin, so check with the kitchen for guests who avoid it.

value.front: What is a Bavarian cream?
value.back: Crème anglaise set with gelatin and lightened with whipped cream: between a mousse and a custard. Ours is milk chocolate, in The Snickers.

value.who: The Brennan's pastry kitchen (chocolate maker not named)
value.history:
The Snickers is Brennan's grown-up version of the candy bar, and the menu prints it plainly: Bavarian milk chocolate, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts, at $15. It appears on the dessert menu and as a choice on the Taste of Brennan's tasting menu, where a diner listing describes it as house made.

Bavarian, on a pastry menu, most often names a preparation rather than a place: a Bavarian cream, or bavarois, is a set custard lightened with whipped cream, between a mousse and a custard. Read that way, the line promises a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, not chocolate made in Bavaria. No public source names the chocolate the pastry kitchen melts into it, and no claim should be made about a maker.

The kitchen's pastry roots are real. Kris Padalino became executive chef in June 2025 after eight years at Brennan's as pastry chef and executive sous chef. Who builds The Snickers now, and with which chocolate, are questions for lineup.
facts: The menu prints Bavarian Milk Chocolate, Caramel Custard, Nougat Ice Cream, Roasted Peanuts, $15.00.
It also appears as a dessert choice on the tasting menu.
A diner listing calls it a house-made Snickers-inspired dessert on the Taste of Brennan's menu.
No public source names the chocolate maker.
Kris Padalino became executive chef in June 2025 after eight years as pastry chef and executive sous chef.
notes: Say a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, light and set, between a mousse and a custard.
Never say the chocolate comes from Bavaria or name a brand; neither is confirmed.
Peanuts are printed on the dish: dietary questions go to the kitchen before ordering.
Bavarian creams are usually set with gelatine; vegetarian questions go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: Our Snickers: a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, between a mousse and a custard, with caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts.
askKitchen: Which milk chocolate goes into The Snickers, and does Bavarian mean a Bavarian cream?
Is the Bavarian set with gelatine?

explain.value:
A caramel custard is eggs, milk or cream and sugar cooked gently until set, flavored with caramel, sugar cooked to amber, which brings a toasty, slightly bitter depth. It is the family of crème caramel and flan.

Gentle heat is everything: too hot and the eggs curdle into a grainy, weeping custard.

In The Snickers it plays the caramel layer of the candy bar, silky and toasty against the milk chocolate Bavarian cream, the nougat ice cream and the salty roasted peanuts. If a guest asks, it is the soft caramel part of the bar.

value.front: What plays the caramel in The Snickers?
value.back: A caramel custard: eggs and cream cooked gently with sugar taken to amber, silky and toasty, from the same family as crème caramel and flan.

explain.value:
Nougat is a confection of honey and sugar whipped into egg whites, usually studded with nuts, almonds, pistachios or hazelnuts; soft nougat is the chewy center of many candy bars. As an ice cream it tastes of honey, toasted nuts and vanilla.

It is the frozen version of the candy bar's nougat layer.

In The Snickers it sits with roasted peanuts, caramel custard and milk chocolate Bavarian cream. Classic nougat often carries tree nuts besides the dish's peanuts, so ask the kitchen what is in it for any guest with a nut question.

value.front: What is nougat?
value.back: Honey and sugar whipped into egg whites, usually with nuts; as an ice cream it tastes of honey and toasted nuts. Ask the kitchen about nuts in ours.

explain.value:
The peanut is not a true nut but a legume, a pod that ripens underground, grown across the American South. Roasting browns its natural sugars and oils, bringing out the toasty flavor, and salting makes it the classic partner to chocolate and caramel.

Salty peanuts against sweet chocolate is the whole appeal of the candy bar.

On The Snickers roasted peanuts give crunch and salt. The guide prints PEANUTS in capitals on this dessert: confirm with every table before it is ordered, and send any dietary question to the kitchen.

value.front: What must you confirm before The Snickers is ordered?
value.back: Peanuts, printed in capitals in the guide: roasted peanuts give the crunch and salt. Confirm with every table and send dietary questions to the kitchen.

explain.value:
The French tarte au citron is sweet pastry filled with a sharp lemon curd, often crowned with meringue. Our Lemon Tart takes it apart: the pastry becomes a sweet pastry crumb, the curd becomes a light yuzu mousse, the sharpness is concentrated in a lemon jelly, and the meringue is piped and toasted.

The deconstruction keeps the flavors and makes the whole dessert lighter.

It is $14 and the lightest dessert on the list. The guide names it, with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, as the dessert to steer to for guests who avoid alcohol, since the flamed desserts and the bread pudding all carry spirits.

value.front: Which desserts do we steer guests who avoid alcohol towards?
value.back: The Lemon Tart, a lighter, deconstructed tarte au citron with yuzu mousse, and the Pineapple Tarte Tatin; the flamed desserts and bread pudding carry spirits.

explain.value:
Yuzu is an East Asian citrus grown in Japan and Korea, about the size of a tangerine, with a bumpy yellow skin and little juice. Its aroma is intense: it tastes like lemon, lime and mandarin at once, with a floral edge. It is the citrus in ponzu.

Its zest and juice perfume a dish far beyond their quantity.

In the Lemon Tart it flavors a light yuzu mousse, the dessert's answer to lemon curd. The guide notes the mousse is likely set with gelatin, so check with the kitchen for guests who avoid it.

value.front: What does yuzu taste like?
value.back: Like lemon, lime and mandarin at once, with a floral edge: an East Asian citrus, the citrus in ponzu. It flavors the mousse in our Lemon Tart.

explain.value:
Meringue is egg white whipped with sugar until glossy and stiff. Italian meringue whips in a hot sugar syrup, and Swiss meringue warms the whites and sugar together first; both are cooked and stable, so they hold their shape on a plate and can be browned with a torch.

Toasting caramelizes the peaks into a marshmallow-like flavor with a crisp shell.

On the Lemon Tart the toasted meringue sits with the yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and sweet pastry crumb, sweet and soft against sharp citrus. Which style the pastry kitchen uses is a question for the chef.

value.front: How is the meringue on the Lemon Tart finished?
value.back: Piped and toasted with a torch, so the peaks caramelize like marshmallow; a cooked Italian or Swiss meringue holds its shape on the plate.

components.name: Lemon jelly and sweet pastry crumb

explain.value:
A lemon jelly is lemon juice, sugar and water set into a soft, clear gel, concentrated and sharp, a burst of acid in each bite. A sweet pastry crumb is sweet shortcrust, butter, sugar, flour and egg, baked and broken into crumbs, so the tart's crust becomes a crunchy scatter.

Splitting the tart this way lets each texture be at its best.

In the Lemon Tart the jelly carries the sharpness and the crumb gives the buttery crunch, around the yuzu mousse and toasted meringue. The guide lists what the pastry contains on the service note.

value.front: Where did the tart’s crust go in our Lemon Tart?
value.back: It became a sweet pastry crumb, crunchy and buttery, beside a sharp lemon jelly, the yuzu mousse and toasted meringue.

explain.value:
Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down tart: fruit caramelized in butter and sugar in a pan, covered with pastry, baked and turned out so the pastry is underneath. It is named for Stéphanie and Caroline Tatin, who ran the Hôtel Tatin at Lamotte-Beuvron in the Sologne. The story of an accident with overcooked apples is a legend; the region already made such tarts, and Maxim's in Paris made the name famous.

Apples are classic. Pineapple is wetter and needs more browning, hence charred.

Our Pineapple Tarte Tatin is $14 with puff pastry, sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse, and a dessert without spirits.

value.front: What is a tarte Tatin?
value.back: A French upside-down tart of fruit caramelized in butter and sugar, baked under pastry and turned out, named for the Tatin sisters. Ours is charred pineapple.

explain.value:
Pineapple is a tropical fruit, sweet and sharp, and much juicier than apple. Charring it, in a very hot pan, under a grill or in caramel, drives off water and caramelizes its sugars until the edges blacken slightly, giving a deep, almost smoky sweetness while keeping the acidity.

That browning is what makes it work in a tart built for apples.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin the charred pineapple sits on puff pastry with a sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse: caramelized, tangy and flaky against cool cream.

value.front: Why is the pineapple charred on the Tarte Tatin?
value.back: Pineapple is much wetter than apple; charring drives off water and caramelizes its sugars for a deep, slightly smoky sweetness that keeps its tang.

explain.value:
Puff pastry is a laminated dough: a block of butter wrapped in dough, then rolled and folded again and again until there are hundreds of layers. In the oven the water in the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, so the pastry rises tall, crisp and flaky with no yeast at all.

It is one of the foundations of French pastry, behind the palmier and the mille-feuille.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin it is the flaky base under the charred pineapple. A classic Tatin is baked with the pastry on top and turned out; whether ours is baked inverted or assembled on the plate is a question for the chef.

value.front: How does puff pastry rise without yeast?
value.back: It is laminated: butter folded into dough into hundreds of layers, and steam from the butter pushes them apart in the oven.

explain.value:
A vanilla mousse is cream, or a light custard folded with whipped cream, flavored with vanilla and whipped until airy, sometimes set lightly so it holds a shape. It is cooler and lighter than ice cream, and softer than a Bavarian cream.

Vanilla's floral warmth suits caramelized fruit.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin the whipped vanilla mousse cools the hot, charred pineapple alongside the sweetened condensed anglaise, so the plate has warm and cold, crisp and soft. Whether it is set with gelatin is a question for the kitchen if a guest asks.

value.front: What cools the hot pineapple on the Tarte Tatin?
value.back: A whipped vanilla mousse, airy and lighter than ice cream, served with the sweetened condensed anglaise so the plate has warm and cold, crisp and soft.

explain.value:
Cheddar takes its name from the English village of Cheddar, and is now made all over the world. Its curds are cut, stacked and turned, a process called cheddaring, which presses out whey and gives the cheese its dense, smooth texture. Young cheddar is mild and creamy; aged cheddar is sharp, nutty and crumbly, with crunchy crystals.

Sharp cheddar melts well and holds its flavor in a sauce.

On our menus it is stirred into the Cheddar Grits, a $7 breakfast side, creamy, rich and a little sharp, and it is the classic cheese of the pimento cheese folded into the Shrimp & Grits cake.

value.front: What cheese is in the Cheddar Grits, and what does it add?
value.back: Cheddar, the English cheese made by stacking and turning curds; sharp cheddar melts smoothly and gives the grits a rich, slightly sharp edge.

explain.value:
A grilled cheese is buttered bread around sliced cheese, cooked in a pan or on a griddle over moderate heat until the bread is golden and crisp and the cheese has melted through. Too hot, and the bread burns before the cheese melts; patience and a lid help.

It is a children's favorite because it is warm, mild and familiar.

The children's menus offer it twice: at breakfast with Brabant potatoes and at dinner with French fries, each within the $25.00 set price. The menu does not name the cheese or bread, so confirm with the kitchen if a parent asks.

value.front: How is a grilled cheese made so the cheese melts?
value.back: Buttered bread and cheese cooked over moderate heat, often with a lid, so the bread turns golden while the cheese melts through. With potatoes or fries.

explain.value:
Good fries are usually cooked twice. A first, lower-temperature fry cooks the potato through until soft; after resting, a second, hotter fry crisps and browns the outside. Starchy potatoes give a fluffy inside, and salt goes on the moment they leave the oil, while it still sticks.

Belgium and France both claim them; the name stuck in America.

Fries come with the children's fried Gulf shrimp and grilled cheese at dinner, and the Roost serves Fries with Pink Sauce at $8, the easy add for a table with drinks and no food. Fryer questions go to the kitchen.

value.front: Why are good fries fried twice?
value.back: A lower first fry cooks the potato soft; a hotter second fry crisps and browns it. Salt them the moment they leave the oil.

explain.value:
Buttered noodles are pasta boiled in well-salted water until just tender, drained and tossed straight away with butter and grated cheese, so the cheese melts into a light, glossy coating with a splash of the pasta water.

It is the plainest comfort food, which is why children love it.

On the children's dinner menu Buttered Noodles with Cheese comes within the $25.00 set price, with salami and cheese to start, ice cream and a drink. The menu names neither the pasta shape nor the cheese, so if a parent asks, the kitchen has the answer.

value.front: What comes with the children’s Buttered Noodles with Cheese?
value.back: Within the $25.00 dinner price: salami and cheese to start, the noodles tossed in butter and cheese, ice cream and a drink.

explain.value:
Whipped cream is cold cream beaten with a little sugar, and often vanilla, until it holds soft peaks; beaten too far it turns grainy and then to butter. Fresh berries, strawberries, blueberries, raspberries or blackberries, bring color and a sharp sweetness.

Together they are the classic topping for French toast and pancakes.

On the children's Vanilla French Toast they finish the plate within the $25.00 breakfast price. Which berries are in season changes, so check at lineup if a parent asks or a child has a favorite.

value.front: What tops the children’s Vanilla French Toast?
value.back: Fresh berries, which change with the season, and whipped cream, cold cream beaten with a little sugar to soft peaks.

explain.value:
Popcorn shrimp are small shrimp, or larger ones cut into bite-size pieces, dredged in seasoned flour or a light batter and fried quickly until golden, so they pop into the mouth like popcorn. The coating crisps in seconds while the shrimp stays sweet and tender.

They are eaten by the handful, which makes them a natural bar snack.

At the Roost, Popcorn Shrimp uses Louisiana shrimp with a Crystal hot sauce gastrique at $15, the step up from fries for a table staying a while. The children's breakfast offers popcorn shrimp with Brabant potatoes. Coating questions go to the kitchen.

value.front: What are popcorn shrimp?
value.back: Small, bite-size shrimp dredged and fried golden in seconds, eaten by the handful; at the Roost with a Crystal gastrique, and on the children’s breakfast.

explain.value:
Spiced nuts are nuts tossed with a little fat, salt and spice and roasted until fragrant and crisp, the classic bowl on a bar. A Creole seasoning brings paprika, cayenne, garlic and herbs: warm, savory and gently hot.

Salt and spice make people thirsty, which is the point of a bar snack.

At the Roost, Creole Spiced Nuts are $6, the cheapest snack on the Bubbles list and the one to suggest the moment a drink lands. The mix of nuts is not printed, so ask the kitchen for any guest with a nut question.

value.front: When do you suggest the Creole Spiced Nuts?
value.back: The moment a drink lands: at $6 they are the cheapest Bubbles snack, warm and salty with Creole spice. Ask the kitchen which nuts are in the mix.

explain.value:
Crawfish are freshwater crustaceans, like small lobsters, and Louisiana produces most of the country's supply, both farmed in rice fields and caught wild in the swamps and bayous. The tail meat is sweet and rich, and the fat from the head, golden and full of flavor, is prized by Cajun cooks.

Spring is boil season, when crawfish are eaten by the pound at backyard parties.

At the Roost they fill the Crawfish Meat Pies with a chive rémoulade, the most Louisiana snack on the Bubbles list at $16. How the kitchen makes the filling is not printed, so ask before describing it.

value.front: What are crawfish?
value.back: Freshwater crustaceans like small lobsters; Louisiana raises and catches most of the country’s supply. Their sweet tails fill our Crawfish Meat Pies.

value.who: Louisiana crawfish farmers and Atchafalaya fishermen
value.where: South Louisiana rice country and the Atchafalaya Basin
value.history:
Louisiana grows nearly all of America's crawfish. Its crawfish ponds covered 120,654 acres in 1990 and about 225,789 acres in a recent count, against roughly 7,500 acres in the whole of the rest of the country.

More than half of that farming happens in rice fields. After the rice harvest in July and August the farmers flood the same fields as crawfish ponds, so the clay soil that suits rice gives a second crop in the cooler months. Farm-raised crawfish make up most of Louisiana's supply, about 80% by one count.

The rest is wild, trapped in the deeper water of the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States, which has historically given about 90% of the state's wild landings.

On the Roost menu the Crawfish Meat Pies come with a chive rémoulade. The menu does not print Louisiana, so whether the tail meat in them is Louisiana crawfish is a question for the kitchen; Louisiana law requires a menu notice when imported crawfish are served.
facts: Louisiana crawfish ponds grew from 120,654 acres in 1990 to 225,789 acres, against about 7,500 acres elsewhere in the US.
More than half of Louisiana's crawfish farming is done in rice fields flooded after the rice harvest.
Farm-raised crawfish are about 80% of Louisiana's crawfish industry by one count; the rest is trapped wild.
Wild crawfish are trapped in the Atchafalaya Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States.
About 90% of Louisiana's wild crawfish landings have historically come from the Atchafalaya Basin.
Louisiana's Act 372 of 2019 requires a menu notice when imported crawfish or shrimp are served.
notes: The menu prints Crawfish Meat Pies, not Louisiana crawfish; do not add the word until the kitchen confirms it.
A good line: most Louisiana crawfish grow in rice fields, a second crop after the rice harvest.
Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.
value.sayIt: Crawfish are Louisiana's own: most are raised in flooded rice fields, the rest trapped wild in the Atchafalaya swamp.
askKitchen: Is the crawfish tail meat in the meat pies from Louisiana, and is it farmed or wild?

explain.value:
Louisiana's hand pies have a long history. The best known is the Natchitoches meat pie from the state's oldest permanent European settlement: a half-moon of pastry filled with seasoned pork and beef in gravy, traditionally fried. It was documented by 1826 and is an official state food; it may descend from Spanish empanadas or French Canadian tourtière.

Crawfish pies fill the same kind of pastry, or a full pie, with crawfish in a seasoned sauce.

The Roost's Crawfish Meat Pies follow that tradition, with chive rémoulade for dipping. Offer them to visitors who want a local taste in the courtyard.

value.front: What is a Natchitoches meat pie?
value.back: A fried half-moon hand pie of seasoned pork and beef from Natchitoches, Louisiana’s oldest settlement; our Crawfish Meat Pies follow that tradition.

explain.value:
Pink sauce is the menu's name for the dip with the Roost fries, and the menu does not say what is in it. Across the South, pink dipping sauces are usually mayonnaise-based with ketchup or tomato, often with hot sauce, garlic and pickle, the family of fry sauce and of New Orleans's own pinkish rémoulades.

Because it is not printed, the guide's instruction is to ask the kitchen what is in it.

Sell Fries with Pink Sauce at $8 as the easy add for a table with drinks and no food: salt sells the next glass. Learn the sauce's ingredients at lineup before a guest asks.

value.front: What is in the pink sauce with the Roost fries?
value.back: The menu does not say; learn it from the kitchen at lineup. Southern pink sauces are usually mayonnaise with tomato, hot sauce and pickle.

explain.value:
Fried pickles are a Southern bar classic: slices or spears of sour pickle dipped in a seasoned batter or cornmeal and fried until crisp, so the outside crunches and the inside bursts sour and juicy. A cool, creamy dip tames the heat and salt.

Ours use a medley of housemade pickles, so the vegetables and flavors vary, with a chive cream for dipping.

At $14 they are a fun share for a group at the bar; the guide suggests selling them with a crisp, acidic drink. Which pickles are in tonight's medley, and the coating, are questions for the kitchen.

value.front: What are the Roost’s Fried Pickles?
value.back: A medley of housemade pickles battered and fried, crisp outside and sour inside, with a cool chive cream; a $14 share best with a crisp drink.

explain.value:
A cheese board sets out a few contrasting cheeses, typically one soft, one firm and one blue or washed rind, with something sweet, something sharp and good bread. Cheeses taste best at room temperature, so they come out of the fridge before service.

The Roost's board offers three cheeses chosen by the kitchen, a seasonal chutney, Brennan's honey, fruit and nut bread.

At $24 it is the largest Bubbles snack and the natural partner for a bottle of rosé. Tonight's three cheeses are learned at lineup: know their names, milk and style before you sell it.

value.front: What must you learn about the Cheese Board at lineup?
value.back: Tonight’s three cheeses: names, milk and style. The $24 board also carries a seasonal chutney, Brennan’s honey and fruit and nut bread.

components.name: Brennan’s honey, chutney and fruit and nut bread

explain.value:
The cheese board's accompaniments each have a job. Honey brings floral sweetness that flatters salty and blue cheeses; the menu calls it Brennan's honey, and its source is a good lineup question. A chutney is fruit cooked slowly with vinegar, sugar and spice into a sweet and sour preserve, here seasonal. Fruit and nut bread is a dense loaf studded with dried fruit and nuts, made to be sliced thin under cheese.

Sweet, sharp and crunchy around three cheeses: that is the balance.

On the Roost's Cheese Board they turn a plate of cheese into a shared snack for a bottle of rosé.

value.front: What goes with the cheeses on the Roost’s Cheese Board?
value.back: Brennan’s honey for floral sweetness, a seasonal chutney for sweet and sour, and fruit and nut bread to slice under the cheese.

value.where: Served at 417 Royal Street; where the honey comes from is not confirmed, so ask the kitchen
value.history:
