value.sayIt: Willett is a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, since 1936; its barrel-strength rye makes Thompson's Dream bigger and spicier than the Classic.
askKitchen: What proof is the Willett 4-year rye we are pouring now?
Does the house tell a story behind the name Thompson's Dream?

explain.value:
Cognac is grape brandy from the Cognac region of western France, double distilled in copper pot stills and aged in oak. Its best cru is Grande Champagne, chalky country that gives long, fine spirits; the name has nothing to do with the sparkling wine region.

The Dudognon family has grown grapes at Lignières-Sonneville, in the heart of Grande Champagne, since 1776. It is a traditional estate that distils only its own grapes and sells its spirits by age, such as a 10-year Réserve and a 20-year Vieille Réserve.

The Origin Story prints Dudognon Cognac without naming the bottling, so which one the bar pours is a lineup question. It gives the drink grape, dried fruit and oak, rounder than rye.

value.front: Where does Dudognon Cognac come from?
value.back: A family estate at Lignières-Sonneville in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first cru, growing grapes there since 1776. Which bottling we pour is a lineup question.

value.history:
The Dudognon family has grown vines at Lignières-Sonneville, in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first cru, since 1776; one history says the present estate was bought in 1852. The vineyard, Le Davore, lies on a chalky hillside tucked away from the village. Paulin Dudognon brought the house its first formal recognition, a gold medal in 1898.

For generations the family supplied its eaux-de-vie to the large Cognac houses. Raymond Dudognon, born in 1927 into a line of distillers going back to Paulin, took over in 1946 and was the first to sell cognac under the family name; one account dates that change to 1970. Raymond died in 2002, having chosen one of his three daughters to succeed him. She runs the house with her husband and their son, and every source found still names the family as its owners.

It is a bouilleur de cru, a grower that distils only its own grapes. The family distils over a wood fire on two copper alembic stills, roughly 100 barrels a year, air-dries the oak for its casks for five years, and adds nothing to the cognac but water. The cognacs are sold by age: a 10-year bottling, a 15-year Napoléon, the 20-year Vieille Réserve and a 60-year cognac named for Paulin.

At Brennan's the Origin Story prints Dudognon Cognac without naming the bottling, so which one the bar pours is a lineup question.
facts: The family has grown vines at Lignières-Sonneville, in Grande Champagne, since 1776; one history says the present estate was bought in 1852.
Paulin Dudognon won a gold medal in 1898, the house's first formal recognition.
Raymond Dudognon, born in 1927, took over in 1946 and first sold cognac under the family name; he died in 2002.
A bouilleur de cru: it distils only its own grapes, over a wood fire on two copper alembic stills, roughly 100 barrels a year.
Water is the only thing added to the cognac.
Oak for its casks is air-dried for five years.
Sold by age: a 10-year, a 15-year Napoléon, the 20-year Vieille Réserve and a 60-year named for Paulin.
notes: Grande Champagne is Cognac's first cru, chalky country; it has nothing to do with the sparkling wine region.
The house is family run; name no living member. Say the family, or Raymond Dudognon's daughter and her family.
Which Dudognon goes into the Origin Story is not printed; never name an age until the bar confirms it.
Guests ask why cognac in a Sazerac. The New Orleans story is that the first Sazeracs were made on cognac and rye took over after phylloxera, so the Origin Story returns to the start.
Describe it as grower cognac: one family's own grapes, distilled and aged on the estate, nothing added but water.
value.sayIt: Dudognon is a family estate in Grande Champagne, growing its own grapes since 1776 and adding nothing to its cognac but water.
askKitchen: Which Dudognon bottling goes into the Origin Story: the 10-year, the Napoléon, the Vieille Réserve or another?

explain.value:
Chicory is a hardy plant whose root is dried, roasted and ground. Brewed with coffee it adds body, a dark color and a roasty, cocoa-like bitterness, and it carries no caffeine of its own.

The French used it to stretch coffee during Napoleon's blockade, and New Orleans, a French city and a great coffee port, kept the habit; the Civil War blockade is said to have fixed it.

Chicory runs through the Brennan's coffee list. The New Orleans-style coffee is blended with it, the Irish Coffee and the walnut and hazelnut coffee use the dark roast with chicory, the Café Glacé is chicory cold brew, and the Espresso Martini prints chicory. How it goes into the martini is a question for the bar.

value.front: What is chicory, and what does it add to coffee?
value.back: The roasted root of a hardy plant: body, dark color and a roasty, cocoa-like bitterness, with no caffeine of its own. New Orleans blends it into its coffee.

explain.value:
Congregation Coffee is a New Orleans roaster with its café at 240 Pelican Avenue in Algiers Point, across the river from the French Quarter. It was founded in 2015; in 2023 it ceased operations while seeking new owners, and reopened in November 2023 under Brennan family ownership, roasting on Tchoupitoulas Street.

The breakfast tasting pours Brennan's private blend from Congregation with chicory, and the coffee list carries a Congregation single origin.

Single origin means the beans come from one place, so the cup tastes of that place rather than a blend, and there is no chicory. Congregation rotates its origins with the seasons, so read today's from the coffee card on shift, never from memory.

value.front: Where is Congregation Coffee, and what is single origin?
value.back: A roaster with its café in Algiers Point. Single origin means beans from one place, no blend and no chicory; read today's origin from the card.

value.where: 240 Pelican Avenue, Algiers Point, New Orleans
value.history:
Congregation Coffee was started in 2015 by two partners who met while working at Cochon Butcher. The name is a local joke and a hope at once: a group of alligators is called a congregation, and the blends High Walk, Low Walk and Gallop are named for an alligator's gaits. Two years after the roastery began, the café opened in a Victorian storefront at 240 Pelican Avenue in Algiers Point, across the river from the French Quarter.

Brennan's was a customer long before it was an owner. By 2023 the restaurant had poured Congregation for seven years, and the buyer called them the best roasters in the city. When the company ceased operations that year while looking for new owners, it came under Brennan ownership, and in November 2023 the Algiers Point café and the wholesale roastery on Tchoupitoulas Street reopened, with a founder collaborating. A second café followed at Magazine Street and Jefferson Avenue.

So the coffee at Brennan's comes from a roaster in the family: the Traditional Breakfast tasting pours Brennan's Private Blend Congregation Coffee & Chicory beside the Bananas Foster, and the coffee list prints a Single Estate-grown Congregation Coffee, Roasted For Brennan's.
facts: Founded in 2015 by two partners who met at Cochon Butcher.
A group of alligators is a congregation; blends High Walk, Low Walk and Gallop are alligator gaits.
The flagship café is at 240 Pelican Avenue, Algiers Point.
It roasts at 1746 Tchoupitoulas Street; the second café is at Magazine Street and Jefferson Avenue.
Brennan's had served Congregation for seven years before it came under Brennan ownership in 2023.
Reopened in November 2023, with a founder collaborating.
The menus print a Brennan's Private Blend with chicory and a single estate coffee roasted for Brennan's.
notes: You can say the roaster is owned by the Brennan family and the blend is made for the house.
The chicory blend is the Traditional Breakfast pour; the single estate coffee's origin rotates, so read it from the coffee card. The chicory story itself lives on the chicory card.
Do not claim Congregation has always been a Brennan company; it was independent until 2023.
The alligator name story is true and guests enjoy it.
value.sayIt: The coffee is Congregation, roasted across the river in Algiers Point; this chicory blend is roasted privately for Brennan's.
askKitchen: Which single estate origin is on the coffee card this week?

components.name: Brown sugar and brown sugar syrup

explain.value:
Brown sugar is sugar that keeps some of its molasses, which gives it a soft, caramel and toffee flavor and a darker color than white sugar. Dissolved with water it becomes brown sugar syrup, the bar's easy way to sweeten a cold drink.

In hot coffee it melts straight in; in cold drinks a syrup is used, because grains do not dissolve in the cold.

Brennan's uses it three times. In the Irish Coffee it sweetens the chicory coffee and helps the cream float. In Rumors are Flying and its spirit-free twin, Personality, a brown sugar syrup rounds the tart cherry juice, which is why a couple can order the same idea with and without spirit.

value.front: Which of our drinks use brown sugar?
value.back: The Irish Coffee, stirred into the hot chicory coffee, and Rumors are Flying and Personality, as a syrup rounding the tart cherry juice.

explain.value:
Tullamore D.E.W. is an Irish whiskey established in 1829 at Tullamore in County Offaly. The letters are the initials of Daniel Edmund Williams, who rose to manage and then own the original distillery, and they also spell the word dew.

It is a blend of the three Irish whiskey styles, pot still, malt and grain, and triple distilled, which makes it smooth, light and gently spicy, well suited to hot coffee.

In Brennan's Irish Coffee it is the named whiskey, with chicory coffee, brown sugar and whipped cream. When a guest asks what the letters mean, the answer is a small, true story to tell while the coffee is poured.

value.front: What do the letters in Tullamore D.E.W. stand for?
value.back: Daniel Edmund Williams, the manager who came to own the distillery. It is a smooth triple-distilled Irish blend, established in 1829, in our Irish Coffee.

value.history:
Tullamore D.E.W. traces its start to 1829, when Michael Molloy founded a distillery at Tullamore in County Offaly, a site most likely chosen for the Grand Canal beside it. After Molloy's death in 1857 it passed in time to his nephew, Bernard Daly.

The letters belong to Daniel E. Williams, who lived from 1848 to 1921; most sources give his middle name as Edmund. By the brand's account he started at the distillery as a stable boy at 15, and he rose to run it as general manager and later came to own it. By one account he added his initials to the whiskey's name in 1887, and they spell dew as well.

The old distillery closed in the 1950s and the brand name was sold in 1965; for decades the whiskey was made at Midleton. In 2010 the Scottish firm William Grant & Sons bought Tullamore D.E.W., and on 17 September 2014 it opened a new distillery at Clonminch, just outside the town, the first new Irish distillery on a greenfield site in over a century.

The whiskey is triple distilled and blended from the three Irish styles: pot still, malt and grain. The result is light and smooth, which suits hot coffee and cream.
facts: Founded in 1829 at Tullamore, County Offaly, by Michael Molloy, beside the Grand Canal.
D.E.W. are the initials of Daniel E. Williams, 1848 to 1921, general manager and later owner; by the brand's account he started as a stable boy.
By one account Williams added his initials to the brand name in 1887.
The original distillery closed in the 1950s and the brand name was sold in 1965.
William Grant & Sons bought the brand in 2010 and opened a new distillery at Clonminch on 17 September 2014.
Triple distilled and blended from pot still, malt and grain whiskey.
The Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco, where Irish coffee was recreated in 1952, has poured Tullamore D.E.W. since 2006.
notes: The menu prints Tullamore Dew; the bottle writes D.E.W. When a guest asks, the letters are the initials of Daniel E. Williams, who by the brand's account rose from stable boy to owner.
Sources spell his middle name Edmund, Edmond or Edward; Daniel E. Williams is the careful form to say aloud.
Do not say it has been made in Tullamore without a break since 1829: the old distillery closed in the 1950s and the new one opened in 2014.
It is owned by William Grant & Sons, the Scottish firm; name nobody from the company.
A good link to tell: the Buena Vista in San Francisco, which made Irish coffee famous in America, has poured Tullamore since 2006.
value.sayIt: Tullamore D.E.W. is a triple distilled Irish whiskey from County Offaly; the letters are the initials of Daniel E. Williams.
askKitchen: Which Tullamore D.E.W. bottling goes into Brennan's Irish Coffee?

explain.value:
Whipped cream is cream beaten until it traps air and thickens. For coffee drinks it is usually whipped only lightly, to a soft, pourable ribbon that floats on hot coffee; a stiff, piped cap is a different texture.

Cool cream on hot coffee is the pleasure of these drinks: the guest sips the hot, sweet coffee through the cold cap. Stirring it in loses that.

At Brennan's whipped cream tops the Irish Coffee and the coffee with Frangelico and Nocello. The guide's Irish Coffee lines say a cap of whipped cream; whether the bar floats it soft or tops it firm is a question to settle at lineup. Questions about cream go to the service note.

value.front: How should whipped cream sit on our coffee cocktails?
value.back: On top, never stirred in: the guest sips hot coffee through cool cream. Whether it is floated soft or set firm is confirmed at lineup.

explain.value:
Chopin is a Polish single-ingredient vodka. Its best-known bottling is made only from potatoes grown in the Polish region of Podlasie and distilled four times at Siedlce; the brand also makes rye and wheat versions from a single grain each.

Potato vodka is fuller and rounder in texture than most grain vodkas, with a soft, creamy feel and a faint earthiness.

In the Flamingo it pairs with Monkey 47 gin under dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger Champagne. The house page prints Chopin Vodka without saying which bottling, so potato is the likely and usual one but not stated; confirm with the bar before saying potato.

value.front: What kind of vodka is Chopin?
value.back: A Polish single-ingredient vodka, best known in its potato bottling from Podlasie, round and creamy. Confirm the bottling before saying potato.

value.where: Krzesk, near Siedlce, east of Warsaw, Poland
value.history:
Chopin is a Polish vodka named for the composer Frédéric Chopin, a favored son of Poland. It is made by Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos of Siedlce, east of Warsaw, at a distillery near the hamlet of Krzesk that has made vodka since 1896. The brand says its still of that year is one of the oldest remaining stills in Poland.

The brand dates from the early 1990s: sources give 1992 or 1993. When its founder bought the distillery itself is less clear: one account says 1993, another 2003. Chopin reached North America in 1997. The company calls itself family owned and run, now in its second generation, and Poland’s last family owned vodka brand.

Chopin is a single-ingredient vodka. Each bottling is made from one raw material, potato, rye or wheat, and distilled four times. The brand grows some of its ingredients on its own farmland and buys the rest from family farms near the distillery, and its water comes from an artesian spring beneath the grounds. The potato vodka, the best known bottling, uses Stobrawa potatoes, which retailers say are grown in Podlasie.

Potato vodka is fuller and creamier in texture than most grain vodkas, with a faint earthiness. Which Chopin goes into the Flamingo is a question for the bar.
facts: Named for the composer Frédéric Chopin, a favored son of Poland.
Made by Podlaska Wytwórnia Wódek Polmos of Siedlce, at a distillery near Krzesk that has made vodka since 1896.
A single-ingredient vodka: each bottling is made from potato, rye or wheat alone and distilled four times.
The brand dates from 1992 or 1993 by different sources; the distillery purchase is dated 1993 or 2003. Chopin reached North America in 1997.
The brand says its ingredients grow on its own land or on nearby family farms, and its water comes from an artesian spring beneath the grounds.
The potato vodka uses Stobrawa potatoes, grown in Podlasie by retailers’ accounts.
Family owned and run, in its second generation; the company calls itself Poland’s last family owned vodka brand.
The brand calls its 1896 still one of the oldest remaining stills in Poland.
notes: The menu prints Chopin Vodka without a bottling. Chopin makes potato, rye and wheat vodkas, so confirm with the bar before you say potato.
Guests ask whether potato vodka tastes of potato. The honest answer: hardly; it is fuller and creamier in texture than most grain vodkas, with a faint earthiness.
Say SHOH-pan, like the composer. If asked who owns it: the founding family, now in its second generation. Name nobody.
Do not quote how many potatoes go into a bottle (seven pounds or five kilos by different sources) or how far away the farms are (20 or 15 miles).
If a guest asks about gluten with a potato vodka, promise nothing from the label: take the question to the bar and the kitchen at lineup.
value.sayIt: Chopin is a Polish single-ingredient vodka, distilled four times at a family-owned distillery that has made vodka since 1896.
askKitchen: Which Chopin goes into the Flamingo: the potato vodka, or the rye or wheat?

explain.value:
Monkey 47 is a dry gin from Germany's Black Forest, the Schwarzwald. Its name gives away its numbers: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. Beside juniper and citrus it uses local plants such as lingonberries, spruce shoots and cranberries, and it rests in earthenware before bottling.

The result is a big, aromatic gin, fruity, green and floral, that stands up in a drink with Champagne.

In the Flamingo it joins Chopin vodka, dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger La Française. The vodka gives body and the gin gives the botanical lift a guest notices first. It is a fine name to drop for a gin lover deciding whether to visit the Roost.

value.front: What do the 47s in Monkey 47 mean?
value.back: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol: a Black Forest gin with lingonberries and spruce. It gives the Flamingo its botanical lift.

value.where: Near Loßburg, in the Black Forest, Germany
value.history:
Monkey 47 tells its own story through a British officer. By the brand’s account, Montgomery Collins, known as Monty, a Royal Air Force officer posted to Berlin after the Second World War, sponsored a monkey named Max at the Berlin Zoo. He left the air force in 1951, settled in the northern Black Forest and opened a guesthouse, Zum Wilden Affen, the Wild Monkey, where his Schwarzwald Dry Gin was the house drink until the 1970s. No archive or independent account of him has been found, so it is told as the brand’s story.

The modern gin began in 2008, when the founder, from a German brandy family, left a job at Nokia to recreate the recipe in the Black Forest. After more than 120 trial distillations the gin came to market, usually dated 2010. In January 2016 Pernod Ricard Deutschland agreed to buy a majority stake, and in March 2020 Pernod Ricard bought the rest, with the founder staying on as an adviser. The distillery near Loßburg, built in 2015, centers on a custom still from a German coppersmith.

The name holds the numbers: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. About a third of the botanicals are Black Forest plants, among them spruce, lingonberries, elderflower, blackthorn and bramble leaves, and the citrus peels go in fresh. They macerate in molasses-based neutral spirit and spring water before distillation in small stills; the gin then rests in large earthenware vessels for about three months, is cut slowly with water and is bottled without chill filtration.
facts: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol give the gin its name; about a third of the botanicals come from the Black Forest.
Black Forest botanicals include spruce, lingonberries, elderflower, blackthorn and bramble leaves; the citrus peels are used fresh.
Botanicals macerate in molasses-based neutral spirit and spring water, about 36 hours by one account, before distillation in small stills.
The gin rests in large earthenware vessels, 90 or 100 days by different accounts, before slow dilution; it is not chill filtered.
By the brand’s account, the RAF officer Montgomery Collins opened the Zum Wilden Affen guesthouse in the Black Forest after leaving the air force in 1951.
The founder began recreating the recipe in 2008, over more than 120 trial distillations; the launch is usually dated 2010.
Pernod Ricard Deutschland agreed a majority stake in January 2016, and Pernod Ricard bought the rest in March 2020; neither price was disclosed.
The distillery near Loßburg was built in 2015 around a custom still made by a German coppersmith.
notes: Tell the Montgomery Collins story as the brand’s story: no archive or independent account confirming the officer, the guesthouse or the recipe was found.
Guests ask about the 47: 47 botanicals and 47 percent alcohol. It is a strong, aromatic gin, which is why it still reads under the Champagne in the Flamingo.
The menu prints Monkey 47 Schwarzwald Gin; the bottle says Schwarzwald Dry Gin. Schwarzwald is German for the Black Forest.
If asked who owns it: Pernod Ricard, the sole owner since 2020 after buying a majority in 2016. Name nobody; the founder is said as the founder.
Do not call it a British gin: it is German, made in the Black Forest.
value.sayIt: Monkey 47 is a Black Forest gin: 47 botanicals at 47 percent, a third of them from the forest, rested in earthenware before bottling.

explain.value:
Dragonfruit, or pitaya, is the fruit of a climbing cactus, with a bright pink or yellow skin covered in green-tipped scales. Inside, the flesh is white or deep magenta, speckled with tiny edible black seeds.

Its flavor is gentle, somewhere between kiwi and pear, mildly sweet, and the red-fleshed kind gives a vivid pink color, which makes it a favorite in bright, festive drinks.

In the Flamingo it brings fruit and almost certainly the drink's color, though how the bar uses it, fresh, as a purée or a syrup, and the color of the flesh are not printed. Describe it as a soft tropical fruit and let the bar confirm the rest.

value.front: What does dragonfruit taste like?
value.back: Gently sweet, between kiwi and pear, from a cactus fruit; red-fleshed kinds give vivid pink color. How the Flamingo uses it is confirmed with the bar.

explain.value:
Champagne is sparkling wine from the Champagne region of north-east France, made from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier by the traditional method, with its second fermentation in the bottle and long aging on the lees. Only wine from that region may carry the name.

Bottle aging gives it fine, persistent bubbles and flavors of citrus, apple, brioche and toast, which is why it lifts a cocktail rather than just fizzing.

Two Brennan's drinks print Champagne by name. Brennan's Champagne Cocktail prints Champagne without a house, and the Flamingo prints Taittinger La Française. Other drinks print sparkling wine, and a server keeps the distinction exactly as the menu does.

value.front: When may a sparkling wine be called Champagne?
value.back: Only when it comes from Champagne in north-east France, made by the traditional method. Our menus print Champagne for two drinks; the rest say sparkling wine.

explain.value:
Taittinger is a Champagne house in Reims whose story begins in 1734; the Taittinger family bought it in 1932, sold it with its group in 2005, led a bid that bought it back in 2006, and runs it today. Its Brut La Française is the non-vintage house style, unusual for its high share of Chardonnay, about 40 percent, with Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, aged close to four years on the lees in the chalk cellars under Reims.

That Chardonnay makes it fresh, light and elegant, with citrus and brioche.

In the Flamingo it tops Chopin vodka, Monkey 47 gin, dragonfruit and lemon. Brennan's also lists Taittinger La Française as a 3 liter double magnum on the Birthday Bubbles list, so the name links the Roost cocktail to the cellar.

value.front: What is distinctive about Taittinger La Française?
value.back: A high share of Chardonnay, about 40 percent, for a fresh, elegant non-vintage Champagne from a Reims house founded in 1734. It tops the Flamingo.

value.founded: 1734, as a Champagne trading house; the Taittinger family bought it in 1932
value.history:
Taittinger traces its start to 1734, when Jacques Fourneaux began trading Champagne wines and worked with the Benedictine abbeys that owned some of the best vineyards. In the 1820s the firm became Forest-Fourneaux, and in 1932 Pierre Taittinger bought it and gave it his name; one source gives 1931.

In the years from 1945 to 1960 the house set up its cellars in the Gallo-Roman chalk pits beneath the site of the Saint-Nicaise abbey in Reims, where the wines still age. In 2005 the family sold its group to the American fund Starwood Capital Group; in 2006 a family-led bid, backed by the bank Crédit Agricole, bought the Champagne house back. A member of the family has been president since 1 January 2020.

Brut La Française is the house’s non-vintage Brut. Its mark is a high share of Chardonnay for a non-vintage blend, about 40 percent, with Pinot Noir and Meunier, which gives the light, fresh, elegant style the house is known for. One reviewer says it spends a year longer on its lees than the Brut Réserve, which ages at least three years.

At Brennan’s it tops the Flamingo in the Roost, and the same wine sits on the Birthday Bubbles list as a 3 liter double magnum.
facts: Traces its start to 1734, when Jacques Fourneaux began trading Champagne wines, working with Benedictine abbeys that owned top vineyards.
Pierre Taittinger bought the house, then called Forest-Fourneaux, in 1932 (one source says 1931), and it took the family name.
Its wines age in Gallo-Roman chalk pits beneath the site of the Saint-Nicaise abbey in Reims, where the house set up its cellars between 1945 and 1960.
Sold with the family’s group to Starwood Capital Group in 2005; in 2006 a family-led bid backed by the bank Crédit Agricole bought the Champagne house back.
Farms about 288 hectares of vines, across 37 crus by most accounts; one source gives 34.
Brut La Française is the non-vintage Brut: about 40 percent Chardonnay with Pinot Noir and Meunier, a high Chardonnay share for non-vintage Champagne.
One reviewer says La Française spends an extra year on its lees beyond the Brut Réserve, which ages at least three years.
Brennan’s lists La Française as a 3 liter double magnum on Birthday Bubbles, and Taittinger Prestige Rosé among the Bubbles rosé bottles.
notes: Say teh-tan-ZHAY. It is true Champagne, from Reims, so the word Champagne is right here: the Flamingo is the Roost drink that prints a Champagne house by name.
Guests ask whether Taittinger is still a family house. The honest answer: yes, the family runs it, after a short spell under an American fund in 2005 and 2006. Name nobody.
Do not quote the La Française blend as fixed: sources split the rest of it differently. Say about 40 percent Chardonnay, which is what makes it fresh and elegant.
Do not explain the name La Française: no source gives its meaning.
A guest who loves the Flamingo’s wine will find the same Taittinger La Française on the Birthday Bubbles list as a 3 liter double magnum; the sommelier handles the cellar side.
value.sayIt: The Flamingo is topped with Taittinger La Française, a Chardonnay-led Champagne from a Reims house whose story begins in 1734.
askKitchen: Is the Flamingo always topped with Taittinger La Française, and what does the bar pour if it runs out?
How long does an opened bottle of La Française stay in service at the Roost Bar?

explain.value:
Bourbon is American whiskey made from a mash of at least 51 percent corn and aged in new charred oak barrels. The corn and the new oak give it sweetness, vanilla, caramel and a soft roundness, rounder than rye.

Most bourbon comes from Kentucky, though it may be made anywhere in the United States.

Two Brennan's drinks use it. The Birdcage is built on Rabbit Hole Dareringer, a wheated Louisville bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks. The Apple Crumble prints bourbon without a brand, so which one is a question for the bar. Its caramel and vanilla are the bridge to the butterscotch, maple and apple in that drink.

value.front: What makes a whiskey bourbon?
value.back: At least 51 percent corn, aged in new charred oak, in the United States: sweet, with vanilla and caramel. The Birdcage names Rabbit Hole; the Apple Crumble does not.

explain.value:
Rabbit Hole is a distillery in Louisville, Kentucky. Dareringer is its straight bourbon of corn, malted wheat and malted barley, aged in new charred oak and then finished in casks that held Pedro Ximénez sherry; it is bottled at 93 proof.

The sherry finish adds dried fruit, raisin and dark berry notes and a little extra richness to the bourbon's vanilla and oak.

In the Birdcage that richness carries the smoke, the Angostura, the orange and the cherry of an Old Fashioned. A useful line for the Old Fashioned drinker: a bourbon with a sweet sherry finish, wrapped in smoke, poured only in the Roost.

value.front: What finish gives Dareringer its dried fruit notes?
value.back: Casks that held Pedro Ximénez sherry, after aging in new oak. That rich, raisiny bourbon is the base of the smoked Birdcage.

value.history:
Rabbit Hole was founded in Louisville in 2012 by a former clinical psychologist who left the profession to distil whiskey. The name, by one account, comes from his wife's warning that the venture would take the family down a rabbit hole from which they could never return. She is a Louisville native and a bourbon lover who had drawn him from Scotch to bourbon, and Dareringer, the sherry-finished bourbon, is named in her honor.

In its first years the brand's whiskey was made at other distilleries while its own was designed and built. The distillery opened in May 2018 in downtown Louisville. In June 2019 Pernod Ricard USA agreed to buy a majority share, at a price never disclosed; at the time the founder kept most of his shares and stayed on to run the company.

Dareringer is a wheated Kentucky straight bourbon. It ages first in new charred American oak, then is finished in casks that held Pedro Ximénez, a dark and very sweet sherry, and it is bottled at 93 proof. The finish lays raisin and dried fruit richness over the bourbon's vanilla and oak, a richness that carries the smoke, the Angostura, the orange and the cherry of the Birdcage.
facts: Founded in Louisville in 2012 by a former clinical psychologist.
Its downtown Louisville distillery opened in May 2018.
Pernod Ricard USA agreed to buy a majority share in June 2019; the founder stayed on to run the company at the time.
Dareringer is a wheated straight bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks and bottled at 93 proof.
Dareringer is named for the founder's wife, a Louisville native who drew him from Scotch to bourbon.
By one account the brand name recalls her warning that distilling would lead the family down a rabbit hole.
notes: The menu pours the Birdcage only in the Roost. From the dining room, invite a whiskey lover there for it; whether one may be sent to a table is a question for the manager.
Say sherry-finished, never sherry-aged: the bourbon ages in new oak first, then rests in the sherry casks.
Name nobody from the founding family; say the founder, a former psychologist, and his wife.
If a guest asks, Pernod Ricard has held a majority of Rabbit Hole since 2019. Do not say who runs it today.
The house page does not say how the Birdcage is smoked: describe the aroma, and let the bar explain the method.
value.sayIt: Dareringer is a Louisville bourbon finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks, rich with dried fruit under the Birdcage's smoke.
askKitchen: How is the Birdcage smoked, and with what wood?
May a Birdcage be sent from the Roost to a dining room table?

explain.value:
Angostura is the world's best-known aromatic bitters, named for the town where it began as a tonic in the nineteenth century. It is a concentrated spirit of gentian and spices, dark red-brown, used a few dashes at a time.

It tastes of clove, cinnamon and bitter root, and it seasons a drink, pulling sweet and strong together.

At Brennan's it is in the Birdcage, the smoked Old Fashioned, and in the Champagne Cocktail, soaked into a demerara sugar cube. It is not in the Classic Sazerac, which uses Peychaud's; mixing the two up at the table is a common slip.

value.front: Which of our drinks use Angostura, and which do not?
value.back: The Birdcage and the Champagne Cocktail use Angostura, a dark, spicy aromatic bitters. The Classic Sazerac uses the red Peychaud's instead; never mix them up.

value.where: Trinidad; begun in Angostura, Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar
value.history:
Angostura bitters began with Dr Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, a German surgeon born in 1796 who served in Simón Bolívar's army and settled around 1820 in the town of Angostura, Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar. The company says he had perfected his Amargo Aromatico by 1824, as a medicine for soldiers; Wikipedia, citing an 1876 court case, says he began selling it that year and set up a distillery in 1830. The bitters took the town's name.

Dr Siegert died in 1870, according to Difford's Guide, and in 1875 the family business, J.G.B. Siegert & Hijos, moved to Port of Spain, Trinidad, amid unrest in Venezuela. It has stayed on the island, adding rum from 1947 through Trinidad Distillers Limited. In 1982 it was listed on the Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange as Angostura Holdings. Reports in 2025 named its largest shareholder as Rumpro, part of the CL Financial group, which has been in liquidation since 2017, with the government's National Investment Fund Holding Company second. The bitters marked their bicentennial in 2024.

The recipe is a trade secret, and the label names only gentian among the botanicals. The oversized label has a legend of its own, most often told as a mix-up between the founder's sons over the bottle and the label that was never corrected. The label still shows a medal from the 1873 Vienna World's Fair.

At Brennan's it seasons the Birdcage, a smoked Old Fashioned, and the menu prints it with a demerara sugar cube in the Champagne Cocktail.
facts: Created by Dr Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, born in 1796, a German surgeon in Simón Bolívar's army, at Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar.
The company dates his formula, Amargo Aromatico, to 1824, made as a medicine for soldiers.
In 1875 the business, J.G.B. Siegert & Hijos, moved to Port of Spain, Trinidad.
The label names one botanical, gentian; the full recipe is a trade secret.
Stories differ on why the label is oversized; the usual one is a mix-up between the founder's sons over bottle and label, never corrected.
The label shows a medal from the 1873 Vienna World's Fair.
Rum came later, from 1947, through Trinidad Distillers Limited.
Listed in 1982 as Angostura Holdings; reports in 2025 named Rumpro, of the CL Financial group, the largest shareholder and the government's National Investment Fund second.
The bitters marked their bicentennial in 2024.
notes: Never confuse it with Peychaud's: Angostura, dark and clove-spiced, is in the Birdcage and the Champagne Cocktail; Peychaud's, red and anise-led, is the Sazerac's.
Guests ask whether it holds angostura bark. The honest answer: the bitters are named for the town, not the bark; published histories say the bark is not in them, and the recipe is secret.
The Champagne Cocktail prints Angostura with a demerara sugar cube; in the classic build the bitters soak the cube, which keeps bubbles rising. Confirm the house build at lineup.
The bitters are named for a town in Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolívar, and are made in Trinidad today.
The Birdcage's measure and how it is smoked are the bar's to confirm; say Angostura seasons it, nothing more.
value.sayIt: Angostura is the classic aromatic bitters, made in Trinidad to a secret recipe begun in Venezuela in 1824.
askKitchen: Is the Champagne Cocktail's sugar cube soaked with Angostura before the Champagne goes in, and with how many dashes?

explain.value:
Orange and cherry are the classic finishing touches of an Old Fashioned. An orange peel is twisted over the drink to spray its oils, then often dropped in; a cocktail cherry, usually a dark, sweet preserved one, sits in the glass.

The peel's oil is aroma first, bright and bitter-sweet; the cherry adds a little sweetness at the end.

The Birdcage prints orange and cherry with Rabbit Hole Dareringer and Angostura. Whether they are a garnish, a peel, a muddled fruit or a cherry liqueur is not printed, so a server says orange and cherry, as the house page does, and lets the bar describe the build and garnish.

value.front: What do orange and cherry add to an Old Fashioned?
value.back: Orange peel adds bright aroma from its oils; the cherry adds a sweet finish. How the Birdcage uses them is not printed, so ask the bar.

explain.value:
Gin is a spirit flavored above all with juniper, the small blue-black cone of a conifer, together with other botanicals such as coriander, citrus peel and angelica. Dry gin is the classic modern style: piney, citrus-bright and unsweetened.

Every gin has its own recipe, which is why the brand matters more with gin than with vodka.

Four Brennan's drinks use gin. The Flamingo names Monkey 47, from the Black Forest, the Spoonbill names Hendrick's, with cucumber and rose, and the OBX names Gentilly Gin, made in New Orleans. The Prisoner of Love prints only gin, so which one is a question for the bar.

value.front: Which botanical must every gin taste of?
value.back: Juniper. Each gin adds its own botanicals: Monkey 47 in the Flamingo, Hendrick's in the Spoonbill, Gentilly in the OBX; the Prisoner of Love's gin is unnamed.

explain.value:
Hendrick's is a Scottish gin launched in 1999 by William Grant and Sons at Girvan. It is made in two stills of different design whose spirits are blended, and essences of Bulgarian rose and cucumber are added after distillation.

That cucumber and rose made it stand apart when it launched, and they give it a cool, fresh, floral character, softer than a classic juniper-led gin.

In the Spoonbill it meets Cap Corse Mattei Blanc quinquina and chive oil, with a spoon of caviar alongside. The cucumber links naturally to the green chive, and the rose to the aperitif wine, which is a neat way to explain why the drink tastes so cool and savory.

value.front: What two flavors set Hendrick's gin apart?
value.back: Cucumber and rose, added after distillation: a cool, floral Scottish gin from 1999. In the Spoonbill they meet chive oil and caviar.

value.history:
Hendrick’s is a Scottish gin made by William Grant & Sons, the family-owned company William Grant founded in 1887, the year his Glenfiddich distillery began production, and still run by his descendants. The gin is made at Girvan, where the company built its grain distillery in 1963 under a great-grandson of William Grant.

That same great-grandson bought two old stills at auction in 1966: a Bennett still of 1860 and a Carter-Head still built in 1948 by John Dore & Co. By the company’s account, in 1988 he set a company distiller the task of making one spirit from both. After years of trials Hendrick’s launched in 1999: the gins of the two stills are blended, then essences of rose and cucumber are added. Because the rose and cucumber go in after distillation, it cannot be labeled a London Dry gin.

Eleven botanicals stand behind the rose and cucumber, among them juniper, orris root, chamomile, cubeb, elderflower, yarrow, caraway and lemon and orange peel. The rose is described as Bulgarian; the cucumbers come from Holland or Belgium. The name, by most accounts, was chosen by a member of the Grant family after Hendrick, a gardener who took particular care of the family’s roses.

On 1 October 2018 the company opened the Hendrick’s Gin Palace in the grounds at Girvan, with new still houses that doubled capacity and glasshouses of exotic botanicals.
facts: Made by William Grant & Sons, the family-owned company William Grant founded in 1887 and his descendants still run.
Distilled at Girvan, Scotland, where the company built its grain distillery in 1963.
Two stills bought at auction in 1966: a Bennett still of 1860 and a Carter-Head still of 1948.
Launched in 1999: the two stills’ spirits are blended, then essences of rose and cucumber are added.
Because rose and cucumber go in after distillation, Hendrick’s cannot be labeled a London Dry gin.
Eleven botanicals besides rose and cucumber, including juniper, orris root, chamomile, cubeb, elderflower, yarrow and caraway.
The rose is described as Bulgarian; the cucumbers come from Holland or Belgium, by one account.
The Hendrick’s Gin Palace opened at Girvan on 1 October 2018, doubling capacity, with glasshouses of botanicals.
Named, by most accounts, after Hendrick, a gardener who tended a Grant family rose garden.
notes: Say Hendrick’s is Scottish, made at Girvan by William Grant & Sons, the family company behind Glenfiddich.
Guests ask why it is not a London Dry: the rose and cucumber are added after distillation, which a London Dry may not do.
Name nobody from the company: say a great-grandson of William Grant, or the master distiller.
The still dates vary by source; if asked, quote the company’s own: the Bennett of 1860 and the Carter-Head of 1948.
In the Spoonbill the cucumber meets the chive oil and the rose meets the Cap Corse quinquina: say cool, green and floral.
value.sayIt: Hendrick’s is a Scottish gin from Girvan, made in two old stills and finished with rose and cucumber; it launched in 1999.

explain.value:
A quinquina is a wine aperitif flavored with cinchona bark, the source of quinine, which gives it a gentle bitterness. Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his house in Bastia in 1872 and made his first quinquina wine in 1875; the aperitif is named for Cap Corse, the northern peninsula of Corsica. The Blanc is Vermentino and Muscat grape must, held from fermenting with spirit, flavored with cinchona, spices and cédrat, a thick-peeled citron.

Cap Corse Mattei Blanc is light, citrusy and softly bitter.

The house page prints it as Cap Corse Mattei Blanc Quinquina vermouth; strictly it is a quinquina, a cousin of vermouth. In the Spoonbill it plays the vermouth's part in a martini-style drink with Hendrick's gin and chive oil, with a spoon of caviar served alongside.

value.front: What is a quinquina?
value.back: A wine aperitif flavored with cinchona bark, the source of quinine, gently bitter. Cap Corse Mattei, from Corsica since 1872, plays the vermouth's part in the Spoonbill.

value.who: L.N. Mattei, makers of Cap Corse Mattei
value.history:
Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his first shop in Bastia, on Corsica, in 1872, selling cigars, coffee, wine and liqueurs. In 1874 he began distilling cédrat, the thick-skinned citron of Cap Corse, the island's northern peninsula, and in 1875 he made a medicinal wine with quinquina, the cinchona bark that gives quinine. Accounts differ on how he came to the bark: his importer says he found it on a voyage to the Caribbean; another source says he meant it against malaria.

The Blanc is a mistelle: Muscat and Vermentinu grape must kept from fermenting with neutral alcohol, so its sweetness is the grape's own. It is flavored with cinchona, cédrat and other plants, fruits and spices, and bottled at 17 percent. The bark brings spice and gentle bitterness to the middle and finish; the cédrat brings citrus perfume and a silky texture.

Its American importer has long called the house family owned, with macerations, aging and bottling done in house, by one report in the Borgo industrial zone. Monocle reports, though, that a Corsican drinks group, Groupe Boisson Corse, has since bought the house, revived the founder's recipe and taken output from about 80,000 bottles to about 400,000. On Cap Corse stands the Moulin Mattei, a windmill a later head of the house turned into an advertisement for the aperitif; the Conservatoire du Littoral bought it in 2004 and restored its 1930s look.

At Brennan's it plays the vermouth's part in the Spoonbill, with Hendrick's gin and chive oil.
facts: Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his first shop in Bastia in 1872, selling cigars, coffee, wine and liqueurs.
In 1875 he made a medicinal wine with quinquina, cinchona bark, the source of quinine.
Cap Corse is Corsica's northern peninsula; cédrat, the Corsican citron, is a signature ingredient.
The Blanc is a mistelle of Muscat and Vermentinu grape must with neutral alcohol, with no added sugar.
Flavored with cinchona, cédrat and other plants, fruits and spices; bottled at 17 percent.
Monocle reports that Groupe Boisson Corse, a Corsican drinks group, bought the house and relaunched it, reviving the founder's recipe.
The Moulin Mattei windmill on Cap Corse, once the brand's advertisement, was bought by the Conservatoire du Littoral in 2004.
Imported to the United States by Haus Alpenz; there is a Rouge as well as the Blanc.
notes: Say quinquina, kan-kee-NAH: a wine aperitif with cinchona bark. Our page calls it vermouth; strictly it is vermouth's cousin.
Guests ask if it has quinine. The honest answer: it is flavored with cinchona bark, the source of quinine, for a gentle bitterness; the amount is not published.
Do not call it a Corsican wine: it is grape must held from fermenting with spirit, a mistelle.
Do not call it family owned: the importer's pages say so, but Monocle reports a sale to a Corsican drinks group.
The founder, Louis-Napoléon Mattei, may be named; name no one at the house today.
The page prints the Blanc; Mattei also makes a Rouge, so check the bottle before describing it.
value.sayIt: Cap Corse Mattei is a Corsican quinquina: Muscat and Vermentinu with cinchona bark and Corsican citron, gently bitter, from a Bastia house founded in 1872.
askKitchen: Is the Spoonbill stirred like a martini, and in what proportion of gin to Cap Corse?

explain.value:
Chive oil is a bright green oil made by blending fresh chives with a neutral oil, then straining it clear. Kitchens use it to finish soups and plates with color and a fresh, gently oniony note.

In a cocktail a few drops float on the surface or bead in the drink, so the guest gets a savory, green aroma before the first sip.

In the Spoonbill it is the savory link between the cool cucumber of Hendrick's gin and the salty spoon of caviar served beside the drink. How the bar makes it and how it is added are not printed; describe the flavor and let the bar describe the method.

value.front: What does chive oil add to the Spoonbill?
value.back: A bright green, gently oniony aroma that links the cucumber of Hendrick's to the salt of the caviar. How it is made and added is confirmed with the bar.

explain.value:
Caviar is the salted roe of sturgeon. The eggs are separated from the membrane, lightly salted and packed; their size, color and flavor depend on the species, and most caviar served today is from farmed sturgeon.

Good caviar tastes clean and briny, buttery and nutty, and the eggs pop softly on the tongue. It is served cold, traditionally on a non-metal spoon of mother of pearl or horn.

The Spoonbill comes with a spoon of caviar alongside, which makes the drink a moment. Which caviar, how much and how it is presented are confirmed with the bar; any question about fish or roe goes to the service note and lineup.

value.front: What is caviar, and how does it come with the Spoonbill?
value.back: Salted sturgeon roe, briny and buttery, served cold. The Spoonbill comes with a spoon of it alongside; which caviar is confirmed with the bar.

explain.value:
Demerara is a light brown, large-grained cane sugar with a gentle toffee note, named for the Demerara region of South America, where it was first made. Pressed into a cube it dissolves slowly.

In a Champagne Cocktail the cube is soaked in bitters, set in the glass and topped with Champagne. As it dissolves it sweetens the wine a little at a time, and its rough surface keeps sending a stream of bubbles up the glass.

Brennan's Champagne Cocktail prints a demerara sugar cube with Angostura and Champagne, the classic build. It gives a faint caramel sweetness that grows as the guest drinks, which is worth telling: the last sip is the sweetest.

value.front: Why does the Champagne Cocktail keep bubbling?
value.back: The bitters-soaked demerara cube dissolves slowly, and its rough surface keeps sending bubbles up the glass. It also sweetens the wine gradually.

explain.value:
Lillet is a French wine aperitif from Podensac, south of Bordeaux, founded in 1872 by the brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet. It is about 85 percent Bordeaux wine, Semillon for the Blanc, and 15 percent citrus liqueurs made from orange peels.

The old Kina Lillet carried more quinine; in 1986 Lillet Blanc replaced it, lighter, fruitier and less bitter. It tastes of orange, honey and blossom, served cold.

Two Brennan's drinks use it. In the Riviera it is topped with sparkling wine and lemon, light and floral; the menu spells it Lilet, but the bottle is Lillet. In To Each His Own it softens Daron Calvados and quince liqueur.

value.front: What is Lillet Blanc made from?
value.back: Bordeaux wine, mostly Semillon, with about 15 percent citrus liqueurs: a light French aperitif from Podensac. It is in the Riviera and To Each His Own.

value.history:
Lillet was founded in 1872 in Podensac, south of Bordeaux, by the brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet, wine and spirits merchants who took up distilling. Their early trade was mainly in fruit liqueurs. Their first wine aperitif came in 1887: Kina Lillet, its name joining the family's to quinquina, the cinchona bark that gives quinine.

The recipe is still about 85 percent wine and 15 percent fruit liqueurs and cinchona. For the Blanc the wine is Semillon, with some Sauvignon Blanc, and the liqueurs are made by steeping the peels of sweet oranges, from Morocco or Spain, and bitter oranges, from Haiti or Peru, in alcohol for several weeks. The blend is matured in oak casks in the Podensac cellars and bottled at 17 percent.

In 1986 Lillet Blanc replaced Kina Lillet: sweeter and less bitter. That is why a Vesper made today does not taste as it did when it was written. The family sold the business in 1985, and in 2008 it passed to a subsidiary of Pernod Ricard, which owns it today.

At Brennan's it appears twice: topped with sparkling wine and lemon in the Riviera, and beside Daron Calvados and quince liqueur in To Each His Own.
facts: Founded in 1872 in Podensac, south of Bordeaux, by the brothers Paul and Raymond Lillet.
Kina Lillet, the first wine aperitif, came in 1887; Kina is from quinquina, the cinchona bark.
About 85 percent wine and 15 percent fruit liqueurs and cinchona.
The Blanc's wine is Semillon, with some Sauvignon Blanc.
The liqueurs steep sweet and bitter orange peels in alcohol for several weeks.
Matured in oak casks in the Podensac cellars; bottled at 17 percent.
Lillet Blanc replaced the more bitter Kina Lillet in 1986.
Owned by a Pernod Ricard subsidiary since 2008.
notes: Say it as a French wine aperitif from near Bordeaux: orange, honey and blossom, served cold.
The Bubbles menu spells it Lilet in the Riviera; the bottle is Lillet, said lee-LAY.
Guests who know the Vesper may ask if ours is the original. The honest answer: today's Lillet Blanc is lighter and less bitter than the Kina Lillet it was written for.
Who owns it: Pernod Ricard, since 2008. Name no owner before that; say the founding family sold in 1985.
value.sayIt: Lillet Blanc is a French aperitif from Podensac, near Bordeaux: Semillon wine with orange-peel liqueurs, light and gently bitter.

explain.value:
Sparkling wine is any wine with bubbles of carbon dioxide trapped in it. The best is made by a second fermentation in the bottle, the traditional method of Champagne; tank-fermented sparkling wines such as Prosecco are fresher and simpler.

Only wine from Champagne may be called Champagne, so a menu that prints sparkling wine is promising bubbles, not a region.

At Brennan's the Riviera and For Sentimental Reasons print sparkling wine without a name, so which wine is a question for the bar. The spritz names Chandon Brut, the OBX names the Bigaro and Personality uses a zero proof rosé. Say sparkling wine exactly where the menu does.

value.front: Why do some menus say sparkling wine, not Champagne?
value.back: Only wine from Champagne may carry that name. The Riviera and For Sentimental Reasons print sparkling wine; which one is a question for the bar.

explain.value:
Rum is distilled from sugar cane, usually from molasses, sometimes from fresh cane juice. White rums are light and clean; aged rums take color and vanilla, caramel and spice from the barrel.

It is the spirit of the Caribbean and of tiki drinks, and it pairs naturally with lime, cream and nuts.

The Bodrum prints rum without naming one, with pistachio, cream, lime and sparkling water, so which rum is a question for the bar. It is the one bubbly cocktail lengthened with sparkling water rather than wine, which makes it the drink for a rum lover, or for a guest who does not care for wine.

value.front: Which rum is in the Bodrum?
value.back: The menu prints only rum, so which one is a question for the bar. It is the one Bubbles cocktail lengthened with sparkling water, not wine.

explain.value:
The pistachio is the seed of a small tree native to Iran and Central Asia, now grown widely in California, Iran and Turkey. Roasted, it tastes sweet, buttery and gently resinous, with a green color that marks pistachio desserts.

In drinks it usually arrives as a syrup, an orgeat-style nut milk or a liqueur, because whole nuts cannot be shaken smooth.

The Bodrum prints pistachio with rum, cream, lime and sparkling water. How the pistachio goes in is not printed, so the bar confirms it. The guide's service note says pistachio and cream, as printed, and any question about nuts goes to that note and lineup, never a guess.

value.front: What do we say if a guest asks about the pistachio?
value.back: That the Bodrum prints pistachio and cream, and how the pistachio goes in is confirmed with the bar. Nut questions go to the service note and lineup.

explain.value:
Fresh citrus juice is the sour side of most cocktails. Lemon is sharp and clean; lime is sharper, greener and a little bitter. Bartenders squeeze it fresh each day, because bottled juice tastes flat and cooked.

Citrus balances sweetness from liqueurs and syrups, brightens fruit and wakes up the spirit; a peel twisted over a drink adds aroma from its oils as well.

Lemon is printed in seven Brennan's drinks: the Flamingo, the Riviera, the OBX, Old Buttermilk Sky, Five Minutes More, Oh! What It Seemed to Be and the Apple Crumble. The Bodrum prints lime. Whether each is juice, peel or both is confirmed with the bar.

value.front: What job does fresh lemon do in a cocktail?
value.back: It is the sour side: it balances sweet liqueurs and syrups and brightens fruit. Seven of our drinks print lemon; the Bodrum prints lime.

explain.value:
Gentilly Gin is made in New Orleans by Seven Three Distilling Co., which opened in 2017 in Tremé; the name Seven Three is a nod to the city's 73 neighborhoods, and Gentilly is one of them.

Its seventeen botanicals were inspired by the traiteurs, the old folk healers of south Louisiana, and include elderflower and persimmon; it is bottled at 87 proof, and the distillery also makes a barrel-aged version.

In the OBX it meets peach, lemon and the softly sweet Elio Perrone Bigaro. A local gin in a courtyard drink is a good story for a visitor; which Gentilly bottling the bar pours is worth confirming.

value.front: Who makes Gentilly Gin?
value.back: Seven Three Distilling Co. of New Orleans, opened in 2017 in Tremé; its botanicals were inspired by the traiteurs. It is the gin in the OBX.

value.who: Gentilly Gin, Seven Three Distilling Co.
value.where: 301 North Claiborne Avenue, Tremé, New Orleans
value.history:
Seven Three Distilling Co. is a New Orleans craft distillery named for the city’s 73 officially recognized neighborhoods, and it names its spirits after them: St. Roch Vodka, Bywater Bourbon, Marigny Moonshine, Irish Channel Whiskey, Black Pearl Rum and Gentilly Gin. A New Orleans husband and wife developed the brand while building a custom distillery, which opened in early 2017 in a warehouse at 301 North Claiborne Avenue, on the corner of Bienville Street, usually described as Tremé. Its first release was a run of 1,000 bottles of St. Roch Vodka, a neutral spirit redistilled and filtered for five days through copper, limestone and charcoal.

Gentilly Gin starts from the same neutral base. Juniper is joined by persimmon and elderflower, 17 botanicals in all, inspired by the traiteurs, the old faith healers of Louisiana. It is bottled at 87 proof, 43.5 percent. Tasters find elderflower, a little anise and vanilla on the nose, honeyed persimmon, ginger and juniper on the palate, and a peppery finish. A Barrel Reserve version rests in barrels before bottling.

Gentilly itself is one of the city’s old neighborhoods. By the common account, in 1727 the colonists Mathurin and Pierre Dreux chose the natural levee along Bayou Sauvage for their plantation and named it after the French community they came from; one recent history argues the name began as Chantilly.
facts: Named for the city’s 73 officially recognized neighborhoods; each spirit takes a neighborhood’s name.
Opened in early 2017 at 301 North Claiborne Avenue, at Bienville Street, founded by a New Orleans husband and wife.
Its first release was 1,000 bottles of St. Roch Vodka, redistilled and filtered for five days through copper, limestone and charcoal.
Gentilly Gin starts from the vodka’s neutral base, with juniper, persimmon, elderflower and other botanicals, 17 in all.
The botanicals were inspired by the traiteurs, the old faith healers of Louisiana.
Bottled at 87 proof, 43.5 percent alcohol; a Barrel Reserve version is rested in barrels before bottling.
The range includes Bywater Bourbon, Marigny Moonshine, Irish Channel Whiskey, Black Pearl Rum and Whiskey Tree bourbons.
Gentilly takes its name, by the common account, from the French home of the colonists Mathurin and Pierre Dreux, who settled there in 1727.
notes: Say Gentilly Gin is made here in New Orleans, at Seven Three Distilling in Tremé.
Guests ask what Gentilly means: one of the city’s neighborhoods, and the distillery names every spirit after one.
Never claim the persimmon or the elderflower is grown in Louisiana: no source says where the botanicals come from.
If asked who owns it: the New Orleans husband and wife who founded it, as the local business press reported. Name nobody.
A curious guest can visit: the distillery has a tasting room and tours, but hours change, so suggest they check before going.
value.sayIt: Gentilly Gin is made here in New Orleans by Seven Three Distilling, named for one of our neighborhoods, with persimmon and elderflower.
askKitchen: Is the OBX made with the standard Gentilly Gin or the Gentilly Gin Barrel Reserve?

explain.value:
The peach is a stone fruit first grown in China and now loved across the American South. A ripe peach is juicy, floral and honeyed, with a soft acidity.

In drinks it comes as fresh fruit, a purée or a liqueur, and it is happiest with sparkling wine: the Bellini is white peach and Prosecco.

The OBX prints peach with Gentilly Gin, lemon and Elio Perrone Bigaro, whose Moscato already brings a peach and orange blossom note, so the fruit runs right through the glass. How the peach goes in is not printed; the bar confirms it before a server describes it.

value.front: What famous drink pairs peach with sparkling wine?
value.back: The Bellini, white peach and Prosecco. The OBX also pairs peach with bubbles, the Bigaro, plus Gentilly Gin and lemon.

explain.value:
Bigaro is a softly sparkling pink wine from Piedmont in north-west Italy, made by the Perrone family near Asti from roughly equal parts Brachetto and Moscato. The two grapes are crushed together, left a few days on the skins, and the fermentation stopped by filtering at about 5 percent alcohol, so it stays gently sweet and lightly fizzy.

It smells of red berries, rose, peach and orange blossom.

In the OBX it tops Gentilly Gin, peach and lemon, adding fruit, a soft sweetness and a light sparkle. It is far gentler than Champagne, which is why the OBX drinks so easily in the afternoon; call it a sparkling wine, never Champagne.

value.front: What is Elio Perrone Bigaro?
value.back: A gently sweet, lightly sparkling pink wine from Piedmont, Brachetto and Moscato, about 5 percent alcohol. It tops the OBX.

value.who: Elio Perrone, a family wine estate
value.where: Castiglione Tinella, province of Asti, Piedmont, Italy
value.founded: The family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century
value.history:
Elio Perrone is a family estate in Castiglione Tinella, in the Moscato hills of the province of Asti in Piedmont. Sources say the family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century, over four generations. One profile dates the present generation’s taking over to 1989, when the son of the man whose name is on the label took the reins; another says the father retired in the late 1990s.

Moscato is the heart of the estate’s production. The family also farms vines at Isola d’Asti, where Barbera leads and Brachetto grows too, and the present generation created Bigaro, a blend of the two aromatic grapes made in the style of Moscato d’Asti.

Bigaro is its pink, softly sparkling wine: half Brachetto and half Moscato, crushed together and left a few days on the skins, with the fermentation stopped by filtering, so that it keeps some grape sugar and a light fizz at about 5 percent alcohol; one listing gives 7 percent for the 2024. Brachetto brings red berries and rose, Moscato brings peach and orange blossom, and the color is salmon. Its importer lists it as Piedmont DOC, and it is served well chilled, as an aperitif or with fruit desserts.

In the OBX it tops Gentilly Gin, peach and lemon, adding fruit, a soft sweetness and a gentle sparkle.
facts: A family estate in Castiglione Tinella, in the Moscato hills of the province of Asti, Piedmont.
The family has made Moscato there since the end of the nineteenth century, over four generations, by the sources’ accounts.
One profile says the present generation took over in 1989; another says the father retired in the late 1990s.
The present generation created Bigaro, a Brachetto and Moscato blend made in the style of Moscato d’Asti.
Bigaro is half Brachetto and half Moscato, crushed together, left a few days on the skins, with fermentation stopped by filtering, leaving a light fizz and some sweetness.
About 5 percent alcohol on most listings; one listing gives 7 percent for the 2024.
Brachetto brings red berries and rose; Moscato brings peach and orange blossom.
A salmon-colored, softly sweet, gently sparkling wine, listed by its importer as Piedmont DOC.
notes: Say bee-gah-ROH. Call it a sparkling wine, never Champagne or Prosecco: it is a softly sweet, low-alcohol pink from Piedmont.
Guests ask why the OBX drinks so lightly. The honest answer: the Bigaro is about 5 percent alcohol, far below Champagne, though the gin still makes it a full cocktail.
Do not say what the name Bigaro means: an earlier note said mottled, but a fresh search could not confirm it.
Elio Perrone is the name on the label and the estate is family run. Name nobody else.
A guest who likes Moscato d’Asti will recognize the style: grapey, floral and gently sweet.
value.sayIt: The OBX is topped with Bigaro, a softly sweet, lightly sparkling pink from Piedmont, half Brachetto and half Moscato, about 5 percent alcohol.
askKitchen: Which vintage of the Bigaro is open, and what alcohol figure does its label print?

explain.value:
A bitter orange liqueur is a spirit sweetened and flavored with the peel of bitter oranges, often with herbs and roots that add a pleasant bitterness. The Italian aperitivo bitters, bright orange or red, are the best-known family.

They are bittersweet rather than sweet: orange peel, gentle bitterness and a light body, made to wake the appetite before a meal.

The Chandon Garden Spritz prints a bitter orange liqueur with Chandon Brut sparkling wine and does not name it. Which liqueur, and whether the bar builds the drink or pours a ready-made spritz, are questions for the bar, so a server describes the taste rather than a brand.

value.front: Which orange liqueur is in the Chandon Garden Spritz?
value.back: The menu prints only a bitter orange liqueur, so name no brand. Describe it as bittersweet orange peel under dry bubbles; the bar confirms the rest.

explain.value:
Chandon is the California sparkling wine house founded in 1973 by Moët Hennessy, the group behind Moët & Chandon Champagne, and based at Yountville in the Napa Valley since 1977, the first French sparkling wine house in California. It makes its wines in the Champagne method.

Brut means dry. Chandon Brut is crisp and fresh, with apple, citrus and a little toast.

In the Chandon Garden Spritz it is the sparkling base under a bitter orange liqueur. Whether ours is the Californian Chandon Brut or Chandon's ready-made Garden Spritz from Mendoza is a question for the bar; either way the menu calls it sparkling wine, never Champagne, and so does the server; the Moët link is a fair and interesting thing to tell a guest who asks.

value.front: Who founded Chandon in California?
value.back: Moët Hennessy, owner of Moët & Chandon Champagne, in 1973; its Yountville winery opened in 1977. Chandon Brut is dry sparkling wine; never call it Champagne.

value.who: Chandon, the sparkling wine house of Moët Hennessy (LVMH)
value.where: Yountville, Napa Valley, California; the Garden Spritz is made in Mendoza, Argentina
value.history:
Chandon is the sparkling wine house the Moët group built beyond Champagne. Its first venture abroad was Chandon Argentina, founded by Moët & Chandon in 1959 at Agrelo, in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza: the first Moët & Chandon subsidiary outside France.

In California it began in 1973, first named M & H Vineyards after its parent, Moët Hennessy. Its founding head, John Wright, found the vineyards; the first vintages were made at the Trefethen winery, and the house moved into its own winery at Yountville in 1977. Wine Spectator calls it the first French sparkling wine house in California. LVMH owns it today.

Chandon Brut is a dry, non-vintage sparkling wine made by the traditional method, its second fermentation in the bottle, with Chardonnay from southern Napa, Mt. Veeder and Carneros in the blend: green apple, pear, citrus and a little brioche.

The Garden Spritz is Argentine. Chandon’s winemakers in Mendoza made a bitter orange Garden liqueur from Valencia oranges, herbs and spices, inspired by Argentina’s taste for yerba maté and Fernet, and blended it with the Chandon Brut made in Mendoza. Chandon announced it in the United States in May 2021 as its first ready-to-drink sparkling aperitif.
facts: Chandon Argentina, founded by Moët & Chandon in 1959 at Agrelo in Mendoza, was the first Moët & Chandon subsidiary outside France.
Chandon California was founded in 1973 by Moët Hennessy, first named M & H Vineyards after its parent company.
Wine Spectator calls it the first French sparkling wine house in California, making wine by the Champagne method.
Its first vintages were made at the Trefethen winery; it moved into its own winery at Yountville in 1977.
Owned today by LVMH, Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy.
Chandon Brut is dry and non-vintage, made by the traditional method; sources disagree on its grape split, and Chandon’s own notes call Pinot Noir the majority.
The Garden Spritz was created in Mendoza by Chandon Argentina’s winemakers, its Garden liqueur made from Valencia oranges, herbs and spices.
Its oranges come from a family farm in Entre Rios, north-east Argentina, by the launch reports.
Chandon announced the Garden Spritz in the United States in May 2021 as its first ready-to-drink sparkling aperitif.
The launch release names the Garden Spritz’s base as Chandon Brut made by the winemakers and growers in Mendoza, not the Californian wine.
notes: Never call it Champagne. Chandon is sparkling wine made by a Champagne group outside Champagne, so the menu says sparkling wine and so do you.
Guests ask whether this is the Moët they know. The honest answer: the same group founded Chandon, and Moët & Chandon’s Imperial Rosé is on our Bubbles rosé list.
The menu prints bitter orange liqueur and Chandon Brut. Chandon’s ready-made Garden Spritz is exactly that, bottled in Mendoza; whether the bar builds it or pours the bottle is a lineup question.
If the bar pours the ready-made bottle, the wine and the liqueur are Argentine, not Californian. Say so only once the bar confirms it.
Offer it to the guest who orders an Aperol spritz or an aperitivo: bittersweet orange under dry bubbles. Chandon suggests ice, an orange slice and rosemary; our glass and garnish come from the bar.
value.sayIt: Chandon is the sparkling wine house the Moët group founded beyond Champagne; its Garden Spritz began in Argentina, bittersweet orange under dry bubbles.
askKitchen: Do we build the Chandon Garden Spritz from Chandon Brut and a bitter orange liqueur, or pour Chandon’s ready-made Garden Spritz?
If we build it, which bitter orange liqueur, and is the Chandon Brut the Californian wine?
What glass, ice and garnish does the spritz get?

explain.value:
A spiced syrup is sugar dissolved in water and simmered or steeped with whole spices. Cardamom, the green seed pod of a ginger relative, brings a cool, floral, slightly citrus perfume; clove, the dried flower bud of a tropical tree, brings warmth and a sweet, almost medicinal depth.

Both turn up in coffee traditions around the world, and clove belongs to New Orleans' flamed café brûlot.

In the Café Glacé de la Maison the syrup sweetens chicory cold brew and gives it warm spice under an orange flower foam. The guide hears an echo of café brûlot in it; how the bar makes the syrup is a question for lineup.

value.front: What do cardamom and clove bring to the Café Glacé?
value.back: Cardamom adds a cool, floral perfume and clove a warm, sweet depth, a nod to café brûlot. The syrup sweetens the chicory cold brew.

explain.value:
Orange flower water is made by distilling the blossoms of the bitter orange tree. It is clear and intensely fragrant, used by the drop in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern pastries, and in the Ramos Gin Fizz, New Orleans' famous cream and gin drink.

It tastes of blossom rather than fruit: a heady, floral perfume that lifts cream and tea.

At Brennan's it appears twice. The Café Glacé de la Maison is topped with an orange flower foam, a floral lift over the cold brew. The Prisoner of Love prints orange flower water with gin, Earl Grey tea and clarified heavy cream. Too much tastes like soap, which is why bartenders measure it in drops.

value.front: What does orange flower water taste of?
value.back: Blossom, not fruit: a heady floral perfume distilled from bitter orange flowers. It tops the Café Glacé as a foam and scents the Prisoner of Love.

explain.value:
The Revive juice prints three fruits. Strawberry gives color and a sweet, red fruit perfume; apple gives body and a clean sweetness; pineapple gives tang and a tropical brightness that keeps the juice from tasting flat.

Pressed together they make a juice that is sweet but lively, fresh rather than cooked, the way cold-pressed juice is meant to taste.

The menu lists it under juices that are locally made and fresh squeezed, at breakfast and lunch. It is the drink for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine, including a child, and it gives a breakfast table a bright option beside the eye openers. Who presses it is confirmed with the bar.

value.front: What fruits are in the Revive juice?
value.back: Strawberry, apple and pineapple: sweet, fruity and tangy. It is the choice for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine.

explain.value:
Allspice dram, also called pimento dram, is a Jamaican liqueur made by steeping allspice berries in rum and sweetening it. Allspice is the dried berry of the pimento tree, and it tastes like clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once, which is how it got its name.

It has been traded since the 1850s, appeared in 1930s cocktail books and was taken up by the tiki bars; a little goes a long way.

In For Sentimental Reasons it sits under pear purée and sparkling wine, giving the drink its warm baking spice finish. Which allspice dram the bar pours is not printed; describe the flavor and let the bar name the bottle.

value.front: What is allspice dram?
value.back: A Jamaican liqueur of allspice berries steeped in rum, tasting of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once. It warms For Sentimental Reasons.

value.who: Pimento dram, the allspice liqueur of Jamaica
value.founded: An article of commerce since the 1850s
value.history:
Allspice dram, called pimento dram in Jamaica, is rum in which allspice berries have been steeped, then sweetened. Allspice is the dried berry of the pimento tree; the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails says its flavor recalls cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg, and records the dram as an article of commerce since the 1850s. Bottles were shown at the International Exhibition of 1862. In Jamaica the berry kept its Spanish name, pimiento, now pimento; the English called it allspice. It is no relation of the pimento pepper.

The National Museum Jamaica records that the liqueur became popular in Europe and North America in the early 1900s, when J. Wray & Nephew bottled and sold it. It appeared in drinks such as the Lion's Tail and was taken up by the tiki bars. Imports to the United States later stopped, and bartenders made their own.

The revival came in 2008 with St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, made in Austria from Jamaican allspice berries, raw sugar and pot-stilled Jamaican rum for an American importer.

At Brennan's it gives For Sentimental Reasons its warm baking spice, under pear purée and sparkling wine. The menu names no brand, so which dram the bar pours is a lineup question.
facts: Allspice dram is rum steeped with allspice berries and sweetened, a Jamaican liqueur.
Its flavor recalls cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg, says the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails.
An article of commerce since the 1850s; shown at the International Exhibition of 1862.
J. Wray & Nephew bottled and sold it in the early 1900s, by the National Museum Jamaica's record.
In Jamaica the berry is called pimento, from the Spanish; it is no relation of the pimento pepper.
St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, made in Austria with Jamaican berries, raw sugar and pot-stilled rum, debuted in 2008.
notes: Say it as Jamaica's spiced rum liqueur: clove, cinnamon and nutmeg in one berry.
The menu names no brand; describe the flavor and let the bar name the bottle.
It is sweet spice, not heat: never call it pepper or say the drink is hot.
A little carries the drink: For Sentimental Reasons is pear and bubbles first, with the spice underneath.
value.sayIt: Allspice dram is Jamaica's pimento dram: rum steeped with allspice berries, tasting of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once.
askKitchen: Which allspice dram goes into For Sentimental Reasons: St. Elizabeth, another brand, or a house infusion?

explain.value:
A fruit purée is ripe fruit blended smooth and strained, sometimes lightly sweetened. Pear purée is soft, honeyed and floral, with the gentle grain of the fruit, and it gives a drink body as well as flavor.

Purées are thicker than juice, so a purée drink feels rounder and softer in the mouth; with sparkling wine they make the Bellini family.

In For Sentimental Reasons pear purée meets allspice dram under sparkling wine, so the guest tastes ripe pear first and warm spice at the end. Whether the purée is made in house or bought in is a question for the bar.

value.front: What does pear purée add to For Sentimental Reasons?
value.back: Ripe, honeyed pear flavor and a soft body, under sparkling wine with allspice dram. Whether it is made in house is a question for the bar.

explain.value:
Earl Grey is black tea scented with oil of bergamot, a fragrant citrus grown mostly in Calabria in southern Italy. It is named for Charles Gray, the second Earl Grey, Prime Minister from 1830 to 1834; the stories of how the blend got his name are uncertain, so tell them lightly if at all.

Bergamot gives the tea a floral, perfumed citrus note over the tannic black tea.

In the Prisoner of Love the tea joins gin, clarified heavy cream and orange flower water. The tea's acidity and tannin help the clarifying, and its bergamot meets the orange flower water, which is why the drink smells so fragrant.

value.front: What gives Earl Grey tea its perfume?
value.back: Oil of bergamot, a fragrant Italian citrus, over black tea. It scents the Prisoner of Love with gin and clarified cream.

explain.value:
Rittenhouse Rye was introduced in 1934 by Continental Distilling of Philadelphia, named for the city's Rittenhouse Square. From 1948 it was bottled in bond, which by law means the spirit of one distilling season, aged at least four years and bottled at 100 proof. Heaven Hill, the Bardstown family firm, bought the brand in the 1990s and makes it in Kentucky.

It is a spicy, robust rye that holds its own in cocktails.

The menu prints Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye in Rumors are Flying. Who aged it for the house, in what cask and for how long are not printed, so a server says barrel-aged for Brennan's and no more until the bar gives the story.

value.front: What does bottled in bond mean on Rittenhouse?
value.back: One distilling season, aged at least four years, bottled at 100 proof. The menu calls ours barrel aged for Brennan's; what that means is a question for the bar.

value.history:
Rittenhouse Rye was first sold in Philadelphia in 1934, just after Prohibition, by Continental Distilling, and named for the city's Rittenhouse Square. In 1948 it was relaunched as a four-year-old bottled in bond rye, the form it keeps. Heaven Hill bought the brand in the 1990s, in 1993 by some accounts and 1999 by others, and moved its production from Pennsylvania to Kentucky.

Heaven Hill itself was founded at Bardstown in 1935 by a group of investors; in time five brothers of one family bought out the rest, and their descendants own and run the company still. On 7 November 1996 fire swept through its warehouses, and some 90,000 barrels burned. In 1999 it bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville, where it has distilled since, while aging and bottling stayed around Bardstown; a new Bardstown distillery filled its first barrel on 7 April 2025.

Bottled in bond means the spirit of a single distilling season, aged at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse and bottled at 100 proof. Rittenhouse is 51 percent rye, with corn and malted barley: a modern Kentucky recipe, lower in rye than the old Pennsylvania ryes it nods to.
