value.back: Melon de Bourgogne, aged on its lees near Nantes: lemon, green apple and a salty finish. The classic oyster wine.

explain.value:
Godello is a white grape of north-west Spain, grown in Valdeorras in Galicia and in Bierzo next door. It was nearly lost in the twentieth century and was revived by a handful of growers.

It gives a white of real weight that stays fresh: lemon, pear, almond and herbs with a saline edge, often textured by time on the lees or in older barrels. Sommeliers compare it to a cross between Chablis and white Burgundy.

Ours is Raúl Pérez's Ultreia from Bierzo. It is a fine choice for a guest who likes white Burgundy and wants something new, and for richer fish and crab.

value.front: How would you describe Godello to a white Burgundy lover?
value.back: A Spanish white of real weight that stays fresh: lemon, pear and almond with a saline edge. Ours is Raúl Pérez's Ultreia from Bierzo.

explain.value:
Pinot Gris is a pink-gray skinned mutation of Pinot Noir. In Italy it is Pinot Grigio, made light and crisp; in Alsace it is a different animal: rich, full and spicy, with ripe pear, quince, honey and a smoky note.

Alsace growers often pick it very ripe, so some bottles carry a touch of sweetness and others are dry; the label does not always say, so the sommelier is the one to ask. It ages well, gaining dried apricot, ginger and mushroom.

We have Albert Boxler's and Trimbach's Réserve Personnelle 2007. Its weight and spice handle rich, smoky dishes, duck and foie gras.

value.front: How is Alsace Pinot Gris different from Pinot Grigio?
value.back: Rich, full and smoky with pear, quince and honey, sometimes a touch sweet, where Pinot Grigio is light and crisp. Ask the sommelier how sweet a bottle is.

explain.value:
Assyrtiko is the great white grape of Santorini. It keeps very high acidity even in the hot, dry Aegean summer, which is rare, and gives bone dry wine tasting of lemon, salt, flint and white flowers.

On Santorini the vines grow in volcanic pumice that phylloxera never reached, so many are ungrafted and very old, trained low into basket shapes against the wind. The result has a savory, almost salty depth.

Ours is Gaia's Wild Ferment, fermented with the island's own yeasts. Sell it as the white for grilled fish, lemon and herbs, and for any guest who loves Chablis or Sancerre.

value.front: What makes Santorini Assyrtiko taste salty and electric?
value.back: Volcanic soil, old ungrafted basket-trained vines and a grape that keeps high acidity in heat. Ours is Gaia's Wild Ferment.

explain.value:
Savagnin is an ancient white grape of the Jura, the hills between Burgundy and Switzerland. It is related to Traminer, the parent of Gewürztraminer, but it is not aromatic in the same way: it is firm, high in acidity and savory.

It is the only grape allowed in Vin Jaune, the yellow wine, which ages for years in barrel under a veil of yeast and tastes of walnut, curry spice and dried apple.

Ours is the Domaine du Pélican Vin Jaune from Arbois. It is a curiosity for adventurous guests, and a famous match for aged Comté cheese, mushrooms and chicken in cream.

value.front: What is the only grape allowed in Vin Jaune?
value.back: Savagnin, an ancient Jura white related to Traminer, firm and savory. Aged under a veil of yeast it tastes of walnut and curry spice.

explain.value:
Gewürztraminer is the most perfumed white grape of all. Gewürz means spice in German; the pink-skinned grapes smell of lychee, rose petal, ginger and cinnamon, with low acidity and a rich, oily texture.

It is at its best in Alsace, where it is made from dry to sweet. In great years, grapes left late on the vine are made as Vendanges Tardives, late harvest, richer and sweeter.

We pour the Trimbach Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives 2007, and it is in the Grgich Hills Violetta blend. Its spice is a natural echo of baked apple, cinnamon and Creole spice desserts.

value.front: What does Gewürztraminer smell of?
value.back: Lychee, rose petal, ginger and cinnamon: the most perfumed white grape. Our Trimbach is a late harvest, Vendanges Tardives, so it is sweet.

components.name: Marsanne, Roussanne and the southern whites

explain.value:
Marsanne and Roussanne are the white grapes of the Rhône. Marsanne gives body, a waxy texture and flavors of almond, pear and honey; Roussanne adds perfume, herbs and freshness. Grenache Blanc and Clairette, two southern whites, add roundness and floral lift.

Together they make full, textured whites that age well, gaining honey and fennel notes, and they suit rich fish and poultry far better than crisp, lean wines do.

Our example is the rare white of Domaine de Trévallon in the Alpilles, Marsanne-led with Roussanne, a little Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette. It is a bottle for a guest who loves white Burgundy and wants something rarer.

value.front: What grapes make the Trévallon white, and what is the style?
value.back: Marsanne-led with Roussanne, Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette: full and textured, apricot, honey, fennel and herbs. A rare Provence white.

explain.value:
Palomino is the white grape of sherry, grown on the bright white albariza chalk around Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda in southern Spain.

As a table wine it is neutral and low in acidity, which is exactly why it suits sherry: it lets the aging speak. Under a layer of flor yeast it becomes fino or, in the sea air of Sanlúcar, Manzanilla, tasting of green apple, almond, bread dough and salt.

Ours is La Cigarrera Manzanilla in a half-bottle. Serve it well chilled as an aperitif; it is a bold, classic match for oysters, fried seafood and salty snacks.

value.front: Which grape makes Manzanilla, and why does it work?
value.back: Palomino, grown on white chalk near Jerez. It is neutral, so the flor yeast and sea air of Sanlúcar give the flavor: apple, almond, bread and salt.

explain.value:
Moscato Bianco, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains in France, is one of the oldest grape families and one of the few whose wine smells of the grape itself: orange blossom, peach and grapes.

It makes Moscato d'Asti, the sweet wines of Beaumes-de-Venise, and, in Montalcino, Moscadello, the sweet wine the town was famous for long before Brunello. Picked late, the grapes concentrate their sugar and give honey, apricot and candied orange.

Ours is Castello Banfi's Florus, a late harvest Moscadello di Montalcino, now fifteen years old. Its orange blossom and honey suit fruit tarts and the Tarte Tatin.

value.front: What was Montalcino famous for before Brunello?
value.back: Moscadello, a sweet wine from Moscato Bianco. Ours is Banfi's late harvest Florus: honey, apricot, candied orange and orange blossom.

explain.value:
Welschriesling is a white grape of central Europe that, despite the name, is no relation to Riesling. It is grown across Austria, Hungary, Slovenia and Croatia.

Dry, it is light and fresh with green apple and citrus. Its real glory is around the Neusiedlersee in Burgenland, where autumn mist off the lake brings noble rot, and the grape keeps its acidity while the sugar concentrates. Blended with Chardonnay it gives creamy, tropical sweet wines.

Ours is the Kracher Cuvée Auslese, Welschriesling with Chardonnay: pear, quince, mandarin and passion fruit, sweet but fresh. It suits fruit desserts and cheese.

value.front: Is Welschriesling a kind of Riesling?
value.back: No, it is unrelated. In Burgenland it makes fresh sweet wines; our Kracher Cuvée Auslese blends it with Chardonnay for pear, quince and passion fruit.

explain.value:
Corvina is the main red grape of Valpolicella, in the hills north of Verona, usually blended with Corvinone and Rondinella. On its own it gives light, cherry-scented red with bright acidity.

Its thick skins are what matter: the grapes can be dried for months after picking without rotting, losing water and concentrating sugar, color and flavor. That process, appassimento, makes dry Amarone and sweet Recioto.

Our bottle is Giuseppe Quintarelli's Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997, from Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella and other local grapes. With chocolate and the richer desserts it is a rare treat.

value.front: Why can Corvina grapes be dried for months?
value.back: Their thick skins resist rot, so they lose water and concentrate sugar and flavor. That makes Amarone and sweet Recioto, like our Quintarelli 1997.

explain.value:
Malvasia, Malmsey in English, is an ancient family of grapes found all around the Mediterranean. On the Portuguese island of Madeira it gives the sweetest of the four classic styles, named for the grape.

A Malvasia Madeira must carry a lot of sugar, yet the island's high natural acidity keeps it tangy and alive. Warm aging in old casks turns it amber and gives coffee, caramel, toffee, orange peel, dried fig and walnut.

Ours is the Broadbent Single Cask Malvasia 2009, in a 500 ml bottle. Opened, Madeira lasts longer than almost any wine. Offer it with the Bread Pudding, nuts and coffee desserts.

value.front: Which Madeira style is sweetest, and what keeps it fresh?
value.back: Malvasia, or Malmsey: rich with coffee, caramel and fig, kept tangy by the island's high natural acidity. Ours is the Broadbent Single Cask.

explain.value:
Port is made from a field of native Portuguese red grapes grown on the steep schist terraces of the Douro valley. The five most prized are Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Spain's Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão; old vineyards mix dozens together.

Touriga Nacional gives floral violet aromas, deep color and firm tannin; Touriga Franca adds perfume and red fruit; Tinta Roriz brings body. The blend is why Port can taste of blackberry, plum, violets and dark chocolate at once.

Every Port on our list, from Dow's and Graham's to Taylor Fladgate, Niepoort, Sandeman and Feist, is a blend of these grapes. Most bottles do not name them, so a guest who asks gets the family, not a recipe.

value.front: What grapes make Port?
value.back: A blend of native Douro reds, led by Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca with Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão: violets, blackberry and plum.

explain.value:
Champagne is a region about ninety miles north-east of Paris, around the cities of Reims and Épernay, and only sparkling wine made there may carry its name. It is one of the coolest places in the world to ripen grapes, so the base wines are tart and light, exactly what a sparkling wine needs.

Under the vines is chalk, which drains well, holds water for dry summers and keeps the wines fresh; the houses age their bottles in miles of chalk cellars beneath the towns. The main districts are the Montagne de Reims, the Côte des Blancs, the Vallée de la Marne and the Côte des Bar to the south.

So when a guest asks for Champagne but means any bubbles, gently say which of ours are Champagne and which are sparkling wine from elsewhere.

value.front: Why can only some of our bubbles be called Champagne?
value.back: Champagne is a place north-east of Paris, around Reims and Épernay. Only sparkling wine from there carries the name; Argyle, Schramsberg and Chapel Down are sparkling wine.

explain.value:
The Montagne de Reims is the wooded hill between Reims and Épernay, more a plateau than a mountain, ringed with vineyards. It is Pinot Noir country, and its Grand Cru villages, Bouzy, Ambonnay, Verzenay and others, give Champagne power, red-fruit depth and structure.

Bouzy is also famous for still red wine, a little of which is blended into rosé Champagne to give it color. Tauxières is a Premier Cru village on its southern slope; Merfy lies on the smaller hills north-west of Reims.

On our list the Montagne speaks through Paul Bara's Grand Cru rosé and Pierre Paillard's Les Parcelles, both from Bouzy, through Chartogne-Taillet of Merfy and Bollinger's PNTX20, led by Tauxières. Say Pinot Noir, body and red fruit.

value.front: What does the Montagne de Reims give Champagne?
value.back: Pinot Noir power and red-fruit depth. Its Grand Cru village Bouzy gives our Paul Bara rosé and Pierre Paillard, and red wine for rosé blends.

explain.value:
The Côte des Blancs is the east-facing slope south of Épernay, planted almost entirely with Chardonnay; the name means the slope of the whites. Its chalk is very near the surface, and the wines are taut, citrus, chalky and long-lived.

Its Grand Cru villages, among them Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, are the source of the great Blanc de Blancs. Vertus, at the southern end, is a Premier Cru village and home to several fine family growers.

From here come Larmandier-Bernier's Longitude and Veuve Fourny's Blanc de Blancs and rosé, and the Chardonnay in Pol Roger's vintage Blanc de Blancs. Say lemon, chalk and finesse: these are the Champagnes for oysters and caviar.

value.front: Which grape rules the Côte des Blancs, and what does it taste like?
value.back: Chardonnay: lemon, chalk and finesse. Our Larmandier-Bernier and Veuve Fourny come from Vertus at its southern end; pour them with oysters.

components.name: Aÿ and the Vallée de la Marne

explain.value:
The Vallée de la Marne follows the river west from Épernay. Its cooler, frost-prone slopes suit Meunier, while Aÿ, on the north bank near Épernay, is one of Champagne's most famous Grand Cru villages for Pinot Noir.

Aÿ has been a wine town for centuries and is home to Bollinger. Its neighbor Mareuil-sur-Aÿ is home to Billecart-Salmon, and Tours-sur-Marne, a little upstream, to Laurent-Perrier.

So three of our great houses sit within a few miles of one another on the Marne. When a guest asks where Bollinger comes from, the answer is Aÿ, the Pinot Noir village, and it explains the house's rich, powerful style.

value.front: Which of our Champagne houses sit on the Marne near Aÿ?
value.back: Bollinger in Aÿ, a Grand Cru for Pinot Noir; Billecart-Salmon in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ; Laurent-Perrier in Tours-sur-Marne, a little upstream, all within a few miles.

components.name: The Aube and the Côte des Bar

explain.value:
The Côte des Bar, in the Aube département, is Champagne's southern outpost, closer to Chablis than to Reims. Its soils are Kimmeridgian clay and limestone, like Chablis, rather than the chalk of the north, and the warmer slopes are mostly Pinot Noir.

For a long time its grapes went north to the big houses; today its growers and houses are prized for ripe, fruity, generous Champagne.

Our Drappier half-bottle comes from Urville, in the heart of the Côte des Bar, and is about three parts Pinot Noir. It is a softer, rounder Brut than many, easy at the start of breakfast.

value.front: Where is the Côte des Bar, and which of ours comes from it?
value.back: Champagne's southern outpost in the Aube, near Chablis, mostly Pinot Noir. Our Drappier Carte d'Or half-bottle comes from the village of Urville there.

explain.value:
Alsace is a narrow strip of vineyards on France's eastern edge, between the Vosges mountains and the Rhine, facing Germany. The mountains block the rain, so it is one of the driest, sunniest places in France, yet cool enough for aromatic grapes.

Unlike most of France, Alsace names its wines by grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Muscat. It bottles them in tall, slender flutes, and its towns, Colmar, Ribeauvillé and Riquewihr, look half German, half French, because the region changed hands several times.

On our list are Pierre Sparr's Crémant d'Alsace rosé by the glass, Albert Boxler and Trimbach. Alsace whites, rich and spiced, are a natural match for duck, pork and Creole spice.

value.front: How does Alsace label its wines, unlike most of France?
value.back: By grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris. A dry, sunny strip between the Vosges and the Rhine; ours include Pierre Sparr, Boxler and Trimbach.

explain.value:
The Loire is France's longest river, and its vineyards follow it for hundreds of miles, from Sancerre in the center of France to Muscadet near the Atlantic at Nantes. It is a cool region of crisp, fresh wines, many of them unoaked.

Each stretch has its own grape: Sauvignon Blanc upstream in Sancerre; Chenin Blanc in the middle, around Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou; Cabernet Franc for reds; Melon de Bourgogne for Muscadet by the sea.

Our Loire bottles show the range: the Durand Sauvignon by the glass, Cotat's Sancerre and Chavignol rosé, Huet's Vouvray in three sweetness levels, Laureau's Savennières, the Baumard Layon and two serious Muscadet bottles. Loire wines, high in acidity, suit seafood and light dishes.

value.front: Name the main grapes of the Loire, from Sancerre to the sea.
value.back: Sauvignon Blanc in Sancerre, Chenin Blanc in Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou, Cabernet Franc for reds, and Melon de Bourgogne in Muscadet near Nantes.

explain.value:
Sancerre is a hilltop town in the upper Loire, and its wine is the benchmark Sauvignon Blanc: lemon, grass and a flinty, smoky edge. A little red and rosé is made from Pinot Noir.

Chavignol, a village below the town, is famous for its steep chalk slopes, above all Les Monts Damnés, the damned mountains, so steep they are worked by hand, and for the Crottin de Chavignol goat cheese. The Cotat family's wines from here are picked riper than most and age remarkably.

We have Pascal Cotat's Les Monts Damnés Sancerre and his rare Chavignol rosé, bottled by lot rather than vintage. A Sancerre with goat cheese is one of the classic pairings.

value.front: What are Les Monts Damnés?
value.back: The damned mountains: a steep chalk slope above Chavignol in Sancerre, worked by hand. Pascal Cotat's Sauvignon Blanc from there is on our list.

explain.value:
Vouvray is a village on the north bank of the Loire just east of Tours, in Touraine. Its wines are all Chenin Blanc, grown on clay and flint over tuffeau, the soft white limestone the châteaux of the Loire are built from and into which the cellars are carved.

Vouvray is made dry (sec), gently sweet (demi-sec), sweet (moelleux) and sparkling, and the vintage decides: warm years with noble rot give sweet wines, cool years dry and sparkling ones.

Domaine Huet is its greatest estate, with three vineyards, Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and the Clos du Bourg. We pour its sec, demi-sec and moelleux. Always say the sweetness word on the label to the guest.

value.front: What three sweetness words appear on our Huet Vouvray labels?
value.back: Sec, dry; demi-sec, gently sweet; moelleux, sweet. All Chenin Blanc from Vouvray, near Tours, on chalky tuffeau. Always say the word to the guest.

components.name: Anjou: Savennières and the Coteaux du Layon

explain.value:
Anjou lies west of Touraine around the city of Angers, where the Loire meets several tributaries. Chenin Blanc is king here, in two opposite styles.

Savennières, on the north bank, is a tiny appellation of steep schist slopes making dry, firm, waxy Chenin that tastes of quince, beeswax and chamomile and ages for decades. Across the river, the Coteaux du Layon follows a small tributary whose autumn mists bring noble rot, and the wines are sweet, honeyed and fresh.

We have Damien Laureau's Savennières L'Alliance and the Baumard Clos Sainte Catherine 2006 from the Layon. Same grape, same few miles: one dry for fish, one sweet for dessert.

value.front: Savennières and Coteaux du Layon: same grape, what difference?
value.back: Both Anjou Chenin Blanc. Savennières is dry, firm and waxy; the Coteaux du Layon is sweet, honeyed and fresh, from autumn mists by the river.

explain.value:
Muscadet is the westernmost Loire wine, made around Nantes near the Atlantic. Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine, named for two small rivers, is its heartland, and its wine is made from Melon de Bourgogne.

The words sur lie on many labels mean the wine stayed on its lees, the spent yeast, through the winter until bottling, gaining texture and a light spritz. The best growers now bottle crus communaux, named villages such as Monnières-Saint Fiacre, Clisson and Gorges, and leave the wine on its lees for two years or more.

Domaine de l'Écu bottles by the rock beneath the vines, so Orthogneiss is named for an ancient rock; Pépière's Monnières-Saint Fiacre is a cru communal. Both are the oyster wine.

value.front: What does sur lie on a Muscadet label mean?
value.back: The wine stayed on its lees, the spent yeast, until bottling: more texture, a light spritz and savory depth. Our two Muscadet bottles rest on them far longer than usual.

explain.value:
Chablis is the northernmost part of Burgundy, nearer Champagne than Beaune, and it makes only Chardonnay. Its cool climate and Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of fossilized oyster shells, give lean, crisp, steely wines that taste of lemon, green apple and a chalky, oyster-shell finish.

The tiers run Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru. The seven Grand Crus, Les Preuses among them, sit on one slope facing south-west across the little Serein river.

We have Louis Michel's village Chablis and Montmains Premier Cru, made in steel with no oak, and Dauvissat's Les Preuses Grand Cru. Chablis with oysters is the oldest pairing advice there is.

value.front: What soil gives Chablis its oyster-shell finish?
value.back: Kimmeridgian limestone and clay full of fossil oyster shells. Chablis is northern Burgundy's Chardonnay: lean, crisp and steely, the classic oyster wine.

explain.value:
The Mâconnais is the southern end of Burgundy proper, around the town of Mâcon, a warmer, gentler landscape of rolling hills. Almost all its white is Chardonnay, riper and rounder than the Côte d'Or's and much kinder in price.

Mâcon-Villages wines may add the village name, so Mâcon-Verzé, Mâcon-Igé and Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine name villages. Pouilly-Fuissé, under the dramatic limestone rocks of Solutré and Vergisson, is its finest appellation and gained Premier Cru vineyards in 2020.

Great Côte d'Or estates now farm here: Leflaive at Verzé and the Lafon family at Milly-Lamartine. Our dinner tasting white, the Fichet Château London, comes from Igé. Say: white Burgundy with sunshine.

value.front: What do Verzé, Igé and Milly-Lamartine have in common on our list?
value.back: They are Mâconnais villages that name our Mâcon whites: Leflaive's Verzé, Fichet's Château London from Igé and the Lafon family's Milly-Lamartine.

explain.value:
The Côte de Beaune is the southern half of the Côte d'Or, the narrow limestone escarpment at the heart of Burgundy, running south from the town of Beaune. It is the home of the greatest white Burgundy, and of silky reds too.

Its white villages, Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet and the hillside Saint-Aubin, share the Grand Cru Le Montrachet. Its red villages include Volnay, known for perfume, Beaune itself, Savigny-lès-Beaune and Pommard.

On our list it gives the Jadot Beaune Premier Cru on the dinner tasting, the Bouchard Clos de la Mousse, d'Angerville's Volnay, Tollot-Beaut's Savigny, and the whole run of Meursault, Puligny and Saint-Aubin. Say elegance: silky reds, rich but precise whites.

value.front: Name four Côte de Beaune villages on our list.
value.back: Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet for white, Volnay and Beaune for red; also Saint-Aubin and Savigny-lès-Beaune. The southern half of the Côte d'Or.

explain.value:
Meursault is the largest white wine village of the Côte de Beaune, and its Chardonnay is the richest of the great three: round, nutty and buttery, with hazelnut, ripe lemon, toast and a stony freshness underneath, usually from fermentation and aging in oak barrels.

It has no Grand Cru, but famous Premier Crus such as Perrières, Charmes and Genevrières, and many named village vineyards, lieux-dits, like Les Tillets, Les Corbins and the Clos de la Baronne. Every November the village holds the Paulée de Meursault, a harvest feast.

Our list carries Meursault from Jadot, Dupont-Fahn, Bitouzet-Prieur, Comtes Lafon and Leflaive's Sous le Dos d'Ane. For a guest who wants a rich, classic white with lobster or crab, this is the page.

value.front: How does Meursault taste compared with Puligny-Montrachet?
value.back: Meursault is rounder and nuttier, hazelnut and butter over a stony core; Puligny is more chiseled and floral. Both are great Côte de Beaune Chardonnay.

explain.value:
Puligny-Montrachet is the most famous white wine village in the world. It shares with Chassagne the Grand Cru Le Montrachet, and its own Grand Crus and Premier Crus give Chardonnay that is elegant, floral and chiseled: citrus, white flowers, hazelnut and a fine, chalky tension.

The water table is high here, so cellars are shallow and wines are often aged above ground. Saint-Aubin, tucked into the hills behind Puligny and Chassagne, makes wines in a similar style at a gentler price.

We have village Puligny from François Carillon and Domaine Leflaive, and Paul Pillot's Le Charmois Saint-Aubin Premier Cru. Recommend Saint-Aubin to a guest who loves Puligny but wants value.

value.front: Which village is our value alternative to Puligny-Montrachet?
value.back: Saint-Aubin, in the hills behind Puligny and Chassagne, in a similar elegant, chalky style: our Paul Pillot Le Charmois Premier Cru.

explain.value:
Beaune is the wine capital of Burgundy, a walled town of négociant cellars, home to houses such as Louis Jadot and Bouchard Père & Fils and to the Hospices de Beaune, whose charity wine auction each November is the most famous in France.

Its own vineyards, on the slope above the town, are mostly red Pinot Noir. Beaune has no Grand Cru, so its Premier Crus are its highest tier; they give silky, generous reds with red cherry, raspberry and a little spice, often walled clos such as the Clos de la Mousse and the Clos des Ursules.

Our dinner tasting pours the Jadot Beaune Premier Cru with the Redfish Véronique, and the Bouchard Clos de la Mousse is on the half-bottle list.

value.front: What is the highest vineyard tier in Beaune?
value.back: Premier Cru: Beaune has no Grand Cru. Our Jadot Beaune Premier Cru pours with the Redfish Véronique on the dinner tasting.

explain.value:
The Côte de Nuits is the northern half of the Côte d'Or, running from near Dijon south to Nuits-Saint-Georges. It is almost all Pinot Noir and home to nearly all of Burgundy's red Grand Crus: Chambertin, Musigny, Clos de Vougeot, Echézeaux, Romanée-Conti.

Its villages each have a voice: Gevrey-Chambertin for power, Chambolle-Musigny for perfume, Vosne-Romanée for silk and spice, Morey-Saint-Denis between them, Nuits-Saint-Georges for firm, earthy structure.

On our list are Gouges and Grivot from Nuits-Saint-Georges, Roumier's Clos de la Bussière in Morey, Grivot's Echézeaux Grand Cru and Faiveley's Bourgogne from a Nuits house. Say depth and structure: the reds for beef and game.

value.front: How does the Côte de Nuits differ from the Côte de Beaune?
value.back: It is the northern half, almost all Pinot Noir and home to most red Grand Crus: deeper, more structured reds, where the Côte de Beaune is famed for white.

explain.value:
Nuits-Saint-Georges is the town that gives the Côte de Nuits its name. Its Pinot Noir is the sturdiest of the Côte: dark cherry and plum, earth, an iron or gamey note and firm tannin for Burgundy, needing a few years to soften.

It has no Grand Cru but many Premier Crus, including Les Saint-Georges and Les Pruliers on the south side of the town. The town is also a center of the Burgundy trade, home to houses such as Faiveley.

We pour Henri Gouges, the reference name of the village, in a village half-bottle and Les Pruliers Premier Cru, and Grivot's Les Charmois. With the filet, the short rib or game, a Nuits-Saint-Georges is the Burgundy with the backbone.

value.front: What is the style of Nuits-Saint-Georges red?
value.back: The sturdiest Côte de Nuits Pinot: dark cherry, earth and iron, firm tannin. Henri Gouges is its reference grower; Faiveley is based there.

explain.value:
Vosne-Romanée is the most celebrated red wine village in Burgundy, home to Romanée-Conti, La Tâche and Richebourg. Its Pinot Noir is silky, spiced and perfumed: dark cherry, rose and baking spice.

Echézeaux is a large Grand Cru just above the Clos de Vougeot, legally within the commune of Flagey-Echézeaux but sold as part of Vosne. Its wines are generous and fragrant, the friendliest entry to Vosne's Grand Crus.

Domaine Jean Grivot is a family domaine of Vosne-Romanée. We have its Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011, now fifteen years old and coming into forest floor, and its Nuits-Saint-Georges Les Charmois. This is a splurge bottle for a guest who knows Burgundy.

value.front: What is our Grand Cru red Burgundy from Vosne-Romanée?
value.back: Domaine Jean Grivot Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011: silky dark cherry, rose and spice, with forest floor from age. Echézeaux sits above the Clos de Vougeot.

explain.value:
Bourgogne is French for Burgundy, and on a label it marks the regional tier: wine from anywhere in the region, or from vineyards just outside the village boundaries. Bourgogne Rouge is Pinot Noir; Bourgogne Blanc is Chardonnay.

From a good grower these are the best value in Burgundy, often from vines next to famous villages and made exactly like the grander wines, just lighter and ready sooner.

We have four: the Damien Martin Pinot Noir by the glass, Faiveley's Bourgogne Rouge, and Bourgogne Blanc from two Meursault growers, Matrot and Jean-Philippe Fichet. Tell a guest: white Burgundy with a Meursault accent, or red Burgundy at its plainest and freshest.

value.front: What does Bourgogne alone on a label mean?
value.back: The regional tier of Burgundy: Pinot Noir if red, Chardonnay if white. From good growers like Matrot or Fichet, the best value in Burgundy.

explain.value:
Beaujolais lies south of the Mâconnais, a land of granite hills planted almost entirely with Gamay. Most of it makes light, fruity red to drink young; Beaujolais-Villages comes from the better villages in the north.

At the top are ten crus, villages that put only their own name on the label: Morgon, Fleurie, Moulin-à-Vent, Brouilly, Chiroubles and five more. Fleurie is known for floral grace; Morgon, and above all its Côte du Py hill of crumbling rock, for depth and grip.

We pour Jadot's Beaujolais-Villages half-bottle, Coudert's Clos de la Roilette Fleurie and the two Morgon bottles from Lapierre and Foillard. A guest who says they do not like Beaujolais usually means the nouveau; a cru is another wine.

value.front: What is a cru Beaujolais, and which do we pour?
value.back: One of ten top villages that label with their own name. We pour Fleurie from Coudert and Morgon from Lapierre and Foillard.

components.name: The Southern Rhône and Côtes du Rhône

explain.value:
The Southern Rhône is the wide, sunny valley around Orange and Avignon, swept by the mistral wind. Its reds are blends led by Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and others, and taste of ripe red fruit, pepper and garrigue, the wild thyme, rosemary and lavender of the hillsides.

Côtes du Rhône is the broad regional name; above it come the villages, such as Beaumes-de-Venise, Gigondas and Vacqueyras, and at the top Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

We pour the Châteaumar Côtes du Rhône on the breakfast tasting, the Durban by the glass, and Gigondas and Châteauneuf by the bottle. Warm, spicy and generous, these are the reds for the filet, lamb and blackened dishes.

value.front: What is garrigue, and where do you taste it?
value.back: The wild thyme, rosemary and lavender of the southern French hills; you taste it in Southern Rhône reds like our Côtes du Rhône, Gigondas and Châteauneuf.

explain.value:
Châteauneuf-du-Pape, the Pope's new castle, is named for the summer castle of the popes who lived at nearby Avignon in the fourteenth century. It became one of the first French appellations, with rules written in the 1920s and 1930s.

Thirteen grape varieties are allowed, red and white; most wines are Grenache-led with Syrah and Mourvèdre. Many vineyards are covered in large round stones, galets roulés, which store the day's heat. Bottles carry the papal keys and tiara embossed on the glass.

Our three tell three stories: Pegau's traditional Cuvée Réservée, Beaucastel's Mourvèdre-rich Oenothèque 2007 and Vieux Télégraphe's La Crau 2014. Decant and sell with beef and lamb.

value.front: What does Châteauneuf-du-Pape mean, and how many grapes are allowed?
value.back: The Pope's new castle, after the papal summer castle near Avignon. Thirteen varieties are allowed; most wines, like our Pegau, are Grenache-led.

explain.value:
Gigondas and Beaumes-de-Venise are neighboring villages under the Dentelles de Montmirail, a jagged limestone ridge whose name means the lace of Montmirail.

Gigondas makes powerful, Grenache-led reds with Syrah and Mourvèdre, from terraces rising up the slopes: ripe red and black cherry, garrigue, pepper and firm tannin, often called a junior Châteauneuf. Beaumes-de-Venise is famous for its sweet Muscat, but its dry red, Grenache and Syrah, is lighter and juicy.

We pour Domaine de Durban's red by the glass, and Gigondas from Raspail-Ay in a half-bottle and Saint Damien's La Louisianne. Say: the value step to Châteauneuf.

value.front: Why is Gigondas called the value step to Châteauneuf?
value.back: Neighboring Grenache-led reds with Syrah and Mourvèdre, powerful and spicy, at a gentler price. It sits under the Dentelles de Montmirail.

components.name: Côtes de Provence and pale rosé

explain.value:
Provence, between the Rhône and the Riviera, has made wine since ancient Greek settlers founded Marseille, and today it is the world's reference for pale, dry rosé. Côtes de Provence is its largest appellation.

The wines are mostly Grenache with Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Rolle, Vermentino in Italy, a white grape that adds freshness. The palest color comes from pressing the grapes gently and quickly, so the juice barely touches the skins.

Our two are Minuty Prestige by the glass, from above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, and Whispering Angel by the bottle. Peach, strawberry and citrus, dry and light: rosé for the courtyard and for Gulf seafood.

value.front: How does a Provence rosé get its pale color?
value.back: Gentle, quick pressing so the juice barely touches the red skins. Mostly Grenache, Cinsault and Rolle; ours are Minuty and Whispering Angel.

explain.value:
Bandol is a small appellation on the Provençal coast between Marseille and Toulon, with terraced slopes in an amphitheater facing the sea. It is the home of Mourvèdre, which needs this heat and sea light to ripen.

Its reds must be at least half Mourvèdre and are aged at least eighteen months in wood, dark, gamey and long-lived. Its rosé, Mourvèdre with Grenache and Cinsault, is the most serious in Provence: salmon-pink, savory and structured, with garrigue and blood orange.

Lucien Peyraud of Domaine Tempier helped make Bandol its own appellation in 1941. We pour the Tempier Bandol rosé, the rosé for a guest who wants pink with real substance.

value.front: What makes Bandol rosé more serious than most?
value.back: Mourvèdre leads it, with Grenache and Cinsault: savory, structured and salmon-pink. Domaine Tempier, the rosé we pour, helped found the appellation in 1941.

explain.value:
The Alpilles are a small range of limestone hills in western Provence, near Saint-Rémy and the hilltop village of Les Baux, a land of olives, wild herbs and vineyards scented with garrigue.

The local appellation, Les Baux-de-Provence, has rules about grapes, and some growers chose to work outside them. Domaine de Trévallon famously planted a blend the rules did not allow, so it labels its wines with the wider regional name, Alpilles, rather than the appellation; they are among the most sought-after wines of the south.

Ours is the rare Trévallon Blanc 2016, Marsanne-led, rich with apricot, honey, fennel and herbs. Sell it as a collector's white.

value.front: Why is Trévallon labeled Alpilles, not an appellation?
value.back: Its grape blend falls outside the local appellation rules, so it uses the regional name. Our Trévallon Blanc 2016 is a rare, collector's white.

explain.value:
Roussillon is French Catalonia, the hot corner of France against the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean, near Perpignan. It is famous for vins doux naturels, sweet wines fortified during fermentation.

Banyuls comes from steep schist terraces above the fishing port of Banyuls-sur-Mer; it must be at least half Grenache noir. Rivesaltes, from the plain and hills further north, uses Grenache in its three colors and Muscat. Both may age for decades in old casks, often in the sun, turning amber and nutty.

We pour the La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva with the dinner tasting's dessert, and the Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 is on the list: fifty-one years in wood.

value.front: What are Banyuls and Rivesaltes?
value.back: Sweet fortified wines, vins doux naturels, from Roussillon in French Catalonia, mostly Grenache. Our Banyuls pours with dessert; the Riveyrac Rivesaltes is a 1975.

explain.value:
The Jura is a small, cool, hilly region between Burgundy and Switzerland, with its own grapes and traditions. Arbois is its main wine town, and it is also where Louis Pasteur grew up and did his research on fermentation.

Its whites, from Chardonnay and Savagnin, are made either topped up in the usual way or deliberately left under a veil of yeast, which gives a nutty, savory, sherry-like tang. The most famous is Vin Jaune, which ages over six years and is sold in a squat 62 cl bottle, the clavelin.

Domaine du Pélican is the Arbois estate founded by the d'Angerville family of Volnay. Our bottle is its Vin Jaune 2016.

value.front: What is special about the Jura's Vin Jaune bottle?
value.back: It is a squat 62 cl clavelin, said to be what remains of a liter after six years of aging under yeast. Ours is Domaine du Pélican from Arbois.

components.name: The Médoc and the Left Bank

explain.value:
The Médoc is the long gravel peninsula north of the city of Bordeaux, on the left bank of the Gironde estuary. Its deep, warm gravel drains well and suits Cabernet Sauvignon, which leads the blends with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.

Four villages hold most of the great estates: Margaux, known for perfume; Saint-Julien, for balance; Pauillac, for power, home to three of the five first growths; and Saint-Estèphe, in the north, for firm, earthy structure. Their châteaux were ranked into five growths in 1855.

On our list are Pichon Lalande and Grand-Puy-Lacoste from Pauillac, Talbot from Saint-Julien, La Chapelle de Meyney from Saint-Estèphe, and the Moulin d'Issan from the team at Château d'Issan in Margaux. These are the classic steak reds.

value.front: Name the four great villages of the Médoc and their styles.
value.back: Margaux for perfume, Saint-Julien for balance, Pauillac for power and Saint-Estèphe for firm structure. All Cabernet-led, on gravel by the Gironde.

explain.value:
Pauillac is the most famous village of the Médoc, home to three of the five first growths, Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild. Its deep gravel ridges give the most powerful, long-lived Cabernet Sauvignon in Bordeaux: blackcurrant, cedar, cigar box and graphite, with firm tannin.

Classic Pauillac smells of what the British trade calls cigar box and pencil shavings, and with age it softens into a long, savory finish.

We have two: Château Pichon Lalande, a second growth across the road from Latour, with more Merlot than its neighbors, and Grand-Puy-Lacoste, a fifth growth often called one of the best values in the Médoc. With the Chateaubriand, a mature Pauillac is the textbook pairing.

value.front: Which two Pauillac estates do we pour, and how were they ranked in 1855?
value.back: Pichon Lalande, a second growth across the road from Latour, and Grand-Puy-Lacoste, a fifth growth known for value. Powerful, cedar-scented Cabernet.

explain.value:
The Right Bank lies east of the Dordogne river, around the medieval hill town of Saint-Émilion and its neighbor Pomerol. Here the soils are clay and limestone, cooler than the Médoc's gravel, and Merlot leads with Cabernet Franc.

The wines are plusher and rounder than the Left Bank's: plum, black cherry, cocoa and a fresh limestone edge, with finer tannin. Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised about every ten years, unlike the fixed 1855 list.

Our bottle is Château Troplong Mondot, on one of the highest points of the Saint-Émilion plateau, in a half-bottle from 2020. Offer it to a guest who wants red Bordeaux that is generous and soft.

value.front: How does Right Bank Bordeaux differ from the Médoc?
value.back: Merlot leads on clay and limestone instead of Cabernet on gravel: plusher plum and cocoa, finer tannin. Ours is Troplong Mondot from Saint-Émilion.

explain.value:
Bordeaux Supérieur is a regional appellation that covers the whole Bordeaux area, with slightly stricter rules than plain Bordeaux: riper grapes and a longer wait before release. It is where great estates often place wine from vineyards outside their village appellation.

Margaux, the most southerly of the Médoc's great villages, is known for perfumed, silky reds. Château d'Issan is one of its oldest estates, a moated castle whose vineyards partly lie on low ground by the estuary that is not entitled to the Margaux name.

Our Moulin d'Issan by the glass is made by the d'Issan team from those vineyards: a Cabernet blend with cassis, plum and cedar, a taste of the Médoc at a glass price.

value.front: Why is Moulin d'Issan a Bordeaux Supérieur, not a Margaux?
value.back: It comes from Château d'Issan vineyards on low ground outside the Margaux appellation. The d'Issan team make it: cassis, plum and cedar by the glass.

explain.value:
Sauternes and Barsac lie about twenty-five miles south of the city of Bordeaux, where the cold little Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne. In autumn the meeting makes morning mist and sunny afternoons, the weather that brings noble rot to Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc and makes some of the world's great sweet wines.

The estates were classified in 1855: Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, then first and second growths. Barsac, on limestone, is a village within Sauternes whose wines may use either name and tend to be a little fresher.

Ours are Yquem, Suduiraut and Gilette from Preignac and Sauternes, and Climens from Barsac. Serve small pours, well chilled, with Bananas Foster, bread pudding or foie gras.

value.front: Why do Sauternes and Barsac make great sweet wine?
value.back: The cold Ciron meets the warm Garonne, giving autumn mist then sun, which brings noble rot. Ours include Yquem, Suduiraut, Gilette and Climens.

explain.value:
The Mosel winds through western Germany from the French border to the Rhine at Koblenz, its vineyards on some of the steepest slopes in Europe. The slate soil, blue or red, holds the sun's warmth and gives Riesling a stony, mineral edge.

Mosel Riesling is light, often only 8 to 11 percent alcohol, with racy acidity and green apple, peach and lime, made from dry to lusciously sweet. The famous villages of the Middle Mosel, Ürzig, Erden and Wehlen, face the sun across the river; the Saar, a cooler tributary, gives the steeliest wines of all, at the Scharzhofberg.

Our Mosel bottles include the Berres and Dr. Hermann by the glass, Stein, Prüm and Egon Müller.

value.front: Why does Mosel Riesling taste so light and stony?
value.back: Steep slate slopes and a cool climate give racy acidity, low alcohol and a mineral edge. Ours include Berres, Dr. Hermann, Prüm and Egon Müller.

explain.value:
The Nahe is a small river and wine region between the Mosel and the Rhine, with an unusual patchwork of soils from volcanic rock and porphyry to slate and sandstone, sometimes changing within a single vineyard.

Its Riesling sits between styles: the Mosel's fine acidity with more body and a smoky, stony depth. Niederhausen's Hermannshöhle, beneath a cliff, is called its greatest vineyard; Dönnhoff of Oberhausen is its most famous grower, with the tiny Brücke by the old bridge over the river.

We have two Dönnhoff gold capsule Auslesen and Hexamer's Rheingrafenberg Spätlese from Meddersheim. Sweet but racy, they suit fruit desserts and the Baked Apple.

value.front: Who is the Nahe's most famous grower, and which vineyards do we pour?
value.back: Dönnhoff of Oberhausen: we pour its Oberhäuser Brücke and Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle Auslese Goldkapsel. Hexamer of Meddersheim is our other Nahe grower.

explain.value:
Rheinhessen is Germany's largest wine region, the rolling land inside the bend of the Rhine south of Mainz. For decades it was known for cheap, sweet export wine; since the 1990s a generation of growers has made it one of the most exciting places in Germany.

Its limestone hills, around villages such as Flörsheim-Dalsheim, give Riesling with depth and a stony freshness; dry wines now lead, but great sweet wines are still made in good years.

Weingut Keller of Flörsheim-Dalsheim is the most admired of those growers. Our bottle is its PIUS Auslese, a sweet blend whose varieties change by vintage, in a half-bottle.

value.front: Which Rheinhessen grower do we pour, and what is the wine?
value.back: Weingut Keller of Flörsheim-Dalsheim, among Germany's most admired. Its PIUS Auslese is a sweet blend; the varieties change by vintage.

explain.value:
The Kamptal and the Wachau are two of Austria's great white wine valleys along the Danube, west of Vienna. The Wachau is a narrow gorge of steep stone terraces; the Kamptal, following the little Kamp river to the town of Langenlois, is a little wider and warmer.

Both grow Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, dry, on loess and on rock. The Kamptal's Heiligenstein is a famous hill of desert sandstone above Zöbing; the Wachau's Honivogl at Spitz is one of its most famous Grüner sites.

Our Kamptal wines come from Bründlmayer and Loimer of Langenlois; our Wachau bottle is Hirtzberger's Honivogl Smaragd. Say: dry, precise and peppery, with food in mind.

value.front: What do the Kamptal and Wachau grow, and in what style?
value.back: Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, dry, on Danube terraces west of Vienna. Ours are Bründlmayer and Loimer from Langenlois and Hirtzberger from Spitz.

explain.value:
Burgenland is Austria's easternmost region, on the Hungarian border. Its heart is the Neusiedlersee, a huge, shallow lake surrounded by reeds and smaller pools.

In autumn, mist rises from the water every morning and the afternoon sun burns it away. That rhythm brings noble rot to the grapes almost every year, which is rare anywhere else, so the village of Illmitz on the eastern shore makes sweet wines that rival Sauternes: Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

Kracher of Illmitz made the region famous for them. Ours is its Cuvée Auslese, Welschriesling with Chardonnay: pear, mandarin and passion fruit, creamy and fresh.

value.front: Why does the Neusiedlersee make sweet wine almost every year?
value.back: Morning mist off the shallow lake and afternoon sun bring noble rot nearly every autumn. Kracher of Illmitz, ours, made the region famous.

explain.value:
Rías Baixas is the Atlantic coast of Galicia, in Spain's green north-west corner, named for its rías, long fjord-like inlets where the sea runs deep into the land. It is cool, wet and windy, and famous for seafood: mussels, octopus, oysters and percebes.

Albariño covers almost all the vineyards, often trained high on granite posts to catch the wind and dry the grapes. The Salnés valley, the coolest and most coastal part, gives the most saline, aromatic wines.

Our Pazo das Bruxas by the glass is made by Familia Torres; Do Ferreiro's Cepas Vellas is from very old vines in the Salnés. Lead with them for oysters, crab claws and Gulf fish.

value.front: What are the rías of Rías Baixas?
value.back: Long fjord-like sea inlets on Galicia's Atlantic coast. The cool, salty air gives Albariño its saline snap: our Pazo das Bruxas and Do Ferreiro.

explain.value:
Bierzo is a mountain valley in north-west Spain, in Castilla y León but next to Galicia, on the old pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela. Its climate mixes Atlantic rain and continental heat, on slate and clay slopes.

It was long a forgotten region until the late twentieth century, when a few growers revived its old vines of Mencía for red and Godello for white. Raúl Pérez, born there, is among the best known of them.

Our bottle is his Ultreia Godello; ultreia is an old pilgrims' greeting on the Camino. It is a white of real weight with lemon, pear, almond and a saline edge.

value.front: Where is Bierzo, and what do we pour from it?
value.back: A mountain valley in north-west Spain beside Galicia, on the pilgrim road. We pour Raúl Pérez's Ultreia Godello, a textured, saline white.

explain.value:
Rioja is Spain's most famous red wine region, along the Ebro river in the north. Rioja Alta, the higher, cooler western part, gives its most elegant wines, and the town of Haro is its historic center, with a cluster of great bodegas in the Barrio de la Estación, the station quarter, built beside the railway in the late nineteenth century to ship wine to France and beyond.

Rioja is defined by Tempranillo and by aging: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva mark longer times in barrel and bottle, traditionally American oak.

La Rioja Alta S.A., founded in the station quarter in 1890, makes our Gran Reserva 904.

value.front: What is the station quarter of Haro?
value.back: The cluster of historic Rioja bodegas built beside Haro's railway to ship wine. La Rioja Alta, maker of our 904, was founded there in 1890.

explain.value:
Sherry comes from a triangle of towns in Andalucía, southern Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda. The vineyards are on albariza, a brilliant white chalky soil that holds winter rain through the scorching summer.

Sanlúcar sits at the mouth of the Guadalquivir river, facing the Atlantic. Its cool, humid sea air keeps the flor yeast thick all year, so its fino-style sherry, called Manzanilla, is the lightest and most delicate, with a salty tang only Sanlúcar gives.

La Cigarrera is a family bodega there. Our half-bottle of its Manzanilla is a bold aperitif, chilled, for oysters and fried seafood.

value.front: Why can Manzanilla only come from Sanlúcar de Barrameda?
value.back: The town's cool, humid Atlantic air keeps the flor yeast thick, giving the lightest, saltiest sherry. Ours is La Cigarrera.

explain.value:
Piemonte, at the foot of the Alps in north-west Italy, is one of the world's great wine regions. Around Alba it makes Barolo and Barbaresco from Nebbiolo; around Asti, in the hills of the Monferrato, it is known for Barbera and for sweet, sparkling Moscato d'Asti.

Barbera d'Asti is the everyday red of the region: juicy, bright and low in tannin, drunk with every kind of food. The villages, such as Castagnole Monferrato, are crowned with old castles and churches above the vines.

La Miraja works from old castle cellars at Castagnole Monferrato, and its Le Masche Barbera d'Asti is our glass.

value.front: Where does our Barbera come from?
value.back: Asti, in the Monferrato hills of Piemonte. La Miraja works from old castle cellars at Castagnole Monferrato; Le Masche is its Barbera d'Asti.

explain.value:
Montalcino is a medieval hill town south of Siena in Tuscany, world famous for Brunello di Montalcino, a long-lived red from Sangiovese.

Brunello is in fact the newcomer. For centuries the town's famous wine was Moscadello, a sweet white from Moscato Bianco, praised by Renaissance writers. It almost vanished in the twentieth century and was revived when its own appellation came in 1984.

Castello Banfi, the large estate founded by an American importing family, makes a late harvest Moscadello called Florus. Our bottle is from 2011: a sweet Tuscan rarity with honey, apricot and candied orange.

value.front: Montalcino is famous for Brunello: what came first?
value.back: Moscadello, a sweet white from Moscato Bianco. Castello Banfi's late harvest Florus, on our list, keeps that old tradition alive.

explain.value:
Valpolicella is a set of valleys running down from the Lessini mountains to Verona in north-east Italy. The Classico zone, around Negrar, Fumane and San Pietro in Cariano, is the original heart of the region.

It makes four wines from Corvina, Corvinone and Rondinella: light Valpolicella; Ripasso; Amarone, dry and powerful from dried grapes; and Recioto, the oldest of them, sweet from dried grapes. Recioto is thought to be the wine of Roman Verona, and Amarone was born as a Recioto that fermented dry.

Giuseppe Quintarelli worked in the hills above Negrar. Our Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997 is a rare, sweet, velvety red.

value.front: What is Recioto della Valpolicella?
value.back: A sweet red from Corvina and partners dried for months before pressing. The oldest Valpolicella style; ours is Quintarelli's 1997 from Negrar.

explain.value:
The Douro valley in northern Portugal is one of the oldest demarcated wine regions in the world. Its vineyards are carved into terraces on schist slopes above the river, baking hot in summer.

Port is made up the valley at the quintas, the wine estates, then traditionally sent down the river to age in the cool lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across from the city of Porto. The Douro Superior, the far eastern end towards Spain, is hottest and wildest; Taylor Fladgate's Quinta de Vargellas is there.

Many great Port houses were founded by British merchants, which is why so many names are English: Taylor, Graham, Dow, Sandeman. Our list carries Ports from Dow's, Graham's, Taylor Fladgate, Niepoort, Sandeman and Feist.

value.front: Why do so many Port houses have English names?
value.back: British merchants founded many of them to ship Port. The wine grows on Douro schist terraces and ages in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia.

explain.value:
Madeira is a volcanic Portuguese island in the Atlantic, west of the coast of Morocco. Its wine was the wine of early America: ships called there on the way west, and the barrels were found to improve in the heat of the hold on long voyages.

Today producers recreate that heat on the island, then age the wine for years; once opened, a bottle lasts for months. The four classic grapes name the sweetness: Sercial, driest, then Verdelho, Bual and Malvasia, sweetest.

Our bottle is the Broadbent Single Cask Malvasia 2009, a 500 ml bottle from one cask of one harvest. Its tang and caramel suit the Bread Pudding and nuts.

value.front: Why does Madeira last so long once opened?
value.back: It has already been heated and aged with air for years, so it cannot be spoiled by more. The island's wine was a favorite of early America.

explain.value:
Napa Valley is a valley about thirty miles long, north of San Francisco Bay, and America's most famous wine region. Fog from the bay cools its southern end, while the north, around Calistoga, is warmer; mountains on both sides give its hillside wines.

It is above all Cabernet Sauvignon country, and its middle, around Rutherford and Oakville, is the heart of it: Rutherford is famous for a dusty, cocoa-like note growers call Rutherford dust. Napa's reputation was made at the Paris tasting of 1976, when its wines beat top French ones.

Our Napa wines include Inglenook Rubicon from Rutherford, Paul Hobbs from Coombsville, Duckhorn, Montelena, Kongsgaard, Grgich Hills and Schramsberg.

value.front: What is Rutherford dust?
value.back: The dusty, cocoa-like note growers find in Cabernet from Rutherford, in the heart of Napa Valley. Our Inglenook Rubicon comes from there.

explain.value:
Coombsville is a small district in the south-east corner of Napa Valley, in the hills east of the city of Napa, and one of the valley's cooler corners. Breezes and fog from San Pablo Bay keep temperatures down, and volcanic soils from an ancient caldera drain well.

The result is Cabernet Sauvignon that ripens slowly and evenly, keeping freshness and fine tannin alongside Napa's dark fruit. It became its own American Viticultural Area in 2011, and it is named for Nathan Coombs, who founded the city of Napa.

Our dinner tasting pours the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet with the Rohan duck: dark fruit and cocoa with the freshness of a cool site.

value.front: Why does the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet stay fresh?
value.back: Coombsville is one of Napa's cooler corners, near San Pablo Bay, so Cabernet ripens slowly and keeps freshness. It pours with the Rohan duck.

components.name: Sonoma County and Dry Creek Valley

explain.value:
Sonoma County lies west of Napa, between the Mayacamas mountains and the Pacific, and it is bigger and more varied, from foggy coast to warm inland valleys.

Dry Creek Valley, north-west of Healdsburg, is warm by day and cool at night, with benchland gravel that has grown Zinfandel since the nineteenth century; many of its old field-blend vineyards survive, including Lytton Springs. The Chalk Hill area, in the hills east of Windsor, is known for rich Chardonnay.

Our Sonoma bottles are Ridge's Lytton Springs, Three Valleys and Essence, and the Chalk Hill Chardonnay. Sell Sonoma as California with a little more variety and old-vine character than Napa.

value.front: What is Dry Creek Valley known for?
value.back: Old-vine Zinfandel field blends on warm benchland in Sonoma County, such as Ridge's Lytton Springs on our list, planted from 1901.

explain.value:
The Santa Cruz Mountains run along the coast south of San Francisco, with vineyards high on ridges above the fog, some over two thousand feet up. Cool nights, thin soils and fractured limestone give Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay with freshness and structure rather than plush ripeness.

Ridge Vineyards' Monte Bello estate sits near the top of one ridge. Its 1971 Cabernet came fifth among the reds at the Paris tasting of 1976 and won the thirtieth anniversary re-tasting outright in 2006.

Our Ridge Estate Cabernet comes from vineyards around Monte Bello: blackcurrant, cedar and graphite, structured and savory, in a half-bottle.

value.front: Which Ridge wine won the 2006 re-tasting of the Judgment of Paris?
value.back: Monte Bello 1971, from the Santa Cruz Mountains. Our Ridge Estate Cabernet half-bottle comes from vineyards around Monte Bello, high on the ridge.

explain.value:
The Sta. Rita Hills are in Santa Barbara County, in the west of the Santa Ynez Valley. The valley runs east to west, unusually for California, so cold Pacific air and fog pour straight in, making it one of the coolest wine areas in the state.

That cool, windy climate gives Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with bright acidity and a lean, Burgundian line. The Sanford & Benedict vineyard, planted in 1971, was its pioneer.

Our wines from here are the Gainey Chardonnay by the glass, Sandhi, and Au Bon Climat's Sanford & Benedict Chardonnay. Sell them as California fruit with Burgundian freshness.

value.front: Why are the Sta. Rita Hills so cool?
value.back: The valley runs east to west, so Pacific fog and wind pour in. Chardonnay keeps bright acidity: our Gainey, Sandhi and Au Bon Climat.

explain.value:
California's North Coast covers Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino and Lake counties. Its coolest corners, near the bay and the ocean, grow Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with the high acidity that sparkling wine needs.

Several producers make sparkling wine there by the traditional method, the same method as Champagne, including second fermentation in bottle and years on the lees. Schramsberg, in the hills of Calistoga, was a pioneer, and its Blanc de Blancs was poured at the Toast to Peace in Beijing in 1972.

On our list are Schramsberg's Blanc de Blancs half-bottle and its Mirabelle rosé, the Louis Pommery rosé from California and Duckhorn's North Coast Sauvignon Blanc. Say sparkling wine, never Champagne.

value.front: What do we call Schramsberg or Mirabelle at the table?
value.back: Sparkling wine, never Champagne: they are made in California by the traditional method. Schramsberg was poured at the 1972 Toast to Peace.

explain.value:
The Willamette Valley in Oregon runs south from Portland between the Coast Range and the Cascades. Its cool, rainy climate is a cousin of Burgundy's, and since the 1960s it has become America's leading home of Pinot Noir and, increasingly, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

Its hills, such as the Dundee Hills with red volcanic soil and the Eola-Amity Hills, give Pinot Noir with red cherry, cranberry and forest floor, light on its feet and earthy.

We pour Argyle's sparkling wine by the glass, and Bergstrom and Ken Wright Pinot Noir. Say: Burgundy's grape with Oregon's bright fruit.

value.front: Why is the Willamette Valley compared with Burgundy?
value.back: A cool, rainy climate suited to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Our Argyle sparkling, Bergstrom and Ken Wright Pinot Noir come from there.

components.name: English sparkling wine: Kent and Sussex

explain.value:
England's south coast is now a serious sparkling wine region. The chalk of the South Downs and the North Downs in Kent and Sussex is the same seam that surfaces in Champagne, and a warming climate lets Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier ripen just enough to keep high acidity.

The wines are made by the traditional method and taste of green apple, lemon and red currant, bright and fine. Ridgeview at Ditchling in Sussex and Chapel Down at Tenterden in Kent, England's largest producer, are among the best known.

We pour Ridgeview's Bloomsbury and Chapel Down's rosé. They make a fun talking point for a guest who has never tried English wine.

value.front: What links English sparkling wine with Champagne?
value.back: The same chalk seam and the same grapes and method. Ours are Ridgeview Bloomsbury from Sussex and Chapel Down rosé from Kent.

explain.value:
Santorini is the volcanic Greek island in the Aegean whose eruption, more than three thousand years ago, left a flooded caldera and a soil of pumice and ash. There is almost no rain, and fierce winds blow across the island.

Growers train vines low into round baskets, kouloura, which shelter the grapes from wind and sand. Phylloxera never reached the island, so the vines grow on their own roots, many very old.

The great grape is Assyrtiko, bone dry, salty and electric. Ours is Gaia Wines' Wild Ferment, fermented with the island's own yeasts.

value.front: What is a kouloura on Santorini?
value.back: A vine trained low into a round basket to shelter the grapes from fierce wind. The island's Assyrtiko, like our Gaia, grows on its own old roots.

explain.value:
Kumeu is a small district north-west of Auckland, on New Zealand's North Island. It is warmer and more humid than the famous South Island regions, with clay soils, and it has a long history of family wineries founded by immigrants from Croatia.

New Zealand is best known for Sauvignon Blanc from Marlborough, but Kumeu has made its name with Chardonnay in a Burgundian style: citrus, white peach, hazelnut and a fine, mineral finish.

Kumeu River, run by the Brajkovich family, is its leader. We pour its Estate Chardonnay, a smart alternative for a guest who loves white Burgundy.

value.front: What is Kumeu River known for, and from where?
value.back: Burgundian style Chardonnay from Kumeu, near Auckland on New Zealand's North Island, made by the Brajkovich family. Ours is the Estate.

explain.value:
The Niagara Peninsula lies in Ontario, Canada, between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. The lakes temper the climate, and a long escarpment traps the lake air, so vines survive the winter.

Canadian winters are reliably cold enough to freeze grapes on the vine, which makes Niagara one of the world's great sources of icewine: grapes are picked frozen, often at night, and pressed while still frozen, leaving only a few drops of very sweet juice.

Inniskillin, founded at Niagara-on-the-Lake in 1975, put Canadian icewine on the world map. Ours is its rare red icewine from Cabernet Franc.

value.front: Why is Niagara one of the great icewine regions?
value.back: Winters reliably freeze grapes on the vine, while the lakes help vines survive. Inniskillin of Niagara made Canadian icewine famous.

explain.value:
The traditional method, méthode champenoise in Champagne, is how every Champagne and our best sparkling wines get their bubbles. First a still, dry, tart base wine is made and blended. Then it is bottled with a little sugar and yeast and capped, and a second fermentation happens inside the bottle; the carbon dioxide cannot escape, so it dissolves into the wine.

The dead yeast, the lees, then rests in the bottle for months or years, adding fine bubbles and a brioche, toasty depth. The bottles are turned and tipped neck down, riddling, the frozen plug of yeast is shot out, disgorging, and a final dose of wine and sugar is added before the cork goes in.

Crémant, Argyle, Schramsberg, Mirabelle and the English wines are all made this way; only the place differs.

value.front: Where does the second fermentation happen in the traditional method?
value.back: Inside the bottle the guest is served. The yeast then rests there on its lees, is riddled and disgorged, and a final dose is added.

explain.value:
Crémant is the name for French sparkling wine made by the traditional method outside Champagne, in regions such as Alsace, Burgundy, the Loire and Limoux, in the Languedoc. The rules are strict and close to Champagne's: hand harvesting, gentle whole-bunch pressing, a second fermentation in bottle and at least nine months on the lees.

Each region uses its own grapes. Crémant d'Alsace is often Pinot Blanc, Riesling or Chardonnay, and Crémant d'Alsace rosé must be all Pinot Noir.

Our Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d'Alsace by the glass shows the point: strawberry and red currant, dry, with a creamy mousse, made the same way as Champagne at a friendlier price. Never call it Champagne; call it Crémant, or French sparkling rosé.

value.front: What is a Crémant, and how is ours different from Champagne?
value.back: French sparkling wine made by the traditional method outside Champagne. Our Pierre Sparr is all Pinot Noir from Alsace: same method, different place, gentler price.

components.name: Dosage: Brut, Extra Brut and Demi-Sec

explain.value:
Dosage is the finishing addition, usually wine with sugar, after disgorgement and before the final cork. The sweetness term on a Champagne label describes the sugar in the finished wine, not simply the amount added at this step.

Extra Brut contains 0 to 6 grams per liter; Brut, less than 12; Extra Dry, 12 to 17; Sec, 17 to 32; Demi-Sec, 32 to 50. Brut Nature requires less than 3 grams per liter and no added sugar after the second fermentation. Extra Brut and Brut overlap, so their names alone cannot rank two bottles by sweetness. Acidity and other features also affect how dry a wine tastes.

Our house Brennan's Essential is Extra Brut. Check the current bottle and producer information before quoting its exact dosage or comparing it with another Champagne. Demi-Sec is a sweeter category to consider with dessert; taste and match the actual dish.

value.front: What do Extra Brut, Brut and Demi-Sec tell you about Champagne?
value.back: Finished sugar content: Extra Brut, 0 to 6 grams per liter; Brut, less than 12; Demi-Sec, 32 to 50. Extra Brut and Brut overlap, so labels alone cannot rank two bottles. Our house Champagne is Extra Brut; confirm its current dosage.

explain.value:
Most Champagne is non-vintage, written NV: a blend of several harvests rather than one. In a cool northern region where some years ripen poorly, blending lets a house make the same style every year.

Each year the cellar master tastes dozens or hundreds of base wines from different villages, grapes and years and builds the blend, using reserve wines, older wines kept back from earlier harvests, to add depth and keep the house style steady. Non-vintage Champagne must rest at least fifteen months in bottle before release; good houses wait much longer.

Krug takes this furthest, blending more than a hundred wines from many years, and numbers each edition. Bollinger keeps its reserve wines in magnums. Say: NV means the house style, the same glass every time.

value.front: What does NV on a Champagne mean, and why do houses do it?
value.back: Non-vintage: a blend of several harvests, with reserve wines, so the house style tastes the same each year. It rests at least fifteen months before release.

explain.value:
A vintage Champagne is made from the grapes of a single year, printed on the label, and houses make one only when the harvest is good enough to stand alone, usually a few times a decade. It must age at least three years before release, and the great ones far longer.

A vintage wine shows the character of its year: the warmth of 2009, the freshness of 2013. Prestige cuvées, such as Rare and Billecart-Salmon's Elisabeth Salmon rosé, are usually vintage wines from the best vineyards with long aging.

On our list: Rare 2012 by the glass and Rare 2013 by the bottle, Pol Roger Blanc de Blancs 2015, Billecart's Elisabeth Salmon 2009, and from elsewhere Argyle 2022 and Schramsberg's Blanc de Blancs 2021. Always read the vintage on the label.

value.front: When does a Champagne house make a vintage wine?
value.back: Only in a harvest good enough to stand alone. It shows that year's character and ages at least three years; Rare, Pol Roger 2015 and Elisabeth Salmon 2009 are ours.

components.name: Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs

say.value: blahn duh BLAHN; blahn duh NWAHR

explain.value:
Blanc de Blancs means white from whites: a sparkling wine made only from white grapes, in Champagne almost always Chardonnay. It is the leanest, most citrus and chalky style, elegant and long-lived.

Blanc de Noirs means white from blacks: a white sparkling wine made only from the black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier, pressed so gently that the juice runs clear. It is fuller and rounder, with red apple and red berry depth.

Ours: Larmandier-Bernier's Longitude, Pol Roger's vintage, Veuve Fourny and Schramsberg are Blanc de Blancs, ideal with oysters and caviar; Bollinger's PNTX20, all Pinot Noir, is a Blanc de Noirs, ideal with richer dishes.

value.front: What is the difference between Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs?
value.back: Blanc de Blancs is from white grapes, Chardonnay: lean and citrus. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier: fuller.

explain.value:
Rosé Champagne is the only French wine allowed to be made pink by blending red and white wine. Most houses add a little still red wine, usually Pinot Noir from villages such as Bouzy or Aÿ, to the white base before the second fermentation, which gives a reliable color and red-fruit flavor.

The other way, saignée or maceration, leaves crushed black grapes on their skins for a short time until the juice turns pink. It gives deeper color and more structure, and is rarer.

Most of our rosés, Moët, Taittinger, Paul Bara, Chartogne-Taillet and Veuve Fourny, use the blending method. Rosé Champagne has a little more body than white, so it suits salmon, duck and the Bananas Foster.

value.front: How do most houses make rosé Champagne pink?
value.back: They blend in a little still red wine, usually Pinot Noir, before the second fermentation. The rarer way leaves black grapes briefly on their skins.

explain.value:
Lees are the spent yeast cells left after fermentation. Leaving a wine in contact with them, instead of drawing it off, slowly changes it: the cells break down and release compounds that add a creamy texture, roundness and flavors of bread, brioche and toast.

In Champagne and every traditional method wine the lees age inside the bottle, which is where the toasty notes and fine, creamy bubbles come from; the longer, the finer. In Muscadet the wine rests on its lees in tank through the winter, sur lie, and the best for two years or more, gaining body and a savory depth.

So when a guest asks why a Champagne tastes of brioche, the answer is the lees, not oak or added flavor.

value.front: Why does a Champagne taste of brioche and toast?
value.back: Time on its lees, the spent yeast in the bottle. Muscadet rests on its lees in tank too, for texture and savory depth.

explain.value:
Most Champagne is fermented in steel tanks, which keeps the fruit pure. A few houses ferment some or all of their base wines in oak barrels instead, the old way, which adds roundness, a gentle oxidative richness and a toasty, nutty depth.

Sous Bois means under wood: Billecart-Salmon's Sous Bois has every base wine fermented in oak. Bollinger ferments part of its wine in old barrels, which is one reason its Special Cuvée is so rich and structured; Krug ferments in small old casks too.

Our Billecart-Salmon Sous Bois magnum, labeled for Brennan's 80th anniversary, and the Bollinger Special Cuvée show the style. Say: richer and nuttier, a Champagne for food.

value.front: What does Sous Bois on a Champagne label mean?
value.back: Under wood: the base wines were fermented in oak barrels, giving roundness and a toasty, nutty depth. Our 80th anniversary magnum is Billecart's Sous Bois.

components.name: Barrel fermentation and oak for white wine

explain.value:
Great white Burgundy is usually fermented and aged in small oak barrels, about 228 liters, called pièces. Oak lets in a little air, which rounds the wine, and new barrels add toast, vanilla and spice; most growers use only a share of new oak so the fruit stays in front.

Many also stir the lees in the barrel, bâtonnage, for a creamier texture. The richness of Meursault, the hazelnut of Puligny and the toast of the best California Chardonnay come from this cellar work as much as from the grape.

On our list, Jadot's Meursault, Lafon, Leflaive, Carillon, Pillot, Kongsgaard and Au Bon Climat use barrels; Dauvissat ages part in old oak; the Fichet Château London has only a touch of old oak. Ask a guest whether they like oaky or crisp before you choose.

value.front: Where do the toast and hazelnut in white Burgundy come from?
value.back: Fermentation and aging in small oak barrels, partly new, and stirring the lees. Ask a guest: oaky and rich, or crisp and unoaked?

explain.value:
Malolactic conversion is a second, gentle fermentation carried out by bacteria, not yeast. It turns the wine's sharp malic acid, the acid of green apples, into softer lactic acid, the acid of milk.

The wine becomes rounder and less tart, and a by-product called diacetyl can give a buttery note. Almost every red goes through it; for whites it is a choice. Most white Burgundy does, which adds to its creaminess; many crisp whites do not, to keep their snap.

The Chateau Montelena Chardonnay is famous for avoiding it, so it stays bright and restrained, while richer California and Meursault styles embrace it. When a guest asks for a buttery Chardonnay, this is what they mean.

value.front: What makes a Chardonnay taste buttery?
value.back: Malolactic conversion: bacteria turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, sometimes with a buttery note. Montelena avoids it to stay bright.

explain.value:
Stainless steel tanks are sealed, neutral and easy to keep cool, so wine fermented and aged in them keeps its fresh fruit, aroma and acidity, with nothing added by wood.

That is the choice for wines whose charm is freshness: Albariño, Sauvignon Blanc, Grüner Veltliner and many Rieslings. In Chablis, Domaine Louis Michel is known for making every wine in steel, with no oak at all, which shows Chardonnay's lemon and oyster-shell purity.

On our list, the Pazo das Bruxas Albariño, Louis Michel's Chablis and Kracher's Cuvée Auslese are made in steel, and the sommelier can name others. For a guest who says no oak, these are the wines to name first.

value.front: Which Chablis do we pour that never sees oak?
value.back: Domaine Louis Michel makes every wine in steel tanks, keeping Chardonnay pure: lemon, green apple and oyster shell. Steel keeps freshness.

components.name: French and American oak for red wine

explain.value:
Most fine reds spend months or years in oak barrels. The wood lets in a trickle of air, which softens tannin and deepens color, and new barrels add their own flavor.

French oak, tight-grained, gives subtle cedar, spice and toast; it is the choice of Bordeaux, Burgundy and most Napa Cabernet. American oak, more open-grained, gives sweeter vanilla, coconut and dill, and is traditional in Rioja and for Zinfandel. Large old casks, as at Pegau, add little flavor and simply let the wine breathe.

La Rioja Alta's 904 ages about four years in American oak from its own cooperage; Ridge's Lytton Springs uses American oak; Duckhorn, Talbot and the Bordeaux use French. Vanilla and coconut say American; cedar says French.

value.front: How can you tell French oak from American oak in a red?
value.back: French oak gives subtle cedar, spice and toast; American oak gives sweeter vanilla and coconut, as in our Rioja 904 and Ridge Lytton Springs.

explain.value:
Most red wine is made from grapes taken off their stems and crushed. In Beaujolais and in some traditional cellars, growers ferment whole bunches instead, stems and all, often uncrushed.

In carbonic maceration the whole bunches sit in a tank filled with carbon dioxide; fermentation begins inside each intact berry, before the skins split. The result is very fruity, perfumed and soft in tannin, with notes of strawberry, cherry and sometimes banana or bubblegum in young wine. Whole bunch fermentation in larger wines adds freshness and spice.

Lapierre, Foillard and Coudert use whole bunches for their Beaujolais; Pegau ferments its Châteauneuf with whole bunches in cement. Say: that is why it tastes so juicy and soft.

value.front: What is carbonic maceration, and which of our wines use whole bunches?
value.back: Whole, uncrushed bunches ferment under carbon dioxide, starting inside each berry: juicy and soft. Lapierre, Foillard and Pegau use whole bunches.

explain.value:
Fermentation needs yeast to turn sugar into alcohol. Many wineries add a chosen, cultured yeast for a reliable, clean result. Others rely on native yeasts, the wild ones that live on the grape skins and in the cellar, often called a wild or spontaneous ferment.

Native ferments start slowly and are less predictable, but many growers believe the mix of yeasts adds complexity and a sense of place. It is a key idea of the natural wine movement, which the Beaujolais growers of the Gang of Four helped start.

Gaia's Wild Ferment Assyrtiko is named for it; La Miraja describes native fermentation for Le Masche; Lapierre and Foillard rely on it. Say it plainly: fermented with the grapes' own yeasts.

value.front: What does Gaia's Wild Ferment name mean?
value.back: Fermented with native yeasts, the wild ones from the grape skins and cellar, not added cultured yeast. Many growers believe it adds complexity.

explain.value:
All red grape juice is clear; the color lives in the skins. To make rosé the winemaker controls how long the juice touches the skins.

For pale Provence rosé, the black grapes are pressed straight away, gently, so the juice picks up only the faintest blush: direct pressing. A short maceration of a few hours before pressing gives a deeper pink and more body. Picking early and keeping the juice cold keeps the freshness.

Minuty and Whispering Angel are pale, direct pressed rosés: peach, strawberry and citrus. The Tempier Bandol rosé and Pascal Cotat's Chavignol rosé have more color and structure. Color is a hint, not a promise of sweetness: all four are dry.

value.front: Does a pale rosé mean a sweet rosé?
