value.back: No: color comes from brief skin contact, not sugar. Minuty and Whispering Angel are pale and direct pressed; Tempier is deeper. All four of ours are dry.

explain.value:
German and Austrian quality wines can carry a Prädikat, a word that names how ripe the grapes were at harvest, measured by their sugar. From least to most ripe: Kabinett, Spätlese, late harvest, Auslese, selected bunches, Beerenauslese, selected berries, Trockenbeerenauslese, selected dried berries, and Eiswein, from frozen grapes.

The word describes ripeness at picking, not sweetness in the glass: a Kabinett is usually light and lightly sweet, but can be dry; Auslese and above are usually sweet, the highest often touched by noble rot.

Our ladder runs from Kabinett at Prüm and Egon Müller, through Spätlese at Stein and Hexamer, to Auslese at Dr. Hermann, Dönnhoff, Keller, Prüm and Kracher. Read the word aloud and explain it simply.

value.front: Put Kabinett, Auslese and Spätlese in order of ripeness.
value.back: Kabinett, then Spätlese, late harvest, then Auslese, selected bunches. The words measure ripeness at picking, not sweetness in the glass; Auslese is usually sweet.

explain.value:
Goldkapsel, gold capsule, is a German grower's signal, not a legal category. A grower bottles a richer, more concentrated selection of the same Prädikat, usually from riper or botrytized berries, and dresses it with a gold foil capsule. A long gold capsule, lange Goldkapsel, marks an even finer selection.

So a Goldkapsel Auslese is richer and sweeter than the same grower's plain Auslese, and usually made in small amounts, often in half-bottles.

Our gold capsule wines are Dönnhoff's two Auslesen from the Brücke and the Hermannshöhle, Prüm's Wehlener Sonnenuhr Auslese in magnum and Dr. Hermann's Würzgarten Kranklei Spätlese. Point to the capsule when you present the bottle.

value.front: What does a gold capsule on a German Riesling mean?
value.back: A richer, more concentrated selection of the same Prädikat, chosen by the grower; not a legal term. Our Dönnhoff and Prüm Auslesen wear one.

explain.value:
An off-dry wine has a little sugar left in it, enough to taste as a soft roundness but not as dessert. In a high-acid grape like Riesling the acidity balances the sugar, so the wine tastes juicy rather than sweet.

German growers use feinherb, or halbtrocken, for wines just off dry. The Berres Old Vines by the glass carries about twenty grams of sugar a liter at only 11.5 percent alcohol; Stein's Weihwasser and Palmberg-Terrassen are feinherb.

Off-dry wine is a server's secret weapon with Creole spice, smoke, sweet glazes and the maple on the duck: the touch of sugar cools heat that would make a dry wine taste bitter and hot.

value.front: Why does an off-dry Riesling work with spice?
value.back: A touch of sugar cools the heat, and acidity keeps it juicy. Our Berres has about twenty grams a liter; Stein's feinherb wines are just off dry.

explain.value:
Botrytis cinerea is a mold that, in the right weather, becomes noble rot. It needs misty, humid autumn mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons. The mold pierces the grape skins and the sun dries the berries, which shrivel, losing water while the sugar and acidity concentrate.

The grapes look ruined but make the most luscious sweet wines in the world, tasting of honey, apricot, candied orange, saffron and marmalade. Because the rot spreads unevenly, pickers go through the vineyard many times, taking only the affected berries.

Sauternes and Barsac, Burgenland, the Loire and the highest Prädikat levels in Germany depend on it. On our list: Yquem, Suduiraut, Climens, Gilette, Kracher, Keller and the Grgich Violetta.

value.front: How does noble rot make sweet wine?
value.back: A mold, in misty mornings and sunny afternoons, pierces and shrivels the grapes, concentrating sugar and acidity. It makes Sauternes like Yquem.

explain.value:
Late harvest wine is made from grapes left on the vine well after the normal picking date, so they lose water, shrivel a little and concentrate their sugar. Some are also touched by noble rot.

The result is sweet wine with the grape's own flavors deepened: honeyed apricot, baked fruit and spice. In Alsace it is called Vendanges Tardives and is allowed only for the four noble grapes in years ripe enough; in California and Italy it is simply late harvest.

Ours are Trimbach's Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives, Ridge's Essence Zinfandel, the Grgich Hills Violetta and Banfi's Florus Moscadello. Each is made only in years the weather allows.

value.front: What does Vendanges Tardives on an Alsace label mean?
value.back: Late harvest: grapes left on the vine to concentrate sugar, making a sweet wine in ripe years only. Our Trimbach Gewurztraminer is one.

explain.value:
Icewine, Eiswein in German, is made from grapes left on the vine into winter until they freeze solid, usually at about minus eight degrees Celsius. They are picked frozen, often at night, and pressed while still frozen.

The water stays behind as ice in the press, so only a few drops of very sweet, concentrated juice run out; a whole vine may make a single glass. The wine is intensely sweet with vivid acidity.

Canada, with reliably cold winters, makes more than anywhere. Our Inniskillin Cabernet Franc Icewine is a rare red one: strawberry, raspberry, rhubarb and candied fruit. Serve a small, well-chilled pour with fruit desserts or cheesecake.

value.front: Why is icewine so sweet and so rare?
value.back: Grapes freeze on the vine and are pressed frozen, so the water stays as ice and only drops of concentrated juice run out. Ours is Inniskillin's red.

explain.value:
Appassimento is the Italian art of drying freshly picked grapes before pressing. In Valpolicella the best bunches are laid on bamboo racks or in shallow crates, or hung, in airy lofts for three or four months over the winter.

The grapes lose much of their water and turn half to raisins, concentrating sugar, color and flavor. Fermented fully dry they make Amarone; stopped while still sweet they make Recioto.

Giuseppe Quintarelli dried his grapes this way on racks and in crates, and our Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997 is the result: dark cherry, fig, raisin and chocolate, sweet and velvety, with fresh acidity.

value.front: What is appassimento, and which of our wines uses it?
value.back: Drying grapes for months before pressing to concentrate sugar and flavor. Quintarelli's Recioto della Valpolicella 1997 is made this way.

explain.value:
A vin doux naturel, naturally sweet wine, is made by stopping fermentation partway by adding neutral grape spirit, a process called mutage. The yeast dies, so the grape's own unfermented sugar stays in the wine, and the alcohol rises to about 15 to 18 percent. Port is made the same way.

In Roussillon, Banyuls and Rivesaltes are then aged either fresh and fruity, or oxidatively for years in old casks or glass demijohns left out in the sun, turning amber and tasting of fig, walnut, caramel and coffee.

The La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva on the dinner tasting is aged the oxidative way; the Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 has spent decades in old casks. Banyuls with chocolate is the classic match.

value.front: How is a vin doux naturel like Banyuls kept sweet?
value.back: Grape spirit is added mid-fermentation, mutage, so the yeast stops and the grape's sugar stays. Ours are La Tour Vieille Banyuls and Riveyrac 1975.

explain.value:
Port is made in the Douro by stopping the fermentation of red grapes with grape spirit when about half the sugar has turned to alcohol. The young wine is sweet, strong at about 20 percent and deeply colored.

Because fermentation is cut short, the color and tannin must be pulled from the skins fast, so the grapes are trodden by foot in shallow stone tanks called lagares or worked in modern machines that copy it.

Then the style is set by aging. Ruby styles, including Late Bottled Vintage and Vintage Port, age briefly in large casks and keep their dark fruit; tawny styles age for years in small casks, turning amber and nutty. Our list carries every kind.

value.front: How is Port made sweet and strong?
value.back: Grape spirit stops the fermentation when about half the sugar remains, leaving it sweet at about 20 percent alcohol. Aging then decides ruby or tawny.

explain.value:
Vintage Port is made only in the best years, when a house declares a vintage, usually about three times a decade. The wine spends only about two years in cask, then is bottled young, unfiltered, to age for decades in bottle.

It throws a heavy crust of sediment, so it must stand upright before service and be decanted. Young, it is dense blackberry and chocolate; with age it becomes dried cherry, fig, spice and cedar, its tannin softened.

In good years that are not declared, houses may bottle a single quinta vintage, such as Taylor's Quinta de Vargellas. Our list has declared vintages back to 1977: Dow's and Graham's 2000, Graham's 1983, Niepoort 1987 and Taylor 1977.

value.front: Why must a Vintage Port be decanted?
value.back: It is bottled young and unfiltered after about two years in cask, so it throws a heavy crust of sediment as it ages in bottle.

explain.value:
Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, is Port from a single year, like Vintage Port, but left in wood much longer, four to six years, before bottling. The longer cask time softens it and makes it ready to drink sooner.

Most LBV is filtered and ready on release; traditional unfiltered LBV keeps aging and may throw a little sediment. It gives much of Vintage Port's dark fruit at a gentler price.

Ours are unusual: Feist's 2006 and Sandeman's 1999 have had long bottle age on top of their years in wood, so they are mature and mellow: dark cherry, plum, fig, cocoa and spice. Check for sediment and decant if any.

value.front: How is a Late Bottled Vintage different from Vintage Port?
value.back: Both are one year, but LBV stays four to six years in wood before bottling, so it softens sooner. Ours, Feist 2006 and Sandeman 1999, are mature.

explain.value:
Tawny Port ages for years in small, old casks, where slow contact with air turns its color from ruby to amber and its fruit to walnut, caramel, dried orange peel and coffee. Most tawnies are blends, sold as 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old.

A Colheita is a tawny from a single harvest, colheita in Portuguese, aged at least seven years in cask and often far longer, with the harvest year and the bottling date on the label. Because it has aged with air in cask, it needs no decanting and keeps for weeks once opened.

Niepoort, a family house of Dutch origin, is famous for its Colheitas. Ours is the 1997 in a half-bottle. Serve it slightly cool with pecan desserts and the Bread Pudding.

value.front: What is a Colheita Port?
value.back: A tawny from one harvest, aged at least seven years in cask: walnut, caramel and orange peel. Ours is Niepoort 1997, no decanting needed.

explain.value:
Flor is a living layer of yeast that grows like a pale film on the surface of certain wines left in barrels that are not quite full. It shields the wine from air and feeds on it, giving a sharp, nutty, salty tang: green apple, almond, bread dough.

In southern Spain this is how fino and Manzanilla sherry are made; Sanlúcar's sea air keeps the flor thickest, which is why Manzanilla is so light and salty. In the Jura the same thing happens to Savagnin in barrels never topped up, for more than six years, making Vin Jaune: walnut, curry spice and dried apple.

Our La Cigarrera Manzanilla and the Pélican Vin Jaune are cousins under the skin. Both are bone dry and love salty food and cheese.

value.front: What do Manzanilla and Vin Jaune have in common?
value.back: Both age under flor, a film of yeast on the wine in part-filled barrels, giving a dry, nutty, salty tang. Ours: La Cigarrera and Pélican.

explain.value:
The solera is sherry's system of fractional blending. Barrels are arranged in tiers, called criaderas, with the oldest wine in the bottom row, the solera itself.

Each time wine is drawn for bottling, only part of each bottom barrel is taken. It is refilled from the tier above, and that from the tier above it, and so on, with new wine entering at the top. The young wine takes on the character of the old, and the solera keeps the style steady for decades; some soleras were begun more than a century ago.

That is why most sherry, including our La Cigarrera Manzanilla, carries no vintage: every glass holds a little of every year.

value.front: Why does our Manzanilla carry no vintage?
value.back: It comes from a solera: tiers of barrels where each draw is topped up from younger tiers, so every glass blends many years and the style stays steady.

explain.value:
Madeira is the only wine deliberately cooked. After fortification it is heated, recreating the long tropical sea voyages that first made it famous.

Estufagem warms the wine in tanks to about 45 to 50 degrees Celsius for at least three months, a faster way for younger wines. Canteiro, the slow way for the finest, ages the wine in casks in the warm lofts of the lodge, under the roof, for years, sometimes decades.

The heat and air turn it amber and give coffee, caramel, toffee, dried fig and walnut, all held up by bright acidity. Our Broadbent Single Cask Malvasia 2009 is a single cask of one harvest, aged warm in old oak.

value.front: What are estufagem and canteiro?
value.back: Two ways to heat Madeira: estufagem warms it in tanks for months; canteiro ages it for years in casks in warm lofts, for the finest wines.

explain.value:
Old vines, vieilles vignes in French, alte Reben in German, cepas vellas in Galician, is not a legal term anywhere, but it matters. As vines age, past thirty or forty years, they give fewer, smaller bunches, and their deep roots reach water and minerals far below the surface.

The wine tends to be more concentrated, textured and balanced, and less affected by drought or heavy rain. Some of our vines are very old indeed: Ridge's Lytton Springs has blocks planted in 1901, and Santorini's ungrafted vines are among the oldest anywhere.

On our list: Berres Old Vines, Châteaumar's fifty year old Syrah, Stein, Bründlmayer's Alte Reben, Do Ferreiro's Cepas Vellas, Saint Damien and Ridge. Say what the label claims, never an age you cannot confirm.

value.front: What do old vines give a wine?
value.back: Fewer, smaller bunches and deep roots: more concentration, texture and balance. Not a legal term, so quote only the age the label or sommelier confirms.

explain.value:
A field blend is a vineyard planted with several grape varieties mixed together, row by row or vine by vine, then picked and fermented together. The blend is made in the vineyard, not in the cellar.

It was the old way in Europe and in early California, where Italian and other immigrant growers planted Zinfandel with Petite Sirah, Carignane, Grenache, Mataro and others for balance: one for color, one for acidity, one for fruit.

Ridge's Lytton Springs, planted from 1901 and holding more than twenty varieties, is a textbook example, and Ridge's Three Valleys draws on old field grapes too. When a guest asks what is in it, the label lists the share of each grape.

value.front: What is a field blend?
value.back: Several grape varieties planted together and picked and fermented together, so the blend is made in the vineyard. Ridge's Lytton Springs is a classic.

explain.value:
Organic farming grows vines without synthetic herbicides, pesticides or fertilisers, using cover crops, compost and copper or sulfur sprays. Biodynamic farming goes further, following the ideas of Rudolf Steiner from the 1920s: it treats the vineyard as a living whole, uses herbal and mineral preparations and plans work by a lunar calendar.

Growers say it brings livelier soils and wines that show their place more clearly. Some are certified; others farm this way without a label.

Leflaive in Burgundy became a leader of biodynamic farming from 1997; Huet, Climens and d'Angerville farm biodynamically; Gouges, Saint Damien and Pépière organically; Châteaumar organically without certification. Describe the farming; never make a health claim for the wine.

value.front: What is the difference between organic and biodynamic farming?
value.back: Organic avoids synthetic sprays and fertilisers; biodynamic adds herbal preparations and a lunar calendar. Leflaive and Huet farm biodynamically. Never make a health claim.

explain.value:
Burgundy ranks land, not producers. Every vineyard sits in one of four tiers, and the label tells you which.

At the base is the regional tier, Bourgogne, from anywhere in the region. Next come the village wines, named for a village such as Meursault or Nuits-Saint-Georges. Above them are Premier Cru vineyards, written 1er Cru, named after the village with the vineyard, such as Beaune Premier Cru Clos de la Mousse. At the top are the Grand Cru vineyards, so famous they carry only their own name, such as Echézeaux or Les Preuses in Chablis; they are a small share of all Burgundy.

So a label that names only a vineyard is usually the grandest. Our list climbs every rung, from the Damien Martin Bourgogne to Grivot's Echézeaux.

value.front: Name Burgundy's four tiers from bottom to top.
value.back: Regional (Bourgogne), village (such as Meursault), Premier Cru (village plus vineyard) and Grand Cru (the vineyard name alone, such as Echézeaux).

components.name: Grand Cru and Premier Cru in Champagne

explain.value:
In Champagne, cru means village rather than vineyard. Each of the region's villages was once rated on a scale, the échelle des crus, which set the price of its grapes. Seventeen villages, such as Bouzy, Aÿ, Cramant and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, are Grand Cru; about forty more, such as Vertus, are Premier Cru.

A Champagne may print Grand Cru or Premier Cru only if all its grapes come from villages of that rank. Most big-house blends draw on many villages and do not, though they use plenty of Grand Cru fruit.

On our list, Paul Bara and Pierre Paillard are Grand Cru from Bouzy; Larmandier-Bernier and Veuve Fourny are Premier Cru from Vertus; Pol Roger's Blanc de Blancs draws on the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs.

value.front: What does Grand Cru mean on a Champagne label?
value.back: Every grape came from one of the seventeen top-rated villages, such as Bouzy. In Champagne a cru is a village, not a single vineyard.

explain.value:
A clos is a vineyard enclosed by walls, many of them built by monks or nobles centuries ago in Burgundy and the Loire. The walls marked a prized piece of land and protected it.

A monopole is a vineyard owned entirely by one producer, rare in Burgundy, where most vineyards are split among many families. A clos can be a monopole, but not always.

Our walled vineyards include Bouchard's Clos de la Mousse in Beaune, a monopole since 1872; Roumier's Clos de la Bussière in Morey; d'Angerville's Clos des Ducs beside its house in Volnay; Lafon's Clos de la Baronne in Meursault; and Coudert's Clos de la Roilette in Fleurie. Say it simply: one family's walled vineyard.

value.front: What is a monopole in Burgundy?
value.back: A vineyard owned entirely by one producer, rare in Burgundy. Bouchard's Clos de la Mousse and d'Angerville's Clos des Ducs on our list are monopoles.

explain.value:
For the Paris Exposition of 1855, Emperor Napoleon III asked for a ranking of Bordeaux's best wines. The brokers ranked the red estates of the Médoc, plus Haut-Brion, into five growths, crus classés, by the prices their wines fetched, and the sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac into first and second growths, with Yquem alone above them as Premier Cru Supérieur.

It has barely changed since: Mouton Rothschild's promotion to first growth in 1973 was the one great change. Second wines and estates outside the list carry no rank.

On our list: Pichon Lalande, second growth; Talbot, fourth; Grand-Puy-Lacoste, fifth; Yquem, Premier Cru Supérieur; Climens and Suduiraut, first growths of Sauternes and Barsac.

value.front: What was the 1855 classification, and where does Yquem stand?
value.back: A ranking of Bordeaux estates by price for the Paris Exposition: Médoc reds in five growths, Sauternes in two, with Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur.

explain.value:
Most great Bordeaux estates make a second wine. After the harvest the team tastes every lot, and only the best go into the grand vin, the château's main wine; younger vines and lots that do not quite make the cut go into the second wine.

A second wine comes from the same vineyards and cellar, is often softer and readier sooner, and costs much less. Famous examples include Les Forts de Latour and Carruades de Lafite.

Our La Chapelle de Meyney is the second wine of Château Meyney in Saint-Estèphe, from younger vines on the estate: blackcurrant, cedar and earth, a taste of the Médoc for a gentler price.

value.front: What is a second wine in Bordeaux?
value.back: Wine from the same estate and cellar that did not make the main blend, often younger vines: softer and kinder in price. Ours is La Chapelle de Meyney.

explain.value:
Rioja labels promise how long a wine has aged before release. Crianza has at least two years, one of them in oak. Reserva has at least three, one in oak. Gran Reserva, made only in good years, has at least five, with at least two in oak and the rest in bottle.

Traditional houses go well beyond the minimums. The long aging softens the tannin and turns the fruit savory: dried cherry, strawberry, tobacco, leather, vanilla and sweet spice.

La Rioja Alta ages its Gran Reserva 904 about four years in American oak barrels from its own cooperage, then years in bottle before release. It is the bottle for a guest who loves mellow, old-style red with lamb or duck.

value.front: What does Gran Reserva on a Rioja guarantee?
value.back: At least five years of aging, two in oak, from a good year. Our La Rioja Alta 904 spends about four years in American oak.

explain.value:
The Wachau's growers, through their association Vinea Wachau, sort their dry wines into three categories by ripeness and weight, each named after something of the valley.

Steinfeder, after a feathery grass of the terraces, is the lightest. Federspiel, after the lure falconers used, is the classic, medium-bodied style. Smaragd, the emerald lizard that suns itself on the stone walls, is the ripest and fullest, still dry, from the best sites.

Our Franz Hirtzberger Honivogl is a Grüner Veltliner Smaragd from Spitz: ripe pear, quince, white pepper and honeyed spice, rich and powerful yet dry. It stands up to roast meats as well as fish.

value.front: What is a Smaragd, and what is it named after?
value.back: The Wachau's ripest, fullest dry wine category, named for an emerald lizard on the terrace walls. Our Hirtzberger Honivogl is a Grüner Smaragd.

explain.value:
A bottle of Champagne holds about six atmospheres of pressure, roughly three times a car tire, so it is opened with care, and quietly.

Chill it to 43 to 46°F. Present the label to the host. Loosen the cage but keep a thumb or a napkin over the cork from then on. Hold the bottle at about 45 degrees, pointed away from guests, grip the cork and turn the bottle, not the cork, easing it out so it leaves with a soft sigh rather than a pop.

Pour a little into each glass to let the foam settle, then top up to about two thirds, guests first and the host last. Return the bottle to the ice bucket, half ice and half water.

value.front: How do you open Champagne at the table?
value.back: Cage loosened, thumb on the cork, bottle at 45 degrees away from guests. Turn the bottle, not the cork, for a soft sigh, never a pop.

explain.value:
Sabrage is opening a bottle of Champagne with a sabre. Legend ties it to Napoleon's cavalry, the hussars, celebrating victories on horseback.

A well-chilled bottle is held at about 45 degrees, pointed into open space. The blunt back of an unsharpened Champagne sabre slides firmly up the seam of the bottle and strikes the lip; the pressure inside and the weak point where the seam meets the collar break the glass cleanly, and the collar flies off with the cork still in it.

The house sabres in the courtyard on Fridays at five; confirm on shift. Only those trained by the house perform it; a new server's role is to know the story and keep guests well clear, never to try it.

value.front: What is sabrage, and when does Brennan's do it?
value.back: Opening Champagne with a sabre struck up the seam to the lip, breaking off the collar with the cork. The house sabres in the courtyard on Fridays at five.

components.name: Coravin: the needle through the cork

explain.value:
The Coravin system lets us pour a glass of a fine still wine without pulling the cork. A thin, hollow needle passes through the cork; the bottle is pressurized with argon, an inert gas, which pushes the wine out through the needle. When the needle is withdrawn, the natural cork closes up again and the argon protects the wine left inside.

So a bottle such as the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé can be poured by the glass over weeks without spoiling, and a guest can taste a great white Burgundy without buying the bottle.

At the table, say: poured by Coravin, so the bottle is never opened. Present the label. Who handles the device and the house's limits are questions for the bar.

value.front: How does Coravin pour the Leflaive without opening it?
value.back: A hollow needle goes through the cork, argon gas pushes the wine out, and the cork reseals, so the rest stays fresh for weeks.

explain.value:
A needle cannot help a sparkling wine, because the bottle must be opened to pour. Coravin Sparkling is a different device: a stopper that clamps onto an opened bottle and a charger that refills the space with gas, so the wine keeps its pressure and its bubbles.

It lets the Rare Champagne be poured by the glass at $75 from an opened bottle. The cork has been pulled, so do not say no cork is pulled; say poured by the glass from a bottle kept fresh under the Coravin Sparkling stopper, and reseal right after each pour.

The maker says a bottle stays fizzy for weeks; how long the house keeps an opened bottle in service is a question for the bar, as is reading the vintage, 2012 or 2013, on the label.

value.front: How is the Rare Champagne kept fresh by the glass?
value.back: Under a Coravin Sparkling stopper that re-pressurizes the opened bottle. The cork is out, so reseal right after each pour and confirm the house limit.

explain.value:
Decanting means pouring a wine from its bottle into a carafe, for one of two reasons.

An old red or a Vintage Port throws sediment. Stand the bottle upright for some hours if possible, open it gently, and pour slowly in one steady motion over a light or candle, stopping when the sediment reaches the neck. A young, powerful red, such as a Napa Cabernet or a Châteauneuf, is decanted for air, which softens tannin and opens the aroma; thirty to forty-five minutes helps.

Very old wines can fade quickly once decanted, so open them close to drinking. The sommelier decides which bottles need it; offer it, explain why, and always show the bottle and keep it beside the decanter.

value.front: Give the two reasons to decant a wine.
value.back: To leave sediment behind in an old red or Vintage Port, or to give a young, powerful red air. The sommelier decides; keep the bottle beside the decanter.

explain.value:
A half-bottle holds 375 ml, half a standard bottle: two or three glasses of table wine, or four or five small pours of a sweet wine. It is the server's best friend at a table of two, or for a table that wants a different wine with each course.

Wine ages faster in a half-bottle, because there is more air and glass for each drop of wine, so mature half-bottles can be at their peak sooner than the same wine in a full bottle.

Our half-bottle list is long and serious: Krug, Yquem, Meursault, Chablis, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Vintage Port. Present it like any bottle, pour smaller first glasses so everyone gets a second, and suggest one white and one red half for a long meal.

value.front: Why suggest half-bottles, and how many glasses do they pour?
value.back: Two or three glasses, or four or five small sweet pours: ideal for two, or a different wine each course, such as a white half then a red half.

explain.value:
A magnum holds 1.5 liters, two standard bottles; a double magnum, called a Jeroboam in Champagne, holds 3 liters, four bottles. Larger bottles still have Biblical names, such as Rehoboam and Methuselah.

Wine ages more slowly and gracefully in large bottles, because there is less air for each drop of wine, which is why collectors prize them. And nothing makes a table's toast like a magnum.

Our large formats include the Billecart-Salmon 80th anniversary magnum, the Bollinger and Piper-Heidsieck magnums, the Taittinger double magnum and Prüm's Auslese in magnum. Carry it with both hands, open it like any Champagne, pour in small first pours, and keep it in a deep bucket.

value.front: How many standard bottles are in a magnum and a double magnum?
value.back: A magnum is 1.5 liters, two bottles; a double magnum is 3 liters, four. Wine ages more slowly in large bottles.

explain.value:
Sweet wines are rich, so they are served in small pours, usually two to three ounces, in a smaller glass. A half-bottle pours four or five.

Serve sweet whites such as Sauternes, Auslese and icewine well chilled, about 45 to 50°F, so they taste fresh rather than syrupy. Serve Port, Madeira and Banyuls a little cooler than room temperature, about 60 to 64°F.

The golden rule of pairing: the wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert, or the dessert makes it taste thin and sour. Offer a sweet wine when the dessert menu arrives, not after. Fortified wines keep for days or weeks once opened; Madeira and tawny Port keep longest.

value.front: What is the golden rule for pairing wine with dessert?
value.back: The wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it tastes thin and sour. Serve small pours, sweet whites well chilled.

explain.value:
A mature wine has spent years, sometimes decades, aging in bottle. Its fruit turns from fresh to dried, its tannin softens, and new notes appear: leather, forest floor and mushroom in reds; honey, nuts and petrol in Riesling; caramel and coffee in Port.

Mature bottles need gentle handling. Carry them as they lay, without shaking; stand older reds and Ports upright ahead of time if you can; open slowly, as old corks crumble, and keep a two-pronged cork puller or a decanter ready. Taste for soundness with the sommelier before pouring for the table.

Our list is rich in age: Pichon Lalande 2004, Beaucastel 2007, Gilette 1989, Riveyrac 1975, Taylor 1977 and more. Tell guests the age is the point: they are drinking time.

value.front: How do you handle an old bottle before serving?
value.back: Carry it gently as it lay, stand reds and Port upright ahead, open slowly as old corks crumble, and check soundness with the sommelier first.

explain.value:
Every bottle from the list follows the same ritual. Bring it to the host before opening and show the label, saying the producer, the wine and the vintage aloud, so the host can confirm it is the bottle ordered. Check the vintage and size against the list yourself before you leave the cellar.

Cut the foil below the lip, draw the cork cleanly and place it beside the host. Pour a small taste for the host; once approved, pour the guests first and the host last, filling red glasses about a third and white glasses a little less.

Ring every bottle in by its bin number, because the list often carries the same wine in more than one vintage or size.

value.front: Why ring a bottle in by its bin number?
value.back: The list often carries one wine in several vintages or sizes; the bin number names the exact bottle. Always show the label and check vintage and size.

explain.value:
A corked wine has been tainted by a compound called TCA, usually from the cork. It smells of wet cardboard, a damp cellar or a musty basement, and the fruit seems flat and muted. It affects a small share of bottles sealed with natural cork, and it is never anyone's fault at the table.

When the host tastes and frowns, smell the cork and the glass, or ask the sommelier to. If the wine is faulty, apologize, take the bottle away and bring another, without debate.

Other faults are rarer: a bottle that is oxidized, flat and brown, or cooked by heat. A wine the guest simply dislikes is a different matter, for the sommelier or manager to handle.

value.front: What does a corked wine smell like, and what do you do?
value.back: Wet cardboard or a damp cellar, the fruit muted. Apologize, remove it and bring another without debate; it is the cork's fault, not the guest's.

explain.value:
Brennan's wine cellar is one of the few in the world to hold Wine Spectator's Grand Award, the magazine's highest honor, given for depth, breadth, mature vintages and harmony with the menu. The house's own notes say it first won the award in 1983.

Then came Hurricane Katrina in 2005. A month without power cooked the cellar, and about 35,000 bottles were lost. After the restaurant reopened, the team rebuilt the collection, and the house notes say it won the Grand Award back in 2021; reports of the 2025 awards name it again, with about 3,000 to 3,600 selections, deepest in Burgundy, Champagne, Bordeaux and California.

Every bottle you present comes from that rebuilt cellar. Confirm the award years from the listing at lineup before quoting them.

value.front: What happened to the Brennan's cellar, and what has it won?
value.back: Katrina's power loss in 2005 cooked about 35,000 bottles. The rebuilt cellar holds Wine Spectator's Grand Award; confirm the years at lineup.

components.name: The wines of the two tastings

explain.value:
The two tasting menus treat their wines differently. The Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's includes its listed drinks. The dinner tasting does not: its wines are an optional pairing at $120 more, five 4 oz pours, each chosen for one course.

At breakfast, the Charles Lafitte Brut pours with the Eggs Hussarde and the Châteaumar Côtes du Rhône with the petite filet. On the dinner pairing, the Charles Lafitte opens with the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, the Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé meets the Louisiana BBQ lobster, the Louis Jadot Beaune Premier Cru the Redfish Véronique, the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet the Rohan duck, and the La Tour Vieille Banyuls the dessert.

Several of these wines are tasting pours only, with no glass price; whether a guest may order one à la carte is a question for the manager.

value.front: Which wines pour on the $120 dinner pairing, course by course?
value.back: Charles Lafitte with the oysters, Fichet Mâcon-Igé with the BBQ lobster, Jadot Beaune with the redfish, Paul Hobbs with the duck, La Tour Vieille Banyuls with dessert.

components.name: Bubbles at Brennan's and Birthday Bubbles

explain.value:
Champagne is woven into the house. Bubbles at Brennan's runs in the Roost Bar and Courtyard on weekday afternoons, with a list of sparkling rosé bottles from the Mirabelle to the Pommery, bubbly cocktails and bar snacks, and Champagne sabering on Fridays at five.

Birthday Bubbles is the page of Champagnes for celebrations: half-bottles of Drappier, Paul Bara and Krug for two, and magnums and a double magnum, Billecart-Salmon's 80th anniversary Sous Bois, Bollinger, Piper-Heidsieck and Taittinger, for a table.

Know which bottles are Champagne and which are sparkling wine from elsewhere: on the rosé list the Mirabelle and Louis Pommery are Californian. Confirm the hours and the sabering on shift.

value.front: What is Bubbles at Brennan's, and when is the sabering?
value.back: Weekday afternoons in the Roost Bar and Courtyard: sparkling rosé bottles, bubbly cocktails, snacks, and Champagne sabering on Fridays at five. Confirm on shift.

explain.value:
Piper-Heidsieck was founded in Reims in 1785 by Florens-Louis Heidsieck, a cloth merchant from Westphalia who set out to make a cuvée worthy of a queen and presented his wine to Marie Antoinette. After his death his nephew's partner, Henri-Guillaume Piper, joined the business, and the two names were joined.

Today Piper-Heidsieck makes our house Champagne, an Extra Brut of Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay bottled under the Brennan's name, poured by the glass and by the bottle, and its Cuvée Brut in magnum on Birthday Bubbles.

Say labeled for us, not made for us; Piper-Heidsieck spells its own cuvée Essentiel, and which cuvée is in the bottle, and its dosage, is for the sommelier to confirm.

value.front: Who makes our house Champagne, and what is the house's royal story?
value.back: Piper-Heidsieck of Reims, founded in 1785 by Florens-Louis Heidsieck, who presented his wine to Marie Antoinette. Say labeled for us, not made for us.

explain.value:
Rare began as Piper-Heidsieck's prestige cuvée, first made from the 1976 harvest, a year of record heat. It is declared only in exceptional years, about a dozen vintages in half a century, and is now run as its own house, Rare Champagne, in Reims.

Its bottle wears a jeweled dress that recalls a design Fabergé made for the house in the nineteenth century. The wine is Chardonnay-led with Pinot Noir from Grand Cru sites, aged about a decade on its lees: white peach, candied citrus and toasted almond.

We pour Rare 2012 by the glass under the Coravin Sparkling stopper and list the 2013 by the bottle; the glass page now prints a 2013, so read the label before naming the vintage.

value.front: When was Rare first made, and how is it poured by the glass?
value.back: From the 1976 harvest, as Piper-Heidsieck's prestige cuvée, declared only in great years. We pour it under a Coravin Sparkling stopper.

components.name: Pommery, Charles Lafitte and Madame Pommery's brut

explain.value:
Pommery is a Reims house that dates itself to 1858, with roots in an earlier wine business of 1836. Its great figure was Madame Louise Pommery, a widow who took over the business and, in 1874, launched Pommery Nature, the first brut Champagne to succeed commercially, at a time when most Champagne was very sweet. The British loved it, and dry Champagne became the world's taste.

Pommery now belongs to the Vranken-Pommery group, which also owns Charles Lafitte, a name with roots to 1834 in Épernay, and makes the Louis Pommery sparkling rosé in California.

So three bottles on our lists share one family: the Charles Lafitte on both tastings, the Pommery rosé and the Louis Pommery rosé, and only the first two are Champagne.

value.front: What did Madame Pommery give the world in 1874?
value.back: Pommery Nature, the first commercially successful brut, dry Champagne. Pommery's group also makes our Charles Lafitte and the California Louis Pommery.

explain.value:
Krug was founded in Reims in 1843 by Joseph Krug, who believed a house's finest Champagne should be its blend rather than a single vintage. That idea still drives it.

Each year Krug builds its Grande Cuvée from more than a hundred wines from ten or more harvests, fermented in small old oak casks, then ages it for years more. Each release is a numbered edition, counted from the founder's first blend, and a Krug ID code on the back label tells which harvest it is built on.

Our menu prints it as Grand Cuvée; Krug spells it Grande Cuvée. We pour it in a half-bottle on Birthday Bubbles, and which edition is inside is a question for the sommelier.

value.front: What makes Krug Grande Cuvée different from other non-vintage Champagne?
value.back: It blends more than a hundred wines from ten or more years, aged long, and each release is a numbered edition. Founded in Reims in 1843.

explain.value:
Billecart-Salmon was founded at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ in 1818, on the marriage of Nicolas François Billecart and Elisabeth Salmon, and it is still family owned, now in its seventh generation. It is famous for finesse and for its rosé.

Its prestige rosé is named for Elisabeth Salmon, whose marriage gave the house its name: our Cuvée Elisabeth Salmon Rosé 2009 is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with long age before release.

For Brennan's eightieth year the house has a Billecart-Salmon Sous Bois magnum labeled for the anniversary, its base wines fermented in oak. It is the Birthday Bubbles bottle with a story the guest can take home: the restaurant began in 1946. Confirm the anniversary bottling with the sommelier.

value.front: What is special about our Billecart-Salmon magnum?
value.back: It is the Sous Bois, oak-fermented, labeled for Brennan's 80th anniversary. Billecart-Salmon was founded in 1818 on the marriage that gave it its name.

explain.value:
Bollinger is a family-owned house in Aÿ, the Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir, and its style is rich and powerful: Pinot Noir-led, part fermented in old oak, built on reserve wines kept in magnum.

It is also James Bond's Champagne. Bollinger appears in the Bond novels and, from Live and Let Die in 1973, in almost every Bond film since. That film was shot partly in New Orleans; its famous jazz funeral scene was filmed in the French Quarter at the corner of Chartres and Dumaine, a few blocks from Royal Street.

We pour the Special Cuvée by the bottle and in magnum, and the PNTX20, an all-Pinot Noir edition led by the village of Tauxières.

value.front: What links Bollinger, James Bond and New Orleans?
value.back: Bond drinks Bollinger on screen from Live and Let Die (1973), a film shot partly in the French Quarter. Bollinger is a family house in Aÿ.

explain.value:
Taittinger is one of the few great Champagne houses still run by its family. Pierre Taittinger bought the old Reims house of Forest-Fourneaux, founded in 1734, in the early 1930s and gave it his name; the house later made its home in the thirteenth century buildings of the Counts of Champagne in Reims, the source of its prestige Comtes de Champagne.

Its style leans on Chardonnay, unusually generous in its house Brut, which gives elegance and freshness.

On our lists: La Française, its house Brut, in a double magnum on Birthday Bubbles, the same Champagne that tops the Flamingo in the Roost; and the Prestige Rosé on the Bubbles rosé page.

value.front: What gives Taittinger its elegance, and where else do guests meet it?
value.back: A generous share of Chardonnay. La Française, its Brut, is in our double magnum and tops the Flamingo cocktail in the Roost.

explain.value:
Moët & Chandon was founded in Épernay in 1743 by Claude Moët and is now one of the largest Champagne producers in the world. His grandson Jean-Rémy Moët was a friend of Napoleon Bonaparte, who visited the house several times; the Impérial name pays homage to the emperor.

Moët is pronounced moh-ET, sounding the t, a name of Dutch origin.

We pour two pinks: the Imperial Rosé on the Bubbles list, a dry Brut rosé Champagne, Pinot Noir-led and colored with red wine, and the Nectar Impérial Rosé on the bottle list, a Demi-Sec, noticeably sweet, for desserts. Never confuse the two at the table.

value.front: Which Moët rosé is dry and which is sweet?
value.back: The Imperial Rosé is dry, a Brut; the Nectar Impérial Rosé is Demi-Sec, sweet, for dessert. Moët is pronounced moh-ET, founded in Épernay in 1743.

explain.value:
Pol Roger is a family Champagne house in Épernay, and its most famous customer was Winston Churchill. He drank it from 1908 and befriended Odette Pol-Roger at the British Embassy in Paris in 1944; she sent him a case every birthday.

When Churchill died in 1965, the house put a black border around the labels of the bottles it shipped to Britain in mourning, and its prestige Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill was created from the 1975 vintage.

Our bottle is its vintage Blanc de Blancs 2015, all Chardonnay from the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs: lemon, white flowers and chalk. A guest who loves history will love the story.

value.front: Whose Champagne was Pol Roger, and how did the house mourn him?
value.back: Winston Churchill's. After his death in 1965 the house put a black border on its labels shipped to Britain. We pour its Blanc de Blancs 2015.

explain.value:
The Drappier family settled at Urville, in the Côte des Bar in Champagne's far south, in 1808, and still runs its house there.

Their most famous customer lived just down the road. General Charles de Gaulle's family home, La Boisserie, was at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, near Urville, and from 1965 he chose Drappier for his private receptions there. The house still makes a Cuvée Charles de Gaulle in his honor.

Our Drappier is the Carte d'Or Brut in a half-bottle on Birthday Bubbles, about three parts Pinot Noir with Chardonnay and Meunier: crisp, with citrus, orchard fruit and a toasty edge.

value.front: Which French president drank Drappier, and why?
value.back: Charles de Gaulle, whose home at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises was near Drappier's village of Urville. He chose it for his private receptions.

explain.value:
Laurent-Perrier was founded at Tours-sur-Marne in 1812. Its name joins two people: Eugène Laurent, a cellar master who took over the house, and his widow, Mathilde Emilie Perrier, who ran it after his death and added her name.

In 1939 it was bought by Marie-Louise de Nonancourt, and her son Bernard de Nonancourt led it for more than fifty years, making it one of the best-selling Champagne houses in the world while keeping it family led and independent. He was a pioneer of rosé Champagne made by skin contact.

Our bottle is the Harmony Demi-Sec in a half-bottle, gently sweet with pear, apricot and honey: a Champagne for dessert.

value.front: Whose two names make Laurent-Perrier?
value.back: Cellar master Eugène Laurent and his widow Mathilde Emilie Perrier, who ran the house after him. Our Harmony is a sweet Demi-Sec.

explain.value:
Champagne is made by three kinds of producer. The great houses, such as Bollinger, Krug and Moët, buy most of their grapes from thousands of growers across the region and blend for a consistent house style. Cooperatives pool their members' grapes; Nicolas Feuillatte, based at Chouilly near Épernay, is the brand of a large growers' cooperative.

Grower Champagne is made by a family from its own vineyards, often in one village, and shows that place: look for RM, récoltant-manipulant, in small print on the label.

Our growers include Paul Bara and Pierre Paillard of Bouzy, Chartogne-Taillet of Merfy, and Larmandier-Bernier and Veuve Fourny of Vertus. Say: one family, its own vines, one village's voice.

value.front: What is grower Champagne, and how is it marked on a label?
value.back: Made by a family from its own vineyards, often one village: RM, récoltant-manipulant. Ours include Paul Bara, Pierre Paillard and Larmandier-Bernier.

components.name: Schramsberg and the Toast to Peace

explain.value:
Schramsberg is an old Calistoga estate at the north end of the Napa Valley, with caves dug into the hillside. Jack and Jamie Davies bought it in 1965 to make sparkling wine by the traditional method, and their first wine was a Blanc de Blancs, described as America's first commercial Chardonnay-based brut sparkling wine.

In February 1972, President Richard Nixon served the Schramsberg Blanc de Blancs 1969 at the Toast to Peace in Beijing with Premier Zhou Enlai, the first American wine poured at such a state event, and Schramsberg says its wines have been served by every administration since.

We pour its Blanc de Blancs half-bottle and the Mirabelle Brut Rosé, its North Coast label. Both are sparkling wine, not Champagne.

value.front: Which of our sparkling wines was poured at the Toast to Peace in 1972?
value.back: Schramsberg Blanc de Blancs, served by President Nixon in Beijing. We pour its Blanc de Blancs and its Mirabelle rosé.

explain.value:
Argyle opened in 1987 in Dundee, in Oregon's Willamette Valley, working out of a former nut processing plant, and sparkling wine was its signature from the very first year. Its founders believed the valley's cool climate was ideal for the traditional method.

Today it farms vineyards in the Dundee Hills and the Eola-Amity Hills and makes Pinot Noir and Chardonnay as well as sparkling wine.

Our glass is the Argyle 2022, printed as Vintage Brut on the glass list and as Brut elsewhere: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with a little Meunier, shortbread, apple and citrus zest with a saline finish. It is not Champagne: say American sparkling wine, and confirm the blend with the sommelier.

value.front: What is Argyle, and what must you never call it?
value.back: A Willamette Valley winery, founded in 1987, with sparkling wine its signature. It is American sparkling wine, never Champagne. We pour the 2022 by the glass.

explain.value:
England's sparkling wine pioneers planted on the same chalk that runs under Champagne. Ridgeview was founded in the mid 1990s near the village of Ditchling, on the South Downs in Sussex, as a family estate devoted to sparkling wine. Its Grosvenor Blanc de Blancs famously won a major international sparkling wine trophy, the first non-Champagne to do so.

Chapel Down, at Tenterden in Kent, grew into England's largest wine producer. Its vineyards face south on chalk and its wines are made by the traditional method.

We pour Ridgeview's Bloomsbury, Chardonnay-led, and Chapel Down's Rosé Brut. Say English sparkling wine with pride: it is a real category now, not a novelty.

value.front: Where do Ridgeview and Chapel Down come from?
value.back: Ridgeview from Ditchling on the Sussex South Downs; Chapel Down from Tenterden in Kent, England's largest producer. Both on Champagne's chalk seam.

explain.value:
Domaine Leflaive is the most famous estate of Puligny-Montrachet, a family name synonymous with great white Burgundy. The family's roots in the village go back to 1717, but the modern domaine was built from about 1920 by Joseph Leflaive, an engineer who replanted and began selling under his own name.

His granddaughter Anne-Claude Leflaive ran it from 1990 until her death in 2015 and converted the whole domaine to biodynamic farming in 1997, a lead the rest of Burgundy followed. The domaine also farms vines at Verzé in the Mâconnais.

On our list: the Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin by the glass and by the bottle, a village Puligny 2016 and the Sous le Dos d'Ane Meursault Premier Cru 2017.

value.front: What is Domaine Leflaive famous for, and what do we pour by the glass?
value.back: Great white Burgundy from Puligny-Montrachet and a biodynamic lead from 1997. We pour its Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin, by the glass.

explain.value:
Domaine des Comtes Lafon is one of the great estates of Meursault. Comte Jules Lafon built it after his marriage in 1894, buying plots in the best vineyards of Meursault and Volnay and a piece of Le Montrachet.

As mayor of Meursault, in 1923 he invited friends to a harvest banquet that became the Paulée de Meursault, now the last of Burgundy's three great November feasts, the Trois Glorieuses, where growers bring their best bottles to share.

The family's Clos de la Baronne is a walled vineyard it owns entirely, and its Mâconnais estate, Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon, makes our Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine: the Lafon touch at a gentler price.

value.front: Which Burgundy feast did Comte Jules Lafon begin?
value.back: The Paulée de Meursault, a harvest banquet he gave as mayor in 1923. We pour Lafon's Clos de la Baronne Meursault and its Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine.

explain.value:
Louis Jadot is one of the great houses of Beaune. The Jadot family came from Belgium and bought its first vineyard, the Clos des Ursules in Beaune, in 1826; Louis Henry Denis Jadot founded the house in 1859.

Like most Burgundy houses it both owns vineyards and buys grapes from growers, and makes wine from Chablis to Beaujolais. The head of Bacchus, god of wine, on every label is its emblem.

Three of our wines carry the Bacchus head: the Beaune Premier Cru on the dinner tasting with the Redfish Véronique, and half-bottles of village Meursault and Beaujolais-Villages. Say: one of Burgundy's great family houses, from the wine capital, Beaune.

value.front: What emblem is on every Louis Jadot label?
value.back: The head of Bacchus. Jadot is a great Beaune house founded in 1859; its Beaune Premier Cru pours on our dinner tasting.

components.name: Bouchard Père & Fils and the Clos de la Mousse

explain.value:
Bouchard Père & Fils was founded in Beaune in 1731, one of the oldest houses in Burgundy. Its wines age in the deep cellars of the Château de Beaune, a fifteenth century royal fortress the house has occupied since 1820, and it is one of the largest owners of Premier and Grand Cru vineyards on the Côte d'Or.

The Clos de la Mousse is a small walled Premier Cru of Beaune, about three and a half hectares, that Bouchard has owned outright since 1872: a monopole, so every bottle of it is Bouchard's.

Ours is the 2022 in a half-bottle: red cherry, raspberry, violet and a little spice, silky and fresh.

value.front: Why is every bottle of Clos de la Mousse made by Bouchard?
value.back: It is a monopole: a walled Beaune Premier Cru that Bouchard has owned alone since 1872. The house, founded in 1731, ages wine in the Château de Beaune.

components.name: Château London and the two Fichets

explain.value:
Two different Fichets are on our lists, and servers mix them up.

The dinner tasting's white, Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé, comes from Domaine Fichet of Igé in the Mâconnais, a family estate farmed by the Fichet brothers. Château London is a named vineyard parcel at Igé, old limestone with some vines over a century old. There is no castle and it has nothing to do with England. It is made mostly in steel with a touch of old oak.

Jean-Philippe Fichet is a separate grower in Meursault, in the Côte de Beaune, known for precise white Burgundy; his Bourgogne Blanc is on the bottle list.

So say Fichet of Igé for the tasting, Jean-Philippe Fichet of Meursault for the bottle.

value.front: Is Château London a castle in England?
value.back: Neither: it is a vineyard parcel at Igé in the Mâconnais, farmed by Domaine Fichet of Igé. Jean-Philippe Fichet of Meursault is a different grower.

explain.value:
Our red Burgundy by the glass comes from a father and son domaine in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy: Domaine Robert et Damien Martin at Davayé, near Pouilly-Fuissé. Robert Martin founded it in 1982, and his son Damien now runs its roughly twenty hectares.

The Mâconnais is white wine country, so their Bourgogne Pinot Noir is a family's red made for drinking: red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, light in tannin and fresh.

It is the easiest red on the list for fish, crab and the lighter dishes, and the gentlest introduction to red Burgundy for a guest who usually orders Cabernet.

value.front: Who makes our Bourgogne Pinot Noir by the glass?
value.back: Domaine Robert et Damien Martin, a father and son domaine at Davayé in the Mâconnais, founded in 1982: light, red cherry Pinot Noir.

components.name: The family growers of the Côte de Beaune

explain.value:
Most of Burgundy is farmed by families with a few hectares spread over several villages, and many of our white Burgundies come from such domaines.

Thierry and Pascale Matrot run a family domaine in Meursault. Domaine Dupont-Fahn, in Tailly just south of Meursault, farms Les Tillets, one of the village's highest vineyards. Bitouzet-Prieur has vines in Meursault's Les Corbins. Paul Pillot is a Chassagne-Montrachet family that makes our Saint-Aubin Le Charmois. François Carillon comes from a family that has farmed Puligny for centuries and set up his own domaine in 2010. Tollot-Beaut, in Chorey-lès-Beaune, makes our Savigny Les Lavières.

Say the family name and the village: in Burgundy that is the whole story.

value.front: Name three family growers behind our white Burgundies.
value.back: Matrot and Dupont-Fahn of Meursault, Paul Pillot of Chassagne, and François Carillon of Puligny, whose family has farmed there for centuries.

components.name: Dauvissat and Louis Michel of Chablis

explain.value:
Two families on our list show the two faces of Chablis.

Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat is one of the two great reference estates of Chablis, a family domaine that ages its wines partly in old oak barrels, which adds texture without the taste of wood. Its Les Preuses Grand Cru 2015 now has years in bottle: lemon peel, oyster shell and a little honey, steely and deep.

Domaine Louis Michel takes the other path: every wine, even its Premier and Grand Crus, is made in steel tanks with no oak at all, for the purest expression of Chablis. We pour its village Chablis and its Montmains Premier Cru half-bottle.

Old oak or none: both are Chablis at its finest.

value.front: How do Dauvissat and Louis Michel differ in the cellar?
value.back: Dauvissat ages part of its Chablis in old oak for texture; Louis Michel makes every wine in steel with no oak at all.

components.name: The great families of the Côte de Nuits

explain.value:
Our red Burgundy pages are full of the Côte de Nuits' most respected families.

Domaine Henri Gouges, farmed organically and run by its fourth generation, is the reference name of Nuits-Saint-Georges. Domaine Jean Grivot is a family domaine of Vosne-Romanée, run today by the next generation of the family, making our Echézeaux Grand Cru and Nuits Les Charmois. Domaine Georges Roumier of Chambolle-Musigny is one of Burgundy's most sought-after growers, and owns the walled Clos de la Bussière in Morey-Saint-Denis outright. Faiveley, a family house based in Nuits-Saint-Georges, makes our Bourgogne Rouge.

These are bottles for guests who know Burgundy. Speak the family name with respect, and let the sommelier lead on the oldest.

value.front: Which family is the reference name of Nuits-Saint-Georges?
value.back: Domaine Henri Gouges, farmed organically, fourth generation. Grivot of Vosne-Romanée and Roumier of Chambolle-Musigny are also on our red Burgundy list.

components.name: D'Angerville of Volnay and Domaine du Pélican

explain.value:
Domaine Marquis d'Angerville is a family domaine in Volnay, farmed biodynamically and known for perfumed, silky Pinot Noir. Its Clos des Ducs is the walled Premier Cru beside the family house, a monopole: no one else makes it.

The same family looked beyond Burgundy to the Jura, where it founded Domaine du Pélican at Arbois, bringing Burgundian care to the Jura's own grapes and its traditions, including Vin Jaune.

So two very different bottles on our list share one family: the Clos des Ducs Volnay Premier Cru 2014, red cherry, rose and violet, and the Pélican Vin Jaune 2016, walnut and curry spice. A lovely link to share with a guest who orders either.

value.front: What links our Volnay Clos des Ducs and the Pélican Vin Jaune?
value.back: One family: d'Angerville of Volnay, which owns the walled Clos des Ducs and founded Domaine du Pélican in the Jura.

components.name: Côte d'Or names in the Mâconnais

explain.value:
The Mâconnais was long seen as Burgundy's humble south. Over the past decades famous families from further north have invested there, drawn by old vines, limestone and fair prices.

Domaine Leflaive of Puligny farms vines at Verzé; the Lafon family of Meursault formed Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon around Milly-Lamartine; and Domaine du Roc des Boutires in Pouilly-Fuissé has been owned since 2016 by the Parinet family of Château du Moulin-à-Vent, whose En Bertilionne is a small east-facing parcel below the Roche de Solutré.

That is why our Mâcon whites taste finer than their prices suggest. Say: a great Côte d'Or name, from the sunnier south.

value.front: Why do our Mâcon whites carry such famous names?
value.back: Côte d'Or families have invested in the Mâconnais: Leflaive at Verzé, Lafon at Milly-Lamartine, and the Parinet family at Roc des Boutires.

components.name: Lapierre, Foillard and the Beaujolais revival

explain.value:
By the 1970s much Beaujolais was industrial, sugared and fermented with cultured yeast. A small band of growers in the village of Villié-Morgon set out to change that, inspired by the oenologist Jules Chauvet: Marcel Lapierre, Jean Foillard, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton, nicknamed the Gang of Four by their American importer.

They went back to old vines, late picking, whole bunches, native yeasts and little or no added sulfur, and their silky, vivid Morgon wines became a root of the natural wine movement. Lapierre's children run his estate now.

We pour the Lapierre Morgon and Foillard's Côte du Py. Coudert's walled Clos de la Roilette in Fleurie is a family estate in the same spirit of fine, honest Gamay.

value.front: Who were the Gang of Four of Beaujolais?
value.back: Marcel Lapierre, Jean Foillard, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton of Morgon, who revived whole-bunch, native-yeast Gamay. We pour Lapierre and Foillard.

explain.value:
Domaine Huet is the great estate of Vouvray. Victor Huet, a veteran of the First World War who had run a bistro in Paris, founded it in 1928 with his son Gaston, who ran it for decades until his death in 2002.

It farms three famous vineyards: Le Haut-Lieu, where it began; the Clos du Bourg, bought in 1953; and Le Mont, bought in 1957. All are Chenin Blanc, farmed biodynamically, and each is made sec, demi-sec or moelleux as the year allows.

We pour Le Haut-Lieu Sec in two vintages, Le Mont Demi-Sec and Le Mont Moelleux 2009. Teach the guest the three words, and let the vineyard name lead.

value.front: When was Domaine Huet founded, and what are its three vineyards?
value.back: In 1928 by Victor and Gaston Huet. Le Haut-Lieu, the Clos du Bourg and Le Mont, all Chenin Blanc, farmed biodynamically.

explain.value:
The Cotat family of Chavignol is one of Sancerre's most famous names among sommeliers. Pascal Cotat farms a few hectares on the village's steepest chalk slopes, including Les Monts Damnés, worked by hand.

His Sauvignon Blanc is picked riper than most Sancerre and made simply in old casks, so it is rich yet taut, and it ages for years in a way Sancerre rarely does. His rosé, Pinot Noir from a tiny parcel the family has farmed for decades, is bottled by lot rather than vintage, which is why our label reads Lot 2024.

Both are small and sought after. Present them as cult bottles of the Loire.

value.front: Why does our Cotat rosé say Lot 2024 instead of a vintage?
value.back: Pascal Cotat bottles it by lot rather than vintage. His Sancerre from Les Monts Damnés is picked ripe and ages unusually well.

components.name: Pépière and Écu: Muscadet's new guard

explain.value:
For years Muscadet was sold as cheap seaside white. A handful of growers changed its reputation by farming carefully and leaving their best wines on the lees for years.

Marc Ollivier founded Domaine de la Pépière near Maisdon-sur-Sèvre in 1984 and farmed organically from the start, long before it was common. The domaine has vines in four of the new crus communaux, among them Monnières-Saint Fiacre, and its cru wines rest on their lees well beyond the seventeen months required.

Domaine de l'Écu, at Le Landreau, bottles its wines by the rock beneath the vines; Orthogneiss is named for an ancient rock.

Together they prove Muscadet can be serious and age.

value.front: How did growers like Pépière change Muscadet?
value.back: Careful, often organic farming and long aging on the lees, bottled by cru or by rock, as at Pépière and Domaine de l'Écu.

explain.value:
Two Anjou families make our Chenin Blancs from either side of the Loire.

Damien Laureau is a grower in Savennières, the small appellation on the north bank famous for dry Chenin from schist. His L'Alliance is waxy and full, quince, beeswax and toasted nuts, with a firm, stony finish: a white for rich fish and poultry.

Domaine des Baumard is a family estate at Rochefort-sur-Loire, across the river. Its Clos Sainte Catherine is a walled vineyard in the Coteaux du Layon, made sweet; our 2006 is golden, with quince, honey, apricot and a little ginger.

Same grape, same few miles, opposite ends of the table.

value.front: Which Anjou Chenin is dry and which is sweet on our list?
value.back: Laureau's Savennières L'Alliance is dry and waxy; Baumard's Clos Sainte Catherine Coteaux du Layon 2006 is sweet and honeyed. Same grape, opposite ends.

explain.value:
Pegau is old Provençal for a wine jug, the kind found in the papal palace at Avignon. The Féraud family has farmed in Châteauneuf-du-Pape since the seventeenth century, and Paul Féraud and his daughter Laurence named the domaine Domaine du Pegau in 1987.

Its style is proudly traditional: mostly Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and other permitted grapes, fermented with whole bunches in cement and aged about two years in large old casks.

The Cuvée Réservée got its name because the family once sold most of its wine in bulk and reserved a small share to bottle themselves. Ours is the 2020: kirsch, plum, garrigue, leather and spice. Ring it in by bin, as the list carries several Pegau lines.

value.front: What does Pegau mean, and why Cuvée Réservée?
value.back: An old Provençal wine jug. The family once sold most wine in bulk and reserved a share to bottle themselves.

explain.value:
Château de Beaucastel has been run by the Perrin family since 1909. It is famous for growing all thirteen grape varieties permitted in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, red and white, and for giving Mourvèdre a far larger role than most neighbors, which makes its wine darker, more savory and longer lived. It has farmed organically since about 1950.

The family also helped found Tablas Creek in California with an American importer, bringing Rhône grapes to Paso Robles.

Its Oenothèque bottles are older vintages held in the château's own cellar and released later, so they arrive in fine condition. Ours is the 2007: dried cherry, leather, truffle and garrigue, with silky tannin.

value.front: What is Château de Beaucastel famous for?
value.back: Growing all thirteen permitted Châteauneuf grapes and a large share of Mourvèdre. Its Oenothèque 2007 was held in the château's cellar before release.

explain.value:
In 1898 Hippolyte Brunier planted vines on La Crau, a high plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape. In 1793 Claude Chappe had built one of his signal telegraph towers there, on the line that sent messages between Paris and Marseille, because it was one of the highest points around. The tower is long gone, but the name stayed.

La Crau is covered in large, round stones, galets roulés, that store the day's heat and give the wine warmth and depth. The Brunier family still runs the estate, and plays on the name: its younger wine is called Télégramme.

Ours is La Crau 2014: kirsch, dried cherry, garrigue, pepper and leather, warm and silky.

value.front: Why is it called Vieux Télégraphe?
value.back: Claude Chappe's signal telegraph tower stood on its La Crau plateau from 1793. The Brunier family planted there in 1898, among large round stones.

components.name: Saint Damien, Raspail-Ay and La Louisianne

explain.value:
Gigondas is a village of family estates, and our two are among them.

Domaine Saint-Damien has been farmed by the Saurel family since the early nineteenth century and is certified organic. Its La Louisianne comes from old vines on the middle terraces of Gigondas: Grenache with Mourvèdre, Cinsault and a little Syrah, co-fermented in concrete. The name, which guests from New Orleans will love, belongs to a lieu-dit, a named parcel; why the parcel carries it is a question for the sommelier, not a story to invent.

Domaine Raspail-Ay is a family estate under the Dentelles de Montmirail; ours is a half-bottle of its Gigondas, Grenache-led with Syrah.

value.front: Why is a Gigondas called La Louisianne?
value.back: It is the name of a lieu-dit, a named parcel, farmed by the Saurel family. Why the parcel bears it is for the sommelier; never invent a Louisiana link.

components.name: Durban and Châteaumar: the Rhône by the glass

explain.value:
Our two Rhône reds by the glass each come with a twist.

Domaine de Durban, high above Beaumes-de-Venise, is famous for its sweet Muscat; the wine we pour is its dry red, Grenache and Syrah: ripe dark cherry, plum, dried herbs and pepper.

Domaine de Châteaumar's Cuvée Vincent, the breakfast tasting's red with the petite filet, is all Syrah from fifty year old vines on two parcels beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, about nine kilometers from Orange, farmed organically without certification. All Syrah is unusual in the south, where Grenache usually leads.

So: the sweet-wine estate's dry red, and the Grenache country's Syrah.

value.front: What is the twist in our Durban and Châteaumar reds?
value.back: Durban is famous for sweet Muscat but we pour its dry red; Châteaumar is all Syrah, unusual in the Grenache-led south.

components.name: Domaine Tempier and the Peyraud family

explain.value:
In 1936 Lucien Peyraud and his wife Lucie Tempier, known to everyone as Lulu, took on her family's farm at Le Plan du Castellet, above the port of Bandol. Lucien fell for an old bottle of Bandol and worked to have it recognized as its own appellation, granted in 1941, and he championed Mourvèdre, the grape that defines it.

Lulu's Provençal cooking, generous and seasonal, inspired Alice Waters of Chez Panisse and a generation of American chefs; she died in 2020 aged 102. Their family still owns the domaine.

Our bottle is the Tempier Bandol Rosé, Mourvèdre-led: wild strawberry, blood orange, garrigue and a savory depth. It is the rosé for a guest who cooks.

value.front: Who were Lucien and Lulu Peyraud?
value.back: The couple behind Domaine Tempier from 1936: Lucien helped found the Bandol appellation and championed Mourvèdre; Lulu's cooking inspired Alice Waters.

explain.value:
Domaine de Trévallon is a family estate in the Alpilles hills of Provence, near Les Baux. Its founder planted vines on land cleared from rock and garrigue and chose the grapes he believed in, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah for the red, rather than the blend the local rules came to require.

So Trévallon left the appellation and labels its wines with the wider regional name, Alpilles, and they have become among the most sought-after wines in the south of France, proof that a great wine does not need an official name.

Its white is rare: Marsanne-led with Roussanne, Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette. Ours is the 2016, apricot, honey, fennel and herbs.

value.front: Why does Trévallon not use its local appellation?
value.back: Its founder chose grapes the rules did not allow, so it labels as Alpilles, yet it is among the south's most sought-after wines.

explain.value:
Château d'Esclans is an estate in the hills of Provence behind the Riviera. It was bought in 2006 by a new owner whose aim was to make the greatest rosés in the world, and its Whispering Angel became the best-known pale Provence rosé in America, credited with starting a rosé boom.

The name came by chance. In the château's chapel, above the altar, is a carving of two cherubs that seemed to be whispering to each other; the label carries a line drawing of them. The estate is now part of LVMH.

Ours is the 2024: Grenache-led with Cinsault and Rolle, white peach, wild strawberry and citrus, dry and mineral.

value.front: Where does the name Whispering Angel come from?
value.back: A carving of two cherubs above the altar in Château d'Esclans' chapel that seemed to whisper. The label shows them.

explain.value:
Château Minuty stands at Gassin, on the hills above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, with vineyards around Gassin and Ramatuelle looking out to sea. Gabriel Farnet bought the estate in 1936, and it has stayed with his descendants, the Matton family, ever since.

In 1955 it was named one of the crus classés of the Côtes de Provence, and today its rosés, built on Grenache, are poured all over the world.

Our glass is the Minuty Prestige 2024: pale, dry, white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest, with a light mineral finish. Sell it as a glass of the Riviera, made for the courtyard.

value.front: Where is Château Minuty, and who runs it?
value.back: At Gassin above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, held by the Farnet and Matton family since 1936. Its Prestige is our rosé by the glass.

explain.value:
Trimbach is one of the oldest family wine houses in Alsace, founded in 1626 by Jean Trimbach and now in its thirteenth generation. It settled in Ribeauvillé after the First World War.

The house is famous for bone dry, high-acid, elegant whites, above all the Clos Sainte Hune, one of the world's greatest Rieslings. Its Réserve Personnelle is its top bottling of Pinot Gris, and in great years it makes late harvest wines, Vendanges Tardives.

We pour two mature Trimbach wines from 2007: the Pinot Gris Réserve Personnelle, dried apricot, honey, smoke and ginger, and the Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives, sweet with lychee, rose and cinnamon. Their sweetness levels are for the sommelier to confirm.

value.front: How old is the Trimbach house, and what is it famous for?
value.back: Founded in 1626, now in its thirteenth generation at Ribeauvillé: bone dry, elegant Alsace whites. We pour its Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer from 2007.

components.name: Joh. Jos. Prüm and the sundial

explain.value:
The Wehlener Sonnenuhr, the Wehlen sundial, is one of the Mosel's most famous vineyards, a steep slope of gray Devonian slate facing south across the river. In 1842 Jodocus Prüm, a vineyard owner, built a large sundial into the rock so the workers on the slope could tell the time, and the vineyard took its name.

The Prüm family has been in Wehlen for centuries; the Joh. Jos. Prüm estate dates from 1911, when the family's holdings were divided. Its Rieslings are delicate, lightly sweet and famously long-lived, sometimes with a little spritz when young.

We pour the Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett 2020 and the gold capsule Auslese 2015 in magnum.

value.front: How did the Wehlener Sonnenuhr get its name?
value.back: Jodocus Prüm built a sundial into its slate in 1842 so vineyard workers could tell the time. We pour Joh. Jos. Prüm's Kabinett and Auslese from it.

explain.value:
The Scharzhofberg is a steep slate hill above the Saar, the coolest corner of the Mosel. For centuries it belonged to a monastery in Trier. When the French revolutionary armies seized church land, the vineyard was sold at auction in 1797 to Jean-Jacques Koch, and it passed to the Müller family through his daughter's marriage.

The family's estate, the Scharzhof, is now perhaps the most sought-after Riesling estate in Germany, and its wines were served at the royal courts of Europe. Its Kabinett is lightly sweet and low in alcohol, with an electric acidity that makes it feel weightless.

Ours is the Scharzhofberger Kabinett 2020. Present it as one of the most famous Rieslings in the world.

value.front: How did the Müller family come to own the Scharzhofberg?
value.back: It was church land sold at auction in 1797 after the French Revolution; it passed to the Müller family by marriage. Our Kabinett 2020 is from there.

explain.value:
Dönnhoff is a family estate at Oberhausen on the Nahe and the region's most famous grower, the name that made the world notice the Nahe.

Its vineyards include the Brücke, a tiny parcel beside the old bridge over the river that the family owns alone, and a share of the Hermannshöhle in Niederhausen, a steep slope under a cliff often called the Nahe's greatest vineyard. Its Rieslings are known for purity, precision and a smoky, stony edge.

We pour two gold capsule Auslesen from 2023 in half-bottles: the Oberhäuser Brücke, lemon curd, peach and honey, and the Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle, peach, honey and stone. Sweet, concentrated and piercing: the Riesling for fruit desserts.

value.front: What are Dönnhoff's two Auslesen on our list?
value.back: Gold capsule Auslesen from the Brücke, a tiny parcel it owns alone by the old bridge, and from the Hermannshöhle, the Nahe's greatest vineyard.

components.name: The Mosel family estates: Berres, Dr. Hermann and Stein

explain.value:
Three small Mosel family estates give us some of our most useful Rieslings.

C.H. Berres is at Ürzig in the Middle Mosel, from a family with roots to 1510; its off-dry Old Vines is our Riesling by the glass. Weingut Dr. Hermann is a family estate at Erden, next door; its Erdener Prälat Auslese 2014 half-bottle pours by the glass with dessert, and its Würzgarten Kranklei Spätlese comes from the red slate spice garden of Ürzig. Weingut Stein is a small estate at Alf run by a grower who has rescued steep slate terraces others abandoned; we pour his Weihwasser and Palmberg-Terrassen.

Three families, steep slate, and Riesling for every course.

value.front: Which Mosel family makes our Riesling by the glass?
value.back: C.H. Berres of Ürzig, a family with roots to 1510. Dr. Hermann of Erden and Stein of Alf are our other Mosel families.

explain.value:
Weingut Keller is a family estate at Flörsheim-Dalsheim in Rheinhessen, and one of the most admired growers in Germany. It helped show that Rheinhessen, long known for cheap, sweet wine, has limestone hills capable of greatness.

The family is best known for powerful dry Rieslings, but in good years it also makes sweet wines from late harvest and botrytis grapes.

Our bottle is its PIUS Auslese 2022 in a half-bottle, a sweet blend whose grape varieties change with the vintage: honeyed apricot, pineapple and spice, rich and pure, with Keller's stony acidity. Keller wines are rare; treat it as a find.

value.front: Why is Weingut Keller admired, and what do we pour?
value.back: It helped prove Rheinhessen's limestone can be great. We pour its PIUS Auslese, a sweet blend whose grapes change by vintage.

explain.value:
Our Austrian wines come from three family estates on the Danube.

Bründlmayer is the leading family estate of Langenlois in the Kamptal, and the best-known grower of the Heiligenstein, the famous steep hill above Zöbing. We pour its Terrassen and Alte Reben Grüner Veltliner and its Heiligenstein Riesling. Loimer, also of Langenlois, makes Lois, a light, fresh Grüner built for food.

Franz Hirtzberger is a family estate in Spitz, at the western end of the Wachau, and Honivogl is its most famous Grüner Veltliner vineyard; ours is a Smaragd, the ripest dry category.

Light and crisp, or full and powerful: all dry, all made with food in mind.

value.front: Which Austrian families make our Grüner Veltliner wines?
value.back: Bründlmayer and Loimer of Langenlois in the Kamptal, and Franz Hirtzberger of Spitz in the Wachau, whose Honivogl is a Smaragd.

explain.value:
Kracher is a family estate at Illmitz, between the village and the shore of the Neusiedlersee in Burgenland. Its vineyards sit among the lake's reeds and pools, where autumn mist brings noble rot almost every year.

Alois Kracher made it world famous from the late 1980s until his early death in 2007, with numbered collections of sweet wines that stood beside Sauternes and Tokaji; the family carries the estate on.

Ours is the Cuvée Auslese 2017, Welschriesling and Chardonnay made sweet and kept in steel: pear, quince, mandarin, passion fruit and orange blossom honey. Lighter than a Sauternes, it is lovely with fruit desserts.

value.front: What made Kracher famous?
value.back: Alois Kracher's sweet wines from the Neusiedlersee, where mist brings noble rot almost every year. We pour its Cuvée Auslese 2017.

components.name: Pazo das Bruxas: the manor of the witches

explain.value:
Pazo das Bruxas is Galician for the manor of the witches. Galicia has a rich folklore of witches, meigas, and spells, and the name plays on it.
